title: Bangor Firefighters Halt Center Street Fire Before It Reaches Nearby Home
text:
Firefighters Keep An Early Morning Fire On Center Street In Bangor From Spreading To Other Buildings; Outbuilding Destroyed
Hard work and a quick response by the Bangor Fire Department kept an early morning fire on Center Street from spreading to other buildings nearby.
Read More: Two Fires Strike Belfast Area Over One October Weekend
Authorities say an explosion and a fire at 382 Center Street was reported just before 2:30 AM Friday morning. Within 5 minute, firefighters from Station 6 and Central Station were on the scene.
When they arrived, they found an outbuilding fully engulfed in flames. Directly next to the fire were two buildings, a home and a garage.
"Crews quickly contained the fire to the building of origin and kept it from spreading to the exposure buildings."
Within 15 minutes of their arrival, firefighters had the blaze under control. We're told that most of the personnel were able to clear the scene by 4 AM.
According to Bangor Fire, no on was injured in the firefighting effort.
"The outbuilding is a total loss. The garage and house sustained minor exterior damage because they were so close to the fire...The explosions are believed to have been caused by items stored in the outbuilding."
Read More: Generator Enclosed In Box Sparked West Bath Halloween Fire
Authorities are still investigating the fire, but don't believe it to be suspicious. The property was insured.
Bangor Fire Officials say that last month alone, they responded to a total of 1,050 incidents.
On October 25th, the Bangor Fire Department transitioned to 24-hour staffing. Within the first week of that changeover, they responded to over 60 incidents.

title: Wild video: Runaway tire flies off a truck and strikes an unsuspecting man
text:
Wild video: Runaway tire flies off a truck and strikes an unsuspecting man
A 19-year-old pedestrian was injured when a flying tire detached from a vehicle and struck him, according to surveillance footage and local authorities.
The incident occurred Oct. 29 in Chile’s capital, Santiago.
The tire came loose from a vehicle traveling through an underpass, collided with another car, and was propelled at high speed before hitting the teenager, Providencia Mayor Jaime Bellolio said.
“Yesterday an accident happened that sounds unbelievable. A vehicle driving on the street Los Leones lost a wheel and had to stop at the underpass. That wheel was propelled at an enormous speed, another car bumped into that wheel and it finally impacted a young man, age 19, that was walking on the pavement," Bellolio said.
Bellolio said the 19-year-old was taken to an area hospital for treatment. He is listed in stable condition, Bellolio said, and has multiple concussions.
The mayor confirmed that the vehicle involved had been identified and stopped at the underpass.
"We will give all the information needed so the young man can take the legal actions he considers necessary. We are also looking into his health and recovery," Bellolio said.

title: Supreme Court to hear North Dakota landowners’ legal fees case
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The Supreme Court is set to hear a case about landowners’ rights that centers on North Dakota but could apply to property owners elsewhere.
The central question is whether a government-backed company should have to pay a property owner’s legal fees if the owner takes the company to court and wins.
In the U.S., someone who takes land under eminent domain must pay the owner for it. The North Dakota property owners in this case went to court to be paid fairly for their land.
WBI Energy, the government-contracted company behind the pipeline in question, eventually gave the owners fair compensation. The landowners were left with nearly $380,000 in legal fees. They say the company should pay that bill.
Sam Spiegelman of Spiegelman Law Group said North Dakota law “clearly says that just compensation includes the legal costs for an owner to vindicate their property rights.”
The 8th Circuit Court of Appeals said that law should not apply when the federal government is on the other side of the lawsuit.
Bob McNamara from the Institute of Justice said North Dakota has broad laws that protect victims of eminent domain and private natural gas pipelines. He said pipeline companies “say they don’t have to follow those laws because they’re just like the federal government.”
The outcome is likely to have consequences beyond North Dakota.
Spiegelman said landowners around the country whose property is seized by the government, or by private companies licensed by the government, “will not have any good incentive to pursue the vindication of the full value of their land” in court.
“What’s at stake here are property rights protections. And really all 50 states that are under threat from private pipeline companies operating with the federal government’s authority” McNamara said.
During oral arguments Monday, the Natural Gas Act is likely to be discussed. The act suggests federal standards should apply to disputes like this one.

title: Much Needed Rain On The Way This Weekend
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A wet weekend is ahead as an area of low pressure moves into the Gulf of Maine, bringing much-needed rain to the region. The highest totals are expected along the coast and islands
Showers have already developed along the coast and steadier, heavier rain will spread from south to north Friday night into early Saturday morning. In far northern Maine, rain may hold off until close to sunrise Saturday.
Patchy fog is possible. Lows will range from the mid-30s in the far north to the upper 40s and low 50s closer to the coast.
Saturday: Soggy With Seasonable Highs
Rain showers will continue Saturday, though there will be a few breaks. Pockets of moderate to heavy rain are most likely closer to the coast, so keep an umbrella handy.
Highs will range from the mid- to upper 40s to the low 50s. Northeast winds will gust to 20 to 25 mph, with peak gusts up to 30 mph possible.
Sunday: Showers Continue & Cooler
As the low moves east and northeast, scattered showers will continue Saturday night into Sunday. Cooler air will move in, allowing rain to mix with or change to snow for a time in the higher elevations.
Precipitation will end from southwest to northeast later Sunday. Highs will range from the upper 30s to the upper 40s, with northwest wind gusts up to 25 mph.
Rainfall totals
- Immediate coast and islands: 2 inches or more.
- Interstate corridor to the coast: 1 to 2 inches.
- Foothills to the interstate: 0.5 to 1 inch.
- Mountains and northern Maine: Less than 0.5 inches.
Early next week: Drier and seasonable
Drier and more seasonable conditions are favored for the first part of the week. Watching a cool-down for the end of the week with highs that may only be in the 30s and low 40s.
First Alert 7-Day Forecast
TONIGHT: Rain spreading from south to north. Lows will range from the upper 30s in the north to the upper 40s and low 50s along the coast. Patchy fog possible with NE winds 5-15 mph.
SATURDAY: Rain showers continue. Highs in the 40s and low 50s. NE wind will gust 15-25 mph.
SUNDAY: Cloudy with scattered showers and even some mixing in the higher elevations. Highs in the 30s & 40s. NW wind will gust 15-25 mph.
MONDAY: Partly to mostly cloudy skies. Highs in the 40s and low 50s.
TUESDAY: Partly to mostly cloudy skies. Highs in the 40s and low 50s.
WEDNESDAY: Partly to mostly cloudy skies. Highs in the 40s and low 50s.
THURSDAY: Mix of sun & clouds with highs in the 40s.

title: P.I. Graves’ Shop & Save Will Become a Hannaford
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Customers in Presque Isle will see a few things change at Graves’ Shop and Save as the business transitions into a Hannaford Supermarket. The new store manager says they are trying to keep things the same to honor the store’s decades-long legacy.
“There isn’t gonna be as big of a change as folks are probably expecting. The Graves family already did a very great job. We just want to get our messaging of value, affordability, and convenience into the store as well. We want to continue the Graves’ high level of customer service. It’s gonna be the same associates working in the building. We retained almost every single current Graves’ associate in the transition to Hannaford. So, I think that’s really exciting. We’re looking on building on the legacy that the Graves family has had in the city of Presque Isle since 1959 but certainly putting our own spin as Hannaford in the community,” said James Redman, the new store manager of the Presque Isle Hannaford.
Redman says the transition has been going smoothly. “Things are going very well. You know, Bob Graves and the family has been super welcoming to us, allowed us to get into the building a few weeks early, start getting to know the community, getting to know the associates that have been working here. So, we’re making really good progress. We are gonna be resetting some cases. Hopefully, installing some new fixtures. We’re looking to add a wing bar and do a bunch of other things. It’s gonna be dependent on the construction sequence next week on how much we’re gonna be able to get done but certainly we have big plans for the next 12 months on really making a positive impact in programs and services throughout the building.”
For those with concerns about the pharmacy that operates independently within the store, Redman says customers won’t have to worry about being able to pick up their prescriptions. “The pharmacy is gonna stay open the regular business hours during the store closure. Be able to come in and pick up their prescriptions, or the pharmacy is gonna offer curbside pickup during the duration. So, there should be no impact to the current independent pharmacy while the grocery side of the business is closed next week.”
Graves’ Shop and Save will officially close Monday, Nov. 9, at 2 p.m. and reopen Friday, Nov. 13, at 7 a.m. as a Hannaford Supermarket. The change will mark a new chapter for the longstanding Presque Isle store.

title: Maine heating oil prices are up 79% from a year ago
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine’s heating oil prices have fallen ever so slightly over the past week.
The average price for a gallon of heating oil is now $6.01, down from last week’s record high of $6.05, according to the Maine Department of Energy Resources.
In eastern and Down East Maine, prices range from a low of $5.68 to a high of $6.40.
That statewide average is 79% higher than this time last year, when heating oil went for $3.35 a gallon.
Mainers will now have to spend an additional $731.50 to fill a standard 275-gallon tank.
Energy prices have been climbing globally since February when President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu launched a surprise war against Iran. Although Trump said that the war would last only weeks, it entered its eighth month in late October.
That war effectively halted fuel shipments out of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s natural gas and oil passes, for much of the year. The ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine also has strained global fuel supplies as both sides have traded blows on each other’s energy infrastructure, and Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen have attacked Saudi energy sites and seized territory along the Red Sea coast, another key trade route.
Last month, the Trump administration released about $37 million in low-income heating assistance for Maine. An additional $1.4 million was awarded to the state’s four federally recognized tribes. The administration also is tapping the Northeast heating oil reserves for the first time since 2012 when Hurricane Sandy devastated the northeastern U.S.
About half of Maine households ( more than 300,000) rely on heating oil to stay warm during the winter, and consumption can average 2 to 7 gallons a day, depending on how cold it is outside. That means the 13.2 million gallons flowing from the Northeast stockpile would amount to approximately nine days of consumption at a rate of five gallons a day.
Rising energy costs and anger over the Iran war contributed to heavy losses for Republicans in Tuesday’s midterm elections, including the ousting of U.S. Sen. Susan Collins after three decades representing Maine in Washington.
It’s unclear whether the election results will mean any relief from high oil prices. Trump has mused for weeks about escalating attacks on Iran after the midterms, and the U.S. in recent days has conducted what it calls “defensive strikes” against Iranian targets in the strait.

title: Stephen Miller to replace Susie Wiles as Donald Trump's White House chief of staff
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, mere days after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections.
On his social media site, Trump praised Wiles and said she’d continue to work for his political organization.
Miller, long a key member of Trump’s inner circle, is a key architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies.
Wiles, the steely political operator and longtime adviser to Trump, was the first woman to ever serve in that post.
Wiles’ departure comes almost immediately after the GOP’s midterm thrashing on Tuesday. She will be replaced by Stephen Miller, a longtime trusted aide to Trump.
The departure also came months after Wiles indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease, a diagnosis she went public with in March 2026.
Wiles is the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.
Story by Seung Min Kim, Associated Press

title: Focus still on quarterbacks in Patriots, Packers matchup
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — The Green Bay Packers and New England Patriots don’t play each other that often.
The most recent time was in 2022, an overtime game at Lambeau Field that Green Bay won with Aaron Rodgers under center during his final season with the Packers.
In the teams’ most recent matchup in New England in 2018, Tom Brady was on the field playing in his penultimate season with the team.
The game between the Packers (5-3) and Patriots (5-3) on Sunday won’t feature either future Hall of Famer. Rodgers is playing what he’s said is his final NFL season in Pittsburgh, and Brady will be calling his first game in Gillette Stadium as an analyst for Fox Sports.
“I think I’m required contractually to catch up with him at some point,” Patriots coach Mike Vrabel joked this week about Brady’s latest return to New England.
But there will be plenty of focus on the quarterbacks that have come behind Rodgers and Brady for their respective former franchises.
Jordan Love appears to be finding his stride in his fourth season as the full-time starter, leading the league in passing yards for a team looking to make the playoffs for the fourth consecutive season.
Meanwhile, Drake Maye has recovered from a rough start to account for at least three touchdowns in each of his past five games, leading the Patriots to victories in four of them.
While the Packers enter the game last in the NFL in rushing, averaging only 60.6 yards per game, Love said he isn’t worried about generating offense.
“The run game isn’t where it needs to be, but I think we’ve still been able to kind of adjust and still make plays,” he said. “There’s a lot more out there, but we’ve done a great job just being able to win these games by putting up some points, and that’s what it comes down to.”
Maye said the matchup is certainly a measuring stick opposite a team that, like them, is trying to keep pace in their division.
“They’re good, they’ve beaten good teams, and they continue to show up every year,” Maye said. “We’ve definitely got a challenge and a chance to see how we look.”

title: Democratic candidates with a Christian message help flip Congress
text:
(AP) - Clergy members and other Democratic candidates with an unapologetically Christian message to “love your neighbor” helped their party flip control of Congress.
It was a striking midterm victory that demonstrated the strength of the religious left as a counter to the stalwart evangelical support for President Donald Trump and his fellow Republicans.
“This attempt to corner the market on Christianity by evangelicals was repudiated,” said Brian Kaylor, a Baptist pastor and editor of a progressive faith and politics site.
Instead, American mainline Protestantism, with its less-strident theology, took the election spotlight.
Seminarian James Talarico in Texas, megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton in Kansas and Iowa ministers Sarah Trone Garriott and Lindsay James flipped key seats in the U.S. Senate and House. They’re part of the mainline Presbyterian, Methodist and Lutheran branches with moderate or progressive beliefs.
Unlike the nationalists wanting America to privilege a particular Christian worldview in public life, the mainline candidates in keeping with their Christian values backed church-state separation and sought common ground across religions, Kaylor said.
“There were so many people in our country who felt so strongly that what was happening in D.C. was not moral,” Hamilton told The Associated Press. “It didn’t reflect our national values.”
That’s why he and the other candidates ran, he said, and why they were elected.
Mainline denominations have historically been part of the country’s civic establishment as the church home of most presidents and other elites. But membership has been sliding for decades. Despite that shift, the wins show these Protestants can still have significant influence — though not with white evangelicals.
Across the board, white evangelical Protestants stayed consistent in their overwhelming midterm support for Republicans. Most Protestants who identify as “liberal” or “moderate,” about 7 in 10, voted for Democrats, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of roughly 100,000 midterm voters.
The four mainline candidates also got a big boost from voters who reject organized religion. At least 7 in 10 religiously unaffiliated voters supported Democratic Senate and House candidates in Texas, Kansas and Iowa, The AP Voter Poll showed.
Others said being a progressive pastor wasn’t the prime factor in these victories.
“If I hear a story about the Democratic Party scouting out pastors to run in 2028 based on Talarico and Hamilton, I think they’ve totally missed the upshot from this election,” said Ryan Burge, a professor at Washington University in St. Louis who studies religious demographics. “It’s about economic issues. It’s about disdain for Trump. It’s about high prices.”
Talarico takes Texas as critique of his Christianity continues
In the longtime GOP stronghold of Texas, Talarico flipped a U.S. Senate seat — the first election in 30-plus years that Democrats won statewide races — by defeating Republican Ken Paxton, an evangelical.
Voters also ousted Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, a Republican who chaired Trump’s Religious Liberty Commission and declared, “There is no separation of church and state.”
In Talarico’s acceptance speech, the 37-year-old state legislator recounted how his grandfather, a Baptist preacher, taught him about Jesus, a “barefoot rabbi” who commanded people to love God and neighbor. And not just the neighbor who looks, prays or votes like him, the Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.) seminarian and former middle school teacher said.
“Two thousand years ago, when the people at the top hurt his neighbors, that barefoot rabbi didn’t stay in his room and pray. He walked into the seat of power, and he flipped over the tables of injustice. … Texas, it’s time to start flipping tables," Talarico said.
A longtime Texas Trump supporter and Southern Baptist pastor, the Rev. Robert Jeffress, maintains that the pluralistic religion promoted by Talarico and other candidates is not actually Christianity, a criticism raised by others during their campaigns.
“People want to choose a religion that’s nice and warm and fuzzy, whether it’s built on truth or not,” said Jeffress, who leads First Baptist Church in Dallas. “What James Talarico believes, according to the words of Jesus, is not true.”
He attributes the Democrats’ success to a trifecta of inflation, the Iran war and “less than ideal candidates.” Jeffress also suspects many evangelicals stayed home.
White evangelical Protestants made up a slightly smaller share of the electorate than in 2024, when Trump was running for president: 21% in 2024, compared with 17% in 2026, The AP Voter Poll showed. That could be due to lower turnout among white evangelicals or higher turnout among other groups. About 2 in 10 voted for Talarico in Texas and Hamilton in Kansas.
Kansas pastor candidate says kindness doesn’t require religion
Burge, the professor who studies religious demographics, asserts that the Democratic clergy members who won were strong candidates but also benefited from very favorable political winds.
“If you ran Adam Hamilton in 2024, he’s beat by double digits and we’re not having this conversation,” Burge said.
Hamilton, pastor of the nation’s largest United Methodist congregation, called for “decency” in politics, drawing on Jesus’ Golden Rule in his victory speech: “Do unto others as you would have them do unto you.”
“I can’t not talk about my faith. It’s just, it’s my life. It’s what I eat, sleep, drink and breathe,” he told the AP. But being religious isn’t required to follow biblical injunctions “to do justice, to love kindness.”
While campaigning for Hamilton’s Republican opponent, Sen. Roger Marshall, Vice President JD Vance questioned Hamilton’s religiosity.
“It was so ridiculous that there was no reason to even respond to it,” said Hamilton, who welcomes a conversation with Vance and other critics about faith and theology.
Iowa pastor candidates prioritize coalition building
Democrats Sarah Trone Garriott and Lindsay James, who flipped U.S. House seats in Iowa, didn’t have political ambitions when they pursued ordination.
Trump’s 2016 election sparked James’ involvement. The Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.) chaplain sees her ministry experience — from church potlucks to the pews — as a strength when connecting with all voters.
“I spent time bringing people together across difference,” she told the AP in March.
Trone Garriott, a state senator and a pastor in the mainline Evangelical Lutheran Church in America, thinks the religious right’s high profile in national politics has made some progressive Christians wary of sharing their faith publicly.
But she sees the power in diverse coalition building. In her acceptance speech, she evoked hope and the power of loving your neighbor. “When people come together on our common ground, we will do powerful things,” she said.
Midterm successes for other Christian candidates
Among Republicans, clergy candidates for Congress also prevailed, including Mark Harris of North Carolina, a Southern Baptist pastor, and Tim Walberg of Michigan, a former pastor.
Black Protestants vote overwhelmingly Democratic and have long comfortably talked faith and politics in a way white mainliners have not. This year, victorious Democrats included at least two Black clergy members — the Rev. Frederick Haynes III, a Baptist from Texas, and U.S. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver II, a United Methodist minister from Missouri.
In North Carolina, Democrat LaKesha Womack unseated a Republican incumbent in the U.S. House. She is an ordained deacon in the African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church, a historically Black Protestant denomination.
Womack told the AP her faith prompts her to advocate for “policies that address poverty and immigration and making sure everybody has access to healthcare.” And she defends religious freedom for all.
“With the white Christian nationalists almost taking over the narrative of what it means to be a Christian, I think there are a lot of people of faith in this country who wanted to reclaim that narrative,” she said.
Womack said that Democrats shouldn’t read too much into this year’s clergy victories.
“I don’t think we should go out and try to recruit ministers to become politicians if that’s not what they’re called to do,” she said. “It has to be authentic.”
___
AP reporter Tiffany Stanley contributed to this report.
___

title: Votes continue to be counted in Mississippi’s Senate race
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Mississippi election officials continued to count ballots in the state’s U.S. Senate race on Friday, which remains without a declared winner.
Democrat Scott Colom leads incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by about 2,500 votes as of Friday night. Thousands more ballots could still possibly be counted in the race.
Emily Ommundsen, a University of Mississippi political science professor, said counties are being particularly judicious in determining that the count is accurate because of the narrow margins of the race.
“Because of this narrow majority, we are we are hesitant to make any conclusions about the outcome of the race, as these final ballots are still being counted, within this legally prescribed period, where counties are ensuring that they are reporting the correct totals,” Ommundsen said.
The total number of remaining ballots remains unclear because of provisional ballots as well late-arriving mail-in ballots.
“Let me be clear. This race is far from being over,” said Mike Hurst, chairman of the Mississippi Republican Party, on Thursday. “We estimate that there could be approximately 20,000 outstanding ballots left to be counted. That includes mail-in or absentee ballots and affidavit or provisional ballots.”
Provisional ballots are ballots that have been set aside because of verification issues. Voters have until Nov. 10 to resolve them.
Both campaigns have deployed legal teams that could address possible legal challenges in the days ahead.
“We got an army of lawyers. Those election commissioners and circuit clerks, they’re not going to be intimidated,” Colom said Friday.
Mississippi is the only state in the nation without any recourse for a vote recount. But challenges are still likely.
The deadline to certify votes in Mississippi is Nov. 13.
“If these margins stay as close as they are, I expect some court ordered considerations, of which ballots should be permitted to be to be counted,” said Ommundsen. “But the 13th is really that first opportunity that I think we will have to see to see how things are going to shake out here in Mississippi.”

title: Voters narrowly reject moving Penobscot County Jail out of Bangor
text:
Penobscot County residents voted down a referendum to move the county jail out of Bangor by just 60 votes.
In total, 32,591 Penobscot County residents voted against the referendum, according to unofficial results gathered by the Bangor Daily News. The outcome of the vote took days to determine as results from Tuesday’s election trickled in from the county’s smallest communities, which largely voted against the measure.
Springfield, east of Lincoln, was the final town to report its results to the BDN along with Kingman and Prentiss townships, with the “no” side winning by nine votes.
Without approval, the plan to build a new Penobscot County Jail seemingly has to start over from scratch. Penobscot County Commissioners Dan Tremble, David Marshall and Andre Cushing will have to plan for a new location for the jail.
Previous plans had a single-story jail being built in Hampden, where the county had paid $100,000 to hold a plot of land, but now the commissioners will be tasked with finding a location in Bangor. Commissioners for years have discussed plans for a new jail, citing its decrepit state, inability to hold all the inmates brought to the facility and lack of space for needed services.
Hampden voted against the referendum 1,686 to 2,286.
Commissioners previously said they had looked at about a dozen slices of land in Bangor, but none were suitable for their plans. It’s unclear how the county’s plans will change.
Approval to relocate the jail garnered 32,531 votes and had approval in 18 of the more than 60 Penobscot County towns that voted on the measure. The county’s largest communities carried the “yes” vote, with six of the 10 biggest towns approving the move.
Of the next 10 largest municipalities, just four approved the referendum.
Penobscot County shared unofficial results that differ from what the BDN has collected from towns, but they confirm the measure did not pass, according to a press release from County Administrator Blair Tinkham.
Officials are waiting for legal guidance on the process and county officials will ratify the results, Tinkham said.
The release did not say if the county will call for a recount. Officials “will determine any additional actions required to properly complete the certification process,” Tinkham said.
“The voters of Penobscot County have spoken, and it is now our responsibility to ensure the results are reviewed and certified in accordance with Maine law,” Marshall said in the release. “Given the close margin and the unique circumstances surrounding certification of a county referendum question, the commissioners are committed to a transparent, deliberate and legally sound process that maintains public confidence in the integrity of the election.”
More information about the certification process and next steps will be shared after commissioners and officials receive legal guidance, Tinkham said.

title: Deven Young does not enter plea in 1st adult court appearance in slaying of Maine paddleboarder
text:
Deven Young made his first appearance in adult court Friday morning.
Young, now 19, is charged with intentional or knowing or depraved indifference murder in Knox County Superior Court. He is accused of killing 48-year-old Sunshine Stewart, who was found dead July 3, 2025, after she failed to return from paddleboarding on Crawford Pond in Union.
Young, who was 17 at the time of Stewart’s death, did not enter a plea, which is standard in felony cases. It will be presented to a grand jury that will decide whether to indict him.
The appearance in adult court comes about 20 minutes after Young waived his right to a bind-over hearing. The case proceeded from juvenile to adult court.
He is held without bail in Knox County Jail in Rockland and is scheduled for a status conference in January.

title: Bedbugs discovery closes Medomak Middle School for days
text:
WALDOBORO, Maine (WABI) - Medomak Middle School in Waldoboro is moving to remote learning for several days after multiple bedbugs were discovered at the school.
In the letter, RSU 40 Superintendent Daniel Welch said that the decision was made “out of an abundance of caution,” and announced that the school would be arranging professional treatment to target the bugs.
Officials said there is currently no indication of an infestation.
Superintendent Welch announced that students will be learning remotely through next Tuesday.
The bedbug treatment is scheduled for next week in accordance with state regulations that mandate five days’ advance notification before treatment can occur.
School officials are asking families to check children’s backpacks, coats and other belongings for signs of bedbugs. Families are also encouraged to inspect bedding, mattress seams and areas where belongings are stored.
The district also said bedbugs are a nuisance but are not known to spread disease.
The school said families should contact the school if they find bedbugs or have questions about the situation.

title: Author talk explores women's suffrage on MDI
text:
BAR HARBOR — Join the MDI Historical Society and the Jesup Memorial Library for a Chebacco Author Chat with Catherine McDonald on Thursday, Nov. 19 at 5:30 p.m. In “Battling for the Ballot: The Long Fight in Maine,” McDonald chronicles the long road to women’s suffrage on MDI, traced through generations of local women and their increasing role in social activism, through an exploration of the public attitudes that accompanied women’s rising power and the voices that tried to halt their progress.
Catherine McDonald graduated from the University of Maine in 2019 with a B.A. in History and Secondary Education, and from the University of Nebraska at Kearney in 2024 with a MA in American History. Catherine started Boundless Local Tour Company in 2023 and offers historical tours in Bar Harbor and Eastport. She lives in Addison with her partner Larry, hopes to pursue a Ph.D., and continues to share local history with visitors to Downeast Maine.

title: Maine looks to its forests to reach climate goals
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.
As the most heavily forested state in the country, about 94 percent of Maine’s forests are privately owned, so focusing on their carbon benefits has both immediate ecological and economic effects.
By creating specific programs and collaborations, the state has been strategic in using its resources to reach its climate goals and has made thoughtful partnerships for years ahead. The story of Maine demonstrates how individuals can collectively make a greater impact and how international alliances can contribute toward global stewardship.
In a four-year climate action plan called “Maine Won’t Wait,” the state sets out four pillars to focus on: drastically reducing greenhouse emissions, strengthening resiliency by adaptation, protecting jobs at risk from climate change and creating clean energy jobs and supporting all of Maine’s residents, even in rural communities.
On the economic side, Maine’s Forest Products Council reported that in 2024 the state’s timber industry produced $8.3 billion for Maine’s economy, representing 3.45 percent of the state’s GDP. Maine’s paper and timber industry also accounted for 29,000 jobs across 16 counties.
But Maine’s 18 million acres of forests also protect the watershed, soil and biodiversity as the largest unfragmented tract across the eastern United States, essential for species migration.
One thing is certain: Maine’s forests are indispensable. In 2021, the state created the Forest Carbon Task Force and implemented a range of programs and legislation to support Maine’s forests and build climate resiliency. Now, as reporting deadlines are approaching, the state can see exactly how successful these conservation efforts have been.
In March, the Maine Forest Service introduced the WoodsWISE Resilience Program, which supports private woodland owners and encourages climate-focused stewardship. The program, which works alongside an existing program called the WoodsWISE Incentives Program, is now funded by two grants totaling $9 million from the Inflation Reduction Act and the U.S. Forest Service Landowner Support Program. One grant requires documentation of pre- and post-treatment inventory and carbon modeling.
Nicole Rogers, formerly the Maine Forest Service landowner outreach forester, said that through the WoodsWise program, landowners can apply for eight approved practices that have climate or carbon benefits. To participate, woodland owners need 10 to 1,000 acres of forest and must agree to work with a practice plan focused on the area of practice implementation that meets their forest’s specific needs for 10 years.
“Our program is a tool for landowners wanting to take action in their own forest,” Rogers said in an email. “By offering financial incentives, landowners have the opportunity to do thoughtful silviculture with a reduced financial burden.”
According to Rogers, since March, more than 150 landowners have participated in the WoodsWISE Resilience Program. Through this program, a trained consulting forester works with each landowner on a plan specific to their forest’s needs so they can gain support while navigating the changes from climate change.
The program focuses on good stewardship, which can mean many things, depending on the forest. It can range from invasive species removal and thinning an overcrowded, young forest; to removing specific trees to encourage regeneration, or removing trees that carry disease or fungus.
“These practices can be costly for a private landowner, so the program aims to reimburse 60 to 90 percent of the financial burden for landowners based on their underserved status by creating an indiviudalized plan the woodland owner agrees to follow for the next 10 years. This could result in up to $20,000 per participant and another program is set to open later this year with a higher landowner cap. With programs like these, the state of Maine could see a collective benefit.”
By purposefully using landowners’ forests, Maine has an advantage in reaching carbon neutrality. According to research by the University of Maine, the state’s forests offset at least 60 percent of overall greenhouse emissions annually. Philip Bartlett II, the former chair of the Maine Public Utilities Commission, said that electricity generation in Maine is already fairly clean, with a mix of renewables in use throughout the state.
Bartlett said it’s important to look long-term when meeting climate goals, and agrees that good forest management practices are key for Maine. He said that, to his knowledge, no fast clear-cutting is being done, and forests are managed for growth and harvesting, creating opportunities for carbon sequestration.
The challenge, he said, is the state’s vastness, which makes residents rely on fuel for transportation and oil to heat their homes. Bartlett said recent international dynamics have emphasized the need for a diversified portfolio of renewable resources to stabilize electricity prices.
“I think what we’re seeing now is that reliance on fossil fuels is really what is driving a ton of volatility and really high prices during certain parts of the year. So the only way you’re going to tackle that is to figure out how to diversify that portfolio,” he said.
Catherine Wolfram, a professor of energy economics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Sloan School of Management, said Maine’s implementation of carbon markets aligns with how Europe and other countries are operating.
She said that while compliance markets run by governments in which polluters are essentially taxed for carbon emissions are “extremely robust and extremely effective,” much of the criticism of carbon markets comes from the voluntary markets where companies buy and sell carbon offsets without formal monitoring, with corruption and manipulation sometimes a factor.
While Wolfram said these potential problems are solvable, she said the issue of large areas of forests being used as carbon sinks is more complex when businesses are also dependent on the area for timber.
“Even if Maine protected all of its forest, then maybe the timber companies will just go to Vermont, and then what have you done? You’ve just displaced where they do their forestry, and you haven’t preserved a carbon sink; you’ve just rearranged things,” said Wolfram.
She said ideas such as global governance of what counts could solve issues like this, and that ultimately clean energy can insulate consumers from the market instability of fossil fuel markets.
“With climate change, it’s a global problem,” said Wolfram, “so what really matters is how what we do in the United States translates to what other countries are doing. China is 30 percent of global emissions, and they’ve made a lot of progress, thankfully, but I think we need to keep things in proportion.”
Maintaining a global perspective is exactly what Maine is doing. In 2019, Maine began a formal collaboration with Finland, encouraging an interchange of sustainable stewardship strategies to build strong bioeconomies. After years of working together informally, Gov. Janet Mills signed the partnership at the 2019 Arctic Circle Conference in Reykjavik.
Dan Berger, director of the Maine North Atlantic Development Office for the Maine International Trade Center, said that since the two regions share a similar profile in which heavily forested lands are economic cornerstones, this “peer exchange” makes sense.
Finland, known for a bioeconomy that makes up 16 percent of its GDP, has focused specifically on the role its forests play. Maine also has research initiatives, including a $20 million award from the U.S. Economic Development Administration to the University of Maine’s Tech Hub to support converting low-value wood into everyday necessities such as fuel and packing materials.
Berger said this focus on Maine’s bioeconomy can “strengthen domestic manufacturing and supply chains, and displace conventional, carbon-intensive materials and fuels.” He said three areas of particular interest are where Maine’s forests can make a sustainable impact on the local economy.
First is construction, replacing petroleum-based materials with lower-carbon alternatives such as mass timber and wood-fiber insulation; second, replacing conventional plastic packing materials with nontoxic ones, such as cellulose nanofiber, which has been developed at the University of Maine. Companies like Poland Spring Bottling Company are already considering biobased packing alternatives. Thirdly, Berger points to replacing fossil fuels used to heat homes in the winter months with low-value wood that is already a byproduct of Maine’s timber companies.
“We measure success in concrete terms,” said Berger in an email. “Investments attracted, jobs created, companies launched or scaled, and Maine businesses reaching new markets, all in a way that is sustainable, science-based, and advances Maine’s economic and climate goals alike.”
Claire Hawkins, director of natural resource markets and economic development for the Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry, agrees that a strong bioeconomy balances thoughtful stewardship with a local, sustainable economy.
Because Finland has a globally renowned, robust bioeconomy that supports innovation, the alliance has provided valuable insights into Maine’s current practices and helps anticipate long-term results. “For every facet of Maine forestry, there’s an equal or a parallel example in Finland,” said Hawkins. “One of the benefits of working with the Finns is that they’ve been doing it longer; they’re an older country, so their bioeconomy is a little bit further down the road in terms of its evolution than ours.”
This summer, about 100 delegates came to Maine. They included Finnish government officials, researchers and forest and conservation workers.
In describing the Maine-Finland collaboration, she said, “We have a lot in common, but Maine and Finland are still their own creatures, so it’s less of the copy and paste and more of the, ‘You have a problem with this pest, we had a problem with this pest. This is the way we dealt with it.’”
Hawkins said that research and development, the commercialization of forest products, forest and exchange policy, and encouraging continuity in the forestry workforce are other topics the two partners frequently discuss.
“Circular economics is something we hear a lot about in the context of bioeconomy, but if not circular, then certainly sustainable, right?” Hawkins said. “So, I think it’s recognition that there has to be a more holistic approach to managing and propelling these natural resource-based economies, but I also think they’re sort of a future-oriented bend to the definition too … the definition of bioeconomy is evolving.”
Maine has taken both an introspective and extrospective approach in thinking about the role its forests play in climate change. By recognizing the connection of sustainability and economics both the individual and world community are considered and asked to take part in effecting change.

title: Chiefs Rashee Rice files for bankruptcy, listing millions in liabilities
text:
Chiefs WR Rashee Rice files for Chapter 7 bankruptcy, listing millions in liabilities
Federal court records show Chiefs wide receiver Rashee Rice has filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy protection.
The court documents were filed Wednesday in Texas.
Video above: Chiefs launch 'redemption tour'
Rice reports $3.46 million in liabilities and about $677,000 in assets.
The documents say there is more than $3.2 million in unsecured debt, with multiple claims connected to civil litigation.
Rice listed assets, including a $53,800 Mercedes-Benz and $165,000 worth of jewelry, including a Super Bowl ring.
The filing comes two years after Rice was involved in a high-speed, multi-vehicle crash in the Dallas area that injured several people.
Multiple lawsuits were filed against Rice as a result of the crash.
Back in July 2025, Rice was sentenced to five years of probation and 30 days in jail for his involvement in the crash.
Rice served the jail sentence after testing positive for THC.
He also served a six-game suspension during the 2025 season.

title: Did Area 51 relocate to Lisbon?
text:
In our series AskME, we explore your questions about Maine's history, culture and customs. What have you been wondering? We’ll work to find an answer. Explore the questions, or submit your own, at pressherald.com/ask-me.
Some people in Lisbon are old enough to remember the night the UFOs came to town.
It was 2001, “The X-Files” was in its eighth season on TV, and the Worumbo Mill was abuzz with activity as a U.S. military convoy delivered top secret materials from Area 51.
That is, if you were to believe a mysterious website run by the Counter Evidence Research Consortium, also known as CERC.
That website no longer exists, but archives of its pages can still be found. In an April 2001 post, an unnamed author spilled the beans on why the government had abandoned its notorious UFO research facility in Nevada: too much public interest. Now the contents of Area 51 were being scattered across five different “sectors,” the most important of them Worumbo Mill in Lisbon Falls, Maine.
The conspiracy theory has survived for 25 years in remote corners of the internet, reappearing periodically in Facebook threads and Quora questions, but who started the rumor remains a mystery.
Across the street from the mill, which was demolished in 2016, is the Kennebec Fruit Company, better known as the Moxie Store, and now called Frank’s Restaurant & Pub. For decades, the store was owned and operated by the late Frank Anicetti, founder of Lisbon’s famed Moxie Festival.
If anyone were to notice a midnight convoy of military gruffs and flying saucers, it would have been “Mr. Moxie.” Naturally, Anicetti was the first stop for Sun Journal reporter Scott Taylor, who in 2002 investigated the claim that Worumbo was the new home of Area 51.
When asked, Anicetti said, “This comes as news to the folks around here.”
Taylor tried to contact the mysterious Counter Evidence Research Consortium at its office in Washington, D.C., but was rebuffed.
Their response: “Please understand that it is the policy of CERC to not grant media interviews. We do not go out of our way to garner external publicity on our findings.”
The lack of evidence didn’t keep the story from finding an audience with Maine’s most famous resident. As a teenager, Stephen King worked at the old textile mill and was sufficiently spooked to tell Taylor, “If ever there was a place to stick aliens, Worumbo Mill was it.”
King later found literary inspiration in the site. His 2011 novel “11/22/63” not only references Worumbo Mill and the Kennebec Fruit Company, but features Mr. Moxie himself: “The proprietor of the Fruit Company, an elderly sweet-natured man named Frank Anicetti, had once told me the world’s population divided naturally (and probably by genetic inheritance) into two groups: the tiny but blessed elect who prized Moxie above all other potables . . . and everybody else. Frank called everybody else ‘the unfortunately handicapped majority.’”
Among Anicetti’s other interests: UFOs. Scott Taylor said as much in his 2002 story, as did Portland Press Herald/Maine Sunday Telegram reporter Ray Routhier in the obituary he wrote when Anicetti died in 2017:
“Anicetti was an avid reader, and he especially devoured fiction about space aliens. … A few years ago, he started telling customers and friends that the closed Worumbo mill building was being used as an alien detention facility by the government. Conjuring up scenes from the ‘Men in Black’ movies, Anicetti told of government agents, dressed in black and wearing sunglasses, ushering aliens into the mill under the cover of darkness.”
So Mr. Moxie wanted to believe. Why, then, did he present as a skeptic in Scott Taylor’s 2002 story? To put it in “X-Files” terms: How did Agent Scully become Agent Mulder?
“For that obit, a lot of people said he told tall tales and was a big self-promoter, and not everyone appreciated that,” Routhier said. “So it would seem plausible to me that 15 years earlier he had never heard the story, but when he did, he took to retelling it.”
Scott Taylor, now an editor at the Colorado Trust For Local News (sister company of the Maine Trust for Local News), concurred. “He loved Lisbon Falls and was happy to embrace anything that promoted it.”
Anicetti ran a beloved shop across the street from the mysterious Worumbo Mill. What better way to draw customers than to exploit the conspiracy theory that the mill was the new Area 51?
As for the mysterious Counter Evidence Research Consortium, one wonders why so many of its reported UFO sightings were in Maine. Could it be that Mr. Moxie is the Counter Evidence Research Consortium? Could it be that Frank Anicetti created the mysterious website and, thus, the myth of Worumbo Mill?
I put the theory to the Sun Journal’s Mark LaFlamme, the foremost expert on Worumbo’s esoteric past and author of the 2013 novel, “Worumbo.”
“Frank and I did talk about Worumbo whenever we connected,” he told me. “But I never got the sense that Frank was into tech at all. I went out to his house once and was surprised he had plumbing.”

title: Rome man pleads guilty in case involving alleged assaults on mother, daughter
text:
ROME, Maine (WABI) - A Rome man accused of assaulting a woman with a baseball bat and sexually assaulting her daughter has pleaded guilty, according to the Morning Sentinel.
David Henry, 79, was arrested in February and charged with attempted murder, sexual assault and aggravated assault. The publication reports that the attempted murder charge was dismissed.
Prosecutors say Henry beat and strangled the woman after she confronted him about her daughter’s allegations. The daughter said Henry sexually assaulted her when she was 12 and 14 years old.
According to the Morning Sentinel, attorneys agreed to limit Henry’s sentence to 30 years. A sentencing hearing is scheduled for next month.

title: Only 29% of faculty say they would choose UMaine again
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
In the spring, more than 70% of faculty at the University of Maine said they felt “extensive stress” related to budget cuts on campus after the flagship public university faced an $18 million shortfall last school year, according to a survey released to faculty on Nov. 5.
Only 29% of faculty said they would choose UMaine again.
The Higher Education Research Institute survey, which was administered by UMaine officials and the Faculty Senate last April, also showed that 81% of faculty felt they were at odds with administrators. Less than a quarter of faculty felt they were sufficiently involved in decision-making processes on campus, and half of faculty said they had considered leaving the university.
Those surveyed include full-time faculty who worked with or taught undergraduate or graduate students, part-time undergraduate faculty and full-time academic administrators.
The survey was distributed at the end of a tense year when the university faced an $18 million shortfall. Last year, the university asked departments to shave 7% of their budgets to address the gap. UMaine shared the results with faculty on Nov. 5.
Faculty and staff also raised concerns last year about the school’s strategic planning process. Some felt that their input in planning for the university’s future — which involved addressing fiscal sustainability — was insufficient.
Faculty Senate president Brian McGill said the results show that people are pretty happy with their jobs and departments, but have strong concerns about the university overall. The spring survey, which had 230 respondents, showed that faculty positively rated their experiences and relationships with their peers and departments, and highly rated their retirement benefits.
“I think that reflects what I hear,” McGill said. “They like their colleagues. They like their students. They like their departments. But they’re not having great feelings about the overall climate on campus.”
UMaine Provost Gabe Paquette said on Friday that the strengths that were highlighted in the survey — such as strong relationships with peers and support for research — will provide a foundation for UMaine leaders as they work with faculty to improve communication and trust on campus, as well as address financial and enrollment challenges.
“As we have repeatedly said and shown, UMaine leaders recognize and respect the contributions of our dedicated faculty and staff, and we remain deeply committed to shared governance,” Paquette wrote in an email to The Monitor. “We believe that transparency, trust, meaningful consultation, clear communication, and collaboration between the administration and our employees are essential.”
He said that the university’s leaders have hosted two sessions to discuss the budget, where faculty and others pitched ideas. He also said administrators provided responses to questions that the Faculty Senate raised about the current budget shortfall and fiscal sustainability.
UMaine is still welcoming suggestions, he said.
This year, the campus faces another hefty $19 million shortfall for the upcoming budget year, which starts in July. UMaine so far has plans to address $16 million of that budget gap, including by laying off faculty and staff, but not the remaining $3 million it must make up.
This week, UMaine sent out offers of retirement payouts to faculty members in an effort to address the gap. They have until January to choose whether or not they wish to accept.
McGill said that, with recent developments, opinions of campus have likely not improved, though he suspects they also have not changed significantly.
“We’ve kind of been building a slow-rolling crisis for a while,” McGill said.
This story was originally published by The Maine Monitor, a nonprofit and nonpartisan news organization. To get regular coverage from The Monitor, sign up for a free Monitor newsletter here.

title: ‘Coastal Cowgirl’ Payton Sullivan ready for Maine debut opening for Sugarland
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Sugarland will play the Cross Insurance Center in Bangor on Wednesday, Nov. 11, as part of a tour celebrating 20 years of “Enjoy the Ride.” Country artist Payton Sullivan is opening the show.
The Grammy Award-winning duo’s show starts at 7 p.m.
Tickets are available at waterfrontconcerts.com.
Sullivan’s sound and Sugarland connection
Sullivan told WABI she lives part time in Nashville, Tennessee, and spends the other half of the year on the Big Island of Hawaii. She described her sound as a “coastal country sound” and said her writing has a “rooted storytelling country-style.”
Sullivan said she grew up listening to Sugarland and that “Something More” was her first karaoke song.
“It was such a full circle moment for me,” Sullivan said of getting the call about touring with Sugarland. “I wish I could tell that little girl, ‘You did it.’”
First trip to Maine
Sullivan said she has not been to Maine. She said she looks for the coffee shops closest to the venue in every city on the tour and asked people with suggestions to send her a direct message on Instagram or TikTok.
What to expect at the show
Sullivan said “Something More” is the Sugarland song she most wants to hear live. She said Kristian told her the night before the interview that he had talked to Jennifer and that they want to start bringing her up on stage for “Something More” at the end of the show.
“No way. This is crazy,” Sullivan said.
Sullivan described her set as “very country” and “light and airy and sunshiny.” She said she will wear a bikini top with a denim jacket and a skirt on stage.
She invited fans to visit the merchandise booth after her set, before Sugarland takes the stage. Sullivan said she plans to meet fans there and hand out a free gift.

title: 10 Pop Songs That Have Become Unofficial Movie Theme Songs
text:
10 Pop Songs That Have Become Unofficial Movie Characters Theme Songs
When a theme song sticks, it sticks. Plenty of famous movie characters and even entire film franchises have their own memorable music—where would Hollywood’s composers be without Jaws or James Bond’s title tracks? Most of the time, these theme tunes have been composed specifically with these characters or stories in mind, meant to be used again and again for however long their legacy lasts. But sometimes a song pops up in a movie and unintentionally becomes a famous character’s anthem, whether it was originally intended or not.
Movies often have pop songs playing over their opening or end credits, and sometimes these songs were composed specifically to be used in the movie. (Aerosmith’s “I Don’t Want to Miss a Thing” for Armageddon is a good example of this.) But today at ScreenCrush we’re talking pop songs that were simply included in the movie either on a whim or because the filmmakers just liked how they fit. Somehow, whether through repetition or because they happened to be included in an iconic scene, these songs become irrevocably tied to a specific character to such a degree that we can’t even listen to them without a certain fictional person instantly popping into our heads.
A lot of the time, these songs don’t even have much to do with the character or the scene or the movie at all—and yet, like Pavlov’s dogs, we just can’t help but associate them together forever. The power of movies and the power of music combine to give us something that is — quite literally — unforgettable.

title: These mall walkers are bringing a ’90s vibe back in Oregon
text:
PORTLAND, Ore. (Aging Untold) — In the 1980s and 1990s, the mall was a place to gather beyond shopping, and one Oregon woman is bringing vibes from that era back to the Lloyd Center mall in Oregon.
Krista Catwood started the Food Court 5000 walking group. Participants wearing spandex, windbreakers, sneakers and scrunchies gather every Sunday morning for three and a half miles of power walking.
“We’ve become sort of B-celebrities of the mall,” Catwood said. “I think most people that come here kind of know who we are.”
How the group started
Catwood started the group while searching for a fun way to move. She knew it had to be silly, social and shared with others.
“I knew when I had this idea that it was a good one,” Catwood said. “I had no idea how many people would be interested.”
Members describe what keeps them coming back
The idea drew people in, and the energy, kindness and inclusion keep bringing them back.
“I’m having the time of my life, and I’ll be 81 in two months,” Leslie Kelinson, one of the walkers, said. “I get so much from those two hours, you have no idea.”
She said the meetups are “fun” and “healthy” and “inspiring.”

title: Bangor auction returns for 40th year, supports sister city in El Salvador
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - An auction supporting Bangor’s sister city in El Salvador returns Saturday for its 40th year.
Power in Community Alliances, or PICA, will host silent and live auctions from 3 to 5:30 p.m. at the Universalist Unitarian Church on Park Street. Books, gift certificates, handmade items, and more will be up for grabs.
Proceeds will support PICA’s Sister City Project and benefit the community council and community organizers in Carasque, El Salvador, as well as delegation trips.
For more than 35 years, PICA members have kept in touch with and visited people in Carasque. Despite the nearly 4,000 miles between the communities, organizers say they have found plenty of common ground.
“You have a relationship with these people that are living, in a way a world apart, a different life, but yet you can get together and you can share conversations and laugh and it’s just very grounding in the world we live in,” said Edward Rudnicki, a PICA board member.
Rudnicki said phone calls and visits also offer opportunities to learn about progress in education and how communities have rebuilt since El Salvador’s civil war, which lasted from the late 1970s to the early 1990s.

title: IRS announces new federal income tax brackets for 2027
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
IRS announces new federal income tax brackets for 2027
The IRS on Thursday announced new federal income tax brackets for 2027.
Related video above: What to know about 401(k) early withdrawals
The higher income thresholds were adjusted for inflation, according to a news release from the IRS.
Marginal tax rates for 2027 listed below:
- 10% for single individuals with incomes of $12,800 or less; $25,600 for married couples filing jointly
- 12% for single individuals with incomes over $12,800; $25,600 for married couples filing jointly
- 22% for single individuals with incomes over $52,025; $104,050 for married couples filing jointly
- 24% for single individuals with incomes over $109,125; $218,250 for married couples filing jointly
- 32% for single individuals with incomes over $208,325; $416,650 for married couples filing jointly
- 35% for single individuals with incomes over $264,550; $529,100 for married couples filing jointly
- 37% for single individuals with incomes over $661,375; $793,650 for married couples filing jointly
The standard deduction, which is applied by about 9 of 10 taxpayers, is also rising in 2027, according to the IRS.
The standard deduction for next year will increase to $33,200 for married couples filing jointly, up $1,000 from 2026. The standard deduction will rise to $16,600 for single taxpayers and married individuals filing separately. The standard deduction will be $24,925 for heads of households.
Child tax credit
The child tax credit will increase by $100 to $2,300 in 2027. The amount of credit that may be refundable is $1,800, also up $100 from last year.
Annual Exclusion for Gifts
The annual exclusion for gifts will increase to $20,000 in 2027, up from $19,000 in 2026.

title: How this Civil Rights-era school helped Black women break office barriers
text:
NEW ORLEANS (InvestigateTV) - Just over 60 years ago, the country took a step toward making good on a promise that all Americans are created equal. The passage of the Civil Rights Act in 1964 desegregated schools, workplaces, and public spaces all while creating protections against discrimination.
A year after the signing of the landmark legislation, an adult education center in New Orleans opened its doors to young Black women. Those women would use the skills they learned to integrate major corporate offices across the South.
In mid-May, a group of women who graduated from the former Adult Education Center in New Orleans came back for a reunion.
During the Civil Rights era, the Adult Education Center, located at Exchange Place in the French Quarter, helped prepare Black women to enter the white-collar workforce by teaching them skills such as typewriting and short handwriting.
Raphael Morgan said back then, office jobs for people like her were few and far between because they could not get training.
“I couldn’t type. I didn’t know shorthand. So, every time I went on an interview, they would say, ‘You don’t have any experience. We’re not going to be able to hire you.’ It’s like a door slammed in your face,” Morgan said. ”I have an older mother, and she had witnessed the same thing. So, all she knew was doing domestic work."
Raphael Morgan enrolled at the Adult Education Center in 1970 after high school. She said she could not afford to go to college and believed going to the center would be her best shot for employment.
“I think my mother was more excited because she really felt badly that she couldn’t afford to send me to college at the time, and to this day, I cannot believe the education that I received. I paid $40 for books only, and we had shorthand, typing and job interviewing skills,” Morgan said.
The vocational school opened in 1965, inspired by Father Timothy Gibbons. But the Catholic priest needed educators. And that’s where Alice Geoffray comes in.
“So, when the school was started by a priest, he wanted an expert teacher in that transition from school into offices. My mother had just won an award, a national classroom teacher’s award,” said Jeff Geoffray, co-founder of the 431 Exchange.
Jeff Geoffray is the son of Alice Jeoffray. He said his late mother wasn’t necessarily a civil rights activist. At that time, Alice Geoffray was a seasoned teacher.
“My mother was not involved in the civil rights movement. She was trying to survive. She was trying to be a teacher and feed her children,” said Geoffray.
Through her seven years at the Adult Education Center, Geoffray said his mom came to love her work and the women she trained, many of whom landed jobs after graduation.
Geoffray said his mother would have been proud of the accomplishments of her former students.
“Many of them were her dearest friends. She communicated, kept in touch with them, but the main thing is that she really did not have blind faith in them. She really felt that these were talented women. Those women were the first African American secretaries in the Deep South. They integrated offices like Shell, Standard Oil, Pan-American Life and even city hall,” said Jeff Geoffray.
Raphael Morgan finished her training at the center in 1971. She went on to get a teaching degree from the University of New Orleans and became a teacher.
Her work career also included jobs at the Orleans Parish School Board and as an insurance adjuster.
“But no matter what, I think I’ll always be a teacher because you have the ability to change so many lives,” Morgan said.
Morgan is among the 431 women — mostly African American — who graduated from the Adult Education Center. The center closed in 1972.
Today, Jeff Geoffray and his sister, Jeanne, run the nonprofit group 431 Exchange. It is named in honor of the 431 graduates of the school and where it once stood in Exchange Place.
431 Exchange advocates for equal and affordable access to education. It also offers scholarships to adults who want to pursue higher learning. The story of the school, its members and the nonprofit’s work will be the focus of an upcoming PBS documentary.
“Jeanne and her brother have done tremendous work to keep their mother’s dream alive. And we can’t wait until this [documentary] comes to a conclusion and the world will get to see what we experienced,” said Morgan.
The documentary is expected to be available in 2027.
To learn more about the 431 Exchange, visit 431exchange.org.

title: Lewiston becomes latest Maine city to restrict syringe service programs
text:
Lewiston will become the state’s largest municipality to restrict syringe service programs, after a majority of voters on Tuesday opted to pass a referendum to bring back needle exchange limits.
The successful citizen initiative reinstitutes a one-for-one needle exchange, mandating that syringe service providers can’t distribute more than 20 sterile syringes per person each day. It also prohibits mobile exchange units and requires exchange programs to operate from one location.
More than 8,200 voters supported the restrictions and 5,700 opposed them, despite a coalition of public health experts, doctors and advocates campaigning against them. Research has shown that syringe service programs help in harm reduction and curb the spread of infectious diseases. The restrictions come as Penobscot County to the north has an active HIV outbreak — primarily among people who are unhoused or who use intravenous drugs — that reached 50 cases, as of Thursday.
Eryn Soule, a former city councilor who led the effort to limit syringe service programs, told Maine Morning Star, “it’s a win for Lewiston and all involved.”
“It’s a fair balance for public health,” added Soule, who on Tuesday lost an independent bid for Maine Senate. “All services (and) programs are still available just as before.”
Democratic Rep. Scott Harriman from Lewiston said he was concerned what the new restrictions would mean for syringe litter.
“Many people don’t understand how important syringe service programs (SSPs) are when it comes to public health: They provide sterile syringes in order to prevent the dangerous practice of reusing or sharing syringes, and they serve as an important avenue to get people with substance use disorder into treatment,” he said. “The SSP in Lewiston also collects and safely disposes of significantly more syringes than they give out, reducing the amount of syringe litter in our community.”
Harriman, who previously served as city councilor, said Lewiston’s city charter has no provision to modify legislation put in place by a citizen initiative except via another citizen initiative, which “leaves our community vulnerable and limits our ability to respond to negative public health results such as a disease outbreak,” he said.
“I’m hopeful that we can make some efforts at the state level to expand SSPs in the immediate area to continue to meet this important need.”
Earlier this year, the Maine Legislature rejected proposals to limit these programs statewide. Maine removed one-for-one limits on needle exchanges in 2022, adopting new rules that allowed participants to bring in one used syringe in exchange for 100 clean ones. The Maine Department of Health and Human Services has backed the expanded program, saying limits on clean needles are not “supported by evidenced based practice, would limit access, and increase infectious disease transmission risk including HIV and Hepatitis C,” according to legislative testimony by Maine CDC Director Dr. Puthiery Va.
But some local officials — citing concerns about discarded syringes littering streets, parks and sidewalks — have pushed for stricter limits on these programs.
Sanford passed similar limits, last December opting to temporarily halt needle distribution for a year. Portland city councilors rejected a proposal attempting to bring back a one-for-one limit in 2024, later introducing a needle buyback program to address syringe litter. Portland Public Health Director Bridget Rauscher said last year the initiative has helped reduce syringe litter by 76% and also resulted in a 58% increase in used syringe return.

title: Faced with a budget gap, UMaine offers one year of pay as incentive for certain faculty to retire
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Faced with a budget gap, UMaine offers one year of pay as incentive for certain faculty to retire
The University of Maine is facing a projected $19 million structural budget gap for FY28. As a way to help close that gap, certain faculty members are being offered an incentive to voluntarily retire.
On November 3, UMaine notified 158 faculty members at the campuses in Orono and Machias of their eligibility for the voluntary Special Retirement Incentive (SRI). To be eligible, faculty must have been at least 55 years old as of Nov. 1 with at least 10 years of full-time equivalent service. Faculty who choose to take the SRI will receive a one-time payment equal to 100% of their base annual salary upon retiring on Sept. 1, 2027.
Eligible faculty at UMaine and UMaine Machias have until Jan. 2, 2027, to decide whether to participate.
University officials say that flagship universities across the nation are dealing with significant budget and position cuts due to declining enrollment and state funding, a changing federal funding and policy landscape, and rising compensation and operating costs, though in comparison, UMaine officials say schools here have largely limited impacts on people and programs.
The retirement incentive is funded through a financial commitment to fund up to $6 million of the one-time payout costs. A portion of that funding will also pay for a separate SRI underway at the University of Maine at Farmington.
UMaine says it is currently projecting $303 million in expenses in the fiscal year that begins July 1, 2027, and $284 million in revenue. Officials say those numbers are based on current modeling that will continue to change based on factors that include, but are not limited to, the outcome of UMS contract negotiations, state appropriation determined by the next Governor and Legislature, actual student enrollment and energy costs.
“I applaud UMaine leaders for confronting these serious budget challenges in a manner that minimizes impacts to their valued employees and maintains Mainers’ access to affordable, high-quality education and upward mobility,” said Chancellor Dannel Malloy. “The System is fully supportive of their efforts to ensure this world-class public research university has the strong financial foundation necessary for the success of our students and the state now and for future generations.”
UMaine’s FY28 budget proposal is due to system leadership in late January 2027.

title: Former staffer of Sen. Collins reacts to election night upset
text:
Former staffer of Sen. Collins reacts to election night upset
Jill Carney's said her first job in Washington was with Sen. Susan Collins, serving as a staffer from 2013 to 2016.
"One of the things that you quickly learn is just how dedicated she is to public service and how the views of Mainers and serving Maine was just at the utmost importance to her and her staff," Carney said.
Reflecting after Collins lost her seat to Democrat Troy Jackson Tuesday night, Carney said the outcome was upsetting but that the senator's record will be unmatched.
Collins conceded Tuesday night after Jackson flipped the red Senate seat to blue for the first time in 30 years.
“It has been the honor of my life to serve the people of Maine in the United States Senate. I'm proud of all I have been able to accomplish for our state and for our country in the past 30 years,” Collins said.
In the new year, Jackson will be the one heading to Washington after campaigning against Collins for about three months.
Collins secured her first term in 1996 and is one of 65 women to serve in the United States Senate to date.
“I think her male colleagues could afford to phone it in sometimes, and she really could not,” Carney said.
With the loss of Collins in the Senate, Maine will no longer have a legislator who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee, which is a high-power role.
"From every corner of the state, she's done a tremendous amount of good and she served thousands and thousands of constituents," Carney said. "That record is remarkable, truly."
The longtime senator ends her fifth term in the Senate in early January. She said she would ensure a smooth transition for Jackson’s team.

title: How to lower prescription costs and still get the medication you need
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — If prescription costs have you doing the math every month, there are options to explore to bring the price down and still get the medication you need.
Start with the health care question
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said prescription affordability is a health care issue.
“A medication sitting on a pharmacy shelf isn’t doing anybody any good, and it’s not going to help anybody feel better,” Cradduck said. “So we have to figure out the best way to get them into your hands.”
Ask your doctor and pharmacist
One place to start is with the doctor or pharmacist.
Doctors may have access to free prescription drug programs, including samples left by drug company representatives. Cradduck said patients who are struggling can ask their doctor whether any free medications or samples are available.
Pharmacists know about programs and may recommend cards that can reduce the cost of medications, Cradduck said.
Review coverage and look for assistance
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke recommended that Medicare Part D coverage be reviewed every year and said it should not be left to renew on its own.
A client was paying $100 a month for her Medicare Part D premium. After a review, the premium was lowered to $30 a month, O’Rourke said.
She also pointed to the Extra Help program that helps with the cost of prescription drugs. If you qualify based on income, you can get medications for free or very little, she said.
If insurance denies a medication, O’Rourke said, appeal the decision rather than assuming it can’t be covered. Getting a doctor’s help in presenting the appeal can lead to coverage, she said.
Compare pharmacies and ask about generics
Many people don’t realize how much prices can differ from one pharmacy to another, O’Rourke said.
“Go to the different pharmacies and see what they’re charging,” O’Rourke said. “You would be amazed at the difference in different places to buy medicine.”
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said patients can also ask about generics drugs.
“Some of these drugs cost a lot of money, and you can ask them, ‘Is there an equivalent, something else equivalent that I can treat the same condition with?’” Rogers said. “We see that all the time, especially with the blood thinners.”
Cradduck said patients should find one pharmacy that will fill all of their medications for the lowest price, rather than using several pharmacies. Using multiple pharmacies means no one is tracking what is interacting, Cradduck said, and keeping track of that is part of a pharmacist’s job.
If a pharmacist suggests a change, aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said, patients should go back to their doctor to make sure the doctor agrees.
Don’t split pills or skip doses
The Aging Untold experts said patients should not split pills, take half doses or skip doses to stretch a refill before deciding they can’t afford a medication.
Instead, the experts said, ask questions, because resources exist to get medication at a lower cost.
Resource
Key takeaways
- Ask about free samples. Talk to your doctor about free medications or samples, and talk to your pharmacist about programs and cards that can lower costs.
- Review Medicare Part D every year. Amy O’Rourtke said a client lowered the premium from $100 to $30 a month after a review.
- Check the Extra Help program. Check to see if you qualify based on income. Participants can get medications for free or very little, O’Rourke said.
- Compare prices, ask about generics, and stay with one pharmacy. Prices vary by pharmacy, and using one pharmacy lets the pharmacist track interactions.
- Appeal denials and don’t ration doses. Get your doctor’s help with an appeal, and avoid splitting pills or skipping doses.
