title: Post-midterms, Trump focuses on DC beautification projects
text:
Post-midterms, President Trump focuses on DC beautification projects
On Thursday, President Donald Trump signed a proclamation naming the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as national monuments while a federal judge temporarily stopped construction of his triumphal arch.
Post-midterms, President Trump focuses on DC beautification projects
On Thursday, President Donald Trump signed a proclamation naming the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as national monuments while a federal judge temporarily stopped construction of his triumphal arch.
Fresh off a historic midterm sweep by Democrats, President Donald Trump is turning his attention away from Congress and instead toward his own Washington pet projects.
On Thursday, he signed a proclamation declaring the Oval Office and Cabinet Room national monuments in a bid to prevent future changes to them.
The proclamation orders the Interior Secretary to manage the Oval Office and requires documentation and review before any substantial changes are made. However, the action does not prevent future presidents from restyling the office or reversing the proclamation itself.
Trump claimed that any major changes would require congressional review, though the requirement is not included in the text of the proclamation.
This is the third time this week Trump has highlighted his personal projects in the nation's capital. Most recently, he signed the final beam being raised for his White House ballroom project and earlier spoke about plans to restore the Reflecting Pool.
Another of Trump's projects faced a legal setback overnight Thursday. A federal judge temporarily blocked construction of the 250-foot triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery, just hours after a committee gave final approval for the project despite significant public backlash.
Historically, Congress has designated funding for White House repairs and decoration, including the Oval Office.
For the ballroom, Trump has insisted it would be entirely funded by private donations. However, Democrats on the Senate Budget Committee claim taxpayer dollars from the One Big Beautiful Bill were directed to the project through the White House Secret Service.
Separately, a White House official also said the Triumphal Arch is expected to be paid for through a mix of public and private money.
Based on the last update made to the Reflecting Pool this past summer, renovations are also expected to be funded with taxpayer dollars.

title: Early morning fire destroys Bangor outbuilding
text:
An early Friday morning fire destroyed an outbuilding in Bangor.
The fire broke out in an outbuilding adjacent to a Center Street home about 2:28 a.m., according to the Bangor Fire Department.
Firefighters got there within five minutes, and when they arrived, the outbuilding was fully engulfed in flames.
Crews kept the blaze from spreading to a nearby garage and house, though they sustained minor damage.
The fire was brought under control within 10 minutes. The outbuilding was a total loss.
The fire isn’t considered suspicious. The investigation is ongoing.

title: Homeless Services of Aroostook to shift shelter beds toward individuals
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Homeless Services of Aroostook will change how it divides its shelter beds between families and individuals starting Jan. 1, because fewer families are asking for help.
The organization said fewer families have come to the shelter over the last year and more individuals need a bed.
Fewer families, more individuals
Executive Director Kari Bradstreet said the shelter plans to open more individual beds and decrease family beds.
“The need for family space has decreased. We’re not seeing a lot of families coming in,” Bradstreet said.
Bradstreet said the shelter has seen the decline over the last year and that she thinks it “ebbs and flows.” She said she is concerned about what winter will bring and that making the change now is concerning.
“We need to make sure that we’re meeting the community needs and right now that’s more individuals than it is families,” Bradstreet said.
Changes to bed structure
The shelter has 36 family beds and 21 low barrier beds, Bradstreet said. That structure will change Jan. 1.
The shelter also will ask people to move rooms when it needs space for a family.
“Being an emergency shelter, we always tell people you may have to move,” Bradstreet said.
Bradstreet said that if a family of four arrives and a room has four beds, the shelter will ask the individuals in that room to relocate to another room. That would allow the shelter to accommodate the family and keep beds available.
Bradstreet said the changes begin Jan. 1 and should help address the growing need for individual beds at the shelter.

title: US Justice Department drops bid to force California to set aside disputed ballots
text:
Los Angeles (AP) — The U.S. Department of Justice on Friday moved to dismiss its own lawsuit that sought to stop California from counting roughly 20,000 ballots it alleged went to noncitizens until their immigration status could be verified.
The request to dismiss the case comes days after Republicans’ significant losses in the midterm elections and about a week before a scheduled hearing where a special master was slated to evaluate the accuracy of the list. California officials have previously said the list is out of date and includes legitimate voters — a sentiment that the federal judge presiding over the case echoed in his blistering order denying the federal government’s request.
The case was at the forefront of President Donald Trump’s administration’s effort to assert control over state-run elections across the country, which Trump has said are rife with illegal voting without providing evidence.
The Department of Justice remains enmeshed in litigation with immigrant and voting rights groups seeking to limit its use of the list of what is says are suspected noncitizens. Another controversial suit it filed in Alaska at Trump’s direction before the election to block the victory of the Democrat in that state’s Senate race was swiftly dismissed by a federal judge. The administration is appealing that ruling but has yet to file a full brief at the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals.
California had processed roughly 9 million ballots as of early Friday, with nearly 5 million still left to be counted, according to state election officials. The motion to dismiss the lawsuit said that, by the time of the upcoming hearing, the state will have already irreparably “commingled the challenged ballots with lawful ones.”
“The relief the United States sought and needed is no longer available—rendering voluntary dismissal necessary,” the motion said.
Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, previously argued in court that the lawsuit would be irrelevant after election day, because there would be no way to sequester the ones allegedly belonging to noncitizens. The lawsuit was filed in mid-October, when ballots had been sent to all of the state’s 23 million registered voters, and after hundreds of thousands of ballots were already processed. Once a ballot is processed, it is completely anonymized.
Essayli said at the time the lawsuit was filed that his goal was to “safeguard the integrity of the election so it doesn’t have an effect on the upcoming election.”
“We want to stop the illegal voting. We don’t want to chase it later,” he said outside of court the week before the election.
The United States Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California referred all questions to the Department of Justice in Washington, D.C., which did not respond to an emailed request for comment on Friday evening.
California prosecutors in recent weeks have arrested over 30 noncitizens who are accused of illegally registering to vote. Some who were arrested were also accused of voting in previous elections. Elections clerks around California in the week before the election were sent subpoenas to testify before grand juries slated to convene in November. It’s not clear who is being criminally charged in those cases, but the department does not typically subpoena people whom it regards as targets of a criminal investigation to appear before a grand jury.
U.S. District Judge David O. Carter appointed the special master in late October, shortly after allowing California to proceed with elections as planned. Carter, who was appointed by former President Bill Clinton, argued in his blistering order that separating ballots at that late stage would risk disenfranchising citizens and warned it would “wreak havoc” on the midterm elections.
The special master would have also considered whether or not California election officials did in fact have a mechanism for separating the ballots.

title: 18-year-old accused of posting Instagram photos threatening to kill Trump, shoot up school
text:
18-year-old accused of posting Instagram photos threatening to kill Trump, shoot up school
A young Massachusetts man is facing federal charges after allegedly posing with guns and threatening to kill President Donald Trump on Instagram.
Trenton Touch, 18, of Tewksbury, was charged with making a threat against the president of the United States. Federal investigators allege that Touch is a white supremacist and also threatened to carry out a school shooting.
He will appear in federal court in Boston on Nov. 9.
According to charging documents, law enforcement officials were alerted to four Instagram accounts that contained violent content, including a threat against Trump, on Sept. 10, 2026.
Investigators allege that Touch owned all four of the accounts.
Touch allegedly posted a photo of a firearm in an Instagram direct message on June 21, 2026, that read:
- "it's time"
- "im gonna kill trump"
- "not yet unc I suck at shooting past 200 yards."
According to the Department of Justice, Touch made multiple references to mass shooters in his postings, specifically those who conducted their attacks based on racially motivated violent extremism.
He also allegedly referred to mass shooters as "heroes" and made references to the Christchurch shootings in New Zealand that killed 51 people.
Authorities found a revolver-style firearm and multiple military-style or military surplus items like camouflage clothing, a ballistic helmet, and military-style knives and a hatchet during a search of Touch's residence, according to the DOJ.
The charge of making a threat against the president carries a sentence of up to five years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000.
State charges
In addition to the federal charges, Touch is also facing state charges following his arrest by the Tewksbury Police Department.
Touch will be charged with possession of a firearm without an FID Card, possession of ammunition without an FID card, and improper storage of a firearm.
He was arraigned in Lowell District Court on these charges on Oct. 26 and was held on $50,000 cash bail. He was also ordered not to possess any firearms.
The arrest startled residents nearby.
Richard Frank, who lived a few houses down, said the flash bangs at 6 a.m. shook the neighborhood.
"When I looked out there had to be at least 12 vehicles," he said. "Next thing you know they're putting [Touch] in the car, there's all kinds of vulgarity going on. About a half hour later, it was all over, everyone was gone."
'Posed a grave threat'
Both federal and state authorities say Touch posed a significant threat to the public.
“Trenton Touch is an individual whose alleged threats could not be ignored,” said United States Attorney Leah B. Foley.
“Trenton Touch is an alleged white supremacist who now stands accused of threatening to kill the President... he allegedly had the means to do it. There’s no question Mr. Touch posed a grave threat to public safety,” said Ted E. Docks, special agent in charge of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Boston Division.
Tewksbury Police Chief Ryan Columbus thanked the FBI for its work and assistance in this case.
"They took these leads seriously, and their work may have prevented a mass casualty incident and saved lives," he said. "It’s unsettling to know that something like this could have happened in our town."

title: 2 Justice Department officials resign in wake of the midterm elections
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The top federal prosecutor in Miami who had been tasked with overseeing an investigation into foes of President Donald Trump has resigned, joining other high-profile Justice Department officials departing in the wake of the midterm elections, officials said Friday.
Jason Reding Quiñones’ resignation follows frustrations among Washington officials with his management of the office assigned to lead the so-called “grand conspiracy” investigation, according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel issues.
The Justice Department’s top national security official, John Eisenberg, also resigned on Friday, Attorney General Todd Blanche said. On Thursday, Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who led a radical overhaul of the department’s Civil Rights Division, also announced her departure.
Quiñones was confirmed by the Senate last year as U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, where the Justice Department had centered its meandering probe into whether former law enforcement and intelligence officials conspired against the Republican president.
His departure comes as the investigation has shown signs of faltering amid a spate of staff turnovers and delays. Investigators in recent weeks have put off scheduled grand jury testimony of several witnesses, according to multiple people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation.
Blanche said in a social media post that the department is grateful for Quiñones’ “leadership in combating violent crime, drug trafficking, sex trafficking, and transnational crime, including the indictment of Raúl Castro.”
Castro, the former Cuban president, was indicted by Quiñones’ office in May on charges related to the 1996 downing of civilian planes flown by Miami-based exiles.
Quiñones said Friday that he is leaving with “immense pride in what we accomplished together and profound gratitude for the opportunity to serve our great Nation.”
“I am grateful to President Trump for his trust and to the extraordinary men and women of the great Southern District of Florida for their dedication, friendship, and unwavering commitment to justice and the rule of law,” Quiñones wrote in a social media post.
The “grand conspiracy” investigation has proceeded in fits and starts for over a year with repeated setbacks and departures. Last April, a lead national security prosecutor in the investigation of former CIA Director John Brennan was replaced on the team after raising questions about the strength of the case.
Shortly afterward, Joseph diGenova, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, took over the probe. DiGenova resigned from the Justice Department in September without bringing any criminal charges.
Eisenberg was sworn in as assistant attorney general in charge of the department’s National Security Division in June 2025 and oversaw cases involving espionage, terrorism, export control violations, cyber crimes and other matters.
Among the division’s most high-profile cases under his watch was the prosecution of former national security adviser John Bolton, who pleaded guilty this year to allegations of mishandling classified information and is awaiting sentencing.
“He has served with distinction, strengthening our nation’s ability to address threats, both foreign and domestic,” Blanche said in a statement.

title: How to use music and art with a loved one living with dementia
text:
(Aging Untold) — Music, dance, poetry, storytelling and art can still tap into emotion and long-held experiences for someone with dementia.
While they do not cure dementia, they can support mood, dignity and connection.
Start by looking locally
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said families can begin by searching for available resources in their own area.
“Dance and dementia. Arts and dementia. Music and dementia,” O’Rourke suggested.
She shared an experience of seeing the impact during her first job out of college.
O’Rourke was an activity director, where residents took part in a bell choir at the time.
“Each resident had a bell and the director would point, and you could just see the impact it had on them,” O’Rourke said.
Don’t set expectations
O’Rourke also described a caregiver who took a client with a memory impairment to an art class, and the client started producing pictures and watercolors.
“She had never done art before. She had never drawn. She had never done any kind of artwork at all,” O’Rourke said. “And so I realized, don’t put any expectation on someone with a memory impairment. Anything is possible.”
“Look locally and just think about the connection that they’re going to have inside and with you,” O’Rourke said.
Tapping into long-term memory
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said the arts often use a different part of the brain.
“You’re tapping into something that maybe hasn’t been affected yet,” Cradduck said. “And it does hold some long-term memories. Think about smells, we oftentimes associate smells and memories, arts and memories. And the old gospels. That’s the one that I find taps in a lot when it comes to music.”
Cradduck described a video of Naomi Feil, who she said is the mother of the validation technique in dementia training. In the video, Feil is with a woman who had not spoken for a number of years.
“She just started tapping her arm and singing ‘Jesus Loves You,’” Cradduck said. “She just kept doing it, and she got faster and faster with the rhythm. All of a sudden, this woman who hadn’t spoken a word in years started singing this song.”
Cradduck said the arts tap into some core memories.
Telling the story a different way
While dementia changes memory, it does not change how a person tells their story, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
“They find a different way to tell the story,” Rogers said. “In terms of creativity and the arts, that is a different area of the brain and a lot of times it’s not impacted by dementia.”
A calming activity
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said the benefits extend beyond memory.
“It’s not just memory. It’s cognition,” she said. “You’re tapping into a creative outlet that might give people a way to express themselves, which is calming.”
Ambrose said the arts also help caregivers.
“It gives you a peaceful activity that everyone can be a part of,” Ambrose said. “Sometimes it can be agitating, but most of the time it’s worth trying because it can be something really powerful for therapy and a powerful form of care.”
Dementia can take away a person’s abilities, but it does not remove a person’s ability to feel, Cradduck added.
“You can feel beauty and you can feel rhythm,” she said.
Key takeaways
- Search locally. Look for local resources such as dance, arts and music programs for people with dementia.
- Set no expectations. A person with a memory impairment may take to art without having done it before.
- Expression can be calming. The arts can give people a way to express themselves and give caregivers a peaceful shared activity.

title: Farmers' Almanac Predicts Thanksgiving Weather For Maine
text:
Believe it or not, Thanksgiving is right around the corner. Thanksgiving remains one of the busiest travel holidays during the year meaning the weather forecast is ultra important.
While local weather professionals in Maine will wait much closer to the actual holiday to make their predictions, the Farmers' Almanac never hesitates to make their Thanksgiving weather outlook available early.
And for 2026, the Farmers' Almanac prediction brings good news.
Farmers' Almanac Predicts Good Weather Over Thanksgiving Weekend For Maine
Typically, Thanksgiving weekend forecasts are not sunshine and rainbows. But the Farmers' Almanac weather prediction for Thanksgiving this year really is sunshine.
The Farmers' Almanac predicts that weather from Maine through New York will be fair. The temperatures could be cool but those that travel both short and long distances should not expect much, if any, precipitation.
The only exception will be places in higher elevation, where snow flurries are part of the Thanksgiving forecast from the Farmers' Almanac.
Farmers' Almanac Has Already Predicted a 'Tricky' Winter For Maine
The Farmers' Almanac 2026-2027 winter forecast is rather bleak for the entire country. The effects of El Nino will be felt from coast to coast.
Throughout New England, the Farmers' Almanac calls for lots of precipitation. In Maine, inland areas and the mountains should see regular snowstorms which will be great for skiers.
It's the coast that is in for a 'tricky' winter. The Farmers' Almanac predicts that the heavy dose of storms from El Nino will bring mixed precipitation to Maine's coast. That will come in form of sleet and the dreaded freezing rain.
The Farmers' Almanac also predicts more dramatic cold snaps for Maine than the state has seen in recent years. Those cold snaps typically produce single-digit or below-zero temperatures.

title: Production of Tesla's Cybertruck will wind down soon with its allure escaping most potential buyers
text:
Tesla’s Cybertruck heads for an exit after years of hype and division
Tesla’s Cybertruck, the hulking, stainless-steel pickup that inspired devotion and derision with its science-fiction looks, will cease production next year.
CEO Elon Musk announced the model’s demise Friday with a curt post on X, his social media site, simply noting production of the vehicle “will be winding down” around the middle of 2027 at its facility outside Austin, Texas. Musk said the move was to allow increased production of its Cybercab robotaxi.
Related video above: Cybertruck fails a "wade mode" test and gets stuck in a lake, leading to an arrest
For the Cybertruck, a pet project of Musk who insisted it was Tesla’s best product, it marks an unceremonious end to one of the auto industry’s most ballyhooed debuts.
“Few vehicles in history have generated as much attention,” said Armen Hareyan, whose Torque News site covers autos. “The Cybertruck became a cultural symbol – loved, mocked and impossible to ignore.”
The Cybertruck rolled onto the scene in a dramatic unveiling in 2019, when a Tesla designer hurled a metal ball at the vehicle to demonstrate its supposedly unbreakable glass, only to see it shatter. He repeated the stunt on another window of the truck only to shatter that one, too.
Even as some critics scoffed, Musk was steadfast.
“I just wanted to make a futuristic battle tank — something that looks like it could come out of ‘Blade Runner’ or ‘Aliens’ or something like that but was also highly functional,” he told Automotive News. He called it “a better sports car than a Porsche 911” and “a better truck than an F-150.”
It struck some as the perfect vehicular reflection of the brash, convention-busting Musk.
“A really controversial vehicle unveiled by a controversial individual into a market where none of the electric trucks have been able to really capture demand,” said Spencer Penn, a former Tesla executive who left the company before the Cybertruck’s launch and now heads procurement software firm LightSource.
Penn remembered watching the unveiling and feeling initially revolted by the sight of the Cybertruck, calling its appearance “madness.” But the more he looked at it, the more his opinion changed. He signed up for a pre-sale reservation, though ended up not getting a Cybertruck when Musk’s promises of a price tag under $40,000 went unmet and the first trucks sold for double or more. Penn called the Cybertruck part of Tesla’s adventurous spirit that drives innovation.
“Some of these bets work and some of these bets don’t,” he said.
While the decision to end Cybertruck production may be driven by sales realities, it's also a reflection of Tesla’s shift to autonomous vehicles, on which Musk is betting the company’s future.
Musk once forecast he’d make 250,000 Cybertrucks a year. Kelley Blue Book estimated Tesla sold just 20,237 of the vehicles last year, down about half from the year prior. Sales through the end of September this year were down another 28%, according to Kelley Blue Book.
If the imposing, sharp-angled, dystopian appearance of the Cybertruck weren’t enough to turn many potential buyers away, Musk did so himself by allying with a panoply of right-wing figures, most notably U.S. President Donald Trump. He alienated some customers as his image morphed from eccentric innovator to polarizing force trading his billions for political influence.
Once-passionate Tesla drivers rushed to sell off their cars, or slapped stickers on the bumper declaring, “I bought this before Elon went crazy.” Organizers staged demonstrations outside Tesla showrooms and urged investors to dump shares of the company’s stock. Anger spilled into violence, with Molotov cocktails hurled at Tesla vehicles, charging stations set ablaze, and dealerships covered in graffiti.
Lovers of the Cybertruck became targets, too, subjected to shouts of “Nazi!” and extended middle fingers.
Ross Blankenship is one of them. When he first laid eyes on the Cybertruck, he felt transported to a world from his childhood, when he would play “Halo,” the sci-fi video game. He had to have it.
“I had that sort of child in me wanting to be part of something cool that would change the future of automotive,” Blankenship said in a call from his Cybertruck as he drove through Sunnyside, Colorado. Even as Blankenship found he agreed with Musk on politics, he hated seeing a vehicle he loved turned into a political symbol. “I never bought it for any other reason than the fascination with the future technology of trucks … so that was a little heartbreaking.”
He would buy another Cybertruck again in a heartbeat, calling its end “a sad moment.”

title: Patchy fog and scattered showers
text:
Patchy fog and scattered showers
Patchy fog and scattered showers
Fog develops Friday morning, and the next round of showers arrives. Expect a few sprinkles and light showers in the morning, with steadier rain in waves during the afternoon and evening.
The rounds of showers impact southern Maine and central Maine through the afternoon and evening, while northern Maine misses out on the moisture during the day. Showers become more widespread and push north late Friday evening and overnight.
One more unseasonably warm day before temperatures return to normal this weekend. Highs are in the mid- to upper-60s for most on Friday afternoon, but will be in the 40s and 50s going forward. A stationary front sets up near the coast, and several waves of low pressure move along the front, bringing rounds of showers and some much-needed rain.
Scattered showers continue on Saturday, though there may be a lull for western Maine in the morning. Showers are expected throughout the day on the Midcoast, an area that needs it most due to ongoing extreme drought.
Showers continue Saturday night with a few pockets of heavy rain in the mix. The gloom continues into Sunday morning before drier air arrives in the afternoon. Showers during the first half of the day give way to just an isolated shower in the afternoon.
Mountain showers likely change to wet snow Sunday as colder air arrives. Next week looks cool and mostly cloudy with occasional showers and flurries.

title: Trump announces new Chief of Staff-Stephen Miller
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump announced Friday he’s making a major personnel change - promoting Stephen Miller to White House Chief of Staff.
Trump announced the move Friday in a Truth Social post. Miller’s first day on the job will be Monday. He’s replacing outgoing Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, who will join Trump’s political operation. Wiles was the first female White House Chief of Staff in American history.
Miller, who served in both Trump administrations, has been the Deputy Chief of Staff since Trump began his second term Jan. 20, 2025. He’s been a long-time aide to the president, serving in a variety of roles in both the first and second term. His appointment sends a very strong message to the new 120th Congress, which will be controlled by Democrats. Miller is not the conciliatory type, which means there will be lots of battles between the White House and the new Congress over the next two years.
“President Trump is the most transformative political leader in American History — and he has single-handedly saved America from those who would destroy it. It has been the privilege of my lifetime to have served on his team from Day One, and I am honored beyond words to serve as his White House Chief of Staff.I want to thank the incomparable Susie Wiles for her years of devoted service to the President and the Country, and for her friendship. The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic,” Miller posted on X Friday.
The move comes days after Democrats scored major wins in the midterm elections, which included flipping control of both the House and Senate by wide margins. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) both criticized the move on X.
“Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands. His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today,” Jeffries wrote.
“Donald Trump learned nothing from his historic defeat. Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn’t have made a worse choice. Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way,” Schumer wrote.
As for Susie Wiles, she merely expressed her gratitude for the opportunity to serve, writing, “More than anything, I’m grateful for the extraordinary people I’ve had the privilege of working alongside. While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will.”

title: Patriots RB TreVeyon Henderson reveals hospitalization for neurological symptoms
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — New England Patriots running back TreVeyon Henderson on Friday revealed he has spent several days in the hospital undergoing tests to determine the cause of unexplained neurological symptoms that have affected his strength and coordination.
While the tests results have been what he called “reassuring” in coming back positive, the cause of the medical condition remains unknown, Henderson said in a lengthy post on his Instagram account.
“I will continue working closely with my specialists and physical therapists to focus on my recovery, as these symptoms have affected my strength, coordination and some of my physical functions,” Henderson wrote. “I am committed to doing everything necessary to return to full health. My health and long-term well-being remain my foremost priorities.”
The 24-year-old Henderson has not practiced since Oct. 29, when he was listed as having an illness, and was ruled out of playing in 24-19 win over Miami on Sunday. The second-year NFL player has been limited to 203 yards rushing and a touchdown, with 45 yards receiving, in six games this season.
That’s a considerable drop off for a player who combined for 1,131 yards from scrimmage (911 rushing) and 10 TDs in his rookie season last year.
With no timeline on Henderson’s recovery, coach Mike Vrabel said he’s focused on providing whatever emotional and informational support to the player and his wife Mackenzie.
“I know he is well-loved and respected on our football team. My support shows up in a lot of different ways,” Vrabel said Friday. “To support him the best way I know is to care for him, listen to him and do whatever we can to get him healthy and get him back and help this football team, and do what he does best.”
Aside from ruling him out from playing against Green Bay on Sunday, Vrabel added it would be premature and unfair to the player to discuss any plans of placing Henderson on a long-term injured list.
Led by Rhamondre Stevenson, the Patriots are carrying three running backs on their roster rounded out by Corey Kiner and Lan Larison.
Vrabel also ruled out receiver A.J. Brown, who has not practiced this week because of ankle and knee injuries. Tight end Hunter Henry (foot) and cornerback Marcus Jones (foot) will be listed as questionable to play, Vrabel said.
Henderson thanked his wife, medical team and the Patriots for their support.
He closed his message by writing: “We respectfully ask for continued prayers and privacy as we focus on my health and recovery. Love Trey.”

title: New fitness studio coming to prominent Yarmouth storefront
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The local fitness chain Reframe will open its fourth studio, setting up shop in the iconic downtown Yarmouth building that formerly housed Andy’s Handy Store.
“We are super excited about this location because it’s such a cool building and spot, and there’s just so much history there,” said Lily Jocham, the owner of Reframe.
Reframe currently has locations in Falmouth, Portland and South Portland. It offers low-impact, high-intensity workouts using reformer machines, as well as strength training on mats. With renovations already underway, Jocham said, the first classes in Yarmouth will likely be offered in mid-January.
Jocham said she was approached by the owner of the building about leasing it, as the owner wanted to bring in a local business that would consistently bring people back. The space was previously occupied by Salsa Mexican Grill, which closed after a year, and prior to that it was Dandy’s Handy Store and a takeout restaurant, both of which closed in 2024.
Jocham, who recently moved to Yarmouth with her family, said she is excited to offer more specialty classes in the Yarmouth location, including private training sessions and classes geared toward participants over 55.
“When you make the decision to come and be a part of a fitness studio and take group classes, it’s an intentional step towards building community,” said Jocham. “Being able to put that in a place like Main Street in Yarmouth, which is just so iconic and such a warm, welcoming community already, just felt really meant to be.”

title: Trump says Susie Wiles is out as Chief of Staff. Here’s who is replacing her
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, mere days after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections.
On his social media site, Trump praised Wiles and said she’d continue to work for his political organization.
“I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026. Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
Miller, long a key member of Trump’s inner circle, is a key architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies.
Wiles, the steely political operator and longtime adviser to Trump, was the first woman to ever serve in that post.
Wiles’ departure comes almost immediately after the GOP’s midterm thrashing on Tuesday. She will be replaced by Stephen Miller, a longtime trusted aide to Trump.
Wiles is the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.

title: Production of Tesla’s Cybertruck will wind down. Here’s why
text:
(AP) - Production of Tesla’s Cybertruck, a stainless-steel electric vehicle with a polarizing allure for potential buyers, will wind down next year.
In a post on social media, CEO Elon Musk said, “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”
The Texas facility is the only location where the Cybertruck is produced.
Teslas, and the Cybertruck in particular because of its unorthodox profile, became a political touchstone as Musk allied himself with President Donald Trump and some right-leaning causes amid a widening political divide in the U.S. and Europe.
European sales of Tesla vehicles tumbled 49% in the first two months of 2025 even as overall sales of EVs grew. Musk’s endorsement of Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany party in national elections drew broad condemnation.
The vehicle was also plagued by quality-control issues, with a handful of recalls within months of its debut.
Despite enormous anticipation, the Cybertruck never caught on with most buyers, and sales declined almost from the moment it hit the market.
While Tesla does not break out sales of its vehicles by model, Kelley Blue Book estimated that Cybertruck sales declined 48% from 2024 to 2025. From January through September of this year, sales were down 28%, according to Kelley Blue Book.

title: ‘This is it’: How Susan Collins’ 30-year run ended in an anti-Trump wave
text:
There was no sign of a problem in U.S. Sen. Susan Collins’ hotel suite.
When a Bangor Daily News photographer was invited in around 10:40 p.m. Tuesday, Collins and about 10 family members were watching CNN at Bangor’s Hilton Garden Inn, chatting quietly and checking their phones over Polar seltzers and whoopie pies.
The photographer told the five-term Republican she wanted to capture what politicians do on election night away from the crowds, and Collins chuckled.
“This is it,” she said.
She led the statewide count at the time, by more than 4 points with 30% of votes in. But her campaign had begun to worry about 90 minutes earlier, when results came in from Auburn. The city, the largest one fully counted at that point, went from backing Collins by 8 points in 2020 to backing Democrat Troy Jackson by nearly 5.
About an hour after the photographer left, as Portland’s votes erased her lead, Collins called Jackson to concede.
“Sen. Collins and I had a hard campaign,” the senator-elect told supporters in Portland. “But to every Mainer who voted for her, you can count on me to be your senator now.”
Collins never came back out to the ballroom, where “Closing Time” by Semisonic was playing by 1 a.m. She lost by about 6 points, becoming the first Maine senator ousted by voters since 1978 after a wave of resentment toward President Donald Trump handed Democrats the Senate.
For three decades, Collins defied the gravity that pulled down other Republicans in New England. She won in 2008 as Barack Obama carried Maine, and in 2020 she beat Sara Gideon by nearly 9 points after trailing in every public poll. She steered $1.5 billion in earmarks to Maine over the past five years as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, by her campaign’s count, and never missed a roll-call vote.
Collins told The New York Times on Wednesday that she was caught up in “the Trump tsunami,” and that voters ignored her breaks with the president, including her vote to convict him in his second impeachment trial.
“Anyone who sides with Trump, I’m not going to go with them,” said Kabala Muka, a 26-year-old nurse anesthetist and unenrolled voter who backed Jackson in Gray.
In the final stretch, her campaign’s tracking polls swung day to day within the margin of error, showing Collins up, down and tied, according to a person familiar with the polling. Her campaign said the picture at the end was that of a close race. Most of the late public surveys showed Jackson with a lead.
On Monday, two buses of staffers and supporters pulled up at a Van Buren bakery on the last day of her bus tour to cheer for Collins, who arrived later in a black car, greeted a handful of locals and left after about 15 minutes. As she and her team headed out, a reporter asked a spokesperson if she could ask Collins questions about what she made of surveys released Sunday showing her behind. One of those polls had Collins down 6 points.
“We’re not going to react to that lie, but you can email them,” the staffer said, and the senator went on to her next stop.
It was a stunning turnabout for Jackson, a former Allagash logger and Maine Senate president who finished third in the June primary for governor. Democrats drafted him in July after Graham Platner, their Senate nominee, quit the race following a sexual assault allegation he denied.
Jackson’s campaign repeated one line from start to finish: Collins votes with Trump 96% of the time. The outdated figure was drawn from 2025 votes on which the president took a position, but David Farmer, a senior adviser to Jackson, said the exact number mattered less than the choice it described in a polarized Senate running increasingly more on majority power.
“There’s no deals to be cut,” he said. “You’re either with Trump or you’re against him, and she was with him.”
While her national party scrambled to save her, Collins tried to reach both ends of the electorate. She attended a Gorham rally in September featuring a live interview with Boston radio host Howie Carr. Last month, she brought former Sen. Joe Manchin of West Virginia, a Democrat turned independent, to Maine to help her argue she was no rubber stamp for Trump.
Her campaign described it as an answer to Jackson’s appearances with national progressives, including Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders and New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. But the two also stopped by conservative radio host Ray Richardson’s studio, where they posed with the “Sword of Truth,” a prop associated with the conservative Maine Wire.
There were few swing voters left to win, with most final public polls finding 5% or fewer undecided. Richardson noted that because Republicans trail both unenrolled voters and Democrats in Maine enrollment, even a perfect base turnout wasn’t enough.
“It seemed noticeable to me that there was a moment where they realized the traditional base was not coalescing,” he said. “It was just no question in my mind that the coalition she was going to need to win is different than any coalition she’s ever had before.”
Both sides went hard at character. WinSenate, a Democratic super PAC, spent about $9 million on ads accusing Collins of getting rich in office, some citing a ProPublica report that FBI agents had sought to widen a bribery investigation that could have involved her. Collins called the allegations false, and FBI leadership reportedly didn’t credit the donor’s claims.
But Republicans outspent Democrats $112.2 million to $85.9 million in ads on the race after Jackson became the nominee, according to AdImpact. They spent a bit more calling Jackson corrupt and another $5.5 million on ads about his personal conduct and temper and temper, including an outside group’s radio ad mocking his family that Collins asked to be pulled.
One of Collins’ closing ads featured retired News Center Maine sportscaster Bill Green, whose spots for her were credited for helping her win in 2020. In it, he said this race wasn’t about “buying a cord of wood” and that Jackson “doesn’t have the tools he needs to be effective.”
Green wrote that line himself, he said. He was trying to say Jackson lacked relevant experience and was frustrated by the attacks on Collins’ character, imploring a reporter to include his statement that he doesn’t know a more honest and decent person than the senator.
Jackson turned Green’s line into a talking point and a punch line. He argued that with heating costs soaring, the election “is about a cord of wood.” Then he dressed as a cord of wood at a Halloween event in Portland. Green called that a smart move by Jackson’s campaign, but he made clear he didn’t care for it.
“How do I think he looked dressed up like a cord of wood? I thought Ed Muskie and George Mitchell didn’t do that. I’ll leave it at that,” Green said, referring to Maine’s legendary senators, adding that he didn’t remember former Sen. William S. Cohen “dressed as an outhouse or anything.”
In about 100 days, Jackson raised $31 million and held more than 100 public events. The campaign’s surveys told the story of the race, Farmer said. More than any other word, voters most associated Collins with Trump. Jackson was defined by “personal attacks,” a line he suspected didn’t work because it doesn’t make “anybody’s life better.”
Green likened his current situation with Jackson to shaking hands at midfield after a football loss. He doesn’t dislike the senator-elect, finds his personal story affecting and hopes he proves him wrong. He also understand why voters are upset with the president.
“I think it was all about Trump,” Green said. “All the way across the nation, I think it was all about Trump.”
BDN writers Benjamin Kail, Linda Coan O’Kresik, Callie Ferguson and Kathleen Phalen Tomaselli and freelancer Sam Shepherd contributed to this report.

title: Hegseth’s future in question days after midterms
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The future of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is in question days after the midterm elections. The Democrats have won back control of the House and the Senate, with some states still counting votes.
President Donald Trump has said repeatedly that Hegseth is doing a “very good job.” Congress is considering impeaching Hegseth.
Members of both parties have indicated support for impeaching the defense secretary. Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) has a privileged resolution to impeach Hegseth.
Under House rules, the resolution must be considered during the next voting session, which is next week.
Massie wrote on X: “There is one contingency in which I won’t reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns.”
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) posted on X Friday: “This is about you: the incompetence you’ve displayed, the bad advice you’ve given to the president, and your shameful and embarrassing episodes from firing our top generals to texting war plans to reporters.”
Hegseth said he is prepared for a fight. He released a video Thursday.
“Their obsession with political theater disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents,” Hegseth said. “It’s all about the politics of personal destruction. It didn’t work with President Trump and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”
If Hegseth leaves his post, the path to confirm him could get a lot trickier in the new year. Trump could potentially get a replacement confirmed by the lame-duck Congress. In January, getting a Democratic-controlled Congress to confirm a new defense secretary would be difficult.

title: Troy Jackson taps longtime aides BJ McCollister, Christine Kirby as transition leads
text:
Senator-elect Troy Jackson is leaning on two longtime aides and advisers to help him get set up in office after Tuesday’s election. On Friday, he announced BJ McCollister will chair his transition, and Christine Kirby will be the deputy chair.
McCollister was chief of staff for Jackson when he was president of Maine’s Senate. Now, McCollister is president of Frame Strategies, which led the advertising strategy and production for Jackson’s campaign and managed his caucus nominating campaign in the summer.
Frame Strategies also lobbies at the state Capitol, records show. It has lobbied for environmental and healthcare organizations, among others, and state lobbying disclosures show Jackson’s son Chace Jackson has been employed by McCollister’s firms.
Kirby worked as Troy Jackson’s communications director during his tenure as Senate president and Senate minority leader and worked for the Maine Children’s Alliance.
Jackson has just under two months until he’s sworn in on Jan. 3. McCollister and Kirby will help him hire staff, receive information about constituent needs from Sen. Susan Collins’ office, and decide his priorities for committee assignments, among other things.
Collins said in a statement early Wednesday morning that she and her staff would “work to ensure a smooth transition.”
Jackson will need to hire staff in Maine and in Washington, D.C., and essentially set up a new small business in a short amount of time, said Kay Rand, who undertook similar work for Sen. Angus King when he was first elected to the Senate in 2012.
In addition to McCollister and Kirby, Jackson will get help early on from two official transition aides. They were identified Friday as Hilary Barrett, Jackson’s Senate campaign manager, and Dan Gottlieb, who served as communications director and deputy campaign manager. Both have spent their careers working for Democratic candidates and causes around the country.
Before he’s seated in January, Jackson will have a role in selecting Democratic leaders in the Senate, said Brookings Institution Senior Fellow Sarah Binder. That selection is expected to happen in December.
Jackson is among seven senators-elect who’ve called for new leadership or said explicitly that they won’t support current Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, but no one else has publicly come forward to challenge him, and Schumer would only need the votes of a majority of the Democrats in the Senate to become majority leader.
As part of Friday’s announcement, Jackson’s staff said that Mainers interested in contacting the transition team can email [email protected], and those interested in working in the senator’s office should submit resumes to [email protected].

title: Man convicted of 2004 killing is put to death in Florida’s 19th execution this year
text:
(AP) - Florida carried out a record-tying 19th execution of the year in an unusual instance of three states administering the death penalty on the same day.
Jesse Guardado was pronounced dead at 6:13 p.m. following a three-drug injection at a state prison in Starke. He had pleaded guilty to fatally stabbing 75-year-old Jackie Malone inside her Walton County home in 2004 before stealing her jewelry box, $80 and other valuables to buy drugs. The woman had helped him get a job and housing.
Hours earlier, Indiana executed a man for killing two children in a house fire in 2010, and in Alabama, a man was scheduled to die by injection later Thursday evening for his conviction in a fatal home robbery.
The executions were taking place the same day California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced he will commute all 548 death sentences in his state, saying that he believes “state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values.”
The announcement was a sharp contrast to Florida, where outgoing Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors. His state has carried out more than half of the 34 executions so far this year in the U.S., where capital punishment has come under renewed scrutiny following Tennessee’s failed execution of Christa Pike in September.
It is the second time since August that three states had organized executions on a single day, although it remains unusual. Prior to this year, the last time it happened was 2010.
Florida inmate apologized before receiving lethal injection
Guardado, 64, was already strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm when the curtain to the Florida death chamber went up promptly at 6:00 p.m. Asked if he had any last statement, he replied, “I would like to once again apologize for the pain and suffering I’ve caused to the victim’s family and my own family as well.”
The drugs began flowing immediately after that. About a minute later, Guardado began breathing heavily, followed by some sputtering and twitching for another minute. As the twitching subsided, the execution team warden shook Guardado and shouted his name, but got no response. A medic checked for a pulse soon after and pronounced Guardado dead.
A federal appeals court said in 2024 that Guardado received a “full and fair” hearing during the death penalty phase of his case. The U.S. Supreme Court denied his last appeal without comment earlier Thursday.
DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said he wants to bring justice to victims’ families who have often waited decades for death sentences to be carried out. He signed the death warrants that led to a state record of 19 executions in 2025. The state will set a new record if two more executions are carried out as planned later this year.
The victim’s son, Patrick Malone, spoke briefly to media witnesses after the execution. Instead of discussing his mother or her murder, he questioned those who oppose the death penalty.
“Do such people ever think about what happened to the victim or consider the unending aftermath the victim’s family endures and relives every time that terrible event comes up?” Malone said.
Alabama man drew the death penalty for a double killing
In neighboring Alabama, Michael Taylor, 54, was set to receive a lethal injection later Thursday. The state changed the execution method after a judge declared a nitrogen gas method unconstitutional.
Taylor’s attorneys objected to the last-minute switch to lethal injection since he selected nitrogen gas as his method years ago, but a judge ruled against Taylor.
In 1991, Taylor, then 19, fatally beat two people, ages 83 and 79, with a metal bar during a robbery in their Gadsden, Alabama, home. Police arrested him with the victims’ Cadillac an hour away in Birmingham.
Death penalty opponents had urged Republican Gov. Kay Ivey to reduce Taylor’s sentence to life in prison, noting his age and immaturity at the time. She declined.
Lawyers had asked for a life sentence for Indiana man
In Indiana, Jeffrey Weisheit, 50, was pronounced dead at 12:45 a.m. at the state prison in Michigan City, said Noelle Russell, spokesperson at the Department of Correction. He had no final words.
Weisheit had publicly acknowledged killing his girlfriend’s two children in a house fire in the Evansville area in 2010 but had hoped Gov. Mike Braun would grant clemency and change his sentence to life in prison. Braun declined.
Lawyers failed to persuade Braun, a Republican, to allow Weisheit to undergo brain scans in an effort to reinforce their argument that he has a history of head injuries and mental health problems that should prevent execution.
Weisheit’s last objection centered on the state’s planned use of lethal drugs purchased from a pharmacy that is facing a disciplinary hearing next week at the Indiana Pharmacy Board. The Indiana Supreme Court declined to intervene Wednesday night, though two of the five justices wanted a 10-day stay for more information about the drugs’ expiration and storage.
The execution provided “long-awaited justice for Alyssa Lynch and her brother Caleb, two innocent children whose lives were stolen in an act of unspeakable cruelty,” Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita said.
Americans have long been uneasy over the death penalty
Americans have long been divided over the death penalty, with nearly half of states banning capital punishment outright and just a handful of others carrying out most of the nation’s executions each year.
____
This story has been updated to correct that Christa Pike’s failed execution was in September, not October.
____
Fischer reported from Starke, Florida, and Chandler from Montgomery, Alabama. Associated Press reporter Ed White contributed from Detroit.

title: Meghan Markle’s father arrested on charges related to child sexual abuse material, AP sources say
text:
(AP) - Thomas Markle, the father of Prince Harry’s wife Meghan, was arrested Friday morning by federal agents in Florida on charges related to child sexual abuse material, people familiar with the matter told The Associated Press.
The people who confirmed his arrest were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation and spoke on the condition of anonymity. Thomas Markle was taken into custody near Tampa.
Meghan Markle recently said she was “deeply distressed” by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her father’s former home. She also revealed that a letter containing “troubling allegations” about him had been sent to London police in 2018.
Meghan, an American citizen who starred in the U.S. television drama “Suits,” married Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018. They have two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet.
Her father, a retired television lighting and photography director, did not attend the wedding, prompting extensive coverage in the British media of Meghan’s estrangement from her father. Meghan said she decided to distance herself from him to protect her children.

title: Foxcroft Academy seeking 2nd-straight state field hockey title on Saturday
text:
The Foxcroft Academy Ponies from Dover-Foxcroft will seek a second consecutive state Class C championship on Saturday as they square off against the Winthrop High School Ramblers at 3:05 p.m. at Edward Little High School in Auburn.
That will be the final state championship game of the day in Auburn.
Cheverus High of Portland will be looking to win its fourth state A title in a row when it kicks off the agenda with an 11:05 a.m. contest against Mt. Ararat of Topsham in a battle of 17-0 teams.
Nokomis of Newport, 16-1, will face 14-3 Freeport in the B final at 1:05 p.m.
Foxcroft Academy is 17-0 and earned its trip to the state final with a hard-fought 1-0 win over arch-rival and neighbor Dexter in the C North title game.
Lilah French’s goal with 10:35 remaining decided it.
The Ponies had previously beaten Orono, 9-0, in the quarterfinals and Stearns/Schenck, 6-0, in the semifinals.
Foxcroft Academy features Penobscot Valley Conference Class C Player of the Year Addie Rayfield along with fellow All-PVC first team selections Ava Dunton, Jenna Hartford and Lili Bisson.
Winthrop is 16-1 and punched its ticket to the Class C South with playoff wins over Oak Hill of Sabattus (3-0), Boothbay Region (4-1) and Spruce Mountain of Jay (3-1).
Winthrop captured four consecutive state titles from 2021-2014.
In Class B, Nokomis of Newport scored 15 goals in its three playoff wins capped by a 4-2 win in the North title game over Leavitt of Turner. Nokomis spotted Leavitt a 1-0 lead but received goals from MaKenzie Watson, Ava Roundy, Annie Nyce and Maeve Rush to win it.
Nokomis avenged its only regular season loss, 2-0, to Leavitt.
Nokomis had previously eliminated Erskine Academy from South China 6-0 and Old Town 5-1 and will be looking for its first state title since 2013..
Freeport, which lost to Belfast 1-0 in the state final last year, advanced to the state game with three one-goal victories: 1-0 over the Gray-New Gloucester/North Yarmouth Academy co-op team, 3-2 over Greely of Cumberland Center and 2-1 over Yarmouth.
The Falcons had split regular season games with Yarmouth.
Freeport won its last state title in 2023.
Mt. Ararat posted playoff victories over Brewer (8-0), Messaslonskee of Oakland (2-0) and Skowhegan (3-2) while Cheverus ousted Noble of North Berwick (6-0), Sanford/Kennebunk (3-2) and Thornton Academy of Saco (2-1).
Mt. Ararat rallied from a 2-0 deficit to beat Skowhegan for its first ever regional championship.

title: North Haven welcomes Hannah Pingree home after election win
text:
Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree was greeted by several dozen well-wishers when she returned home to North Haven on an evening ferry Wednesday, the day after winning the election to become Maine’s next governor.
As Pingree walked off the ferry in the dark, she was met by a cheering crowd holding signs and waving flags. She stopped to hug many of them, captured by drone footage posted on the North Haven Facebook group by North Haven High School and Mid-Coast School of Technology student King Arthur.
Other photos posted on the page show well-wishers holding handmade signs with messages like “Welcome home governor” and “Hannah is the best.”
Pingree and her mother, U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, both won overwhelming majorities on the offshore island in Penobscot Bay.
Hannah Pingree won 222 of the 284 votes cast for governor on North Haven, a whopping 78% of the vote. Republican Bobby Charles won 16% and independent Rick Bennett won 5%.
Both Pingrees received more votes on North Haven than District Attorney Natasha Irving, who ran unopposed and received 203 votes.

title: The hidden risks of denial in caregiving: When a loved one’s decline is hard to accept
text:
(Aging Untold) — When a loved one starts to need extra support, admitting how much has changed is one of the hardest hurdles families face.
Denial can step in naturally to protect us from overwhelming grief, but avoiding reality for too long can risk caregiver burnout and compromise care.
Recognizing where you and your loved ones stand emotionally is the first step toward navigating the aging journey with clarity and compassion.
The hidden purpose of denial
“I think denial gets a bad rap,” Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “Denial is a really healthy stage of grief. It’s a shock absorber. It allows the body to kind of catch up and process what’s going on. You can’t let this situation take you all over. And I don’t think people realize that you go in and out of it.”
O’Rourke recalled visiting a client whose husband was actively dying. When she arrived, the wife put the conversation on hold.
“She just stopped me and said, ‘You know, we’re having dinner right now, and we’re enjoying each other,’” O’Rourke noted. “I thought, good for you, and I left, and I was so happy for her that she was aware that she was going to keep it away and enjoy him.”
The caregiver blind spot: ‘I’m not a caregiver’
Denial also shows up when family members take on heavy workloads without acknowledging their actual role as a caregiver.
The National Alliance for Caregiving estimates that 63 million Americans, nearly one in four adults, serve as a family caregiver, but Cradduck said that number is likely higher based on her experience with people who don’t recognize themselves as caregivers.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said many people who are cooking the meals, getting the groceries, keeping the house and paying the bills will tell her that they are not a caregiver. They are doing these tasks for someone who is independent and living alone.
“I’m like OK, when do you become the caregiver? Well, when I give them a shower — when I help with the personal care,’” Cradduck said.
“The denying that someone needs help, or saying ‘I’m fine,’ can be detrimental. Not just the caregiver doing it, but the person themselves,” Cradduck said.
Another facet of denial is when the caregiver who is at a breaking point says they are fine, Cradduck said.
Meeting loved ones where they are
Another facet of denial, aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said, is not facing a loved one’s decline.
If you can’t wrap your head around that, you could actually do harm and have a lot of regrets, she said.
Examples she gave include:
“She’s just being stubborn,” Or, “He’s just giving me a hard time.”
“Because you could be in denial about what is really going on,” Ambrose said.
Seeing a loved one decline is a harsh reality, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
“You really have to meet people where they are. But it’s really, really hard because when you start to accept that, you also start to understand that they can actually change and decline very quickly,” Rogers said.
Ambrose emphasized reorienting your daily mindset: “You want to think about: Who does my loved one need me to be right now, in this moment, and serve them best?”
When older parents are the ones in denial and resist assistance, O’Rourke advises patience over confrontation: “Don’t try to push your way through the denial in that moment.”
She recommends asking gentle, open-ended questions such as, “What do you see?” or “Are you having a hard time?”
Preventing caregiver burnout and collision
True support cannot happen without an honest assessment of both your loved one’s decline and your personal limits.
“We have to reach a point of acceptance even in our grief,” Cradduck said. “I can’t meet you where you’re at if I don’t know where that’s at. I have to be honest enough to say, ‘You know what? You are declining. This is too hard.’”
Unacknowledged stress can lead to exhaustion and relationship friction.
“It’s not just denying that the person themselves is declining and you’re losing someone that you love; it’s how hard and how insurmountable being that caregiver is,” Cradduck said. “When you’re not admitting it, you’re not taking care of yourself. We’re seeing that caregiver burnout and we’re seeing those struggles so frequently because it’s so hard and you’re just saying, ‘Oh, I’m good, I don’t need help.’”
O’Rourke said she also sees people collide at different stages of grief — one person is in denial and the other is in anger.
“They can collide if you’re not really aware of where are you in the stages of grief because everybody is grieving, whether it’s the caregiver or the person,” O’Rourke said.
Key Takeaways
- Denial acts as an emotional shock absorber: Denial is often a stage of grief that shields families from acute crisis and creates space to process painful news at a manageable pace.
- Find value in being present in the moment: Compartmentalizing the illness sometimes helps families block out the crisis and just enjoy the moment.
- Focus on today’s needs: Stop living in yesterday’s memories. Focus instead on the needs of the person in front of you today.

AI voice cloning: An $11 tool recreates your voice so well, even family members may be tricked
text:
AI voice cloning: An $11 tool recreates your voice so well that even family members may be tricked
What if someone called your family pretending to be you, using not only your name but also your actual voice?
It may be easier than you think.
An investigation from sister station KMBC 9 put artificial intelligence to the test to see how easily someone could copy a person's voice and fool someone who knows them.
The results were unsettling.
Using videos that were already posted publicly on YouTube and Facebook, Tenfold Security's cybersecurity expert Aaron Weissenfluh collected 32 minutes of audio of KMBC 9 reporter Byra Berry speaking.
Weissenfluh then used artificial intelligence voice-cloning software that cost just $11 to create a digital version of her voice.
Some programs are available for free.
Berry didn't have to sit in a recording studio or read a script. The audio was already online, available for anyone to hear.
Then came the test.
Berry called her cousin using the AI-generated voice to see whether she could tell the difference. She had no idea she was part of an experiment, and she believed she was speaking to Berry.
Although the cousin eventually noticed pauses in the conversation, the voice itself was convincing enough to make her believe Berry was on the other end of the phone.
That raised the question: If the pauses hadn't been there, how much more convincing could the call have been?
Scammers can use this technology to impersonate someone you love. A familiar voice can create an immediate sense of trust, especially when the caller claims there's an emergency or asks for money.
How can you protect yourself from voice cloning?
If you receive an unexpected call from someone claiming to be a family member, especially if they're asking for money, don't rely on their voice alone.
Be cautious if the caller pressures you to act immediately or insists that you keep the conversation a secret.
Hang up and call that person using a number you already know. You can also establish a family code word to help verify someone's identity during an emergency.
Also, use caution when posting videos of yourself online. With so many people sharing videos on social media, scammers may not need much help finding audio to work with.
This experiment showed just how little it can take: publicly available recordings, inexpensive software, and a phone call.
The biggest takeaway from the investigation is simple: Hearing a familiar voice is no longer proof that you're speaking to the person you think you are.

title: Fryeburg Academy football upsets Lawrence in B North semifinal
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
FAIRFIELD — When the Fryeburg Academy football team lost 27-14 to Lawrence at Keyes Field on Sept. 11, it immediately wanted to return for a rematch in the Class B North playoffs.
On Friday night, the Raiders got their long-sought revenge.
Fourth-seeded Fryeburg beat No. 1 Lawrence 20-13 in a regional semifinal and will meet No. 2 Cony next weekend — a rematch of last year’s Class B North title game.
The Raiders (6-4) were powered by senior quarterback Marcus Sutton, who was 7 of 9 passing for 147 yards, with a touchdown and an interception. He added 51 yards and a touchdown on four carries. It was an especially sweet night for Sutton, who injured his ankle in the regular-season game against the Bulldogs and was unable to return.
“We’ve been waiting for this all week,” Sutton said. “I was super motivated, because I was mad about losing the first one because of my ankle. I just wanted to get this win back so bad.”
Senior running back/receiver Lars Bruhn was Sutton’s primary target, with five receptions for 102 yards and a touchdown. Bruhn also had 81 yards on eight carries, including a 52-yard scoring run in the third quarter.
Lawrence, ranked No. 3 in the Varsity Maine Top 10, finished 8-1. The Bulldogs were led by senior running back Keegan Littlefield, who had 94 yards on 22 carries. Junior fullback Jaiden Hebert gained 81 yards on 16 carries, with two touchdowns.
The Raiders set the tone from the first offensive series. On the second play, Sutton ran for a 46-yard gain. Eight plays later, he hit Bruhn with a pass in the flat, and Bruhn was able to scamper around multiple defenders to finish a 21-yard touchdown for a 6-0 lead.
“It was a crazy game,” said Bruhn, a native of Germany. “They couldn’t guard us.”
Fryeburg also scored on its next possession, going 80 yards in just over four minutes. A 2-yard run by Sutton gave the Raiders a 13-0 lead. The touchdown was set up by a 60-yard pass from Sutton to Bruhn at the beginning of the drive.
Lawrence responded with a 78-yard touchdown drive just before halftime, punctuated by a 1-yard dive from Hebert.
Fryeburg scored its last touchdown on the first drive of the second half, when Bruhn took a handoff from Sutton and sprinted 52 yards up the middle for the touchdown and a 20-7 lead.
“We felt, going into the year, that Lawrence was the best team (in B North) and we wanted to come back and win, at some point,” said Fryeburg coach David Turner. “(Lawrence) is a great team, and they were great tonight … You’re just trying to be the best team on one night. And we were the better team tonight.”
Hebert scored another touchdown for the Bulldogs on a 3-yard scoring run, cutting the margin to 20-13 with 7:45 remaining. Lawrence had an opportunity to tie or win after junior Landas Mansfield intercepted a Sutton pass at the Fryeburg 43 with 3:19 remaining, but the Raiders quickly held on downs.
“We came out a little slow, but credit to (Fryeburg), they played a great football game,” Lawrence coach Pete Curtis said. “To get that turnover near the end, it at least gave us a chance, but we couldn’t get anything going offensively. I’m super proud of the guys, it was a really tight group this year.”
Fryeburg fell 40-7 to Cony in the regional final last year. The Raiders also lost in this year’s season opener, 25-21 on a touchdown pass with 2.9 seconds remaining.
“(Cony) can do everything, they throw the ball well,” Turner said. “(Cony coach) B.L. (Lippert) does great, scheme-wise. And now (Anderson) Noyes is back, so their running game is there. They’re playing as well as anybody, maybe in the state. We’ll have our hands full.”

title: Medomak Middle School Closes For Bedbug Treatment, Classes Move Remote
text:
Maine Middle School Closes To Address Bedbug Issue
Several bedbugs were found in a school Waldoboro this week, prompting school officials to close the school down to have the school professionally treated.
What's the issue?
According to the RSU 40 website, classes at the Medomak Middle School, which shares it's campus with the Medomak Valley High School on Manktown Road, were cancelled for part of this week after the insects were found.
Read More: What Led To Bangor Mall's Sudden Condemnation
School officials say there is no indication of an infestation, as of yet, on the campus, which serves over 350 middle school students from area towns of Friendship, Waldoboro, Union, Washington and Warren. But administrators are proactively addressing the situation before it can spread into something bigger that affects not only the school, but students and staff.
"We are following established protocols to minimize any potential spread and are monitoring the situation closely. Out of an abundance of caution, we have also made the decision to arrange for a comprehensive professional treatment of the entire school."
"Although there is no evidence of a larger problem, we feel this proactive approach is the best way to provide peace of mind to our students, staff and families."
How will this impact students and teachers?
Classes were canceled entirely on Thursday. Families were informed that students would take part in remote learning Friday, and continue remote learning Monday and Tuesday of next week. Schools were already scheduled to be closed for Wednesday November 11th in observance of Veterans Day.
The notice went on to recommend that all families and staff members check their own home and belongings for signs of bedbugs.
What should families be looking for at home?
The U.S. Department of Environmental Protection (aka the EPA) says finding bedbugs early can help you prevent an infestation that could get costly to clear out later. Here are some of the things they suggest you look for:
The first thing they say to check the actual bodies of people living in your home for bedbug bites.
"Bed bug bites can look like bites from other insects (such as mosquitoes or chiggers), rashes (such as eczema or fungal infections), or even hives. Some people do not react to bed bug bites at all."
The second thing you should check is your bedding and furniture.
Read More: Bangor School Buses Canceled As Flu Hits Drivers
"A more accurate way to identify a possible infestation is to look for physical signs of bed bugs. When cleaning, changing bedding, or staying away from home, look for:
Rusty or reddish stains on bed sheets or mattresses caused by bed bugs being crushed, dark spots (about this size: •), which are bed bug excrement and may bleed on the fabric like a marker would, eggs and eggshells, which are tiny (about 1mm) and pale yellow skins that nymphs shed as they grow larger, and live bed bugs."
If you find signs of bedbugs, the school asks that you reach out them and let them know, and then contact professionals immediately to begin treatment.
Here's a good video that explains how and what to look for when it comes to bedbugs.
The Centers for Disease Control says that while they are certainly not fun to deal with, as they can interrupt your sleep (they feed on your blood at night. I know, not pleasant to even think about!) the silver lining is bedbugs are not known to carry or spread disease. So I guess that's a plus? While some folks aren't bothered by their bites, others can have allergic reactions to them, so checking often for bedbugs or signs of bedbugs is advised.

title: Dolly Parton’s manager moves to drop complaint accusing late singer’s nephew of threatening estate
text:
(AP) - Dolly Parton’s longtime manager moved Thursday to drop a complaint that accused the late singer’s nephew of threatening her estate and its employees.
She’s Alive, the entity founded to manage and protect Parton’s estate, had secured a temporary restraining order against Bryan Seaver and his security company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services, in September.
A hearing, pushed several times over the course of a month, was slated for Tuesday.
A very brief filing in a Tennessee court Thursday gives no reason why the complaint is being withdrawn.
It says only that a proposed order was being drafted for the judge’s approval to dismiss the case without prejudice, meaning it can be refiled again. A court filing from a day earlier said the two sides had reached an agreement, but that also gave no details.
The Associated Press sent emails seeking comment from lawyers for She’s Alive, Seaver and his company.
