title: Brunswick police officer accused of excessive force, false arrest
text:
A Brunswick police officer who is facing charges for allegedly assaulting a 17-year-old during a 2025 traffic stop is being sued.
The lawsuit, filed in federal court Friday, names Officer Nathan Day, an additional unnamed officer and the town of Brunswick as defendants.
The filing alleges that Day, 27, used excessive and unprovoked force against the teenage girl, slamming her head into her car and onto the ground and knocking her out, leaving her with severe injuries. It also says Day and the other officer falsely arrested her without cause to believe she had committed a crime.
Day was charged with Class D assault in March. He waived arraignment and has pleaded not guilty to the misdemeanor charge.
Brunswick police Chief Scott Stewart confirmed that Day was placed on administrative leave a day after the Dec. 18, 2025, incident. Stewart said he was unaware of the lawsuit when asked to comment Friday.
The name of the teenager — who is now an adult — is included in the lawsuit, but the Portland Press Herald does not name victims of alleged crimes without their permission.
The lawsuit alleges that, on the day of the traffic stop, officers pulled over the teen’s boyfriend in the parking lot of the Cook’s Corner shopping plaza. She had been following him in a separate car while they were driving to a body shop to repair a taillight on his vehicle, and she followed her boyfriend into the parking lot when he was pulled over.
The filing says the then-17-year-old was waiting across the parking lot when Day ordered her out of her vehicle and assaulted her, knocking her unconscious.
Officers arrested her for traffic violations that were dismissed in September. She was transported to the hospital in handcuffs. She suffered a head wound that required staples, a concussion and foot fractures, and she experienced seizures, the lawsuit alleges.
In an email Friday, Day’s attorney, Marc Beaudoin, denied the allegations outlined in the complaint and detailed a different narrative of the arrest.
Beaudoin said that, while in the parking lot, Day asked the teenager multiple times to come over to him, intending to give her a ticket for using her cellphone while driving. When she refused, Day approached and began to handcuff her, at which point she attempted to move away from him and kicked him in the knee, Beaudoin said.
Day “did not use any excessive force” during the arrest, Beaudoin said, and the teen’s injuries were “inadvertent and due to her own refusal to comply.”
The teen’s lawsuit also cites multiple instances in which Day was disciplined by the department.
According to department records obtained by the Press Herald through a public records request this year, Day was formally disciplined three times before the alleged assault — in September 2023, July 2025 and August 2025.
In the August 2025 incident, Day was disciplined and required to complete remedial training after reportedly tackling a suspect. The other two disciplinary reports involve Day driving a police cruiser and pursuing another vehicle in ways that violated department policy.
The suit accuses the town of failing to properly discipline Day for his “escalating misconduct,” and of demonstrating a broader pattern of deliberate indifference toward reports of officer misconduct.
“While Nathan Day’s actions last December are at the heart of this suit, this case is also about the lack of discipline in the Town of Brunswick’s police department, which allowed Mr. Day to stay on the force despite repeated flouting of the Constitution and departmental regulations,” attorneys representing the plaintiff said in a joint statement Friday.
The plaintiff is seeking compensatory and punitive damages, plus attorney’s fees, and has requested a jury trial.
Staff Writer Drew Johnson contributed to this story.

title: KVCAP opens 37 affordable apartments in Waterville
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WATERVILLE, Maine (WABI) -KVCAP celebrated the opening of 37 new affordable apartments in Waterville on Thursday with a ribbon cutting at a site that holds decades of memories for the city.
The event marked the end of a multi-year redevelopment project in the city’s South End.
David Pelton, president and CEO of KVCAP, said the apartments can take some responsibility off residents.
“If they have an affordable, nice place to live that isn’t going to have things breaking down in it because it’s new...If we can play some role in taking that off their plate, then it allows people to focus on something else like, you know, their job or taking care of their kids or taking care of an elderly parent,” Pelton said.
Apartment details
The complex includes a range of unit types, including accessible units.
Justin Amoroso, construction superintendent for E.W. Littlefield, described the apartments.
“There’s one, two and three bedroom apartments. There’s ADA units for handicapped. It’s for basically any families. There’s nice kitchens, walk-in showers,” Amoroso said.
Former South End Arena site
The apartments stand on the former site of Art Gagne’s South End Arena, a skating rink and arcade.
The grandchildren of Art Gagne said the site remains part of the family’s memories.
“I can remember 40 years plus of history in this place. So, it’s really sentimental and we did a lot of things,” grandchild Shane Gagne said.
The new complex includes a first-floor community room named Art’s Place.
“It was just really nice and that they named the room after Pepe is just very special. Very special,” grandchild Tara Bradstreet said.
How to apply
The apartments are intended for low- to moderate-income households. Applicants must meet income guidelines.
For more information on applying, contact the Waterville Housing Authority or visit its website.

title: Bicycle Coalition of Maine and state spotlight 1,000 miles of bike routes
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine is well known for hiking and boating — perhaps less so for cycling.
Two organizations want to change that with the publication of maps showcasing 32 biking routes totaling 1,000 miles.
The Maine Adventure Collection, created by the Bicycle Coalition of Maine and the Maine Office of Outdoor Recreation, has routes ranging from mountain biking to road cycling.
Each route includes information to help cyclists plan their rides, such as difficulty ratings, distances on paved and unpaved surfaces and recommended bike and tire widths.
“We worked hard to map some very unique routes highlighting some of what Maine has to offer — whether riders are looking for an all-day epic or a relaxed off-road ride,” said Dan Bassett, deputy director of the coalition. “We purposefully wanted to find routes and areas that are less explored by bike to show the range of what is available in Maine for cyclists.”
Options include varying experience levels. For example, the beginner-friendly 37-mile Common Ground Gravel ride is rated three out of 10 for difficulty. The 22-mile Mt. Vernon North ride is considered a challenge, with a difficulty rating of eight out of 10.
“Our partnership with the Bicycle Coalition of Maine reflects our commitment to supporting outdoor recreation opportunities that benefit Maine communities, local businesses and visitors alike,” said Jeff McCabe, director of the Maine Office of Outdoor Recreation.
To see the collection, visit the “where to ride” tab on Bicycle Coalition of Maine’s website.

title: Looks Like Maine Is Getting Its First Jimmy John's Restaurant
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
It Looks Like Maine Could Be Getting Its First Jimmy John’s Restaurant
It's pretty exciting when a popular restaurant or business that seems to be everywhere else finally makes its way to Maine.
I remember when news about the first Chick-fil-A coming to Bangor in 2016 was a shocking yet pleasant surprise. The lines on that first day were insanely long, too.
Well, it looks like Bangor could be getting another "first" with what appears to be Maine's first Jimmy John's.
Jimmy John's Job Listings Point to a Bangor, Maine, Location
As of November 6, 2026, there are no Jimmy John's restaurants open in Maine.
Yet, there are some clues out there that point to the very first one in the state coming to Bangor.
On both the job website the official Jimmy John's career web page, there are hiring listings for crew members and shift managers in Bangor.
The Jimmy John's page narrows down the location even further to Bangor Mall Boulevard. Exciting!
A Second Restaurant Is Planned Alongside a New Arby's in Bangor, Maine
Back in March 2026, WABI reported that a brand-new Bangor Arby's would be taking over the location where a previous Arby's once was: 57 Bangor Mall Boulevard.
That original Bangor Arby's closed after 32 years in 2015 when its owner chose to retire, according to the Bangor Daily News. Kind of neat to have a revival of a fast-food spot that used to be there, right?
But apparently that's not the only business expected to move into the building.
WABI also revealed that Arby's would only take up half the space at the Bangor Mall Boulevard spot, "with another unknown business slated to take over the other half."
Could Jimmy John's Be Sharing a Location With Arby's in Bangor, Maine?
It certainly appears that Jimmy John's might just be that mystery business moving into 57 Bangor Mall Boulevard with Arby's.
The dots seem to line up.
Additionally, several people have said on the Bangor subreddit that they've driven by the location recently and have seen an Arby's and Jimmy John's sign on the building.
I've emailed Inspire Brands, which owns both Arby's and Jimmy John's, for confirmation but haven't heard an official word back yet.
READ MORE: 9 New Maine Restaurants That Opened in September 2026 You Can Try
Are you excited for a Jimmy John's to come to Maine? The closest one to the state, or even New Hampshire, is in Massachusetts.
I've never had it but certainly interested to check out the popular chain spot. Guess I'll have to pick between the sandwiches and wraps.
And with Bangor seemingly being the place for new "first" national restaurants in the state, fingers crossed a Sonic is next? Maybe? At the very least, just one somewhere in the state?
Anyway, hopefully we'll get more opening timeline details for 57 Bangor Mall Boulevard soon!

title: InvestigateTV+: Measles outbreaks in the U.S.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Once declared eliminated in the U.S., measles is making a comeback as cases reach a decades-high peak. InvestigateTV+ digs into the highly contagious disease’s return and how one state is fighting its worst outbreak in years.
Plus, Black women who integrated industries during the Civil Rights era reunite at the adult education center that changed their lives.
Then, we visit a tasting room opened by a volunteer firefighter to honor first responders and celebrate the brotherhood of the fire service.
Measles outbreaks in the U.S.
Measles is one of the most contagious diseases on Earth and can cause serious health complications, including death.
Measles is most often associated with a rash and fever, according to the CDC. Health experts warn it can cause severe complications, particularly in babies and young children.
When more than 95% of a community is vaccinated, most people are protected through what’s known as herd immunity.
This school helped break barriers
Just over 60 years ago, the country took a step toward making good on a promise that all Americans are created equal. The passage of the Civil Rights Act in 1964 desegregated schools, workplaces, and public spaces all while creating protections against discrimination.
A year after the signing of the landmark legislation, an adult education center in New Orleans opened its doors to young Black women. Those women would use the skills they learned to integrate major corporate offices across the South.
The need for housing
America’s population is aging and a recent study found there may not be enough senior-friendly homes to meet demand. In 2019, one in six Americans were 65 or older and by 2060 it will be one in four.
A 2019 U.S. Census data analysis found that “the stock of aging-ready homes across the nation may be inadequate for the growing number of older households.”
An old fire station distillery
A Wisconsin family runs a distillery in an old fire station along Highway 96 in Dale, with a business designed to support the fire departments that keep them safe.

title: Camden, Maine, goes to the polls: A Day to Remember
text:
It is November 3 in Camden, Maine and the coastal town is alive with energy. The fire station serves as the focal point of election day — a public space where citizens have been casting their ballots for more than 19 years. In Camden, voting is not just civic duty. It is a day to celebrate community, differences, and taking a stand.
“It was absolutely mandatory for me to be here to vote,” said Jennifer Currier, a Camden citizen. “Every single vote — it is going to impact you one way or another.”
This was very much the tone of the town on election morning. Citizens showed up in a steady stream to cast their ballots. Though everyone voted on the same candidates and issues, the experience was different for everyone.
Citizens like Currier showed up not only to have a say in statewide politics, but also in issues seen throughout the town. For many, these local decisions are just as important as statewide politics.
“You’ve also got a lot of people who are drastically affected by little things; we were just voting on the Camden parking fees and I know for a fact there are quite a few people who can’t afford to park downtown,” said Currier.
Meanwhile, for some people the 2026 midterms meant their first time voting. Andreina Norton moved to the United States in 2009 and became an official U.S. citizen in 2025. On November 3, she finally got to exercise her right to vote.
“[I’m feeling] very proud, very happy, it’s a little bit emotional, because I’m just very grateful to live here, to be part of this community, and I’m happy to participate in the process,” said Norton.
The voting process would not have been as accessible without local officials like Chris Farley. Farley is the Camden fire chief, and his station is the host of the midterm election.
“Ideally we’re in a participatory democracy,” he said.” It takes an engaged community to make community work. Part of that is the voting process, and it’s important that the community has a safe, reliable place to come and vote.”
Everyone has different experiences that affect the way they vote. For Currier, a big part of this is local affordability. For Norton, it is about gratitude. For Farley, it’s making the voting process accessible for all. There is no doubt that when citizens can come together, there is plenty of space for common ground to be found.
“I really believe that everybody has so much more in common than they have different,” said Dave Morrison, a Camden citizen, poet, and manager of the municipally-run Camden Opera House. “Everybody wants their kids to do well, they want their parents to do okay, they want to have a decent job. We get riled up to get upset about stuff when it doesn’t have to be that way.”
Regardless of how people feel about the results of the election, the citizens of Camden showed up to vote and made their voices matter. November 3 was a day of firsts, a day of community, and a day to remember.
This article first appeared in the Penobscot Bay Pilot on Nov. 6, 2026. The original article can be viewed on PenBayPilot.com.

title: Maine governor-elect Pingree meets with Gov. Mills on transition
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Maine Governor-elect Hannah Pingree visited the State House on Friday to meet with Gov. Janet Mills about the transition of power in January.
Meeting begins in the Cabinet Room
The meeting between Maine’s first and second female governors began in the Cabinet Room, where Mills pledged her administration’s support.
“I intend to do everything I can to ensure that she and her team have everything they need to hit the ground running,” Mills said.
Pingree names transition co-chairs
Pingree said the work starts now. She has named former state Sen. Roger Katz and former Penobscot ambassador Maulian Bryant to co-chair her transition committee. The group will help identify candidates for Pingree’s Cabinet.
“Mainers don’t have time to waste and neither do I. Winter is coming. The work does not pause between administrations. So my team and I are committed to a seamless, peaceful, efficient transition,” Pingree said.
Budget talks to start next week
The state budget is one of the largest tasks for a new governor. The two teams will begin discussing the budget next week as Maine families face a difficult economy.
Pingree said seeking heating assistance will be a priority.
“If we don’t see relief from the federal government, then I would look forward to working across the aisle in a bipartisan way around an emergency relief plan,” Pingree said.
Mills gives Pingree pendant
Mills gave Pingree her State of Maine pendant, a necklace Mills described as a lucky talisman, before showing her the governor’s office.
They later had lunch at the Blaine House, the governor’s residence, where Pingree plans to move with her family.

title: Supreme Court to hear North Dakota landowners’ legal fees case
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The Supreme Court is set to hear a case about landowners’ rights that centers on North Dakota but could apply to property owners elsewhere.
The central question is whether a government-backed company should have to pay a property owner’s legal fees if the owner takes the company to court and wins.
In the U.S., someone who takes land under eminent domain must pay the owner for it. The North Dakota property owners in this case went to court to be paid fairly for their land.
WBI Energy, the government-contracted company behind the pipeline in question, eventually gave the owners fair compensation. The landowners were left with nearly $380,000 in legal fees. They say the company should pay that bill.
Sam Spiegelman of Spiegelman Law Group said North Dakota law “clearly says that just compensation includes the legal costs for an owner to vindicate their property rights.”
The 8th Circuit Court of Appeals said that law should not apply when the federal government is on the other side of the lawsuit.
Bob McNamara from the Institute of Justice said North Dakota has broad laws that protect victims of eminent domain and private natural gas pipelines. He said pipeline companies “say they don’t have to follow those laws because they’re just like the federal government.”
The outcome is likely to have consequences beyond North Dakota.
Spiegelman said landowners around the country whose property is seized by the government, or by private companies licensed by the government, “will not have any good incentive to pursue the vindication of the full value of their land” in court.
“What’s at stake here are property rights protections. And really all 50 states that are under threat from private pipeline companies operating with the federal government’s authority” McNamara said.
During oral arguments Monday, the Natural Gas Act is likely to be discussed. The act suggests federal standards should apply to disputes like this one.

title: Watch: Giant pandas make much-anticipated debut at Zoo Atlanta
text:
Watch: Giant pandas make much-anticipated debut at Zoo Atlanta
Zoo Atlanta’s newest pandas munched bamboo and lounged Friday during their public debut as smiling visitors lined up to welcome them.
Ping Ping, a male, and Fu Shuang, a female, arrived in September from China under a 10-year loan agreement, bringing the cuddly black-and-white bears back to the zoo after a two-year absence. After spending the past weeks getting acclimated to their habitat, the 6-year-old pandas greeted visitors in the newly renovated Arthur M. Blank Panda Grove.
Eight-year-old Rachel Sutherland and her family were visiting from Sacramento, California, and extended their vacation by a day to see the pandas.
“They’re amazing,” said Rachel. She said she was partial to Ping Ping because the name reminds her of the color pink.
Ping Ping has distinctive dark circles around his eyes, while Fu Shuang has a protruding forehead, according to Xinhua News Agency. Both were born at Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding in China.
The Atlanta zoo's panda enclosure had been empty since 2024, after four other pandas returned from the United States to China, ending a 25-year partnership amid strained relations between the two countries.
During a news conference Friday morning, Xie Feng, the Chinese ambassador to the U.S., said the pandas' arrival “marks the renewal of a decade-long bond between China and Zoo Atlanta.”
“We trust that under the loving care of Zoo Atlanta, the two pandas will eat happily, sleep soundly and grow healthy and strong in their new home, bringing twice the joy and happiness to everyone who loves them,” the ambassador said.
Georgia Tech student Kevin Wei, 18, said he'd been counting down until “panda day,” and felt especially connected to the animals because they are from his hometown of Chengdu.
“It's kind of like having a familiar bond,” Wei said. “Although I'm living in the U.S., I still can connect with myself and to China.”
China has long used pandas as part of its diplomacy globally, deploying the bears in loan programs as expressions of goodwill and letting loan agreements lapse when tensions arise.
Zoo Atlanta is one of three U.S. zoos that now house the popular bears.
The National Zoo in Washington returned three pandas to China in 2023 before accepting new arrivals Bao Li and Qing Bao in October 2024. The San Diego Zoo debuted two pandas in August 2024.
A decade ago, the International Union for Conservation of Nature reclassified giant pandas from endangered to vulnerable, reflecting pandas' growing numbers in the wild in China.
Resident Kim Herres, 76, said she has been visiting Zoo Atlanta ever since the city first received pandas in 1999. She said she sees pandas as a symbol of the world “doing the right thing” to protect animals.
“I'm just glad we've gotten them back,” she said. “Hopefully we won't make the Chinese mad, and they won't come get them.”

title: Woman rescued after being chained to bed for years when maintenance worker hears cries for help, police say
text:
FARGO, N.D. (KVLY/Gray News) — A woman was rescued in North Dakota after being chained to a bed for years when a maintenance technician working in the apartment building heard her cries for help.
According to court documents, Fargo police were called to an apartment complex Tuesday after a maintenance technician heard someone crying for help.
The maintenance technician told police he entered the apartment where he found a woman chained to a bed with a security camera pointing at her. Court documents also said the windows of the bedroom were covered with tin foil.
The responding officer said the woman was in a bedroom with a chain and padlock secured around her right ankle, with the other end of the chain secured to the bed.
The woman told authorities she was brought to Fargo from Mexico in 2024 by her ex-husband, identified as 40-year-old Arturo Calzada Becerril. She said she had been chained up in his apartment and had not been outside for two years.
The woman said Calzada Becerril brought her food twice a day but did not let her go outside or use the bathroom. She was given a bucket to relieve herself.
Court documents said that police freed the woman from the chains and interviewed her using Language Link because she did not speak English.
Investigators noted bruising to her body and face. She was then brought to the hospital.
Police said that shortly afterward, 41-year-old Erendira Amoles arrived at the apartment with her 8-year-old daughter.
While being interviewed at the hospital, the woman told investigators that both Calzada Becerril and Amoles would beat her and sexually assault her.
Calzada Becerril told investigators that the three of them were from the same town in Mexico. Court documents show that he told investigators he locked the victim up so “she did not run away.” Amoles told police she is the one who often locks the woman up.
Calzada Becerril and Amoles were arrested on kidnapping and assault charges. They were booked into the Cass County Jail.
Border Patrol assisted Fargo police.

Milestone recognizes Stanton’s decade of leadership, growth and impact at the Portland communications firm
PORTLAND – Broadreach Public Relations, a woman-owned strategic communications firm located in Portland, is recognizing Paula Stanton as she celebrates 10 years with the firm.
Stanton joined Broadreach in 2016 as a client manager, advanced through several roles and now serves as vice president of client services, leading the firm’s day-to-day operations and coordinating a team of communications professionals and a network of specialized partners.
Over the past decade, Stanton has played an important role in Broadreach’s evolution. From leading international events and complex client initiatives to developing emerging talent, she has helped strengthen client relationships, build a high-performing team and guide the firm through significant change, including the pandemic and implementation of the Entrepreneurial Operating System .
“Paula and I have navigated a lot together over the past 10 years, including more than a few ‘how are we going to pull this off?’ moments,”Linda Varrell, president and founder of Broadreach, said. “Through the growing pains, unexpected challenges and occasional chaos, she’s brought a level head, a sense of humor and a determination to get things done. She’s grown into an exceptional leader, and Broadreach is a stronger firm because of her. I couldn’t be prouder of what we’ve accomplished together.”
Stanton earned a bachelor of arts in journalism from the University of Massachusetts-Amherst and holds a graduate certificate in Digital and Social Media from Kennesaw State University. Prior to joining Broadreach, she built a diverse marketing and communications background through roles in e-commerce, professional services and higher education.
Founded in 2007, Broadreach Public Relations is a women-owned, award-winning strategic communications firm located on Portland’s historic waterfront. Broadreach runs on the Entrepreneurial Operation System and has partnered with over 350 businesses, government agencies and nonprofits to deliver creative strategies, effective storytelling and measurable results for more than 450 projects. title: Dramatic video: Mother rescues man drowning
text:
Dramatic video: Mother of three rescuing man drowning in flooded waters
A West Palm Beach, Florida, mother of three risked her own life Monday night to rescue a man who had driven his vehicle into a lake.
Annmarie Sanchez said Willow Pond Road was so flooded it was impossible to tell where the road ended and the lake began.
Sanchez said her daughter told her that there was a vehicle in the lake, and Sanchez ran to see if she could help.
She said many residents were standing on the bank using their phones to record the vehicle, but nobody was helping.
Sanchez decided to act.
"I had no idea if there were crocodiles, alligators, anything. I just kind of went for it. I wasn't going to let him die," Sanchez said.
Video below: Boat video shows heavy flooding in McCaysville, Georgia
She dove into the water and swam toward the vehicle, which was completely submerged by the time she reached it.
The driver was struggling to stay afloat.
Sanchez began pulling the man toward the shore, but the effort was difficult.
"Then I got really desperate, where I really couldn't hold him anymore, and I started asking for a helping hand, and I'm yelling," Sanchez said.
Video shows Sanchez pulling the man, screaming, "Somebody, pull my hand, please."
However, nobody helped.
"That was very frustrating, and it made me feel, kind of, like, very inhumane," Sanchez said.
She continued pulling the man and said she was seconds away from giving up.
"I have him by the arm. I can't keep up," she is heard saying in the video.
That's when a woman swam out to help her, and together they brought the man to shore safely.
On Thursday afternoon, Sanchez received a knock on her door.
It was the man she had saved, introducing himself as Bill.
"I was so happy to see his face," Sanchez said. "We hugged. That's the first thing that we did."
Video from Sanchez's home security system shows the two hugging while Sanchez said, "I'm so glad you're OK."
"The first thing he said was, 'Thank you for having the courage to jump in when nobody else did. Thank you for saving me,'" Sanchez said.
Sanchez told him it was something she felt she had to do.
"I just couldn't sit there and let a stranger die in front of me and not do anything," she said.
Sanchez said she hopes to keep in touch with Bill and is also searching for the woman who helped her during the rescue to thank her personally.

title: How this Civil Rights-era school helped Black women break office barriers
text:
NEW ORLEANS (InvestigateTV) - Just over 60 years ago, the country took a step toward making good on a promise that all Americans are created equal. The passage of the Civil Rights Act in 1964 desegregated schools, workplaces, and public spaces all while creating protections against discrimination.
In mid-May, a group of women who graduated from the former Adult Education Center in New Orleans came back for a reunion.
During the Civil Rights era, the Adult Education Center, located at Exchange Place in the French Quarter, helped prepare Black women to enter the white-collar workforce by teaching them skills such as typewriting and short handwriting.
Raphael Morgan said back then, office jobs for people like her were few and far between because they could not get training.
“I couldn’t type. I didn’t know shorthand. So, every time I went on an interview, they would say, ‘You don’t have any experience. We’re not going to be able to hire you.’ It’s like a door slammed in your face,” Morgan said. ”I have an older mother, and she had witnessed the same thing. So, all she knew was doing domestic work."
Raphael Morgan enrolled at the Adult Education Center in 1970 after high school. She said she could not afford to go to college and believed going to the center would be her best shot for employment.
“I think my mother was more excited because she really felt badly that she couldn’t afford to send me to college at the time, and to this day, I cannot believe the education that I received. I paid $40 for books only, and we had shorthand, typing and job interviewing skills,” Morgan said.
The vocational school opened in 1965, inspired by Father Timothy Gibbons. But the Catholic priest needed educators. And that’s where Alice Geoffray comes in.
“So, when the school was started by a priest, he wanted an expert teacher in that transition from school into offices. My mother had just won an award, a national classroom teacher’s award,” said Jeff Geoffray, co-founder of the 431 Exchange.
Jeff Geoffray is the son of Alice Jeoffray. He said his late mother wasn’t necessarily a civil rights activist. At that time, Alice Geoffray was a seasoned teacher.
“My mother was not involved in the civil rights movement. She was trying to survive. She was trying to be a teacher and feed her children,” said Geoffray.
Through her seven years at the Adult Education Center, Geoffray said his mom came to love her work and the women she trained, many of whom landed jobs after graduation.
Geoffray said his mother would have been proud of the accomplishments of her former students.
“Many of them were her dearest friends. She communicated, kept in touch with them, but the main thing is that she really did not have blind faith in them. She really felt that these were talented women. Those women were the first African American secretaries in the Deep South. They integrated offices like Shell, Standard Oil, Pan-American Life and even city hall,” said Jeff Geoffray.
Raphael Morgan finished her training at the center in 1971. She went on to get a teaching degree from the University of New Orleans and became a teacher.
Her work career also included jobs at the Orleans Parish School Board and as an insurance adjuster.
“But no matter what, I think I’ll always be a teacher because you have the ability to change so many lives,” Morgan said.
Morgan is among the 431 women — mostly African American — who graduated from the Adult Education Center. The center closed in 1972.
Today, Jeff Geoffray and his sister, Jeanne, run the nonprofit group 431 Exchange. It is named in honor of the 431 graduates of the school and where it once stood in Exchange Place.
431 Exchange advocates for equal and affordable access to education. It also offers scholarships to adults who want to pursue higher learning. The story of the school, its members and the nonprofit’s work will be the focus of an upcoming PBS documentary.
“Jeanne and her brother have done tremendous work to keep their mother’s dream alive. And we can’t wait until this [documentary] comes to a conclusion and the world will get to see what we experienced,” said Morgan.
The documentary is expected to be available in 2027.
To learn more about the 431 Exchange, visit 431exchange.org.

title: The Trump fever has broken
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Bernard Campbell is a semi-retired businessman who lives in Deer Isle.
Donald Trump has been a millionaire since he was 8 years old. He eventually inherited more than $400 million in today’s dollars. Incredibly, he seemingly single-handedly captured the working man and saved the Republican Party, which owes him a great debt.
How did he accomplish this? I think the Democrats screwed up for a really long time. I believe they became the party of elites and know-it-alls, and lots of regular people didn’t like them. Trump was no everyman, but he sounded like one. He was different, and people were ready for different. He was angry, and he channeled the anger of the people who had been ignored for too long.
But here is the thing: It takes a carpenter to build a house, but all it takes is a drunk with a sledgehammer to knock one down. Criticizing others is easy. You need to be competent to actually do a job right. And we now know something is really wrong.
People know what gas costs, and what heating oil costs, and what health care costs, and what food costs, and what mortgages cost, and nothing is making much sense.
Our tax dollars may fund a $200 billion exercise in futility in the Middle East. Is it possible we are actually losing a war with Iran?!
ICE is a $75 billion clown show.
The East Wing ballroom project looks like a $400 million investment to support the narcissism of a reality show host, playing at being president.
Combined with tax cuts disproportionately favoring the rich, the federal government has become a financial basket case, like an adolescent who believes that as long as there is still room on the credit card, everything is fine.
Economically, everything is not fine. And yes, competence does matter. But that might not even be the hard part. We were a great country, but we aren’t one any more.
No decline this dramatic happens overnight. Our loss of community has been happening for decades. The wealth difference between the haves and have-nots has grown immensely, and government, no matter who was in power, did essentially nothing, leaving a lot of angry, scared people.
Elon Musk spent close to $500 million on the election, apparently to protect the billionaire class and keep the working class in their place, and it did not move the needle. At all.
The Trump fever has broken. Maybe we have tired of being angry.
This could be a turning point. Republican elected officials were in the unenviable position of supporting an unsupportable president. Many of them have now been put out of their misery, and the remainder can rebuild their party in the spirit of a group that truly cares about the many, not the few.
In a similar way, Democrats have a real chance to fix decades of mistakes; to reconnect with their FDR roots, and remember one of Franklin Roosevelt’s most famous quotes: “The test of our progress is not whether we add more to the abundance of those who have much; it is whether we provide enough for those who have too little.”
Only then can we return to the intention of our founding fathers, and start rebuilding our collective will. Maybe this will come to matter more than Democrats versus Republicans.
We aren’t called the United States of America for nothing.

title: Row house fire in Brooklyn kills 6 people and injures 9
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A fire barreled through a multifamily row house in New York early Thursday, killing six people and injuring nine others, including some firefighters and police officers, the city’s fire department said.
More than 200 first responders descended on the two-story building in Brooklyn’s Sunset Park neighborhood, where Kevin Woods, the department’s chief of fire operations, said they were met with “fire on every floor.”
The severely charred wooden home had “fire blowing out every window, meeting us at the front door,” he said at a news conference. Fire marshals were still investigating what caused the blaze.
Firefighters rescued four people, using a rear entrance in the two-unit home to reach people trapped behind window bars, Woods said. A staircase partially collapsed inside the home, he added.
First responders brought the fire under control in about three hours, and eight people who were displaced were taken to hotels. Woods said the fire spread to one adjacent row house, but damage could be seen on buildings to both its left and right.
Row houses share common walls and exteriors and are usually built in blocks. Fire officials said the Sunset Park home was one in a block of 25 wood-frame homes.
“This was a devastating fire,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at the news conference. “It will take a long time for this neighborhood to mourn the neighbors they lost this morning and to recover from this immense grief.”
The nine injured people were expected to survive, including three firefighters and two police officers who had minor injuries. No names have been released.
The home was built in 1915, according to property records.
City records show that the building was sold by a family a few years ago to a company called One Golden Sunshine Corp. Complaints filed with the city’s building department in 2025 said that the home’s basement level was illegally being converted into an apartment and that construction had been going on without a permit for a month.
City inspectors visited several times, including in August, but were unable to gain access.
A lithium-ion battery was found at the scene, but it was unknown whether it was related to the cause of the fire, the department said.
Last week, an e-bike battery fire killed four people in the Bronx. It is among more than 400 fires in the city that have been linked to lithium-ion batteries this year, leading to at least six deaths and more than 70 injuries, according to fire officials.
Fatal home fires are not uncommon, though the death toll in the Brooklyn blaze was unusually high. A townhome fire in Chicago the same day killed four people, including a teenager.
The U.S. Fire Administration says at least 1,555 people have died in home fires this year. Among them were an Amish woman and her six children who were killed in a swift-moving house fire in April in rural Pennsylvania.
Last month, five people, including four children, died in a mobile home fire in Canton, Texas. And in Riverdale, Utah, a man and his four children were killed Oct. 1 in a house fire started by a power strip that overheated, officials said.
——
McCormack reported from Concord, New Hampshire. Associated Press reporters Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut, Yuki Iwamura in New York and Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City contributed.

title: How to lower prescription costs and still get the medication you need
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — If prescription costs have you doing the math every month, there are options to explore to bring the price down and still get the medication you need.
Start with the health care question
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said prescription affordability is a health care issue.
“A medication sitting on a pharmacy shelf isn’t doing anybody any good, and it’s not going to help anybody feel better,” Cradduck said. “So we have to figure out the best way to get them into your hands.”
Ask your doctor and pharmacist
One place to start is with the doctor or pharmacist.
Doctors may have access to free prescription drug programs, including samples left by drug company representatives. Cradduck said patients who are struggling can ask their doctor whether any free medications or samples are available.
Pharmacists know about programs and may recommend cards that can reduce the cost of medications, Cradduck said.
Review coverage and look for assistance
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke recommended that Medicare Part D coverage be reviewed every year and said it should not be left to renew on its own.
A client was paying $100 a month for her Medicare Part D premium. After a review, the premium was lowered to $30 a month, O’Rourke said.
She also pointed to the Extra Help program that helps with the cost of prescription drugs. If you qualify based on income, you can get medications for free or very little, she said.
If insurance denies a medication, O’Rourke said, appeal the decision rather than assuming it can’t be covered. Getting a doctor’s help in presenting the appeal can lead to coverage, she said.
Compare pharmacies and ask about generics
Many people don’t realize how much prices can differ from one pharmacy to another, O’Rourke said.
“Go to the different pharmacies and see what they’re charging,” O’Rourke said. “You would be amazed at the difference in different places to buy medicine.”
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said patients can also ask about generics drugs.
“Some of these drugs cost a lot of money, and you can ask them, ‘Is there an equivalent, something else equivalent that I can treat the same condition with?’” Rogers said. “We see that all the time, especially with the blood thinners.”
Cradduck said patients should find one pharmacy that will fill all of their medications for the lowest price, rather than using several pharmacies. Using multiple pharmacies means no one is tracking what is interacting, Cradduck said, and keeping track of that is part of a pharmacist’s job.
If a pharmacist suggests a change, aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said, patients should go back to their doctor to make sure the doctor agrees.
Don’t split pills or skip doses
The Aging Untold experts said patients should not split pills, take half doses or skip doses to stretch a refill before deciding they can’t afford a medication.
Instead, the experts said, ask questions, because resources exist to get medication at a lower cost.
Resource
Key takeaways
- Ask about free samples. Talk to your doctor about free medications or samples, and talk to your pharmacist about programs and cards that can lower costs.
- Review Medicare Part D every year. Amy O’Rourtke said a client lowered the premium from $100 to $30 a month after a review.
- Check the Extra Help program. Check to see if you qualify based on income. Participants can get medications for free or very little, O’Rourke said.
- Compare prices, ask about generics, and stay with one pharmacy. Prices vary by pharmacy, and using one pharmacy lets the pharmacist track interactions.
- Appeal denials and don’t ration doses. Get your doctor’s help with an appeal, and avoid splitting pills or skipping doses.

title: Congress needs to hold ICE to account
text:
I was sickened and incensed to read about the arrest of Jessie Laurel Tepler-Mujambere by New Hampshire immigration authorities last week. As a teen, Jessie fled violence in Burundi, was adopted by Sen. Denise Tepler (D-Topsham) and Sheldon Tepler, and had a pending asylum application. He had obtained a Canadian passport and was arrested on his way to the border.
It used to be that a person with a pending asylum application was authorized to live and work in the U.S. “Trump 2.0” demonstrates daily its goal to intimidate, instigate cruelty and unabashedly enact unprecedented levels of corruption.
I want to add my voice to the call for change. We call out the senseless arrests of immigrants. Anyone with a sense of history knows that this country was built by immigrants. We, in fact, are all immigrants or descendants of immigrants.
It’s time to expose the diabolical actions of ICE. It’s past time for Congress to do its job and demand accountability for the ongoing terrorism exercised on our immigrant population.
I believe that change is coming. We all need to do what we can to reestablish an America where all are treated with dignity and respect.
Rosie Hartzler
Windham

title: Hegseth’s future in question days after midterms
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The future of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is in question days after the midterm elections. The Democrats have won back control of the House and the Senate, with some states still counting votes.
President Donald Trump has said repeatedly that Hegseth is doing a “very good job.” Congress is considering impeaching Hegseth.
Members of both parties have indicated support for impeaching the defense secretary. Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) has a privileged resolution to impeach Hegseth.
Under House rules, the resolution must be considered during the next voting session, which is next week.
Massie wrote on X: “There is one contingency in which I won’t reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns.”
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) posted on X Friday: “This is about you: the incompetence you’ve displayed, the bad advice you’ve given to the president, and your shameful and embarrassing episodes from firing our top generals to texting war plans to reporters.”
Hegseth said he is prepared for a fight. He released a video Thursday.
“Their obsession with political theater disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents,” Hegseth said. “It’s all about the politics of personal destruction. It didn’t work with President Trump and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”
If Hegseth leaves his post, the path to confirm him could get a lot trickier in the new year. Trump could potentially get a replacement confirmed by the lame-duck Congress. In January, getting a Democratic-controlled Congress to confirm a new defense secretary would be difficult.

title: Actress Kimmarie Johnson, who appeared in 'Dude, Where's My Car?' and 'Beverly Hills, 90210,' dies at 50
How Medicare for All would work in practice
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WMTW) - Senator-elect Troy Jackson said establishing Medicare for All is one of his top goals in Congress, but how would such a program work, and how much support would it have in Congress?
Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced a Medicare for All bill in 2025 that could serve as a framework. If enacted, it would create a single-payer healthcare system in which the government pays for covered care for U.S. residents of all ages.
People would be automatically enrolled at birth or when they establish U.S. residency. Coverage would include primary and preventive care, emergency services, mental health treatment, vision, dental and prescription drugs.
The bill would eliminate copays and coinsurance for covered services, though people above a certain income threshold could pay up to $200 a year for prescription drugs.
Private insurance would still exist, but insurers could only sell coverage for services not included in the national health insurance program.
“We’re going to get more spending, more inefficiency and lower quality care, rather than what Medicare for All advocates are promising,” said Michael Cannon, a health policy expert at the Cato Institute.
Some policy experts like Cannon argue Medicare for All is not the right path to universal coverage, saying private options create competition that pushes providers to offer higher-quality care.
“It would leave us with less freedom, less control over our health care,” Cannon said. “It would enrich inefficient healthcare providers. It would reduce the quality of care.”
An analysis by the Congressional Budget Office also outlined potential concerns about single-payer systems, though it noted that such a system would reduce the number of people who are uninsured and could encourage people to seek more frequent preventative care since they wouldn’t have gaps in coverage.
Including Sanders, the bill had 19 cosponsors, and 18 are expected to return to Washington, D.C., next year.
They would be joined by at least four incoming senators who have expressed support for Medicare for All, including Jackson. Supporters would need to recruit dozens of other lawmakers in both chambers to pass the proposal.

title: Bates Volleyball Celebrates Seniors in End to Hard-Fought Season
text:
Volleyball ended its season on Saturday, Oct. 31, falling to Colby in a hard-fought, five-match game. Bates held their own against the highly ranked Colby team, forcing a fifth match in their final game of the season.
Underhill Arena was decorated to celebrate the seniors on Halloween Day, with friends, family, and President Gerry Jenkins coming out to cheer on the Bobcats. Before the game, the team honored its three seniors, Isabel Bettencourt ‘27, Sofia Castiglioni ‘27, and Logan Yogi ‘27, as they played their last game for Bates.
“I couldn’t have asked for a better group of people to share my last game with,” said Castiglioni, who was named Bobcat of the Week and NESCAC Co-Player of the Week this past September. She contributed twelve kills in her final game as a Bobcat.
The Bobcats won the first set 25-23 in an electric opening set featuring nineteen ties and six lead changes. Each team was neck and neck the entire first set, with the Bobcats pulling ahead at the end to secure the hard-fought victory.
“We knew we had nothing to lose,” said Yogi, who came back to play this year after stepping down her junior year due to injuries. “We all agreed that we would be more disappointed in ourselves if we walked off the court knowing we had played with any doubt or hesitation.”
The second match led to another 25-23 victory for Bates, where the Bobcats quickly pulled ahead and maintained dominance throughout the entire set.
However, with Bates winning 2-0, Colby came back with force during the third and fourth matches, winning each 25-16.
With a tie of 2-2, the atmosphere intensified for the fifth and final match as Bates lost 10-15. This solidified the victory for Colby, who ranks second in NESCAC and now third nationally.
“Although we ultimately came up short, I’m incredibly proud of the fight we put up and how we played together,” Castiglioni said after the game. “Going into the game, we were very aware of [Colby’s caliber] and knew we were going to have to bring our best to compete with them.”
As the seniors stepped off the court after their final game, Yogi said, “I told myself that I was going to play every single point like it was my last, because this time, it really was. I couldn’t be more grateful to have ended my volleyball career surrounded by a team that fought for each other until the very end.”
Bates volleyball finishes their season ranking with an overall record of 11-9 and a 2-8 NESCAC record.

title: ALS is on the rise, tracking cases could tell us why
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, has no cure, and the number of cases is projected to rise. The number of people in the U.S. with the disease is not known because doctors are not required to report cases to their health departments. A growing number of states are making reporting mandatory.
ALS is also known as Lou Gehrig’s disease. It affects the nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord. It is considered a rare disease, and experts say there is no explanation for why the numbers are rising.
Living with ALS
In two years, ALS has taken Jennifer Robb’s ability to walk and to eat most solid food. It is now taking her ability to talk.
Using the text-to-speech tool, Jennifer told us it’s a “constant challenge” where “every day gets harder with loss of function.”
Her hands are her main source of communication, but Jennifer admitted they are getting weaker.
ALS destroys the nerve cells that control voluntary muscle movement. As motor neuron cells die, people lose the ability to walk, talk, swallow and breathe. There is no cure, and the disease is fatal.
Jennifer’s husband, Eric Robb, quit his job as a teacher to become her full-time caregiver. He said the disease is progressing quickly.
“Every month it seems like we have to change up our routine, we have to do things differently,” Eric said. Bedtime for the couple took about 30 minutes when Jennifer was first diagnosed. It now takes two hours to get her to bed and two hours to get her up.
“The disease doesn’t get better. It only gets worse, and that’s what’s tough about it. It’s painful to see somebody go through that because you know that she’s never going to get any of that back,” Eric said.
Research and treatment
Researchers across the country are working to change the course of the disease.
“We hope to put ourselves out of business. We don’t want to be doing this,” said Dr. Stephen Goutman, associate professor of neurology at the University of Michigan and director of its ALS clinic.
Goutman said he has seen people living with ALS for 14 years and has cared for more than a thousand people with the disease. He said the clinic follows close to 300 people at any given time.
Goutman and Ben Murdock, an associate professor of neurology, of the University of Michigan Medical School have spent more than a decade researching the disease. Their work includes constant tests of patients’ blood. The average life expectancy after diagnosis is three years.
“These people are really scared, they’re really terrified by what’s going to happen to them, and it’s really heartbreaking, and so it’s incredibly important to, you know, give people hope or some options,” Murdock said.
Murdock said only a handful of treatments exist for ALS. He said there hasn’t been much meaningful discovery in treatment since the drug Riluzole came on the market more than 30 years ago.
“That’s still the gold standard. It provides an extra, I want to say, two or three months of life,” Murdock said.
Murdock said he would like to see a treatment that provides at least six months to a year, but ultimately the end goal is a cure.
But a cure is much more complicated to find than a treatment, in part because no one knows why people get ALS, how to stop it or what causes it. Among experts, there are suspicions that pollutants in the environment play a role.
“Individuals exposed to metals seem to have this higher risk of ALS, and we don’t entirely know why that is, but it’s giving us something to dig into,” Goutman said.
Researchers said they could better study that if they knew where ALS patients were located.
State reporting requirements
ALS is not a mandated reportable disease. Most illnesses that must be reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention are contagious. Only a few non-communicable diseases, such as cancer, are on the list.
A growing number of states have chosen to require reporting themselves. According to the ALS Association, they are Massachusetts, Vermont, Maine, California, Louisiana, New York, New Jersey and, as of 2025, Michigan.
More than a year after Michigan implemented its rule, the state had not collected a single case.
“We’re waiting on guidance from the health department,” Goutman said.
The Michigan health department declined interview requests. It said that once a pilot collection system is tested at the University of Michigan and is working properly, it will start collecting data statewide.
Goutman and Murdock advocated for the tracking. Murdock said the information will be helpful for studies of environmental exposure.
“Now we can kind of figure out where people have been living, where they come from, and hopefully we can start putting some of those puzzle pieces together,” Murdock said.
Cases are expected to rise nationwide. The projected number of cases in 2022 was nearly 33,000. The projected number for 2026 is 35,000.
Murdock said ALS is the most common rare disease. When asked if it is becoming more common, he said, “Yes, the rates have been going up.”
“The number of people that I care for in the 14 years that I’ve been here has almost doubled, and so there has to be a reason why,” Goutman said.
The rate of ALS is about 1 in every 100,000 people. Jennifer is the third person from her home county in Missouri to get ALS. The county has fewer than 40,000 people.
Missouri health leaders would not know that because it is not among the states tracking the disease.
“I think it needs to be mandated,” Eric Robb said. “People need to be aware of it. And the more they’re aware of it, the more funding there will be, the more help there will be for people with ALS.”
Jennifer told us she thinks the disease is being ignored. When asked if more people with ALS would be seen and the disease would be harder to ignore if reporting were mandated, she said yes.
She advocates for mandated reporting with ALS groups. She said she does not know how much time she has left.
“You have to have hope,” Jennifer said.
National registry and funding
A national ALS registry exists with the CDC. It relies on people self-reporting their disease. The CDC acknowledges it is missing cases because reporting is not mandatory. The CDC also says that even if reporting is mandated, it will rarely capture 100% of cases.
Advocates say more funding could help bring an end to ALS. In early 2026, Congress approved the highest level of funding ever for ALS, $315 million.
Funding for other diseases is in the billions: $8.1 billion for cancer, $3.9 billion for Alzheimer’s disease and $3.3 billion for HIV/AIDS.
The ALS Association says more funding will lead to more answers about ALS and hopefully lead to a cure.

title: School janitor accused of trading vapes for nude photos from girls, sharing photos with a teacher
text:
KINGMAN, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — A school janitor in northwestern Arizona is accused of giving vape pens and alcohol to girls in exchange for naked photos of them.
The Mohave County Sheriff’s Office said Thursday that Pierce Anthony Eller, 41, is facing more than a dozen charges.
Investigators said Eller works as a janitor at a Kingman-area school through a private contractor, and the vape-for-explicit-photos trades started in February with an underage family friend.
The sheriff’s office said there have been 10 trades between Eller and the victim.
Detectives said the victim then told her friends about the deal, and the friends reached out to Eller on social media.
The sheriff’s office said Eller gave three additional girls, ages 14 to 16, vapes and alcohol in exchange for nude photos of them.
Deputies said Eller admitted to the allegations Wednesday and that they found more evidence on his phone.
He was arrested and booked into jail on 10 counts of sexual exploitation of a minor, four counts of luring a minor and four counts of commercial exploitation of a minor.
While processing digital evidence, investigators said they found that the photos were being shared with a teacher, identified as 57-year-old Ronald Wayne Bowman. Bowman taught for the Kingman Unified School District for 24 years, officials said.
Bowman was detained and allegedly admitted to being involved. He was arrested and faces nine charges of sexual exploitation of a minor.
Deputies said none of the victims were students at the school where Eller worked.

title: Mills, Pingree meeting to discuss transition of power
text:
Maine Governor-elect Hannah Pingree meets with Gov. Janet Mills to discuss transition of power
Maine Gov. Janet Mills met with Governor-elect Hannah Pingree on Friday to discuss the upcoming transition of power in Augusta.
In a statement shared after Pingree won the gubernatorial election, Mills said she will ensure a smooth transition. The governor echoed those sentiments while standing beside Pingree during a news conference with members of the media.
"Hannah Pingree is ready to lead on Day One, and I intend to do everything I can to ensure that she and her team have everything they need to hit the ground running," Mills said. "That's why I've pledged my administration's full cooperation in providing the smooth and effective transition that Maine people expect and deserve."
Pingree served in the Mills administration as director of the Governor's Office of Policy Innovation and the Future from January 2019 until she resigned in May 2025 and announced her run for governor a month later.
"I couldn't be prouder that the person Maine chose to lead our state is my friend and former colleague in the Legislature, and former Speaker of the House, Hannah Pingree," Mills said. "I believe Maine people selected Hannah Pingree for the very same reasons that I asked her to serve in my administration eight years ago: her deep experience, her sound judgment, her leadership qualities and her relentless optimism for Maine's future."
"Governor Mills, you have led this state with strength and compassion through some incredibly difficult and important times. You gave me the chance to lead on issues that matter, and you inspired me and encouraged me to take this on," Pingree said. "I thank you for your leadership, for your friendship and for everything you have done for Maine over your very, very long career that I've been so proud to be a part of. I thank you for the grace that you and your team have already shown me in the last couple of days, and I know you'll continue to share for the next couple of months. That means a great deal."
Pingree went on to say that Mainers do not have time to waste, and neither does she.
"Winter is coming. The work does not pause between administrations, so my team and I are committed to a seamless, peaceful and efficient transition," the governor-elect said. "I'm grateful to the governor and her staff for opening their doors and for sharing what they know so that on Jan. 6, when I am officially sworn in, the people of Maine do not miss a beat."
Mills and Pingree also answered questions from members of the media. You can watch their answers to those questions in the YouTube video embedded below.
More about Pingree's transition team
The meeting between the governor and governor-elect comes one day after Pingree announced the staff and volunteers who will lead her transition and plan her inauguration for Wednesday, Jan. 6. Pingree's Transition Committee, which is tasked with identifying candidates for her cabinet, will be co-chaired by former State Sen. Roger Katz and former Penobscot ambassador Maulian Bryant.
"They will be leading a group of volunteers from across Maine who will help me find leaders who put results first and reflect the best of Maine," Pingree said in a statement. "We’ll assemble the most capable and collaborative team possible and start delivering on our vision for Maine’s future."
Pingree will also have a professional staff transition team, which will be co-directed by Scott Ogden, a former congressional aide, and former Portland Mayor Karen Geraghty.
“This transition team brings the energy, experience, optimism, and determination we need to tackle the challenges ahead," the governor-elect said.
The state budget includes an allowance of $5,000 for the governor-elect to spend on support for their transition and inauguration. Under state law, they are required to establish two separate committees to do so. Any additional funds spent must be raised by the governor-elect.
The transition team is expected to make further personnel announcements, including the full membership of the Transition Committee, in the coming days. Interested applicants can apply to serve in Pingree's cabinet and executive office on her new transition website.

title: Letter to the Editor: Medicare Advantage in rural Maine: What seniors need to know before choosing
Financial help available for most CoverME.gov plan enrollees
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A KFF analysis of 276 insurers participating in the Affordable Care Act Marketplace from 50 states and the District of Columbia showed a median proposed premium increase of 15% for 2027. It is the second consecutive year of double-digit premium hikes. (Adobe Stock) Listen to this story HERE Nov 2, 2026 By Kathryn Carley Mainers shopping for health insurance during […]
A KFF analysis of 276 insurers participating in the Affordable Care Act Marketplace from 50 states and the District of Columbia showed a median proposed premium increase of 15% for 2027. It is the second consecutive year of double-digit premium hikes. (Adobe Stock)
Listen to this story HERE
Nov 2, 2026
By Kathryn Carley
Mainers shopping for health insurance during the open enrollment period for CoverME.gov may experience sticker shock from high monthly premiums but health care advocates said financial help is still available.
The Maine Bureau of Insurance has approved an average premium rate increase of roughly 15% for the individual market and about 13% for small businesses.
Ann Woloson, executive director of the Augusta-based Consumers for Affordable Health Care, said most people still qualify for premium subsidies and trained assisters can help them apply in person or online.
“Individuals, for example, who aren’t offered or who can’t afford employer-based coverage. It’s the best place for people to research what their most comprehensive coverage options will be,” Woloson explained.
She stressed people should remain cautious of non-marketplace plans, which often lack comprehensive coverage and make sure they are applying at the official CoverME.gov website. Open enrollment runs through Jan. 15. Enrollment in Maine’s marketplace fell more than 9% this year after hitting record levels of adult enrollment in 2025. Enrollment in dental plans also declined nearly 7% this year.
Woloson urged people to call the Consumers for Affordable Health Care hotline before giving up on health insurance. She noted more than half of Maine households reported carrying medical debt, the majority of which stems from hospital stays.
“Anything that can be done to make it easier for people to get the preventative health care they need so they don’t end up sicker and in a more expensive setting is beneficial, and that’s what health insurance is supposed to be able to do – to help people get the services they need,” Woloson emphasized.
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has developed new identity requirements for marketplace applications but the new rules do not apply to state-based marketplaces like CoverME.gov. New federal rules will prevent many lawfully present immigrants from qualifying for premium subsidies.
Woloson added Consumers for Affordable Health Care can help link people to hospital free care, prescription drug assistance programs and clinics with sliding-scale services.

title: 1 officer killed, 3 wounded in a shooting on a transit bus
text:
LAKEWOOD, Colo. (AP) — A suburban Denver officer was killed and three others were wounded during a firefight on a transit bus that ended with police fatally shooting the gunman, law enforcement authorities said Friday. A bystander also was injured.
The Lakewood officers had responded to a call Thursday evening about a suspicious person attempting to get on a public bus, police spokesperson John Romero said during a news conference. The person may have been involved in a hit-and-run earlier that day, he said.
The man began shooting when officers boarded the Regional Transportation District bus and they fired back, killing the man, authorities said in an update on social media.
The three surviving officers were in stable condition at local hospitals, police said. The bystander’s condition wasn’t known, and it wasn’t clear how they were injured. The names of those involved have not been released.
“Words cannot express the profound sorrow our department and community feel tonight over the loss of our fallen hero, who made the ultimate sacrifice in service to Lakewood,” the police department posted on social media. “Our hearts are heavy, and we stand shoulder-to-shoulder with their loved ones, lifting them up in unwavering support, love, and prayer during this unimaginable time.”
Police said they planned to give another update on Friday.
The shootout happened at a busy intersection about 5 miles (8 kilometers) west of downtown Denver.
A witness, Teddy O’Brien, told NBC affiliate KUSA-TV that he and several other drivers were stopped next to the bus at a red light when the shooting happened. He said several police cruisers surrounded the bus before officers rushed to it with guns and flashlights drawn.
“They hopped on and then shots instantly started ringing from there,” he said. “I instantly just saw shots firing and I ducked down, because you know I’m freaking out at that point.”
O’Brien said he saw only one or two people on the bus besides the driver. He said he heard about 30 or 40 gunshots and saw smoke and flashes of light coming from both the front and back of the bus.
At a hospital after the shooting, dozens of area police officers gathered outside and a bagpiper played “Amazing Grace” in tribute to the officer who was killed. A long procession of police vehicles then left the hospital.
Condolences to the officers and their families poured in on social media.
Gov. Jared Polis and others said they were heartbroken.
“Law enforcement put their lives on the line for our safety everyday,” Polis said in a statement. “Thank you to law enforcement who run into danger to keep us safe and to protect our communities.”
Denver Mayor Mike Johnston said police from his city were assisting Lakewood officials.
The Regional Transportation District said it is deeply concerned by the shooting and is fully cooperating with police as they conduct their investigation.
Colorado State Patrol said in a statement that their hearts are broken over the death of the officer.
“To the three additional Lakewood Agents who were injured in tonight’s shooting, we are sending our deepest prayers, strength and best wishes for a full recovery,” the statement said.
