title: Finish 2026 feeling organized: a year-end money checklist for Maine families
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Why the last weeks of the year matter
Mainers know how to get ready for winter. The wood is stacked, the snow tires are on and the camp was closed up weeks ago. Your finances deserve the same kind of attention, and late fall is the right time to give it.
Several important financial moves have a hard deadline of December 31. Payroll contributions to your retirement plan, required withdrawals from IRAs, and charitable gifts all have to happen inside the calendar year to count. Medicare’s open enrollment window closes even sooner, on December 7.
This year also brings new rules. Federal tax changes that took effect in 2026 change how charitable gifts are deducted, add a new deduction for people 65 and older and require some higher earners to make catch-up contributions as Roth. Those changes land hard in Maine, the oldest state in the country, with a median age of 44.9 and nearly one in four residents 65 or older. A lot of Maine households are making decisions about retirement income, Medicare and passing on a home or camp right now.
You don’t need to do everything at once. The checklist below covers the items that tend to matter most. This year’s dollar limits are in a reference guide at the end.
Your year-end checklist
1. Top off your retirement savings
If you have room in your budget, the last few paychecks of the year are your final chance to add to your workplace plan for 2026. Payroll changes can take a cycle or two to process, so make them in November.
401(k), 403(b) and 457 plans: Check how close you are to the annual limit. If you are 50 or older, you can add extra catch-up contributions, and savers ages 60 to 63 get an even higher limit.
New Roth rule: If you earned more than $150,000 in wages in 2025, any catch-up contributions you make in 2026 must go in as Roth (after-tax) dollars. Check your pay stub to confirm your catch-up is set up correctly.
IRAs: You have until the April 2027 tax filing deadline to contribute for 2026. Income limits may affect whether you can contribute to a Roth IRA or deduct a traditional IRA contribution.
Health savings accounts: If you have a qualifying high-deductible health plan, you also have until April 2027 to contribute for 2026.
2. Plan your retirement income and tax bracket
For retirees and near-retirees, December decisions shape next year’s taxes and Medicare premiums.
Required withdrawals: If you are 73 or older, take your required withdrawal from traditional IRAs and old workplace plans by Dec. 31. If this is your first one, you may be able to wait until April 1, though that means two taxable withdrawals next year. Missing a required withdrawal can trigger a federal penalty of up to 25% of the amount you should have taken, reduced to 10% if it is corrected promptly.
Roth conversions: The years between retirement and the start of Social Security or required withdrawals are often a low-tax window. Converting part of a traditional IRA to a Roth IRA can reduce future required withdrawals and leave more flexibility for you and your heirs. Keep in mind that the converted amount counts as taxable income this year, and a conversion generally makes the most sense when you can pay that tax from savings outside the IRA. Future tax rates are uncertain, so the benefit is not guaranteed.
Watch two income thresholds: Extra income from a conversion or a large withdrawal can shrink the new tax deduction for people 65 and older. Higher income can also raise your Medicare Part B and Part D premiums two years later. A conversion that looks smart on its own can cost more than expected once those are counted.
3. Give with the new rules in mind
Mainers are generous, and 2026 changes how that generosity is treated at tax time.
If you itemize: Only the portion of your charitable giving above 0.5% of your income is deductible. On $200,000 of income, the first $1,000 you give produces no deduction. Grouping two or three years of gifts into one year, sometimes through a donor-advised fund, can help you clear the floor. Contributions to a donor-advised fund are irrevocable, so be sure of the commitment before you make one.
If you take the standard deduction: You can now deduct up to $1,000 of cash gifts ($2,000 for married couples filing jointly) made directly to qualifying charities. Gifts to donor-advised funds do not count toward this deduction.
If you are 70½ or older: You can give directly from your IRA to charity, known as a qualified charitable distribution. The gift doesn’t count as federal taxable income (so it is not also deductible), can count toward your required withdrawal and is not affected by the new 0.5% floor. Custodians need time to process these, so start by early December.
4. Review Medicare and insurance before Dec. 7
Medicare open enrollment runs through Dec. 7, and any changes take effect Jan. 1, 2027. Plans, premiums, and drug coverage change every year, and provider networks can change too. Confirm that your doctors and your pharmacy will still be covered next year before you let your current plan roll over.
If you are still working, use your employer’s open enrollment to revisit your health plan, use any flexible spending account balance you would otherwise lose, and check that your life and disability coverage still fits your family. If you are in your 50s or 60s, it is also worth looking at long-term care coverage, which is generally easier to qualify for, with lower premiums, at younger ages. And ask your property insurance agent whether your homeowners, camp and umbrella coverage keeps pace with today’s replacement costs.
5. Update beneficiaries and estate documents
The beneficiary forms on your retirement accounts and life insurance override your will. If you have had a marriage, divorce, death or new grandchild in the family, check that those forms still say what you want them to say.
Maine also has its own estate tax, and in 2026 it starts at less than half the federal threshold. Between a home, a camp, retirement accounts and life insurance, some Maine families may be closer to that threshold than they expect. Life insurance you own generally counts toward the total. For some families, an irrevocable life insurance trust set up with an estate attorney can hold a policy outside the taxable estate; the trade-off is giving up control of the policy.
A few practical steps:
– Confirm you have a current will, durable financial power of attorney and health care directive, and that the people named in them know where to find them.
– If you want the family camp to stay in the family, talk with an estate attorney about how ownership, expenses and decisions will be shared among the next generation.
– If you plan to help children or grandchildren, gifts up to the annual IRS limit generally don’t require a gift tax return. Married couples who combine gifts may need to file one.
6. Have the family conversation
The holidays bring families together, and that makes them a natural time to talk about the practical side of getting older. Many Mainers are helping an aging parent while still supporting their own children. A short, calm conversation now about where documents are kept, who will step in if help is needed and what a parent wants for their care can prevent a crisis later. If you are the one being cared for someday, your family will thank you for having it.
Your next steps, by date
Put these on the calendar now so nothing sneaks up on you.
This week: Pull your latest pay stub and check how much you have contributed to your retirement plan and HSA so far this year. Log in to your retirement accounts and confirm your beneficiaries.
By mid-November: Submit any payroll changes to increase contributions. If you are 73 or older, request your required withdrawal if you haven’t already.
By December 7: Finalize any Medicare plan changes for 2027.
By early December: Request qualified charitable distributions and any Roth conversions so your custodian has time to complete them. Make your charitable gifts.
By December 31: Confirm every distribution, conversion and gift has been completed and posted to your account.
In January: Gather your tax documents and schedule a review of your full plan for the year ahead.
Start the new year with a plan
A checklist is a good start. Just as important is seeing how the pieces connect: how a Roth conversion affects your Medicare premiums, how a charitable gift can satisfy a required distribution and how your beneficiary forms line up with your estate plan.
That is the work we do every day at Lebel & Harriman Retirement Advisors, an independent, Maine-owned firm in Falmouth that has been helping families and employers since 1978. Our Personal Financial Services team brings financial planning, investment management, and insurance guidance together in one coordinated relationship, whether you are still building savings or drawing income in retirement. We work alongside your attorney and accountant so the pieces fit together. You get straight answers in plain English, recommendations built around your goals and a relationship meant to last for decades.
If you would like a second set of eyes on your year-end checklist, we are happy to help. Reach our team at [email protected] or (207) 773-5390, or visit lebelharriman.com.

title: Cornell faculty vote ‘no confidence’ in university leadership
text:
Cornell faculty vote ‘no confidence’ in university leadership
Cornell University's Faculty Senate approved a resolution Friday declaring “no confidence” in the school's top leaders, a symbolic gesture reflecting deep discontent on campus in the wake of a former student's lawsuit saying she was gang raped at a fraternity party in 2024.
The resolution passed 75-50, with five faculty senators abstaining and five others not voting, according to an email sent to Faculty Senate members on Friday afternoon.
The vote followed weeks of debate among professors over whether Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff and other administrators handled the woman’s allegations properly and have done enough to curtail sexual misconduct at the prestigious university.
Related video above: 'You deserve to be safe': bipartisan campus safety bill promises help for survivors
While the faculty body has no power over the university's top leaders, backers of the resolution had said they hoped it would pressure Cornell's trustees to address longstanding institutional failures they identified.
Board of Trustees Chair Anne Smalling said in a statement the faculty vote “reflects the deep anger across our campus” and sent a clear signal that what happened to the woman was unacceptable, but added that Kotlikoff and his administration were the right leaders to “thoughtfully and comprehensively” address the issue.
Thomas Giuffra, an attorney for the woman who filed the lawsuit, said in a statement Friday that “we are hopeful that this will be yet another step forward to educate and support the Cornell community by addressing the longstanding scourge of sexual assault on campus.”
Lawsuit sparked outrage on campus
The Cornell community has been distressed since mid-September, when a former student, identified only by the pseudonym Jane Doe in court documents, filed a lawsuit against the university and seven former members of the Chi Phi fraternity, saying she was given ketamine and raped at a fraternity house in October 2024.
All of the men have denied her allegations, saying the sex was consensual or that they weren’t involved. The local district attorney initially decided the woman had consented to the encounter and that no crime had been committed, but the investigation has since been reopened and handed to New York’s attorney general.
Cornell disciplined several of the accused students following a monthslong Title IX investigation. Two were expelled, two received suspensions and probation, and two were required to write “reflection” papers and complete bystander training. A seventh man had already graduated and was barred from campus, according to records obtained by The New York Times.
Kotlikoff also convened a task force to study the problem of sexual misconduct on campus, which released certain recommendations.
Some faculty members have criticized Kotlikoff for not acting more forcefully to strengthen the school's disciplinary process, push for criminal investigations and change campus party culture.
Paul Ortiz, a labor history professor who co-sponsored the no-confidence resolution, said last week that hundreds of students, staff, alumni and faculty approached the resolution’s sponsors to emphasize that “the Jane Doe case is but a tip of the iceberg” and that “a veritable fortress of silence has been breached” around sexual violence since the resolution’s introduction.
Cornell's president defended his leadership
Speaking to Faculty Senate members on the first day that they debated the no-confidence resolution, Kotlikoff pledged to make the university a leader in addressing sexual assault and asked for more time to make changes.
Kotlikoff defended his leadership, arguing that replacing him would do little to solve complex problems and could damage Cornell’s reputation. He acknowledged he had not read the campus police report, explaining that university policy barred top administrators from interfering in criminal investigations. He also rejected suggestions he had been indifferent to the woman’s case, though he acknowledged only recently learning she had left Cornell.
Kotlikoff said the university needed to determine whether fraternities could operate safely and left open the possibility of sweeping restrictions on Greek life. He argued that decisions should be based on research and evidence rather than emotion.
Some professors had said faculty should wait to vote until the release of an independent investigation by former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates, whom the university hired to examine how Cornell responded to the woman's initial rape report in 2024 and its overall procedures for handling similar reports from other students.
Yasmeen Masoud, a Cornell junior who spoke Friday at a news conference organized by the resolution’s sponsors, called the vote encouraging for students frustrated with the university’s response.
“We should not have to beg for answers, demand basic transparency or generate media attention just to get our concerns acknowledged,” she said. “It reminds us that there are people across this university who care deeply about its future and are willing to stand together to demand a better Cornell.”
Iris Packman, a co-sponsor of the no-confidence resolution, said Friday that the vote was “only the beginning” and that faculty would push for sweeping reforms.
The no-confidence resolution did not call for Kotlikoff’s resignation.

title: Graduation ceremony held for new loggers from KVCC logging program
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
HINCKLEY, Maine (WABI) - After the conclusion of a 20-week program, students from the KVCC logging program will soon be entering their new “office” in the woods.
The 10th graduation ceremony was held near the Harold Alfond campus farm Thursday afternoon, recognizing 15 new graduates from Kennebec Valley Community College’s Mechanized Logging and Forestry Trucking Program.
The program, now in its 10th year, runs from June to November. The program is designed to help students operate mechanized logging equipment, identify commercial wood, and prepare contract work in the logging industry.
“We’re going to be half a million-dollar machines all the time. Being able to understand what you’re going to do with them all the time and when you go into the real workforce. You help keep contractors going,” said graduate Jackson Newton.
Throughout the course, students trained on nearly $5 million worth of forestry equipment loaned by regional equipment dealers, helping prepare students in managing both old and state-of-the-art machinery for contract workers.
“People who want to hop in one of these machines, you can’t do. Like people just don’t want. some random person running their multi-million dollar or half a million-dollar machine with no experience,” said graduate Samuel Armstrong.
Instructors say that generous support gives young operators invaluable seat time in modern machinery before entering the workforce.
“We love to see them come in the first day, not really sure about what they were doing and what they know. Some of them didn’t know the difference between hardwood and softwood. We’ve taken them from there to merchandising some of the big money wood,” said Program Coordinator Donald Burr.
Graduates are now preparing to take their commercial driver’s license (CDL) exams before beginning full-time jobs with logging contractors across the state.
“I bet when we get into the real world it’ll be a lot more different, a lot faster pace,” said Newton, “I’ve learned a lot and I’m ready.”

title: Aging Untold: What older adults should know about sexual health and protection
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we address sexual health after 60, discussing essential screenings and how older adults can stay protected while dating.
We explore how creative outlets like music, dance and art can support mood, dignity and connection for loved ones living with dementia.
Finally, we celebrate the historic Morehouse College Glee Club and its century-old legacy of brotherhood, leadership and community service.
“Getting older does not make you immune to getting a sexually transmitted disease,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said. “Just because you retired, your sexual health didn’t.”
If you are dating again for the first time in decades, there have been changes in sexual health.
Rogers said appearances do not show whether someone has a sexually transmitted disease, and age does not change the risk.
So older adults have to take precautions to protect themselves against several diseases, and condoms are about more than preventing pregnancy, she said.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said she has seen the impact the arts can have on people with memory impairments.
She saw it with a client when a caregiver took her to art classes and the woman started creating pictures and watercolors.
Music, dance, poetry, storytelling and art can tap into emotion and long-held experiences for someone with dementia. While they do not cure dementia, they can support mood, dignity and connection.
O’Rourke said families can begin by searching for available resources in their own area.
Some patients say they find that paying cash for medical procedures rather than filing insurance claims can be significantly cheaper for certain services.
When Greta Fuller’s 10-year-old son needed an MRI for severe abdominal pain in fall 2024, they went to a provider that doesn’t accept insurance.
Patients pay about $500 out of pocket for an MRI scan.
“That was amazing because we had talked with friends who’ve spent $2,000 after insurance,” Fuller said.
The Morehouse College Glee Club has performed at presidential inaugurations, Super Bowls and the Atlanta Olympics.
Behind every performance is a deeper mission — their voices rise not just in song, but in leadership.
“At Morehouse College, Glee Club is an immediate expression of brotherhood, a united force of dedication and commitment, and an unselfish labor of love,” said Desmond Thompson, a proud member of the 38-member group.
That Morehouse message is one of service and leadership, producing men of distinction for nearly 158 years.

title: Hearing scheduled in Deven Young murder case as prosecutors seek adult trial
text:
Deven Young agrees to be tried as an adult in Crawford Pond murder case
Young, who was 17 at the time he was accused of killing Sunshine Stewart, waived his right to a bind-over hearing
Deven Young agrees to be tried as an adult in Crawford Pond murder case
Young, who was 17 at the time he was accused of killing Sunshine Stewart, waived his right to a bind-over hearing
Deven Young, the Maine teenager who stands accused of killing a paddleboarder at Crawford Pond in Union, has agreed to be tried as an adult in the case.
Young waived his right to a bind-over hearing during a status conference that was held in Knox County Superior Court on Friday.
A judge confirmed Young will be tried as an adult, and he will be held without bail at the Knox County Jail. The case will now go before a grand jury, and another status conference is scheduled for January.
Now 19 years old, Young was 17 when he was charged with the July 2025 murder of Sunshine "Sunny" Stewart.
Prosecutors and the defense team were expected to address issues related to the potential bind-over hearing, which would have determined whether Young would be tried as an adult or a juvenile.
The Maine Attorney General's Office has sought to have Young tried as an adult. A judge would have made that determination after a bind-over hearing, a proceeding in which the court considers evidence, including the seriousness of the alleged offense and evaluations of the defendant.
At a status conference in September, a judge expressed frustration with the delays in scheduling a bind-over hearing after Young's defense team said they needed more time to evaluate Young at the Long Creek Youth Development Center in South Portland. The judge originally had wanted to schedule a bind-over hearing in December.
However, the defense said their expert needed about three months to complete a report after meeting with Young, and the Attorney General's Office would then need time to review it. The judge then said the process could push the bind-over hearing into 2027.
Since Young will be tried as an adult, he could face a sentence of at least 25 years and up to life in prison if convicted.
Sunshine Stewart's death on a pond in Union
Stewart, 48, was found dead by Maine Game Wardens on July 3, 2025, on or near 100-Acre Island in Crawford Pond in Union, one day after she went paddleboarding.
Authorities said a medical examiner determined that Stewart died from strangulation and blunt force trauma.
Young was arrested in connection with the death and has been held at Long Creek Youth Development Center.
A judge ruled in April that Young is competent to proceed with the case, finding that he has a factual and rational understanding of the proceedings and is able to consult with his attorneys.
Much of the evidence in the case remains sealed because the prosecution began while Young was a juvenile.

title: These researchers can trace a World War II veteran’s service for families
text:
NEW ORLEANS, La. (InvestigateTV) — A program at the National World War II Museum in New Orleans is helping families learn about their loved ones’ service by tracking down veterans’ official records.
Researchers can find details that include training, medical history, units, battles and promotions.
InvestigateTV’s own Tisha Powell used the program to learn more about her grandfather, Ulysses Reed Sr.
On Dec. 7, 1941, Japan launched a surprise military attack on the U.S. naval base at Pearl Harbor in Oahu, Hawaii. The attack killed more than 2,400 Americans, sank or damaged 21 ships and destroyed 188 airplanes. The U.S. officially entered the war the next day.
Of the 16.4 million Americans who served in the war, fewer than 46,000 are still alive. Many families are left with unanswered questions about what their loved ones did and endured during the war.
“There’s one half of one percent of American World War II veterans that are still with us today. And so, every time we can bring a veteran to campus or someone who experienced the war in some sort of way, it is a joy and it is an honor,” said Chrissy Gregg of the National WWII Museum.
Gregg said it’s up the museum and researchers “to continue to tell their stories.”
Records trace Reed’s service
Reed was laid to rest April 28, 2012, in a small Louisiana cemetery. He was 100 years old and a U.S. Army World War II combat veteran. Powell said many details of his military service had remained unknown.
Reed was a laborer from the community of Chackbay who was drafted and traveled thousands of miles to Europe during the war.
Dr. Mike Bell, executive director of the Jenny Craig Institute for the Study of War and Democracy at the museum, said researchers can now trace Reed’s service from the time he joined his company after basic training at Camp Beauregard, Louisiana, until he was released from the company at Camp Shelby, Mississippi, to go home. According to Bell, that was likely the winter of 1945.
Bell shared the findings with Powell this spring, after researchers spent weeks searching documents.
“We went in, we found his 1940 registration for the draft, so you can confirm it’s him. Where he lives” Bell said.
Reed’s official military personnel file from the National Archives Records Administration in St. Louis was lost in a 1973 fire. The fire destroyed 80% of Army and Army Air Corps records from 1912 to 1960.
“Millions of records were wiped out in that. And these were the personnel files of the individuals,” Bell said.
Museum researchers, who are veterans themselves, then turned to the Bayou History Center and Nicholls State University in Thibodaux, Louisiana.
“Now, why that was incredibly powerful, though, is it gave us the company he was in,” Bell said.
Unit moved ammunition across Europe
Reed served in the 679th Ordnance Company, which managed ammunition. “Morning reports” detailed the company’s movements.
Records showed the company was formed with soldiers who went to a camp outside Wilmington, North Carolina. Other soldiers who formed the company came from Fort Bragg.
The two groups went to Fort Stewart, Georgia, outside Savannah, for field training. They then traveled by train to Camp Kilmer, New Jersey.
“From there, they’ll board a secret ship. I haven’t figured out exactly which ship yet,” Bell said. He said the records list the ship as secret.
The ship sailed from the United States to Lancashire, England. The 679th then traveled to Wales and later deployed into France, where the company set up miles of ammunition supply points. The company later moved into Germany.
“They’re breaking down ammo, categorizing it, issuing ammunition, you know, moving the supply point to the next phase,” Bell said. “And so in Germany, his unit actually moves into the Rhineland. They’ll support 7th Army as they cross the Rhine River.”
Bell said the company’s “incredible work” allowed Allied troops to advance the campaign in Europe. “Without fuel and ammo, you know, you’re not going to win the war.”
The company pushed forward into Czechoslovakia and then headed back to France after Germany’s surrender in May 1945. The men were still in France when Japan surrendered on September 2, 1945.
“From there, we found the ship that he leaves France on,” Bell said. “He’s on the ship. Yeah, the General R.E. Callen, it leaves Marseille and comes back to the United States.”
The General R. E. Callen would dock near Taunton, Massachusetts and Camp Myles Standish on September 12, 1945. Back on US soil, then PFC Reed and the 679th head to Monterey California to Fort Ord in route to the Pacific.
Research services help families fill gaps
“I wish I had asked more questions when he was alive,” Powell said.
“Well, you know, I think our task is to try to recapture some of that. You know, to give a little agency and voice to these people,” Bell said.
That is the goal of the museum’s Historical Research Services. Research historians work to verify records that can help family members learn about a World War II veteran’s service when their own searches have stalled.
If historians determine the available records contain substantial information about the veteran’s service, families can receive the veteran’s WWII story in the form of a book.
“That generation, in many cases, they just came home and went back to work. And, you know, or they didn’t talk about it just among everybody. How would you understand what they did? Or, uh, I just did my job,” Bell said.
After the war, Reed returned to Louisiana to his wife and young daughters.
During the war, he was able to send home about $900 and his wife bought “upwards of 20 acres of land.”
“So, this service changed the trajectory of my family’s life,” Powell said.
“It’s interesting in the 1950 census, he’s a landowner, you know, in the 1940 census, he’s unemployed,” Bell said.
To Bell and others who work to find information in the records, they feel like they are giving the veterans agency and a voice. “So that we understand what they did, but also to understand why they did it and the importance of it and what they achieved.”
Fee and POW/MIA program
The museum’s research services have a fee. It costs $165 to obtain a veteran’s file.
The museum is also part of the Department of Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency’s Hub and Spoke Program.
The program is a national initiative working to locate and identify American service members who remain unaccounted for from World War II and other conflicts.

title: Recalled playsets sold on Amazon and Walmart pose a risk of injury or death, commission says
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(CNN) - Playsets sold on Amazon and Walmart have been recalled because a child’s head or neck could get trapped, posing a risk of serious injury or death.
Arlopu is recalling about 10,000 of its slide playsets.
The Consumer Product Safety Commission said the playsets have openings that a child’s torso can fit through but a child’s head cannot. It said that poses the risk of injury or death due to potential neck entrapment.
Regulators said one of the models also features basketball nets that can detach and pose dangers.
The recalled playsets have model numbers KTCS17 and LY31. They’re for indoor or outdoor use and come in tan, red, blue, yellow, gray and green.
The CPSC said Amazon and Walmart sold the playsets online from April 2023 through August 2026.
Arlopu said it received one report of a child getting trapped in the playset, resulting in abrasions to the child’s neck.
Customers are advised to stop using the playsets and keep them away from their children. They can contact Arlopu for a free repair kit that includes redesigned panels, basketball hoops and installation instructions.

title: Trump makes the Oval Office a national monument
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Thursday signed a proclamation that he says will preserve the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as a national monument, his first official action after his party was swept aside in midterm elections on Tuesday.
But the action does not prevent future presidents from restyling the iconic office that Trump has filled to the brim with gold flourishes, nor does it prevent a successor from rolling back the proclamation itself. Trump himself has reversed national monument designations made by his predecessors.
Trump, however, described the Oval Office order in expansive terms. “It will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape,” Trump said. “We like the Oval Office, and it’s a symbol, like the White House itself.”
It was the third day this week that the president, a real estate mogul, delivered remarks fixated on his pet projects in Washington. On Wednesday, a day after Republicans suffered defeats in key races across the country, Trump gathered reporters to sign the final beam being raised during construction of his opulent ballroom project. On Monday, he went to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to talk about his renovation of the landmark.
The proclamation, released after Trump’s remarks, says that nothing in it will “restrict the President’s authority to redecorate the monument, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument’s historic structure or architectural character.”
It orders the Interior secretary to manage the Oval Office and requires “documentation, review, and consideration of alternatives before any action that would substantially alter or demolish the monument.” Trump separately said any major changes would need review from Congress, though such a requirement is not in the document’s text.
“If they want to say, ‘Let’s not have oval anymore, let’s make it square,’ what happens is they have to go back to Congress and hopefully the Congress, the people in Congress, will be smart enough not to let that happen,” said Trump — who notably demolished the East Wing of the White House to make room for his ballroom.
A red baseball cap with “VETO” on the front was sitting on the Resolute Desk as Trump signed the document, a not-so-subtle nod to the shifting of powers in Congress.
His effort to preserve changes at the White House comes as Democrats gear up for new scrutiny of Trump. Connecticut Sen. Richard Blumenthal, the top Democrat on the Homeland Security Committee’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, sent a flurry of letters Thursday to known donors to Trump’s ballroom, demanding that they provide information or face “alternative measures to obtain compliance.”
Since returning to the White House, Trump has overseen numerous design changes to various rooms, including the Oval Office, where he has filled the wall space with portraits, a copy of the Declaration of Independence and numerous golden accents.
As he talked about his interior decorating decisions, Trump highlighted new chandeliers that he says were installed in the Cabinet Room to address “very bad lighting.” His other additions to the Oval Office include numerous gold wall appliqués and gold-framed portraits.
Trump did not elaborate on precisely what he was hoping to prevent but suggested that the Oval Office might face some threat in the future. Trump himself has faced several lawsuits alleging that his Washington beautification projects were done without the necessary approval.
“If anybody ever decides to come and start knocking down walls, you call me wherever I may be,” Trump said, “and I’ll come back here and I’ll make sure it never happens.”

title: Douglas Carlisle Jr. prepares to represent Maine House District 5
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Republican Douglas Carlisle Jr. is preparing to represent Maine House District 5 in Augusta after winning Tuesday’s general election.
Carlisle defeated Democrat Lori Kenneson. He will succeed Republican Joseph Underwood, who did not seek reelection.
First term in Augusta
This is Carlisle’s first time as a representative for Aroostook County in Augusta. He said property tax reform and rising energy costs are among his top priorities, along with addressing homelessness in the community.
Carlisle said he is grateful for the support he received and is ready to get to work.
“It’s been a long process. It was thankful that it was over and that we were moving forward in the process. We know that there’s a lot of work that needs to be done in our state,” Carlisle said.
Working across party lines
Carlisle also emphasized the importance of working across party lines. He said he has already reached out to Kenneson to discuss areas where they can find common ground.
“I know there’s a lot of issues we don’t agree on, but we have to find those areas where we can agree and push those things forward,” Carlisle said.
Plans for the term
Carlisle said he plans to seek input from residents throughout his first two-year term. He also wants to improve transparency in the legislative process.
He said he intends to continue coaching local youth while serving in Augusta.

Owner charged after several horses die in flood; refused to let neighbors help move animals to higher ground, sheriff says
text:
CAMP VERDE, AZ (AZFamily/Gray News) — An arrest has been made following an investigation involving several horses that died during recent flooding in Arizona.
The Camp Verde Marshal’s Office said on Thursday that the suspect, whose name has not been released, is facing animal cruelty charges.
On Sunday, first responders were called to a property following reports that several horses were trapped in rising floodwaters. Investigators said emergency personnel and neighbors offered to help move the horses to higher ground, but the owner refused to release them from their enclosures.
The marshal’s office said the owner received repeated warnings about worsening weather but didn’t move the horses before floodwaters overtook them.
Crews spent the following days searching for the horses. While four horses were rescued, three were found dead. Four other horses are missing and presumed dead.
Investigators collected evidence, spoke with witnesses and emergency responders and reviewed veterinary evaluations before arresting the horses’ owner.
“The Camp Verde Marshal’s Office recognizes and appreciates the extraordinary efforts of Copper Canyon Fire and Medical Authority, Emergency Equine Evacuation, veterinary professionals, neighboring residents, and volunteers who worked tirelessly under extremely dangerous conditions to save these animals,” the agency posted on Facebook. “Animal welfare is a responsibility that should never be taken lightly. Animals depend on their owners for appropriate care, protection and safety, particularly during emergencies and natural disasters.”
More than 100 homes were damaged, a dozen of which are a total loss, after severe flooding in Camp Verde.

title: How to use music and art with a loved one living with dementia
text:
(Aging Untold) — Music, dance, poetry, storytelling and art can still tap into emotion and long-held experiences for someone with dementia.
While they do not cure dementia, they can support mood, dignity and connection.
Start by looking locally
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said families can begin by searching for available resources in their own area.
“Dance and dementia. Arts and dementia. Music and dementia,” O’Rourke suggested.
She shared an experience of seeing the impact during her first job out of college.
O’Rourke was an activity director, where residents took part in a bell choir at the time.
“Each resident had a bell and the director would point, and you could just see the impact it had on them,” O’Rourke said.
Don’t set expectations
O’Rourke also described a caregiver who took a client with a memory impairment to an art class, and the client started producing pictures and watercolors.
“She had never done art before. She had never drawn. She had never done any kind of artwork at all,” O’Rourke said. “And so I realized, don’t put any expectation on someone with a memory impairment. Anything is possible.”
“Look locally and just think about the connection that they’re going to have inside and with you,” O’Rourke said.
Tapping into long-term memory
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said the arts often use a different part of the brain.
“You’re tapping into something that maybe hasn’t been affected yet,” Cradduck said. “And it does hold some long-term memories. Think about smells, we oftentimes associate smells and memories, arts and memories. And the old gospels. That’s the one that I find taps in a lot when it comes to music.”
Cradduck described a video of Naomi Feil, who she said is the mother of the validation technique in dementia training. In the video, Feil is with a woman who had not spoken for a number of years.
“She just started tapping her arm and singing ‘Jesus Loves You,’” Cradduck said. “She just kept doing it, and she got faster and faster with the rhythm. All of a sudden, this woman who hadn’t spoken a word in years started singing this song.”
Cradduck said the arts tap into some core memories.
Telling the story a different way
While dementia changes memory, it does not change how a person tells their story, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
“They find a different way to tell the story,” Rogers said. “In terms of creativity and the arts, that is a different area of the brain and a lot of times it’s not impacted by dementia.”
A calming activity
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said the benefits extend beyond memory.
“It’s not just memory. It’s cognition,” she said. “You’re tapping into a creative outlet that might give people a way to express themselves, which is calming.”
Ambrose said the arts also help caregivers.
“It gives you a peaceful activity that everyone can be a part of,” Ambrose said. “Sometimes it can be agitating, but most of the time it’s worth trying because it can be something really powerful for therapy and a powerful form of care.”
Dementia can take away a person’s abilities, but it does not remove a person’s ability to feel, Cradduck added.
“You can feel beauty and you can feel rhythm,” she said.
Key takeaways
- Search locally. Look for local resources such as dance, arts and music programs for people with dementia.
- Set no expectations. A person with a memory impairment may take to art without having done it before.
- Expression can be calming. The arts can give people a way to express themselves and give caregivers a peaceful shared activity.

title: 25 years after 'Britney,' 5 new Britney Spears songs showcase a pop icon at a transformative moment
text:
25 years after 'Britney,' 5 new Britney Spears songs showcase a pop icon at a transformative moment
Britney Spears was at a crossroads — and not just because the film “Crossroads” was soon to be released, marking her acting debut.
Video above: Britney Spears' memoir sells 1.1M U.S. copies in first week
The year was 2001. Spears, then just 19, was one of the most famous people on the planet, championed as the ultimate teen dream by legions of fans across the globe and a leering celebrity industry. That year, she'd performed during the Super Bowl halftime show and changed the course of fashion forever — first, showing up with beau Justin Timberlake in matching denim at the American Music Awards and then with an albino python around her neck during her performance at the MTV Video Music Awards.
She was entering adulthood, full steam ahead, after enjoying a meteoric run with her first two albums, 1999's “… Baby One More Time” and 2000's “Oops! … I Did It Again.” Her third album, “Britney,” was being released just ahead of her 20th birthday and would prove transformative.
Legacy Recordings on Friday is releasing “Britney (25th Anniversary Edition),” an expanded reissue of her pivotal record, which went quadruple platinum in less than two months. The collection features two remixes and five previously unreleased songs from that era, her first new (or is it old?) music since she announced she would “never return to the music industry” in a 2024 Instagram post.
The release is an opportunity to reflect on the album and Spears' unique position in popular culture's imagination — particularly following the news of the last few years. In 2021, she was released from a court conservatorship that controlled the pop singer’s life and money for nearly 14 years. And in February, it was announced that she had sold the rights to her music catalog to Primary Wave for an undisclosed sum.
Listening to 'Britney,' 25 years later
The album opens with a spoken-word declaration. Back in 2001, it was considered a provocation — as it often is when a young woman expresses her own prerogative.
“I know I may be young,” Spears seduces over choppy R&B production, courtesy The Neptunes, the award-winning duo of Pharrell Williams and Chad Hugo. “But I’ve got feelings, too.”
The song is the single “I'm A Slave 4 U,” where Spears made it clear that the bubblegum pop of her previous releases had been traded in for something decidedly more mature. And that's true even of the album's songs written and produced by previous collaborators Max Martin and Rami Yacoub — tracks like “Bombastic Love” still sparkle, but with newfound edge.
If Spears was borrowing from the teen-to-adult pop star trajectory laid forth by forebears like Madonna or Janet Jackson on “Britney,” she did so while keeping it PG-13 — hinting at developed sensuality as a means to express self-definition, but remaining accessible and agreeable to her younger audience. To put it another way, she toes the line: “I'm not a girl, not yet a woman,” as the single goes.
That's all while proclamations of autonomy — sexual and otherwise — punctuate the album. “Say hello to the girl that I am,” she invites on “Overprotected.” “Now I live for me,” she flips the script on “Lonely.” “She's in control,” on the funky, erotic “Boys.”
A sense of self-reflection is amplified by the fact that the album is self-titled, and that Spears co-wrote five songs on the original album: “Lonely,” “Anticipating,” “Let Me Be,” “That's Where You Take Me” and the spiky “Cinderella.”
The previously unreleased 'Britney' songs add to Spears' mythology
The first of the five archival tracks is “She’ll Never Be Me,” co-written with Timberlake, her then-boyfriend, who also sings background. Timberlake cowrote a track on the original album, but the new release comes after Spears wrote about their relationship in her 2023 memoir, sharing deeply personal details about a pregnancy, abortion and painful breakup.
As far as how it fits in with the rest of the album, the song slots in nicely with its vocal effects and propulsive Y2K production — by any measure, it makes for a fine B-side.
The same could be said of the rest, from the slow-burn fake-out “Am I A Sinner" and Latin pop-informed rhythms of “Right Now (Taste the Victory)” to the glitchy, proto-hyperpop “When I Say So” and soulful, unusually lengthy “My Big Secret,” which features Spears' strongest vocal performance of the whole album. It's a stunning falsetto.
Thematically, a number of these tracks could be read as a response to the tabloid press' obsession with Spears' virginity at the time of its release. “I don't want to mislead you,” she sings on “When I Say So.” “You'll get some when I say so.”
And on “Am I A Sinner” she may very well be reflecting back on an unjust media — or any bad relationship: “Tell me, am I a sinner? / Tell me, am I wrong? / Something's wrong with the picture / This is not my fault.”
Since the release of her bestselling memoir, “The Woman in Me” — which details her childhood, rise to stardom, marriages, motherhood and conservatorship — fans have worked to recontextualize how Spears was portrayed early on in her career. These songs will no doubt inspire more detective work. But others may approach it more simply, through the rose-colored glasses of easy nostalgia.
In the end, it is an album written and recorded in the space between adolescence and adulthood, from the woman a generation looked to for guidance on doing the same.

title: Democrats take huge majorities in Maine Legislature, setting up a powerful trifecta
text:
The new Maine Legislature, when it convenes next month, will look much bluer.
Riding a national wave, Maine Democrats flipped 17 Republican-held seats across both chambers on their way to huge majorities — their largest in the House since the 2008 election, and their largest in the Senate since the 1984 election.
Battleground districts all across the state went to Democrats, and some non-battlegrounds, too. Even the district currently held by Rep. Laurel Libby flipped this cycle. One of the stars of the Maine Republican Party, she did not run for reelection.
In the upper chamber, Maine Democrats will hold a two-thirds supermajority: 24 seats to Republicans’ 11. In the Maine House, Democrats and the independents who caucus with them will hold a 90-61 majority.
With Hannah Pingree being elected governor, Democrats will have a solid trifecta, leaving Republicans with little power to affect the legislative agenda.
Both parties announced their leadership positions on Friday.
Senate Democrats reelected Mattie Daughtry of Brunswick as Senate president, Sen. Teresa Pierce of Falmouth as majority leader and Sen. Jill Duson of Portland as assistant leader.
House Democrats said they would renominate Rep. Ryan Fecteau of Biddeford for another term as speaker. Rep. Matt Moonen of Portland will continue as the majority leader and Rep. Ambureen Rana of Bangor will serve as assistant majority leader.
The Senate Republicans reelected Sen. Trey Stewart of Presque Isle to serve as minority leader, while Sen. David Haggan of Hampden will serve in the assistant role. The House Republicans tapped Rep. Kenneth Fredette of Newport to serve as leader and Rep. Alicia Collins of Sidney as assistant leader.
Let’s take a look at the flips in each chamber of the Maine Legislature after Tuesday’s sweeping elections.
SENATE SWEEP
In Maine’s 35-seat upper chamber, Democrats will hold their first two-thirds supermajority in a generation. Democrats invested in these Senate races heavily, outspending Republican outside groups handily.
In Senate District 15, Democrat Amanda Heath flipped a seat held by Republican Sen. Dick Bradstreet, who didn’t run for reelection, by a four-point margin. That Augusta-based Kennebec County district hadn’t been won by a Democrat since 2012.
Senate District 16, based in Kennebec and Somerset counties, flipped to the Democrats, too. Patric Moore defeated incumbent Sen. Scott Cyrway, a Republican from Albion, by more than 1,000 votes. Cyrway himself flipped that district two years ago, but Democrats have reclaimed it.
The Oxford County seat held by Republican-turned-independent gubernatorial candidate Rick Bennett, Senate District 18, also flipped to Democrats. Elizabeth Bosworth defeated John Andrews by just 50 votes.
And in the Auburn-based Senate District 20, incumbent Republican Sen. Bruce Bickford was defeated by Democrat Michael Scott by about 960 votes.
Those four flips — and Democrats’ successful defense of every seat they already held — means a historic 24-11 majority.
“I’m incredibly proud of this supermajority, and it was not the result of national political environment,” Senate President Mattie Daughtry, D-Brunswick, said in a statement Friday. “It took two years of hard work from our candidates, our staff, and folks all across Maine who knocked on hundreds of thousands of doors.”
HOUSE MAJORITY GROWS
Having started the campaign with just a three-seat majority, Democrats will now have a comfortable 90-61 hold over the House; 87 Democrats won, as well as three independents who plan to caucus with them.
This was the chamber of the Maine Legislature that Republicans were much more bullish on their chances of winning control of. Spending was even in their favor in the most competitive seats.
But every incumbent Democrat won, and Democrats flipped 13 seats, while Republicans only flipped one.
“We’re certainly glad to have won, especially after going into this election defending one of the narrowest majorities in Maine’s history and coming out with one of the largest,” Sean Smith, director of the House Democratic Campaign Committee, said in a statement Friday. “But the real victory will be making life a little more affordable for Maine people.”
The only Republican flip came in the consistently competitive House District 96 in Lewiston, where Republican Kerryl Clement defeated Democrat Luke Jensen by 30 votes. Two years ago, retiring Democratic Rep. Mike Lajoie had won that district by 39 votes.
Meanwhile, Democrats and aligned independents picked up districts all across the southern half of the state.
Two Auburn-based House districts flipped, with incumbent Republican Rep. Quentin Chapman losing in District 88 and Democrat Pamela Hart winning District 90, currently held by Libby.
In the Midcoast, independent Clint Collamore made a remarkable return to the House in District 45. He had resigned three years ago amid a signature-forging scandal and Republicans flipped the seat in a 2023 special election. After previously running as a Democrat, Collamore ran unenrolled this year and regained the seat.
Democrat Abigail Geer flipped House District 86 in Casco, Raymond and Poland by about 56 votes. This district had changed hands in 2024, too, when Rep. Rolf Olsen, R-Raymond, flipped the seat.
Democrats defeated two incumbents in Windham, too: House District 106 saw Bradley Youngs defeat Rep. Barbara Bagshaw by about 150 votes, and Joseph Campbell won House District 107 over Rep. Mark Cooper by 328 votes.
In one of the more remarkable flips of this cycle, Charles Tilburg defeated incumbent Republican Rep. Nathan Carlow by 135 votes in the Buxton and Hollis seat, House District 137. Carlow had won this district by comfortable margins in the two previous elections, and Buxton and Hollis hadn’t elected a Democrat to the Maine House since 2012.
Democrat John Henkelman flipped the Sanford-based House District 143 by a 364-vote margin, taking a district that President Donald Trump won by more than 12 percentage points and that had been held by Republicans since maps were redrawn in 2021.
House District 145 in Wells flipped back to blue, with Democrat Kristin Davis defeating Republican Caleb Chase in a seat that has changed parties twice now since maps were redrawn.
And the Berwick-based House District 148 also flipped to Democrats, with Marissa Tasker defeating incumbent Rep. Thomas Lavigne. Lavigne had comfortably won this district twice, and Trump won this district by more than six points in 2024.
The Legislature convenes for the first time Dec. 2 in Augusta.

title: Trump says Susie Wiles is out as Chief of Staff. Here’s who is replacing her
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, mere days after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections.
On his social media site, Trump praised Wiles and said she’d continue to work for his political organization.
“I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026. Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
Miller, long a key member of Trump’s inner circle, is a key architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies.
Wiles, the steely political operator and longtime adviser to Trump, was the first woman to ever serve in that post.
Wiles’ departure comes almost immediately after the GOP’s midterm thrashing on Tuesday. She will be replaced by Stephen Miller, a longtime trusted aide to Trump.
The departure also came months after Wiles indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease, a diagnosis she went public with in March 2026.
Wiles is the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.

title: Kennebunk football posts impressive win over Biddeford in B South semifinal
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
KENNEBUNK — Kennebunk High produced the type of playoff effort that high school football coaches covet.
Three Rams running backs powered for big chunks, and each scored a first-half touchdown. The defense shut down Biddeford’s big-play attack and didn’t allow a point. Kennebunk didn’t turn the ball over and forced four turnovers by Biddeford.
It all added up to a 27-0 Class B South semifinal win for second-seeded Kennebunk on a rainy Friday night. The Rams advance to a fourth straight regional final, at 2 p.m. next Saturday against longtime rival Marshwood, the No. 1 seed, which advanced with a 30-22 win over Falmouth. In the regular season, Marshwood beat Kennebunk in South Berwick, 32-16.
“We started slow in this round the last couple of years. Credit to the kids, we started faster this week, scored on our first drive,” Kennebunk coach Keith Noel said. “It was a really good game by our kids and by our coaches.”
No. 3 seed Biddeford finishes 6-4, the Tigers’ first winning record since 2019. Biddeford had won a total of four games the previous three seasons.
“Sometimes you have to give the other team credit. That’s a good team and they did a really good job tonight,” said Biddeford coach Steve Allosso. “Very positive (season). Wonderful kids with great character. That’s the main thing.”
HOW IT HAPPENED
Kennebunk controlled the line of scrimmage on both sides in the first half. Bradley Farrell, Peter Langenberger and Ethan White each had a touchdown run and combined for 159 yards as the Rams built a 20-0 lead. The offensive line consistently got a big push and opened sizable creases, like when White scored untouched from the 12 with 16 seconds left in the half.
Kennebunk junior center Braylon Zambrano said the offensive efficiency was a result of “working as a team in total, just bringing everyone together and getting everyone to have that push that we needed.”
The Rams’ defense bottled up Biddeford’s home run threats, Estevao Lembissa and Stanley Richerson. Neither had a run or catch longer than 9 yards.
“We wanted to stay in our gaps, defend our gaps, make sure we had our guy, and if the running back came up, then that was our tackle,” Zambrano said.
Biddeford was held to 179 yards, compared to 326 for Kennebunk. The Rams’ defense forced three turnovers, including a fumble by quarterback Ernest Dore that halted Biddeford’s first drive just outside the red zone. Kennebunk had three fourth-down stops and intercepted Dore twice.
“They played phenomenal,” Noel said of his defense. “The linebackers did a really good job communicating. The secondary did a great job. We repped it all week long. Credit the kids, they asked for extra film sessions, and that started on Monday.”
UNSUNG HEROES
Kennebunk senior Hunter Boulette made huge contributions on consecutive plays. On his only target of the game, Boulette hauled in a well-thrown deep ball by quarterback Giovanni D’Elia, kept his feet, and scored the final touchdown on a 67-yard reception.
On the ensuing kickoff, Richerson was a step away from breaking free when Boulette came from behind, smacked the ball out of Richerson’s hands and jumped on the loose ball.
Kennebunk freshman Brooks Reid also impressed in a two-play sequence.
Biddeford started its first drive of the second half at the Rams 29 after a 31-yard return by Ropati Harrison. On third-and-3, Reid knifed throught the right side of Biddeford’s line and threw Lembissa for a 5-yard loss. On the next play, Dore swung a safety-valve pass to the flat to Richerson. Reid, the lone defender in the area, avoided a block and took Richerson down with a secure solo tackle.
Later, Reid ended Biddeford’s final possession with an interception at the goal line.
STATISTICS
Biddeford: Ernest Dore (11 for 22, 79 yards, 2 interceptions; 6 carries, 35 yards), Stanley Richerson (14 carries, 51 yards), Estevao Lembissa (10 carries, 14 yards)
Kennebunk: Giovanni D’Elia (3 of 6, 127 yards, 1 TD), Ethan White (22 carries, 104 yards, 1 TD), Bradley Farrell (10 carries, 51 yards, 1 TD), Peter Langenberger (9 carries, 44 yards, 1 TD), Brooks Reid and Charlie Pentland (one interception each)

title: No charges to be filed in fatal Presque Isle pedestrian crash
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - No charges will be filed after the Oct. 3 fatal pedestrian crash on Ginn Road in Presque Isle.
Shelby Sanborn, 68, was walking along Ginn Road when he was struck and killed by a GMC Sierra pickup truck.
Investigators cite sun glare
Investigators determined the driver’s visibility was limited by the glare of the setting sun.
Investigators performed tests at the scene under similar lighting conditions. They found that a person wearing a reflective vest could not be seen from the driver’s seat until the truck was approximately 100 feet away.
Other factors ruled out
Police said the driver showed no signs of impairment, and speed was not a contributing factor.
Investigators also found no evidence that phone use contributed to the crash. The only phone activity was a hands-free call, which the driver’s father said had ended before the collision.
Weather, traffic and road conditions were also ruled out as contributing factors.
Investigation closed
The crash reconstruction was reviewed and approved by Maine State Police, and the investigation is now closed.
Police thanked the fire, EMS and law enforcement personnel who responded to the scene that night.

title: Market Basket opens at the Downs in Scarborough
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Market Basket will open its fourth Maine supermarket today in Scarborough, bringing an 80,000-square-foot grocery store and 350 jobs to the growing Downs development.
It joins a Maine portfolio that includes stores in Topsham, Westbrook and Biddeford. The company was founded in Lowell, Mass., in 1917 and now operates 90 stores across four states. At the Downs, it’s at the corner of Market Street and Scarborough Downs Road.
“Market Basket is delighted to be opening its fourth Maine store at the Downs, a dynamic town center complex in Scarborough,” Chuck Casassa, president of Market Basket, told Mainebiz. “We look forward to being an integral part of the community and its future growth.”
“Our relationship with Market Basket spans 35 years, so seeing this project come to fruition after years of collaboration is especially meaningful,” said Peter Michaud, managing partner of M&R Development. “We’re grateful they believed in our vision for the Downs and had the confidence to become the first retailer in Scarborough’s new Town Center. Their arrival is already generating tremendous excitement, and it will be a game changer for attracting more restaurants, retailers and visitors to the region.”
“Market Basket’s opening is a win for both consumers and the local economy,” added Michaud. “Not only does it bring more choices and competitive prices to shoppers, but it also creates 350 new jobs in our community. This is exactly the kind of investment we envisioned, one that delivers real value to residents, creates economic opportunity and builds momentum for future growth.”
The supermarket is located near a Costco warehouse that opened in 2023 in the Downs’ Innovation District, north of the Town Center. The arrival of Market Basket is part of a collection of businesses planned for the Town Center section of the Downs. It’s expected to be the first retail tenant in the development’s Town Center, with Costco and Allagash Brewing open in other parts of the 550-acre Downs.
The Downs spans 550 acres and includes residential, commercial and recreational development. The Town Center is being built as a gathering and shopping area within the larger mixed-use neighborhood.

title: Mother and daughter killed by grizzly bear while hiking in Canada
text:
(AP) - Selah Reed’s family first knew something was wrong when the 20-year-old missed a routine Saturday night call with her sister.
When no one had heard from Reed or her mother, Jenny Balcarras, by the next morning, they asked the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to check on their home in Bella Coola on British Columbia’s central coast. Balcarras’ car was gone and the doors were locked. They found the car at a trailhead up the road, but Balcarras and Reed were nowhere to be found.
Family members across Canada and the U.S. started mobilizing. Jenny Balcarras’ brother, Matt, headed north from Vancouver Island, and his brother left from Calgary. They met and drove through the night but got a call late Monday that their sister had been killed, likely by a grizzly.
When they arrived at the trailhead Tuesday morning, ready to join the search for Reed, her remains had also been found. The search was now a tragic recovery effort.
The killings of Jenny Balcarras, 48, and her daughter happened only 3 to 4 kilometers (1.8 to 2.4 miles) from where a grizzly attacked a group of schoolchildren and teachers last year as they walked on a trail. Eleven were injured, two of them critically, in the Nov. 20, 2025, attack.
Jeff Tyre, an inspector with the Conservation Officer Service, said that aggressive bear was never captured, but officials were able to collect its DNA. Officials have set new traps in the hopes of catching the bear involved in last weekend’s attack and to learn whether it was the same bear from a year ago. They also are not sure whether more than one bear was involved.
Terry Webber, chief administrative officer for the Nuxalk Nation, said the killings were triggering for the families who were traumatized by last year’s attack.
“Our community is still healing,” he said, adding that they’ve imposed a curfew and are providing mental health services for the community. “Our priority is to ensure they’re safe and ensure our community is supported.”
Bear attack complicated the search
The delay in finding the remains of the two women was complicated by difficult terrain, even though it was close to the trailhead, and the grizzly bear’s behavior.
Searchers found Jenny Balcarras first, then her daughter. The search was helped by more resources and a cadaver dog, Matt Balcarras said.
Searchers found his niece’s remains in a bear cache — a place where bears stash food, sometimes by digging a small hole and covering it with branches and vegetation to keep other animals and birds away.
“Even though it was within 100 or so meters (330 feet), locating remains in a cache is difficult,” he said.
By the time officials located his niece, she could only be identified by her clothing, he said. His sister was in a similar condition, but they knew who she was thanks to several tiny tattoos, he said.
“There’s no obvious body to identify,” he said. “The coroner’s investigation will include DNA and dental work. But there is no doubt that the remains that were found are theirs.”
Balcarras was comfortable in challenging environments
Grizzly bears are common in the area surrounding the Bella Coola community, officials said. Conservation officials maintain a hotline where people can report problem bears, but no calls had been received recently, Tyre said during a media briefing.
Balcarras, an art therapist, had moved to Bella Coola during the summer. She had previously lived in Alaska, where her children were born, and was “the central organizing person in our family,” Matt Balcarras said.
“In classic, strong single-mother style, she scraped together a career and a life for herself and her kids,” Balcarras said. She was small in stature but strong in character and physical abilities, he said.
She was comfortable living among the wildlife, he said.
“She lived in the Bush when her kids were babies,” he said. “She and my niece were not naive or foolish or uninformed. They’ve lived in these areas and have been around animals of countless types for years and years and decades.”

title: Husson will offer free tuition to Aroostook students
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Husson will offer free tuition to Aroostook County students starting next fall.
It’s the third county to be covered by such a scholarship program at the Bangor-based university, Husson announced Friday morning. Students from Penobscot and Piscataquis counties already have had the opportunity to attend Husson without worrying about paying for classes.
The scholarship is made possible by Bruce and Cynthia Grainger, who graduated from Husson in 1990. The couple met there in 1988 and have been married for more than three decades.
“We are thrilled to expand the Opportunity Scholarship program to a third Maine county thanks to the generosity of Husson University Board of Trustees Vice Chair Bruce Grainger and his wife Cynthia Grainger. Both are proud Husson graduates who know the value of a Husson education,” President Lynne Coy-Ogan said in a statement.
Qualified students must have at least a 3.0 high school GPA, an adjusted gross family income of less than $80,000 and live in Aroostook County, according to Husson. The scholarship will be available to students applying to begin classes in the fall of 2027.
Students must attend Husson full time and enroll in a four-year degree at the Bangor campus.

title: Middle school principal arrested for suspected child sex crimes
text:
TOPEKA, Kan. (WIBW/Gray News) - A principal at Jardine Middle School was arrested for suspected child sex crimes on Thursday.
According to the Topeka Police Department, officers arrested Todd W. Haag, 56, at Jardine Middle School.
Haag was booked into the Shawnee Co.Department of Corrections on charges of the following:
- Aggravated Criminal Sodomy
- Sexual Exploitation of a Child
- Indecent Solicitation of a Child, and Electronic Solicitation
School officials said Haag has since been placed on administrative leave.
“We know this information is concerning; please be assured that the district is working closely with law enforcement and we will have district staff on site in support of students and staff. Additionally, we thank law enforcement for their support for the Jardine Campus as they investigate this matter,” a statement from Topeka Public Schools said in part.
According to Haag’s bio on Jardine’s website, he has worked in education for 30 years, serving Topeka Public Schools at Williams, Jardine, and Scott Dual Language.
No additional information was immediately provided by authorities.

title: Crown Jewel on Portland’s Great Diamond Island up for sale
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Acclaimed seasonal restaurant Crown Jewel on Great Diamond Island is on the market.
The business and real estate are listed at $1.25 million by LandVest. The 1,500-square-foot, 30 seat restaurant is situated in Diamond Cove in the Fort McKinley Historic District.
Owner Alex Wight, who also owns the Old Port’s French-inspired wine bar and restaurant Elizabeth, said she wanted to be able to spend more time with her kids, who were all very young when she first opened Crown Jewel.
“My kids don’t remember having a summer with me, and I just decided it was time,” Wight said. “That place has brought me a ton of joy over the past decade, but I needed to simplify, and that meant putting it up for sale.”
Crown Jewel is currently closed for the season, but is fully equipped and outfitted for continued restaurant use, according to the listing. All furnishings and equipment are included in the sale.
Since it launched in 2018, Crown Jewel has been praised locally and in national media outlets including the Wall Street Journal, Condé Nast Traveler and Food & Wine magazine.

title: Turner family, police searching for missing 14-year-old
text:
Family members and authorities are searching for a Turner teen who they say ran away Tuesday and may be in danger.
Skylar Rowe, 14, must have left the house out a back window while her grandmother was playing with a young child in a different room at their County Road home, Armand Rowe, Skylar’s grandfather, said Friday. Otherwise, they would have seen her leave, he said. She was last seen about 1 p.m.
Skylar had been staying since late May with their daughter, Tiffani Rowe, who has legal guardianship of her in Maine, the grandfather said. She may be headed with her biological mother toward Tennessee, where she once lived, police said.
The Androscoggin County Sheriff’s Office has issued an alert and posted one on Facebook seeking the public’s assistance in locating Skylar, Chief Deputy William Gagne said. A deputy has been assigned to the case.
Skylar is described as about 5 feet, 3 inches tall, weighing about 140 pounds with brown hair and brown eyes. She was last seen wearing black leggings and a camouflage shirt.
She may be in the company of her biological mother, Kasey Rowe, or an adult male identified as Michael Rias who is a friend of her mother’s, Gagne said.
Investigators have received information that she may be traveling toward Memphis, Tennessee.
Due to Skylar’s age and the circumstances surrounding her disappearance, there are serious concerns for her safety and well-being, Gagne said.
Skylar called the Sheriff’s Office this week after leaving her grandparents’ house and said she was “safe,” but would not give her location and would not confirm who she was with, Gagne said. They need to set eyes on her to make sure she is OK or would like to talk to her biological mother to make sure she is safe, he said.
Armand Rowe said they have their granddaughter’s journal and are concerned about what they read in it and who she may be with.
A complex family situation has added to the stress of finding Skylar, Rowe said. In addition, his wife, who is called Mimi by their grandchildren, was just diagnosed with leukemia, he said.
They are not mad at Skylar, he said, they just want to make sure she is safe and want her to come back to Turner.
Her grandparents believe Skylar had been planning to run away with Rias and her mother, Rowe said.
She was enrolled in the Turner-area school system but had not been to school yet, he said.
Anyone with information regarding Skylar’s whereabouts is urged to contact the Androscoggin County Sheriff’s Office immediately at 207-753-2599 or 911.

title: President Trump names Stephen Miller chief of staff amid debate over immigration enforcement
text:
President Trump names Stephen Miller chief of staff amid debate over immigration enforcement
President Donald Trump's new chief of staff is considered the architect of the president's immigration policy, something Democrats are targeting in the next Congress.
President Trump names Stephen Miller chief of staff amid debate over immigration enforcement
President Donald Trump's new chief of staff is considered the architect of the president's immigration policy, something Democrats are targeting in the next Congress.
President Donald Trump has named Stephen Miller, one of the architects of his administration's hardline immigration policies, as his new White House chief of staff, elevating a key adviser as the administration faces new political challenges following Republican losses in Tuesday's midterm elections.
Miller, currently the White House deputy chief of staff, will replace Susie Wiles on Monday, Nov. 9. Wiles will transition to Trump's political operation.
When asked about the change, Trump told reporters, “I just wanted to make a change.”
The leadership shakeup comes as Vice President JD Vance raises the possibility of shifting immigration enforcement priorities toward businesses that employ undocumented immigrants.
In a post reflecting on Tuesday's election losses, Vance said he is open to changing immigration enforcement by focusing more on businesses employing undocumented workers.
The idea was previously discussed by border czar Tom Homan in July, when he proposed using private contractors to expand workplace audits.
Federal contracting records show Immigration and Customs Enforcement has already awarded millions in contracts supporting such efforts.
In September, the agency awarded a five-year contract worth up to approximately $21.5 million to a Maryland company to help investigate employment records and business documents.
Amy Peck, a workplace immigration compliance attorney based in Omaha, Nebraska, said she expects workplace audits to increase.
“I speak with them every day. Businesses are very concerned. The government hasn’t made it easy for employers to be 100% compliant because of the difficulty maneuvering through the regulations,” Peck said.
Meanwhile, Miller's promotion comes as Democrats prepare to use their incoming congressional majorities to investigate ICE's enforcement tactics and spending.
Rep. Bennie Thompson, who is in line to lead the House Homeland Security Committee, has demanded that the Department of Homeland Security preserve its records and respond to outstanding requests for documents.
While Democrats can investigate ICE, they cannot directly dictate how the agency carries out day-to-day immigration enforcement, authority that remains with the Trump administration.
Despite the looming investigations, Trump and some incoming Democrats have expressed openness to discussing immigration legislation.
Trump said he has long believed immigration is an area where compromise is possible. Texas Senator-elect James Talarico also expressed interest in working with the president on border security and expanding legal immigration.

title: Death row inmate asks for a stay of execution until after holidays
text:
COLUMBIA, S.C. (WHNS/Gray News) - A South Carolina death row inmate is petitioning to have his execution pushed back to after the holidays.
Steven Bixby was convicted in 2007 of killing State Constable Donnie Ouzts and Sergeant Danny Wilson of the Abbeville County Sheriff’s Office during a standoff in 2003.
Bixby and his parents were part of a land dispute with the state, which planned to take 20 feet of land from their property to widen a highway.
The dispute escalated into a standoff.
In a petition submitted to the South Carolina Supreme Court, Bixby is asking that the clerk of court not issue a notice of execution until after the winter holidays.
The petition cites a previous stay of execution granted to a death row inmate in 2024, whose execution date would have fallen near Thanksgiving and Christmas.
The South Carolina Supreme Court has not yet made a ruling on the petition.

title: U.S. adds 165,000 jobs in October as hiring rebounds
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - U.S. job growth accelerated in October, beating economists’ expectations, while the unemployment rate edged lower.
Employers added a seasonally adjusted 165,000 jobs, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday. That was nearly three times the 59,000 economists surveyed by Dow Jones had expected, according to CNBC.
The unemployment rate fell from 4.2% in September to 4.1% in October.
However, the U-6 rate, a broader measure of unemployment that also includes discouraged workers and people working part time for economic reasons, rose from 7.6% to 7.9%.
The report, released three days after the midterm elections, also showed stronger job growth in the months leading up to the vote.
The bureau revised August’s job gains upward by 53,000, from 133,000 to 186,000. It revised September’s gains upward by 31,000, from 29,000 to 60,000.
Together, the revisions show employers added 84,000 more jobs over those two months than previously reported.
Professional and business services led October’s gains with 70,000 jobs, followed by health care with 42,000. Transportation and warehousing added 25,000 jobs, and manufacturing added 19,000.
Average hourly earnings rose 3.1% from a year earlier, more than economists expected but below the latest reported inflation rate.
October’s consumer price report is due Tuesday and will show how those wage gains compare with inflation over the same period.
