title: Fourth Market Basket opens in Maine
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine's fourth Market Basket opens at The Downs in Scarborough
The new Market Basket at The Downs in Scarborough is considered the first major retailer at the new Town Center, which is under construction on the former race track property.
Friday marked the grand opening of Maine's fourth Market Basket location. The new 80,000-square-foot grocery store in Scarborough had every register up and running when the doors opened for the first time.
"A lot of people may have never been to a Market Basket and seeing the great prices we have to offer, the great food we have to offer, and also being able to hire a lot of people from this area is exciting," said store manager Eric Beaulieu.
Market Basket hired 350 new employees to work at the Scarborough store. Beaulieu said the new location was strategically placed, as shoppers who came for the grand opening found a whole new neighborhood.
"I've never been out here before. I was shocked," said shopper Elizabeth Watson.
The Downs redevelopment project at the former Scarborough Downs horse racing track has been under construction for years. Developers said the opening of the Market Basket has been nearly a decade in the making.
"This is a big deal, and Market Basket is really going to be a catalyst for other retailers to locate in the town center," said Dan Bacon, development director at M&R Development. "We've been working with them for almost eight years, honestly."
Unlike Maine's other Market Basket locations in Biddeford, Westbrook and Topsham, where customers came from far and wide, the new store in Scarborough has built-in customers who live right outside the front doors.
The Downs features The Breakaway building, which is a combination of commercial space on the ground level and 76 residential apartments on the upper floors.
Bacon said more mixed-use construction is underway at The Downs, and that an InterMed office is coming in January.

title: Democratic candidates with a Christian message help flip Congress
text:
(AP) - Clergy members and other Democratic candidates with an unapologetically Christian message to “love your neighbor” helped their party flip control of Congress.
It was a striking midterm victory that demonstrated the strength of the religious left as a counter to the stalwart evangelical support for President Donald Trump and his fellow Republicans.
“This attempt to corner the market on Christianity by evangelicals was repudiated,” said Brian Kaylor, a Baptist pastor and editor of a progressive faith and politics site.
Instead, American mainline Protestantism, with its less-strident theology, took the election spotlight.
Seminarian James Talarico in Texas, megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton in Kansas and Iowa ministers Sarah Trone Garriott and Lindsay James flipped key seats in the U.S. Senate and House. They’re part of the mainline Presbyterian, Methodist and Lutheran branches with moderate or progressive beliefs.
Unlike the nationalists wanting America to privilege a particular Christian worldview in public life, the mainline candidates in keeping with their Christian values backed church-state separation and sought common ground across religions, Kaylor said.
“There were so many people in our country who felt so strongly that what was happening in D.C. was not moral,” Hamilton told The Associated Press. “It didn’t reflect our national values.”
That’s why he and the other candidates ran, he said, and why they were elected.
Mainline denominations have historically been part of the country’s civic establishment as the church home of most presidents and other elites. But membership has been sliding for decades. Despite that shift, the wins show these Protestants can still have significant influence — though not with white evangelicals.
Across the board, white evangelical Protestants stayed consistent in their overwhelming midterm support for Republicans. Most Protestants who identify as “liberal” or “moderate,” about 7 in 10, voted for Democrats, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of roughly 100,000 midterm voters.
The four mainline candidates also got a big boost from voters who reject organized religion. At least 7 in 10 religiously unaffiliated voters supported Democratic Senate and House candidates in Texas, Kansas and Iowa, The AP Voter Poll showed.
Others said being a progressive pastor wasn’t the prime factor in these victories.
“If I hear a story about the Democratic Party scouting out pastors to run in 2028 based on Talarico and Hamilton, I think they’ve totally missed the upshot from this election,” said Ryan Burge, a professor at Washington University in St. Louis who studies religious demographics. “It’s about economic issues. It’s about disdain for Trump. It’s about high prices.”
Talarico takes Texas as critique of his Christianity continues
In the longtime GOP stronghold of Texas, Talarico flipped a U.S. Senate seat — the first election in 30-plus years that Democrats won statewide races — by defeating Republican Ken Paxton, an evangelical.
Voters also ousted Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, a Republican who chaired Trump’s Religious Liberty Commission and declared, “There is no separation of church and state.”
In Talarico’s acceptance speech, the 37-year-old state legislator recounted how his grandfather, a Baptist preacher, taught him about Jesus, a “barefoot rabbi” who commanded people to love God and neighbor. And not just the neighbor who looks, prays or votes like him, the Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.) seminarian and former middle school teacher said.
“Two thousand years ago, when the people at the top hurt his neighbors, that barefoot rabbi didn’t stay in his room and pray. He walked into the seat of power, and he flipped over the tables of injustice. … Texas, it’s time to start flipping tables," Talarico said.
A longtime Texas Trump supporter and Southern Baptist pastor, the Rev. Robert Jeffress, maintains that the pluralistic religion promoted by Talarico and other candidates is not actually Christianity, a criticism raised by others during their campaigns.
“People want to choose a religion that’s nice and warm and fuzzy, whether it’s built on truth or not,” said Jeffress, who leads First Baptist Church in Dallas. “What James Talarico believes, according to the words of Jesus, is not true.”
He attributes the Democrats’ success to a trifecta of inflation, the Iran war and “less than ideal candidates.” Jeffress also suspects many evangelicals stayed home.
White evangelical Protestants made up a slightly smaller share of the electorate than in 2024, when Trump was running for president: 21% in 2024, compared with 17% in 2026, The AP Voter Poll showed. That could be due to lower turnout among white evangelicals or higher turnout among other groups. About 2 in 10 voted for Talarico in Texas and Hamilton in Kansas.
Kansas pastor candidate says kindness doesn’t require religion
Burge, the professor who studies religious demographics, asserts that the Democratic clergy members who won were strong candidates but also benefited from very favorable political winds.
“If you ran Adam Hamilton in 2024, he’s beat by double digits and we’re not having this conversation,” Burge said.
Hamilton, pastor of the nation’s largest United Methodist congregation, called for “decency” in politics, drawing on Jesus’ Golden Rule in his victory speech: “Do unto others as you would have them do unto you.”
“I can’t not talk about my faith. It’s just, it’s my life. It’s what I eat, sleep, drink and breathe,” he told the AP. But being religious isn’t required to follow biblical injunctions “to do justice, to love kindness.”
While campaigning for Hamilton’s Republican opponent, Sen. Roger Marshall, Vice President JD Vance questioned Hamilton’s religiosity.
“It was so ridiculous that there was no reason to even respond to it,” said Hamilton, who welcomes a conversation with Vance and other critics about faith and theology.
Iowa pastor candidates prioritize coalition building
Democrats Sarah Trone Garriott and Lindsay James, who flipped U.S. House seats in Iowa, didn’t have political ambitions when they pursued ordination.
Trump’s 2016 election sparked James’ involvement. The Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.) chaplain sees her ministry experience — from church potlucks to the pews — as a strength when connecting with all voters.
“I spent time bringing people together across difference,” she told the AP in March.
Trone Garriott, a state senator and a pastor in the mainline Evangelical Lutheran Church in America, thinks the religious right’s high profile in national politics has made some progressive Christians wary of sharing their faith publicly.
But she sees the power in diverse coalition building. In her acceptance speech, she evoked hope and the power of loving your neighbor. “When people come together on our common ground, we will do powerful things,” she said.
Midterm successes for other Christian candidates
Among Republicans, clergy candidates for Congress also prevailed, including Mark Harris of North Carolina, a Southern Baptist pastor, and Tim Walberg of Michigan, a former pastor.
Black Protestants vote overwhelmingly Democratic and have long comfortably talked faith and politics in a way white mainliners have not. This year, victorious Democrats included at least two Black clergy members — the Rev. Frederick Haynes III, a Baptist from Texas, and U.S. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver II, a United Methodist minister from Missouri.
In North Carolina, Democrat LaKesha Womack unseated a Republican incumbent in the U.S. House. She is an ordained deacon in the African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church, a historically Black Protestant denomination.
Womack told the AP her faith prompts her to advocate for “policies that address poverty and immigration and making sure everybody has access to healthcare.” And she defends religious freedom for all.
“With the white Christian nationalists almost taking over the narrative of what it means to be a Christian, I think there are a lot of people of faith in this country who wanted to reclaim that narrative,” she said.
Womack said that Democrats shouldn’t read too much into this year’s clergy victories.
“I don’t think we should go out and try to recruit ministers to become politicians if that’s not what they’re called to do,” she said. “It has to be authentic.”
___
AP reporter Tiffany Stanley contributed to this report.

text:

title: ‘Help us get justice’: Eighth grader dies after being shot in stolen car, family says
text:
BATON ROUGE, La. (WAFB/Gray News) - An eighth-grader was shot and killed in Louisiana, according to authorities.
Officers were called around 11:39 p.m. when they located 13-year-old Madison Harris.
Harris was taken to a hospital, where she later died from her injuries.
Investigators said Harris was in a stolen car when she was killed. Officials confirmed Harris was a student at Inspire Charter Academy.
“As a school community, we were heartbroken to learn of the passing of one of our students and are making support resources available to those who need them.”

title: Maine private schools sue Maine DOE over special education rule
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The Maine Association of Independent Schools and seven Maine private schools are suing the Maine Department of Education over new special education regulations that they say will have a “significant effect” on the safety of students and staff.
Foxcroft Academy and Washington Academy are named in the lawsuit.
Safety Concerns
Tara Walker, a Portland-based attorney from Fisher Phillips who is representing the plaintiffs, said the schools are concerned about what the rule says, what it leaves out and how it was enacted.
Walker said a judge or hearing officer would have to sign off on a change in placement for a student with special needs. She said that could prevent schools from taking immediate action when a student’s behavior puts them or others at risk.
Walker said private schools sometimes have more resources than public schools to care for children with disabilities—leading some districts to choose to place students in a private institution to have their needs met.
“The incentives for this rule run backwards. So, the school district may have risk by changing the students’ school or enrolling them in a different school — but no risk or very limited risk if the student does something unsafe on the premises. Whereas a private school has a lot of the risk,” Walker said.
Emergency rule
The complaint says the policy was enacted as part of an emergency rule—something Walker said prevented those most affected by the change from making their voices heard.
“The agency used an emergency shortcut when it passed the rule in June,” Walker said. “That shortcut is supposed to be used for real emergencies and this wasn’t one.”
Earlier negotiations
The complaint says the rule’s enactment was preceded by six months of discussion regarding a “Master Contractual Agreement” involving several schools, districts, and providers. Walker said that agreement would have mirrored the policies of of Massachusetts’; providing a mechanism for schools to raise concerns expeditiously when they believe students’ health and safety is at risk. The complaint says in April, the Maine DOE announced the agreement would be put on hold until the 2027-2028 school year.

According to the complaint, the emergency rule was enacted just a few months later with no safety assessment process in place, which surprised some of the parties involved in prior negotiations.
The DOE has a few weeks to respond to the filing. The department was contacted for a response and had not replied.

title: Poetry Foundation awards $30,000 to sustain the work of Alice James Books
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NEW GLOUCESTER — Alice James Books is pleased to announce that it has received a $30,000 grant from the Poetry Foundation. The award will support the press’s ongoing commitment to publishing groundbreaking contemporary poetry, championing emerging and established voices and connecting poets with readers nationwide.
Alice James Books is among 52 nonprofit poetry organizations, presses and publications awarded a combined $1.52 million by the Poetry Foundation. The funding will help AJB strengthen its publishing program, expand author support, and engage new audiences.
“We’re grateful to the Poetry Foundation for its generous and vital support, which helps us bring ambitious, thought-provoking poetry to more readers and give our poets the meaningful resources, greater visibility and new opportunities they need to connect with their audiences,” Carey Salerno, executive director & publisher, said.
This funding comes as Alice James Books embarks on a new five-year strategic plan focused on strengthening support for poets, expanding its reach and building a sustainable future. The grant will help advance these priorities and reinforce the press’s longstanding mission to amplify voices and perspectives that deserve to be heard.
Read the Poetry Foundation’s full announcement at PoetryFoundation.org.
For more information, email Adam Vitcavage, publicist, at adam@alicejamesbooks.org or call 207-926-8283.
Founded in 1973, Alice James Books publishes books that matter, preserves a place of belonging for poets who inspire us and seeks to broaden our collective interpretation of what constitutes the American poetic voice. AJB provides a platform from which to elevate established and emerging voices and literary artists of excellence with an emphasis on supporting artists whose voices have been historically marginalized or who offer overlooked perspectives. The press emphasizes collaborative partnership with authors, supporting writers throughout their careers, connecting them to a broad audience, and helping them tell stories that matter. Alice James Books is named after the sister of the philosopher William James and novelist Henry James, Alice James. Keenly self-aware, Alice started writing a journal in 1889 as a vehicle for self-expression within the confines of the Victorian period in which she lived and its narrow view of womanhood. Since the publication of her journal in its entirety in 1964, Alice James has been celebrated as a feminist icon and diarist.

title: Tropical Storm Pena forms in the Pacific Ocean south of Hawaii
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Tropical Storm Pena formed Friday in the Pacific Ocean, well south of the Hawaiian islands.
Pena had maximum sustained winds of 45 mph (72 kph) and was centered about 650 miles (1,046 kilometers) southeast of South Point, Hawaii, and about 1,350 miles (2,173 kilometers) east-southeast of Johnston Island, according to an advisory from the Miami-based U.S. National Hurricane Center.
Pena was moving west at 12 mph (19 kph). It was forecast to strengthen over the next day or so, then have no significant change through next week.
The system is expected to remain offshore of Hawaii. No watches or warnings were in effect, and no hazards were affecting land.
The Pacific Ocean has had an active hurricane season due in part to El Niño.

title: How measles outbreaks are impacting people across the U.S.
text:
(InvestigateTV) — The CDC reported 4,852 measles cases in the U.S. between Jan. 1 and Oct. 30, 2026, the most the country has seen since an outbreak that stretched from 1989 to 1991. According to the CDC, cases are at a 35-year high.
One out of every 1,000 cases will develop encephalitis, which often results in permanent brain damage, the CDC said.
Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine offer the strongest protection against measles, according to the CDC.
Families describe complications
Christine Castle said her sister Fonda is a ball of energy and often smiles and giggles. Fonda is 66 years old. Her room is filled with baby dolls and cartoons.
“She has a lot of love to give,” Castle said. “She basically just didn’t develop past a five or six year old.”
Castle said their mother was seven months pregnant with Fonda when she contracted rubella, a virus different from measles that causes similar symptoms. According to the CDC, a rubella infection during pregnancy can lead to serious illness and developmental delays for babies after birth.
“She can’t read or write. She can kind of memorize colors,” Castle said.
Fonda was born during the U.S. rubella epidemic. According to the National Foundation for Infectious Diseases, between 1965 and 1966, more than 11,000 pregnant women lost their babies and 20,000 were born with congenital rubella syndrome, including Fonda.
“They can basically look at the timeframe when my sister’s brain stopped developing,” Castle said.
Another family carries the effects of measles. Emmi Herman said her sister Marcie was a pianist.
“She was a wonderful piano player. My parents bought her a piano, which went wherever she went,” Herman said.
Herman said that in 1960, Marcie became ill with measles at age 9 and developed encephalitis. The CDC estimates this happens to 1 in every 1,000 children who contract measles.
“She had to learn to walk again; she had to learn to feed herself,” Herman said.
Herman said Marcie faced mental health challenges until her death in 2020 from COVID-19.
“You don’t know about the hardships and the heartaches and the way measles in particular can break up a family and really change the trajectory of that person’s life and also shape the future of the siblings’ and the parents’ lives,” Herman said.
Marcie contracted measles three years before a vaccine became available to the public, according to the World Health Organization. Herman was 6 years old at the time of Marcie’s diagnosis.
South Carolina outbreak timeline
Dr. George Haddad Jr. and Dr. Jennifer Grier are professors at the University of South Carolina School of Medicine – Greenville. They studied medicine in the 1990s and early 2000s, when national measles cases were at their lowest in years.
“I never saw it in training, and I never saw it in practice... until now,” Haddad said.
“I didn’t really think about measles too much other than it’s sort of a disease you see in the textbooks,” Grier said.
According to the S.C. Department of Public Health:
- South Carolina’s first measles case was reported July 9, 2025.
- By Oct. 1, state health officials confirmed five new infections were related, meeting the criteria for an outbreak, defined as three or more linked cases.
- New cases peaked by mid-January 2026, and hundreds of people were in quarantine or isolation.
- State health officials declared the outbreak over April 26, 2026.
A total of 997 people contracted measles during the outbreak.
“Many of them, the majority being children, especially some young children who were sick,” said Dr. Brannon Traxler, the department’s chief medical officer, who oversaw the state’s effort to fight measles.
Traxler said 15 of the 21 hospitalizations were children.
“As a parent myself I can imagine the anguish of the family, of the parents,” Traxler said.
No one died during the outbreak, which Traxler said came to an end largely due to an aggressive vaccination campaign.
“Everything from, you know, making new connections with faith-based, you know, entities, and non-profits,” Traxler said.
Partnerships produced mobile vaccine units, including one at Mount Moriah Baptist Church in Spartanburg. Spartanburg saw a 94% year-over-year increase in MMR vaccinations.
Of the 997 cases in the outbreak, more than 93% (932) were unvaccinated.
Daughter’s reaction to the vaccine
For some South Carolinians, vaccine hesitation is rooted in personal experience.
“She was a completely healthy toddler,” Deidre Downs said of her daughter, Shaylee.
Downs said that a few weeks after Shaylee received the MMR vaccine in 2024, she developed immune thrombocytopenia purpura, also known as ITP. According to Johns Hopkins, ITP is a disorder that affects the ability to form blood clots.
“And within a 24-hour period, they went from small bruises to her whole body covered in bruises,” Downs said.
According to the CDC, ITP can happen after a natural measles infection and after the MMR vaccine. The agency says it occurs in 1 in every 40,000 vaccinated children.
“It doesn’t feel like a rare occurrence when it happens to your child,” Downs said.
Downs said Shaylee is now symptom-free. According to Johns Hopkins, ITP typically doesn’t return. Downs said that after her daughter’s reaction, she will never be too sure of the odds.
“As a whole when this hot topic comes up, I would just like there to be more understanding and compassion,” Downs said.
Castle said she wonders about her sister’s life had the MMR vaccine been available when their mother was infected.
“We don’t know who is going to be affected and who is not, but we definitely would not want a five-year-old for the rest of your life, it is very difficult,” Castle said.
Castle, Herman and Downs each shared a different experience. All three have one message for parents with questions about measles or the vaccine: speak with a trusted doctor.
“If that could save one life, it’s a legacy that, you know, many people can’t claim,” Herman said.

title: Jay Rockefeller, former West Virginia governor and US senator who was part of a dynasty, dies at 89
text:
CHARLESTON, W.Va. (AP) — Jay Rockefeller, the last member of his family’s political dynasty — and the only Democrat — who served as West Virginia’s governor and later a longtime U.S. senator, has died. He was 89.
Rockefeller died Thursday night at his home in Washington, said Mary Stewart, vice president for external affairs at WETA, the public broadcasting station where Rockefeller’s wife, Sharon, serves as president and CEO.
Rockefeller came from one of the nation’s richest families to spend a half century in public service in one of the poorest states. He arrived in 1964 as a worker in an anti-poverty program, was elected governor a dozen years later and served two terms, then spent 30 years as a U.S. senator.
“I could not imagine a more rewarding career,” Rockefeller said upon his retirement in 2015.
He was born John D. Rockefeller IV in New York City. His great-grandfather, Standard Oil Co. founder John Rockefeller, died a month before Rockefeller’s birth. His father, John D. Rockefeller III, was a well-known philanthropist. Uncles Winthrop (Arkansas) and Nelson (New York) were Republican governors. Another uncle, David Rockefeller, ran Chase Manhattan Bank.
A detour from his family’s path
Jay Rockefeller went in a different direction.
A few years out of college at age 27, Rockefeller moved to the West Virginia mining community of Emmons to participate in the Volunteers in Service to America program, a time that Rockefeller said proved transformative.
“It explains every policy I pursued and every vote I have cast. It was where my beliefs were bolted down, and where my passions met my principles,” he said in an emotional farewell speech from the Senate floor on Dec. 4, 2014.
While he intended for his stay in the state to be brief, Rockefeller broke from his family’s Republican tradition and was elected to the state House of Delegates as a Democrat in 1966. By combining money with hard work in a traditionally Democratic state, Rockefeller overcame suspicions of political opportunism and rose from state legislator to secretary of state to governor.
A turning point came after Rockefeller’s only political defeat in the 1972 governor’s race to Republican Arch A. Moore Jr., whose daughter, Republican Shelley Moore Capito, was elected in 2014 to Rockefeller’s Senate seat upon his retirement. Capito on Friday called Rockefeller “a true gentleman” who treated her with respect, kindness and encouragement.
“Over the years, we developed a wonderful friendship that transcended politics, and I will always be grateful for that,” she said in a statement.
After the defeat, Rockefeller remained in West Virginia, a decision he called the most important of his career. He became the first without a theological degree to become president of West Virginia Wesleyan College in 1973. His popularity there — and a change in his stance to embrace strip mining — translated to a landslide win over Republican Cecil Underwood in the 1976 governor’s race.
As governor, Rockefeller emphasized development of the state’s infrastructure, such as roads, sewers and bridges. Those issues, he said, are “not very sexy things, I grant you but very, very necessary in West Virginia.”
Current Gov. Patrick Morrissey said Rockefeller helped shape the state and left a lasting mark on the lives of generations of West Virginians.
“From his early work in some of our state’s most disadvantaged communities to his efforts to strengthen healthcare, protect coal miners and their families, and support our veterans, Senator Rockefeller demonstrated a deep commitment to the people of West Virginia,” Morrissey said in a statement.
Onward to Washington
After Rockefeller defeated Arch Moore in a rematch in 1980, he won a U.S. Senate seat in 1984 after the retirement of longtime Democrat Jennings Randolph. It came despite a landslide victory that year for Republican President Ronald Reagan.
Rockefeller and his wife, Sharon, daughter of former Republican Sen. Charles Percy of Illinois, fit easily into the capital’s social scene, purchasing a multimillion-dollar estate for their family. Never shy or apologetic about using his inherited $150 million fortune to win his races, he spent millions upon millions from his own pocket. He won by comfortable margins in each of his five terms.
Rockefeller’s vast wealth was always a source of conversation and an undercurrent in his political races. He spent at least $21 million of his own money in his political campaigns, including $9 million to win a close 1984 Senate race against Republican novice and fellow multimillionaire John Raese. In Rockefeller’s 1980 gubernatorial race against Republican Arch Moore Jr., bumper stickers appeared saying: “Make Him Spend It All, Arch.”
The state’s junior senator for 25 years, Rockefeller carved his own path of influence in Sen. Robert C. Byrd’s immense shadow. Byrd died in 2010 as the longest-serving senator in U.S. history, winning an enduring reputation for steering billions of dollars over many decades to boost his impoverished state.
Rockefeller’s influence was less showy. As chairman of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, he championed consumers’ rights, upgrading broadband infrastructure and sponsoring a bill to block companies from tracking online activity of their customers. He authored legislation in 1997 that created the Children’s Health Insurance Program, which assists poor families whose incomes are too high to qualify for Medicaid.
He also was head of committees on Veterans’ Affairs and Intelligence, frequently sparring with President George W. Bush over foreign policy. Rockefeller said he regretted his 2002 vote to authorize the war against Iraq.
But Rockefeller also differed with the Democratic administration of President Barack Obama over mining-related regulations. With his state the nation’s second-biggest coal producer, Rockefeller was among several West Virginia officials who opposed the Obama-era Environmental Protection Agency’s oversight of the mountaintop removal method of surface mining.
College studies in Tokyo laid the groundwork for Rockefeller’s efforts to bring business from Japan to West Virginia. He had known Toyota’s founding family since the 1960s and was instrumental in helping the Japanese automaker pick a Buffalo, West Virginia, cornfield for an engine parts plant in 1996. The $2 billion plant now employs about 2,200 workers.
___
Associated Press writer Holly Ramer in Concord, New Hampshire, contributed to this report.

title: Cliff Booth Is Back in New ‘Further Mis-Adventures’ Trailer
text:
Cliff Booth Is Back in the New ‘Further Mis-Adventures’ Trailer
Directed by David Fincher, written by Quentin Tarantino, starring Brad Pitt, and a sequel to Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is sure to be one of the most-discussed movies of the holiday season. How is David Fincher at making a Tarantino movie? Does the film miss the presence of Leonardo DiCaprio? (The trailer offers an explanation why he’s not in the movie.) And most importantly: Does it live up to its fantastic predecessor?
We’ll see. I will say this trailer does look pretty good, and definitely better than the previous ones. It also gives us a much better sense of the story of the film, which involves Cliff hooking up with another TV actor, this one played by with Scott Caan, to protect him from some bad dudes. It also shows off a fun dynamic between Cliff and his dad — played by none other than RoboCop himself, Peter Weller.
Watch the new Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth trailer below:
READ MORE: Every David Fincher Movie, Ranked From Worst to Best
There’s a new poster for the film as well.
Here is the official synopsis for the film:
Brad Pitt returns to his Academy Award-winning role as Cliff Booth, only this time it’s 1977 and it’s a very different Hollywood. Directed by David Fincher from a screenplay by Quentin Tarantino, the film also stars Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Carla Gugino, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II and Peter Weller.
The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth open in IMAX theaters on November 25. It premieres on Netflix on December 23.

title: Cornell faculty vote ‘no confidence’ in university’s leadership over handling of sexual assault allegations
text:
(AP) - Cornell University’s Faculty Senate approved a resolution Friday declaring “no confidence” in the school’s top leaders, a symbolic gesture reflecting deep discontent on campus in the wake of a former student’s lawsuit saying she was gang raped at a fraternity party in 2024.
The resolution passed 75-50, with five faculty senators abstaining and five others not voting, according to an email sent to members of the Faculty Senate on Friday afternoon.
The vote followed weeks of debate among professors over whether Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff and other administrators handled the woman’s allegations properly and whether they’ve done enough to curtail sexual misconduct at the prestigious university.
While the faculty body has no power over the university’s top leaders, backers of the resolution had said they hoped it would pressure Cornell’s trustees to urgently address what they viewed as longstanding institutional failures.
Voting took place electronically over more than a week, with the results released Friday.
The Cornell community has been in a state of distress and dismay since mid-September, when a former student filed a lawsuit against the university and seven former members of the Chi Phi fraternity, saying she was given ketamine and raped at a fraternity house in October 2024.
All of those men have denied her allegations, saying either the sex was consensual or they weren’t involved. The local district attorney initially decided the woman had consented to the encounter, and that no crime had been committed, but the investigation has since been reopened and handed to New York’s attorney general.
Cornell disciplined several of the accused students following a months-long Title IX investigation. Two were expelled, two received suspensions and probation, and two were required to write “reflection” papers and complete bystander training. A seventh man had already graduated and was barred from campus, according to records obtained by The New York Times.
Some faculty members have been furious with Kotlikoff for not acting more forcefully to strengthen the school’s disciplinary process, push for criminal investigations and change campus party culture.
Speaking to Faculty Senate members on the first day that they debated the no-confidence resolution, Kotlikoff pledged to make the university a leader in addressing the problem of sexual assault, and he asked that he be given the time to make more changes.
Kotlikoff defended his leadership, arguing that replacing him would do little to solve complex problems and could damage Cornell’s reputation. He acknowledged he had not read the campus police report, explaining that university policy barred top administrators from interfering in criminal investigations. He also rejected suggestions that he had been indifferent to the woman’s case, though he acknowledged not having known until recently that she left Cornell.
Kotlikoff said the university needed to determine whether fraternities could operate safely and left open the possibility of sweeping restrictions on Greek life. He urged faculty to give him time to make changes, arguing that decisions should be based on research and evidence rather than emotion.
Some professors also urged patience and said faculty should wait until the release of an independent investigation by former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates, whom the university hired to examine both how Cornell responded to the woman’s initial rape report in 2024 and its overall procedures for handling similar reports from other students.
The no-confidence resolution did not call for Kotlikoff’s resignation.

title: Federal judge orders 14-day delay on any work beginning on Trump’s monumental arch
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge late Thursday blocked the Trump administration from breaking ground on a towering memorial arch for 14 days.
The temporary restraining order by U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan halting the work represents a major setback for one of President Donald Trump’s most prominent projects in his vision to remake Washington.
The decision followed a series of steps taken earlier Thursday by the government, including the final approval of the arch by the National Capital Planning Commission in an 8-4 vote after a 9 ½ hour hearing where scores of witnesses opposed the construction.
The administration said the work could begin as soon as the approval and the Interior Department issued a final decision authorizing construction and the proper notification was published by the National Park Service.
In approving the temporary stop, Chutkan said Virginia and the District of Columbia had shown that the immediacy of the construction would cause real harm to the plaintiffs.
“The harm is certain,” she wrote. ”Defendants initially notified the court that construction could begin as early as November 5, 2026, if the NCPC approves the project at its meeting that day and the Department of the Interior authorizes construction.” In their filing, Virginia and D.C. warned of traffic pattern distortions as well as concerns about the impact on mutual aid emergency calls if the arch were to proceed.
“Second, the District and Virginia will incur high unrecoverable costs. As soon as construction begins, DDOT will need to expend staff time and operating resources to affirmatively and proactively manage temporary detours, crashes or disabled vehicles,” Chutkan wrote.
The judge ordered the government to provide a status report next Monday to ensure they are complying with the order.
The judge’s decision came just over an hour after the National Capital Planning Commission hearing ended. The vote by the commission broke along federal and local lines. Those in favor worked for the administration or were connected to the president, who was pushing for the immediate construction. Opponents represented the city of Washington.
The remote, call-in hearing — which crashed repeatedly in the first few hours and was accompanied by a nearly universally negative comment section — drew witnesses who gave impassioned comments opposing an arch they said would destroy the solemnity of the nearby Arlington National Cemetery, where hundreds of thousands of fallen service members and military veterans are buried.
The panel’s Trump-appointed chairman launched the meeting with a gushing appraisal of the towering monument and lauded Trump for wanting to build it.
“President Trump understands as president and a superb builder that it’s important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments,” said Mark Paoletta, the commission’s chairman.
As Trump has often remarked, “the great cities around the world have arches: Paris, Rome, London,” said Paoletta, who also serves as general counsel for the White House Office of Management and Budget.
Commissioner Paul Ingrassia, a lawyer for the General Services Administration, said the arch was “not about politics. It’s about remembrance. It’s about celebrating our history. It’s about commemorating veterans. And it’s really something that’s a noble tribute to our nation and something that we can all rally behind.”
But D.C. City Council Chairman Phil Mendelson, who also serves on the planning panel, said the project has not received required approval from Congress, nor has Congress appropriated any money for it. The plan submitted to the commission does not include a reference to military use cited by Trump and other administration officials, Mendelson said.
“We cannot approve final site and building plans until we have the final site and building plans,” he said.
The commission oversees construction on federal land in the city and began reviewing the arch plan in June.
The arch is one of several projects around Washington that the Republican president has undertaken as he alters the capital to his tastes — from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Those projects could soon face intense scrutiny after Democrats gained control of Congress in the midterm elections this week.
Rep. Jared Huffman, a California Democrat who is set to chair the House Natural Resources Committee, called the project ill-advised and illegal.
“This arch would dishonor America,” Huffman told the commission. He called the proposed arch “a tribute to Donald Trump,” not veterans, as Trump administration officials claim. The monument is similar to those built for emperors or kings, Huffman said, adding that Trump was using veterans as a pretext to build a memorial to himself.
Other critics, including the plaintiffs, argue that the Trump administration must seek congressional approval. The administration maintains that Congress cleared the way for a monument at Memorial Circle decades ago.
Several members of the Planning Commission used that logic in approving the project. Paoletta said it was a “national disgrace” that a memorial arch had not been placed there, despite a 1925 law that designated such a memorial, he said.

title: These researchers can trace a World War II veteran’s service for families
text:
NEW ORLEANS, La. (InvestigateTV) — A program at the National World War II Museum in New Orleans is helping families learn about their loved ones’ service by tracking down veterans’ official records.
Researchers can find details that include training, medical history, units, battles and promotions.
InvestigateTV’s own Tisha Powell used the program to learn more about her grandfather, Ulysses Reed Sr.
On Dec. 7, 1941, Japan launched a surprise military attack on the U.S. naval base at Pearl Harbor in Oahu, Hawaii. The attack killed more than 2,400 Americans, sank or damaged 21 ships and destroyed 188 airplanes. The U.S. officially entered the war the next day.
Of the 16.4 million Americans who served in the war, fewer than 46,000 are still alive. Many families are left with unanswered questions about what their loved ones did and endured during the war.
“There’s one half of one percent of American World War II veterans that are still with us today. And so, every time we can bring a veteran to campus or someone who experienced the war in some sort of way, it is a joy and it is an honor,” said Chrissy Gregg of the National WWII Museum.
Gregg said it’s up the museum and researchers “to continue to tell their stories.”
Records trace Reed’s service
Reed was laid to rest April 28, 2012, in a small Louisiana cemetery. He was 100 years old and a U.S. Army World War II combat veteran. Powell said many details of his military service had remained unknown.
Reed was a laborer from the community of Chackbay who was drafted and traveled thousands of miles to Europe during the war.
Dr. Mike Bell, executive director of the Jenny Craig Institute for the Study of War and Democracy at the museum, said researchers can now trace Reed’s service from the time he joined his company after basic training at Camp Beauregard, Louisiana, until he was released from the company at Camp Shelby, Mississippi, to go home. According to Bell, that was likely the winter of 1945.
Bell shared the findings with Powell this spring, after researchers spent weeks searching documents.
“We went in, we found his 1940 registration for the draft, so you can confirm it’s him. Where he lives” Bell said.
Reed’s official military personnel file from the National Archives Records Administration in St. Louis was lost in a 1973 fire. The fire destroyed 80% of Army and Army Air Corps records from 1912 to 1960.
“Millions of records were wiped out in that. And these were the personnel files of the individuals,” Bell said.
Museum researchers, who are veterans themselves, then turned to the Bayou History Center and Nicholls State University in Thibodaux, Louisiana.
“Now, why that was incredibly powerful, though, is it gave us the company he was in,” Bell said.
Unit moved ammunition across Europe
Reed served in the 679th Ordnance Company, which managed ammunition. “Morning reports” detailed the company’s movements.
Records showed the company was formed with soldiers who went to a camp outside Wilmington, North Carolina. Other soldiers who formed the company came from Fort Bragg.
The two groups went to Fort Stewart, Georgia, outside Savannah, for field training. They then traveled by train to Camp Kilmer, New Jersey.
“From there, they’ll board a secret ship. I haven’t figured out exactly which ship yet,” Bell said. He said the records list the ship as secret.
The ship sailed from the United States to Lancashire, England. The 679th then traveled to Wales and later deployed into France, where the company set up miles of ammunition supply points. The company later moved into Germany.
“They’re breaking down ammo, categorizing it, issuing ammunition, you know, moving the supply point to the next phase,” Bell said. “And so in Germany, his unit actually moves into the Rhineland. They’ll support 7th Army as they cross the Rhine River.”
Bell said the company’s “incredible work” allowed Allied troops to advance the campaign in Europe. “Without fuel and ammo, you know, you’re not going to win the war.”
The company pushed forward into Czechoslovakia and then headed back to France after Germany’s surrender in May 1945. The men were still in France when Japan surrendered on September 2, 1945.
“From there, we found the ship that he leaves France on,” Bell said. “He’s on the ship. Yeah, the General R.E. Callen, it leaves Marseille and comes back to the United States.”
The General R. E. Callen would dock near Taunton, Massachusetts and Camp Myles Standish on September 12, 1945. Back on US soil, then PFC Reed and the 679th head to Monterey California to Fort Ord in route to the Pacific.
Research services help families fill gaps
“I wish I had asked more questions when he was alive,” Powell said.
“Well, you know, I think our task is to try to recapture some of that. You know, to give a little agency and voice to these people,” Bell said.
That is the goal of the museum’s Historical Research Services. Research historians work to verify records that can help family members learn about a World War II veteran’s service when their own searches have stalled.
If historians determine the available records contain substantial information about the veteran’s service, families can receive the veteran’s WWII story in the form of a book.
“That generation, in many cases, they just came home and went back to work. And, you know, or they didn’t talk about it just among everybody. How would you understand what they did? Or, uh, I just did my job,” Bell said.
After the war, Reed returned to Louisiana to his wife and young daughters.
During the war, he was able to send home about $900 and his wife bought “upwards of 20 acres of land.”
“So, this service changed the trajectory of my family’s life,” Powell said.
“It’s interesting in the 1950 census, he’s a landowner, you know, in the 1940 census, he’s unemployed,” Bell said.
To Bell and others who work to find information in the records, they feel like they are giving the veterans agency and a voice. “So that we understand what they did, but also to understand why they did it and the importance of it and what they achieved.”
Fee and POW/MIA program
The museum’s research services have a fee. It costs $165 to obtain a veteran’s file.
The museum is also part of the Department of Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency’s Hub and Spoke Program.
The program is a national initiative working to locate and identify American service members who remain unaccounted for from World War II and other conflicts.

title: As Americans get older, the need for ‘aging-ready’ homes grows
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ROANOKE, Va. (InvestigateTV) - America’s population is aging and a recent study found there may not be enough senior-friendly homes to meet demand. In 2019, one in six Americans were 65 or older and by 2060 it will be one in four.
The Census categorized “aging-ready homes” as dwellings with a bedroom and full bathroom on the first floor and a step-free entryway.
Experts say multi-generational housing is in demand, but inventory is low.
Heather Simon has spent the last 35 years helping thousands of families find homes as a mortgage lender.
She said she’s seen a lot of trends over the years.
However, in the last six to seven years, she’s seen a change in what her clients need in a home.
“Couples that have maybe lived in their house for 30-plus years, and their house no longer is conducive for them to be able to live in it, like multiple levels. It seems to be a problem,” Simon said.
She said many clients who are living in a home with 4,000 to 5,000 square feet of space find themselves needing one level, smaller homes with aging-in-place features, like a master suite on the first floor, wider hallways, fewer stairs and zero-step showers.
Inventory on those types of homes is low.
“Here in Virginia, there does seem to be a lack of one stories, one level, that would be the right size for a couple that’s downsizing,” she explains.
“But all over the country, we’re having problems with moving our parents into the right place that’s going to fit their health needs, their lifestyle,” Simon said.
Beth Powell agrees. She owns Home with Heart and helps clients downsize their homes. She said there’s inventory out there, but not that helps the aging population.
“Some folks will say, well, a patio home is the answer. A patio home is not the answer because, one, they’re not accessible. Two, they’re very expensive. And if somebody has lived in their home and they’ve paid their home off, why should they go into debt at the end of their life for an enormous amount of money?” Powell said.
Both agree experts need to help the aging population do a cost analysis of the pros and cons of their options: retrofitting an existing home, purchasing a new home, or building a home.
But that takes time and planning.
“If you have a couple that have lived in their house for 30, 40, 50 years and they’ve lived in this 5,000 square foot house and now they have to downsize to a 2,000 square foot house. That’s a huge transition. And it’s a very emotional transition and it is also something that takes months of planning,” Simon said.
Powell and Simon both agree finding that right place for loved ones starts with a conversation before a worst case scenario happens.
Experts say too often that worst-case scenario is after a fall or a crisis hits, and the homeowner is forced to make a choice, a choice they say that is both more expensive and more limited in options.
Both agree the best advice is to work with a team that can spend the time to find the right fit for everyone.
Until the inventory for this population increases, retrofitting an existing home to accommodate multiple generations will likely continue to be a growing trend.

title: Kennebunkport cafe celebrates 2 years of positive community impact
text:
Kennebunkport cafe celebrates two years of positive community impact
Caring Community Cuisine is a nonprofit providing free meals to cancer patients and their families.
Kennebunkport cafe celebrates two years of positive community impact
Caring Community Cuisine is a nonprofit providing free meals to cancer patients and their families.
Since November 2024, chefs Jonathan Cartwright and Selena Roy have been serving a unique clientele in southern Maine. Caring Community Cafe in Cape Porpoise operates as a typical business, but Cartwright and Roy take their profits to fund something more.
"Our mission is to provide family nutrition and human interaction to help people battling cancer," Roy said. The cancer patients, fondly referred to as warriors, get a week's worth of free dinner meals for themselves and their families.
Cartwright said, "We thought if we can do the bit that we do quite easily, cooking, it'll give them more time to be a family together, heal, and focus on battling the illness." The menu is catered to the individual needs and personal preferences of the warrior.
Roy calls them medically tailored meals. She said, "It's a necessity. You have to eat, and unfortunately due to some of the treatment, you don't always have that appetite... Sometimes we do bone broth, simple pastas, you know, stuff that's a little more helpful to the stomach when you're going through these treatments."
When crafting the menu, Cartwright considers comfort food and nutritional value. In two years, they've helped feed more than 62 families.
"You're going to do all the hard work. We'll just do a little bit of cooking and help you out as much as we can," he said.
A team of volunteers makes deliveries within a 30-mile radius of the cafe on Pier Road, formerly Musette Cafe and The Wayfarer restaurant. Cartwright and Roy are hoping to expand this nonprofit model into other locations so they can help even more families.
"No matter how good the doctor said your chances are of beating it or whatever, it's always very, very sad – very disheartening," Cartwright said. "We want to try to build up that kind of feeling that you're not alone, and together we're going to beat this."

title: Midwife convicted of practicing medicine without license after near-fatal home birth
text:
ATLANTA (WANF/Gray News) - A woman in Georgia was convicted of practicing medicine without a license after a near-fatal home birth in 2022, according to authorities.
Cynthia “Cindy” Rene Morrow, 64, was found guilty of all nine counts she faced Wednesday, according to the Blue Ridge Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, which covers Cherokee County.’
During labor and following the 2022 birth at a Woodstock home, Morrow performed multiple medical procedures she wasn’t licensed to perform, including administering an injection of Pitocin – a drug used to help induce labor – and intravenous fluids, inserting a catheter and performing a manual uterine procedure, prosecutors said.
The mother experienced significant blood loss after giving birth. Despite her worsening condition, Morrow did not tell the woman’s family she was experiencing a medical emergency, and requested a non-emergency medical transport when she eventually called 911, the DA’s office said.
By the time Morrow called 911, the victim was vomiting, had lost consciousness and was experiencing hypovolemic shock.
Cherokee County Fire & Emergency Services stabilized the woman and took her to the hospital for emergency treatment of a severe postpartum hemorrhage.
Medical records show the woman’s blood pressure dropped to 63/55, her heartrate reached 139 beats per minute and she lost approximately 50 percent of her blood, prosecutors said.
Doctors administered medication to control bleeding, provided multiple blood transfusions and performed emergency surgery.
Medical experts who testified at the trial said that they would have taken the woman to a hospital at least five hours earlier, based on her condition.
The jury also heard testimony from two other former clients and their family members. They described similar experiences with Morrow’s midwifery practice in separate incidents that happened outside of Cherokee County.
One of those women nearly died during childbirth, while the other lost her baby. The DA’s office said their testimony gave the jury additional evidence to consider regarding Morrow’s practices and conduct.
Prosecutors also introduced more than 100 exhibits, including the Cherokee County 911 call, the victim’s medical records, client logs Morrow maintained for her business, Birth Servant Midwifery, LLC, along with cellphone records and records showing Morrow was not licensed as a physician, nurse, or certified nurse midwife.
Photographs taken during the execution of the search warrant at the Woodstock home showed expired, dangerous drugs – the Pitocin – and needles, sutures, intravenous supplies and other medical equipment.
Seven of the charges Morrow was convicted of stemmed from the 2022 Woodstock home birth:
- One count of practicing medicine without a license
- One count of practicing nursing without a license
- Two counts of unlawful practice of midwifery
- Two counts of reckless conduct
- One count of possession of a dangerous drug (Pitocin)
Morrow was also found guilty of the “lesser-included offense of criminal attempt (for possession of expired Pitocin that was recovered during a 2024 search warrant of her home)” and unlawful practice of midwifery, involving a second victim in Cherokee County.
Sentencing is set for Nov. 10.

title: Oscar-winning Chilean filmmaker Sebastián Lelio dies at 52
text:
Oscar-winning Chilean filmmaker Sebastián Lelio dies at 52
Oscar-winning Chilean filmmaker Sebastián Lelio, whose acclaimed drama “A Fantastic Woman” broke ground with its portrayal of a transgender woman, has died in Santiago, Chile, at 52.
His family announced his death Friday in an Instagram post, citing health reasons but not specifying the cause.
“His memory will remain forever among us,” the family said. “He was a beautiful person who contributed to Chilean culture in great moments of its history.”
Lelio won the 2018 Academy Award for best international film (formerly known as foreign-language film) for “A Fantastic Woman," starring trans actress Daniela Vega as a waitress and nightclub singer whose life is torn by the death of her boyfriend.
It was Chile's second Academy Award, following the animated short “Bear Story” in 2016.
Lelio’s other films include "Gloria," "The Wave," "The Wonder," “Disobedience,” and “The Year of the Tiger.” Throughout his career, he collaborated with Julianne Moore, Rachel Weisz and Florence Pugh.
Lelio had begun filming “Poeta Chileno” (Chilean Poet) based on the book by Alejandro Zambra in September.
He was born in the Argentine city of Mendoza and moved to Chile at the age of 2. He studied journalism for a year before enrolling at the Chilean Film School.

title: Dolly Parton’s manager moves to drop complaint accusing late singer’s nephew of threatening estate
text:
(AP) - Dolly Parton’s longtime manager moved Thursday to drop a complaint that accused the late singer’s nephew of threatening her estate and its employees.
She’s Alive, the entity founded to manage and protect Parton’s estate, had secured a temporary restraining order against Bryan Seaver and his security company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services, in September.

title: Deven Young will be tried as an adult in slaying of Maine paddleboarder
text:
A Maine teenager accused of killing a woman in 2025 will be tried as an adult.
Deven Young, now 19, waived his right to a bind over hearing from juvenile court to adult court. Young, then 17, was charged as a juvenile with intentional or knowing or depraved indifference murder in Knox County Juvenile Court.
Young is accused of killing 48-year-old Sunshine Stewart, who was found dead July 3, 2025, after she failed to return from paddleboarding on Crawford Pond in Union.
Friday’s hearing in Knox County District Court was supposed to include arguments from both sides about whether or not Young should be tried as an adult. Instead, by waiving the hearing, the case will proceed directly to adult court.
More than 15 of Stewart’s friends and family attended the hearing, many of them wearing yellow, one of her favorite colors. She was described as a “strong” and “self-made” woman by friends. She rehabbed her home in Tenants Harbor, where the community was shocked to learn of her death. Stewart also worked as a bartender, waitress, carpenter and fisherman.
Young was originally charged as a juvenile on July 18, 2025. Shortly after, the case was made confidential. The case moving to adult court means proceedings will be public moving forward.
The Maine medical examiner’s office ruled that Stewart died from strangulation and blunt force trauma, according to the Maine Department of Public Safety.

title: 4 Cornell lawsuit defendants join effort to oust Letitia James from criminal investigation
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Four men named in a former Cornell University student’s lawsuit are joining a co-defendant’s effort to block New York’s attorney general from leading a reopened criminal investigation into the woman’s gang rape allegations, according to court filings on Thursday.
The co-defendant’s lawyers said the men agreed to be added to a court petition that seeks Attorney General Letitia James’ removal from the case because of social media posts she made prior to her involvement in which she condemned the alleged assault and expressed support for the accuser.
The development comes a day after James appointed Jacqueline Kelly, a former federal prosecutor who oversaw sex crimes cases against music mogul Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs, as outside counsel for the investigation. She and a team of lawyers and investigators will be responsible for evidence gathering, witness interviews and other investigative steps. They will report to James.
A judge heard arguments last week on one of the accused men’s request to remove James but said he wouldn’t rule without knowing if the six other lawsuit defendants backed the effort. He gave the man’s lawyers until Thursday to try to get them to join.
Lawyers for one of the four men agreeing to join had separately filed court papers seeking to have James removed. Two other men named as defendants in the lawsuit didn’t have lawyers who could speak for them and did not provide a response, court filings said.
James’ office declined to comment.
A former Cornell student identified in court papers as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit in September alleging that several men raped her at a fraternity party in 2024. The woman said some of the men pressured her into using ketamine and marijuana and that she drank alcohol that left her too intoxicated to consent. Not all of the men named were accused of rape.
James, a Democrat, posted about the case on X and Facebook on Sept. 28, linking to a news article about the lawsuit. “I’m holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you’re not alone. We stand with you.”
On Oct. 1, Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed James as special prosecutor overseeing the criminal investigation, saying that she had lost faith in the local district attorney, who declined to bring charges in 2024 but had said he would restart the investigation following the former student’s lawsuit.
James initially declined to comment about her social media posts but addressed them at an Oct. 8 debate, saying: “Those comments demonstrate empathy, and what we need now more than ever in our body politic is more empathy.”
In court, the state’s lawyers argued that Hochul has wide latitude to appoint special prosecutors and said she picked James because of her track record handling sensitive cases in the national spotlight.
In a statement on Wednesday, James said she is confident that Kelly “will lead a fair and comprehensive investigation.”
Andrew Miltenberg, a lawyer for the man spearheading the removal effort, said in a court filing that Kelly’s appointment “changes the face of the investigation” but ”does not establish any change in ultimate authority.”

title: Woman rescued after being chained to bed for years when maintenance worker hears cries for help, police say
text:
FARGO, N.D. (KVLY/Gray News) — A woman was rescued in North Dakota after being chained to a bed for years when a maintenance technician working in the apartment building heard her cries for help.
According to court documents, Fargo police were called to an apartment complex Tuesday after a maintenance technician heard someone crying for help.
The maintenance technician told police he entered the apartment where he found a woman chained to a bed with a security camera pointing at her. Court documents also said the windows of the bedroom were covered with tin foil.
The responding officer said the woman was in a bedroom with a chain and padlock secured around her right ankle, with the other end of the chain secured to the bed.
The woman told authorities she was brought to Fargo from Mexico in 2024 by her ex-husband, identified as 40-year-old Arturo Calzada Becerril. She said she had been chained up in his apartment and had not been outside for two years.
The woman said Calzada Becerril brought her food twice a day but did not let her go outside or use the bathroom. She was given a bucket to relieve herself.
Court documents said that police freed the woman from the chains and interviewed her using Language Link because she did not speak English.
Investigators noted bruising to her body and face. She was then brought to the hospital.
Police said that shortly afterward, 41-year-old Erendira Amoles arrived at the apartment with her 8-year-old daughter.
While being interviewed at the hospital, the woman told investigators that both Calzada Becerril and Amoles would beat her and sexually assault her.
Calzada Becerril told investigators that the three of them were from the same town in Mexico. Court documents show that he told investigators he locked the victim up so “she did not run away.” Amoles told police she is the one who often locks the woman up.
Calzada Becerril and Amoles were arrested on kidnapping and assault charges. They were booked into the Cass County Jail.
Border Patrol assisted Fargo police.

title: Containment nearly doubles around the Wild River Fire in the White Mountains
text:
Containment nearly doubles around large wildfire along the Maine-New Hampshire border
Crews have nearly doubled their containment as they battle a large wildfire in the White Mountains along the Maine-New Hampshire border.
As of late Friday morning, White Mountain National Forest officials said the Wild River Fire was holding at 856 acres and containment was up to 20%, compared to 11% the day before. Earlier this week, officials said the fire had burned 1,000 acres, but updated and more precise mapping showed the area at 856 acres.
A total of 140 personnel from as far away as Nevada were battling the fire, including using two helicopters, a bulldozer, six engines, five suppression modules and one drone. The weather was also helping, with rain falling on Friday and showers expected to continue through the weekend.
On Thursday, officials said the cause of the fire was under investigation, but they believed it was caused by humans. Officials at the U.S. Forest Service were reminding people to never leave a campfire unattended and to make sure a fire is completely out before leaving.
The Wild River Fire was first reported at about 1 p.m. on Sunday just southeast of Gorham, New Hampshire, and just south of Gilead, Maine, near Evans Notch. As of about 3:30 p.m. on Monday, the fire had burned about 288 acres.
On Thursday, crews used the drone to check on hot spots and used the helicopters to put them out.
Crews also conducted burnout operations on the north side of the fire to help strengthen the containment line. On Friday, crews were working to continue to keep the fire in its current footprint by securing and strengthening fire containment lines using both ground and aerial resources.
A forest closure is in effect for the White Mountain National Forest. The closure order and map can be found at https://www.fs.usda.gov/r09/whitemountain/alerts/wild-river-fire-androscoggin-ranger-district.
A community meeting was held on Thursday evening to share information with people who live in the area and to answer questions.

title: 'We brought him home': A WWII soldier killed 82 years ago has finally been laid to rest
text:
A WWII hero missing for 82 years has been laid to rest in Massachusetts with full military honors
A World War II hero from Massachusetts whose remains were missing for more than 80 years after his death was buried Thursday in his hometown outside of Salem.
Private Joseph A. Gala of Lynn, Massachusetts, killed in action in 1944 in Myanmar, which was then known as Burma, was finally laid to rest Thursday, 82 years after his death.
Gala was a graduate of Lynn English High School and entered the service on May 24, 1943. He was a member of the U.S. Army's "Merrill's Marauders," a special operations jungle-warfare unit, and was 21 when he was killed in the line of duty.
His family said his mother, Adeline, spent years waiting and hoping for news of her son.
"Horrible — she couldn't talk about him," said one of Gala's nieces.
For decades, Gala's remains were classified as missing in action, but advances in DNA technology allowed his remains to be identified using DNA provided by his nieces.
"Our family, mother, uncles, grandparents, I know they're really happy," said a family member.
On Friday, Gala's remains arrived at Logan Airport in Boston, where his family welcomed him home. A police escort then brought his casket to Solimine Funeral Home in Lynn, where members of the community gathered to honor him.
"We brought him home, to Lynn," said 91-year-old Air National Guard veteran David Solimine Sr., who was moved to tears during the service.  
On Thursday, people from across generations in Lynn came together to pay their respects to Gala during a graveside service with full military honors in the World War II section of Pine Grove Cemetery.
"I am so happy about my city of Lynn, and how everybody has come together for this family," said Solimine Sr. "Any veteran that, we're very proud of them. And we're honored to have them part of our world," said Solimine Sr.
Gala's return and burial marked the end of a decades-long journey to bring him home and provided closure for his family and community.

title: This weekend might be the last chance this year to drive up Acadia’s Cadillac Mountain
text:
This could be the final weekend this year for Acadia National Park visitors to drive to the summit of the park’s highest peak — and they won’t need a reservation to do it.
Cadillac Summit Road will close Monday so the park can resume construction on a pedestrian pathway connecting the summit’s east and west parking lots, a project aimed at preventing visitors from walking along a busy roadway at one of the park’s most frequented sites.
The roadway, which requires a vehicle reservation during the park’s busy season between May and October, will reopen Nov. 25 for Thanksgiving weekend, marking the final chance for visitors to ascend Cadillac Mountain by vehicle this year — if the weather cooperates.
Officials could close the summit road to vehicles for the winter sooner if it snows, as the park typically avoids plowing the mountain road. In the past, the park has closed the road due to snow in November, but has reopened it again temporarily if the snow melted away again before Dec. 1.
The road, which typically is closed to vehicles between December and April, will be closed to all users — including hikers and cyclists — from Dec. 1 through Dec. 18, according to a park Facebook post. After that cyclists and pedestrians will be able to resume using Cadillac Summit Road, but motorists will not be able to use the road again until spring.
Hiking trails on the mountain will be open throughout the construction closures.
The park has already shuttered most of its seasonal amenities, including the visitors centers in Trenton and Hulls Cove.
The park’s popular Jordan Pond House restaurant, famous for its popovers and sweeping mountain views, and its adjoining retail store have already closed as of late October and early November.
The gift shops on the summit of Cadillac Mountain and Thunder Hole also closed in late October, according to the park’s website.
The Sieur de Monts Nature Center closed in mid-October. The center was the site of multiple climate change-related displays that were flagged for removal following the Trump administration’s order to remove signage from national parks that could “disparage Americans past or living” and distract from the “grandeur of the American landscape.”
Some of those signs were removed and later restored after a coalition of environmental groups challenged their removal in federal court. Other displays that were removed in fall 2025 have yet to reappear.
Much of Park Loop Road, Acadia’s 27-mile scenic drive running along the east side of Mount Desert Island, will close for the season on Dec. 1, according to the park. The road will remain open along the portion known as Ocean Drive — between Schooner Head Road and Otter Cliff Road in Bar Harbor — and between Jordan Pond Road in Seal Harbor and the Jordan Pond House.
Wildwood Stables, which offers horse-drawn carriage rides during the summer, is also closed for the season and will reopen in late May.
The park’s various campgrounds — including Blackwoods, Seawall and Schoodic Woods — each closed in mid-October. Winter camping in Acadia is strictly prohibited.
Public restrooms at Sand Beach, Jordan Pond, Brown Mountain, Parkman Mountain trailhead, Fabbri Picnic area and Eagle Lake boat launch and carriage road are all open through the winter, according to the park website.

title: Man gets stolen car back, then faces $2,398 fine and other expenses
text:
BALTIMORE, Md. (WJZ) — A Mount Vernon man says his car was stolen in October and returned with damage. He also says he is dealing with fines and tickets that came in while the car was missing. Trace Thompson wants police to do more to track down stolen vehicles.
Car reported missing Oct. 17
Thompson said he was trying to go to work around 6 a.m. on Oct. 17 when he realized his car had been stolen from his Mount Vernon neighborhood.
“I was in a bit of panic. I was trying to get to work at the time. It was about 6 in the morning,” Thompson said.
He called 311 for help. Thompson said the operator told him his car may have been moved for the marathon. He then asked for police to come out. When officers arrived two days later, they determined the car was stolen.
Car found at Wawa in Lansdowne
Baltimore police said the car was tracked on license plate reader cameras in the city. Thompson said he worked with the car manufacturer to track the location to a motel.
Baltimore County police found the car in the middle of the night last Friday at a Wawa in Lansdowne.
“I was actually able to pass my location information to the police department, and two days later, at three o’clock in the morning, I received a call that my car had been found next to a Wawa,” Thompson said.
Police arrested the driver, identified as Bobby Hamlett. He is charged with unlawful taking of a vehicle. Charging documents say Hamlett claimed he knew Thompson and was borrowing the car.
“I don’t think I would ever let somebody borrow my car and take it to a highway motel,” Thompson said.
Damage, tolls and insurance fine
Thompson said he is now dealing with the damage left behind. He described how the car was entered.
“The individual actually, through the left side port window, was able to pop the rubber out and then pried out the window from there,” Thompson said.
Thompson said he received tickets in the mail for unpaid tolls incurred while the car was stolen. He also received a fine from the MVA for lapsed insurance.
“So I got two within an hour of each other between Baltimore Tunnel South and Fort McHenry. I received a fine for $2,398 in the mail for insurance,” Thompson said.
The MVA said the vehicle being reported as stolen triggered the fine notice to be mailed. The agency said it is reaching out to Thompson, who said he had insurance the entire time. Thompson said he is not sure if more tickets are coming.
Thompson said the inside of the car was also damaged.
“In the back there were trash bags full of stuff,” Thompson said.
He said the bags contained trash, drugs and bodily fluids.
“I think the car was more of a crime scene than a vehicle recovery,” Thompson said.
Thompson asks city for action
Thompson is asking the city to do more to protect neighbors from crimes like this.
“If stuff like this keeps happening to your young professionals, we’re going to leave,” Thompson said.
Thompson said he now parks his car in a garage nearly a mile away.
Hamlett is due back in court in December.
