title: 98-year-old twin Army veterans reunite after years apart
text:
98-year-old twin Army veterans reunite after years apart in hospice care
Twin brothers Jack and Jesse Kennedy, 98-year-old Army veterans, reunited on Monday after years apart, thanks to the efforts of hospice care providers.
Craig Kennedy, Jack’s son, shared how much the reunion meant to his father.
"Dad is always talking about Jesse, and I'm sure Jesse sometimes asked about dad," Craig Kennedy said.
Craig said that the brothers’ connection became even more evident as they both began experiencing the effects of dementia.
"When the dementia seemed to start affecting them the most is when I seemed to notice the connection there more," he said.
Bayada Hospice in High Point, North Carolina, facilitated the reunion by transporting Jack to see Jesse at Pennybyrn Nursing Homes, overcoming the challenges posed by their age and health conditions.
"I feel like, if you watch these two together and you don't feel something, you know, something's broken inside you," Bobby Ashley with Bayada Hospice said.
The brothers grew up in Thomasville, North Carolina, working jobs like tobacco farming before joining the U.S. Army together.
"My dad and Jesse were twins, so they were both together," Craig Kennedy said. "They were in Camp Polk, Louisiana. I think down in Georgia, Fort Monmouth."
Their military service was recognized with certificates and pins, honoring their contributions.
"One generation did their time and served their country, and then myself and my generation are stepping up and continuing the legacy," Capt. Victor Littleton with Fort Bragg said.
Despite the years they spent apart, the bond between the brothers remains unbroken.
"What stuck out the most was when I walked in here and saw both of them, holding each other's hand," Craig Kennedy said.
Their family described the reunion as a moment of positivity, something they believe the world could use more of.

title: 2 Justice Department officials resign, including US attorney who oversaw 'grand conspiracy' probe
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The top federal prosecutor in Miami who had been tasked with overseeing an investigation into foes of President Donald Trump has resigned, joining other high-profile Justice Department officials departing in the wake of the midterm elections, officials said Friday.
Jason Reding Quiñones’ resignation follows frustrations among Washington officials with his management of the office assigned to lead the so-called “grand conspiracy” investigation, according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel issues.
The Justice Department’s top national security official, John Eisenberg, also resigned on Friday, Attorney General Todd Blanche said. On Thursday, Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who led a radical overhaul of the department’s Civil Rights Division, also announced her departure.
Quiñones was confirmed by the Senate last year as U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, where the Justice Department had centered its meandering probe into whether former law enforcement and intelligence officials conspired against the Republican president.
His departure comes as the investigation has shown signs of faltering amid a spate of staff turnovers and delays. Investigators in recent weeks have put off scheduled grand jury testimony of several witnesses, according to multiple people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation.
Blanche said in a social media post that the department is grateful for Quiñones’ “leadership in combating violent crime, drug trafficking, sex trafficking, and transnational crime, including the indictment of Raúl Castro.”
Castro, the former Cuban president, was indicted by Quiñones’ office in May on charges related to the 1996 downing of civilian planes flown by Miami-based exiles.
Quiñones said Friday that he is leaving with “immense pride in what we accomplished together and profound gratitude for the opportunity to serve our great Nation.”
“I am grateful to President Trump for his trust and to the extraordinary men and women of the great Southern District of Florida for their dedication, friendship, and unwavering commitment to justice and the rule of law,” Quiñones wrote in a social media post.
The “grand conspiracy” investigation has proceeded in fits and starts for over a year with repeated setbacks and departures. Last April, a lead national security prosecutor in the investigation of former CIA Director John Brennan was replaced on the team after raising questions about the strength of the case.
Shortly afterward, Joseph diGenova, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, took over the probe. DiGenova resigned from the Justice Department in September without bringing any criminal charges.
Eisenberg was sworn in as assistant attorney general in charge of the department’s National Security Division in June 2025 and oversaw cases involving espionage, terrorism, export control violations, cyber crimes and other matters.
Among the division’s most high-profile cases under his watch was the prosecution of former national security adviser John Bolton, who pleaded guilty this year to allegations of mishandling classified information and is awaiting sentencing.
“He has served with distinction, strengthening our nation’s ability to address threats, both foreign and domestic,” Blanche said in a statement.

title: Votes continue to be counted in Mississippi’s Senate race
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Mississippi election officials continued to count ballots in the state’s U.S. Senate race on Friday, which remains without a declared winner.
Democrat Scott Colom leads incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by about 2,500 votes as of Friday night. Thousands more ballots could still possibly be counted in the race.
Emily Ommundsen, a University of Mississippi political science professor, said counties are being particularly judicious in determining that the count is accurate because of the narrow margins of the race.
“Because of this narrow majority, we are we are hesitant to make any conclusions about the outcome of the race, as these final ballots are still being counted, within this legally prescribed period, where counties are ensuring that they are reporting the correct totals,” Ommundsen said.
The total number of remaining ballots remains unclear because of provisional ballots as well late-arriving mail-in ballots.
“Let me be clear. This race is far from being over,” said Mike Hurst, chairman of the Mississippi Republican Party, on Thursday. “We estimate that there could be approximately 20,000 outstanding ballots left to be counted. That includes mail-in or absentee ballots and affidavit or provisional ballots.”
Provisional ballots are ballots that have been set aside because of verification issues. Voters have until Nov. 10 to resolve them.
Both campaigns have deployed legal teams that could address possible legal challenges in the days ahead.
“We got an army of lawyers. Those election commissioners and circuit clerks, they’re not going to be intimidated,” Colom said Friday.
Mississippi is the only state in the nation without any recourse for a vote recount. But challenges are still likely.
The deadline to certify votes in Mississippi is Nov. 13.
“If these margins stay as close as they are, I expect some court ordered considerations, of which ballots should be permitted to be to be counted,” said Ommundsen. “But the 13th is really that first opportunity that I think we will have to see to see how things are going to shake out here in Mississippi.”

title: Foster mother charged with murder after missing 10-year-old girl found dead
text:
PHILADELPHIA -- Philadelphia officials announced Thursday that the foster mother of a 10-year-old girl who went missing last month has been charged with murder.
Caprice Williams, 36, the foster mother of Malayshia Alford, is charged with murder, abuse of a corpse and several related offenses, authorities said. Authorities said Alford was found dead in New Jersey late Wednesday night.
Search and discovery
Alford was last seen at her Philadelphia home Oct. 22. Her disappearance led to a search by locals, the police department and the FBI.
On Wednesday, law enforcement found surveillance video from the early morning hours of Oct. 26.
“There was video that shows what we believe to be her body being moved out of the home. It was that video that then led law enforcement officials to a suspect vehicle,” said Ashley Toczylowski, assistant district attorney with the Philadelphia District Attorney’s Office.
Investigators found Alford’s body late Wednesday night in the trunk of a car in New Jersey.
“It was immediately apparent that she had been there for a while,” Toczylowski said.
Officials said Alford’s cause of death is believed to be blunt force trauma.
Community reaction
A community in Philadelphia reacted with shock and grief after authorities said Alford was found dead.
Malcolm Jordan, who helped search for Alford, said, “I wanted to cry. I wanted to cry.”
“It’s just so heartbreaking that this is the end result. I just wish it was a different result, man, and uh we just got to do what we can to prevent this stuff from happening,” Jordan said.
A neighbor, who was not named, said, “Everybody failed this baby. Everybody.”
Alford’s uncle, Nafis Horne, spoke Thursday.
“I need everybody held accountable, from the foster parents who were picked to take care of my niece. I want you held accountable,” Horne said.
CNN is working to determine whether Williams has legal representation.

title: Obituary: Jason Elvin Leyro
text:
SCARBOROUGH – Jason Elvin Leyro, 54, of Scarborough, passed away unexpectedly but peacefully in his home on Nov. 1, 2026.
Jason was born at Mt. Sinai Hospital in New York City, N.Y. on June 15, 1972, to Maria and Elvin Leyro. The eldest of his siblings, he was raised in the Bronx, New York, until 1980, when his parents relocated to Bangor.
In Bangor, he attended St. Mary’s Catholic School before continuing his education in the Hampden school system, attending Weatherbee Middle School and graduating with the Hampden Academy Class of 1990. Following graduation, he briefly attended UMaine, Presque Isle, where he played basketball, before relocating to Florida in pursuit of sunnier skies and warmer weather.
Despite his best efforts to convince family to make the move to Florida, Jason ultimately gave in to the lure of New England and, more importantly, the desire to be closer to those he cherished most. In 2017, he returned, settling in southern Maine.
Although he never had his own children, Jason fully embraced his role as big brother, uncle, and, more recently, bonus dad. His genuine interest, patience, kindness, outgoing nature, and “joie de vivre” were best in class. He was truly adored by family and friends alike.
Professionally, Jason found his calling with JM&A, where he excelled as a dealer performance manager for the past decade. Jason was the ultimate maximizer, making the most of every precious moment nurturing his hobbies and, above all, spending time with family and friends.
Some of his best memories were made travelling abroad with family; enjoying annual JM&A vacations with his partner, Laura Baer, and her children, Elise and James, whom he cherished; boating in Casco Bay during the summer; and hitting the links with his dad, brother, and, most recently, his mom.
With his easygoing spirit and appreciation of life’s simple pleasures, Jason had a quality about him that was a reminder not to take life too seriously. He enjoyed charcuterie, oysters, reggae music, and, most of all, the company of the people he loved.
Jason was taken too soon and will continue to be deeply mourned and celebrated by his parents, Elvin and Maria Leyro; his brother Brandon Leyro and sister-in-law Jessie Cmaylo, his sister Teresa Leyro and brother-in-law Sandro Colacicco; as well as his nephews, Benicio and Wesley Leyro, and nieces, Kaia and Jordan Colacicco.
Jason was a central figure to his large Puerto Rican family, including his godparents, Titi Gladys and Uncle Ralph; his Titis, Nellie, Beryl, and Noeli; and his Uncle Pie, with whom he shared the most special bond. And we would be remiss not to mention the cousins with whom he shared his life and to whom he was considered a brother, including Linda (Antonio), Kimberly Ann, Christopher, Michelle, Rizalina, and Idalis.
He was predeceased by his grandparents; his dear Uncle Verne (Nellie); and Titi Elvie, who we know have welcomed him in Heaven. Fly away home.
Celebration of life will be held on Saturday, Nov. 14, from 2 p.m. to 3:30 p.m. at Hobbs Funeral Home, 230 Cottage Rd., South Portland. A reception will follow next door at the Elizabeth Hobbs Hospitality Center from 3:30 p.m. to 5 p.m.
In lieu of flowers, donations may be made to Friends of Casco Bay: https://www.cascobay.org/

title: Arizona Democrats gain trifecta to control the state House, Senate and governor’s office for first time in 60 years
text:
PHOENIX (AP) — Democrats in Arizona won control of both legislative chambers and retained the governor’s office, giving the party its first trifecta in the state since 1966 as Democrats made major gains nationwide in this week’s elections and took control of both chambers of Congress.
In her first term, Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs had vetoed more than 540 measures passed by the Republican-led Legislature on policies including taxes, immigration and voting laws. Hobbs has said she’s looking to address water issues and affordability, and take on fraud and abuse in the state’s school voucher program.
The Associated Press called enough legislative races to confirm that both chambers flipped on Friday. The news organization calls races individually and it can take several days after voting, depending on when election officials tally the votes and how close the elections are. There have not been major disputes or disruptions this year.
In Arizona, Republicans have held the House for 60 years and the Senate since the early 1990s.
Overall, Democrats took full control — both statehouse chambers and governors’ offices — in at least six states where they previously shared power with Republicans. Besides Arizona, those wins were in the battleground states of Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Nevada and Wisconsin.
The flips weren’t just in states that are normally competitive. Democrats won control of the Texas House, which Republicans have held since 2003, and elected Gina Hinojosa as the state’s first Democratic governor since George W. Bush ousted Ann Richards in 1994. Republicans held onto the state Senate.
Democrats also flipped the lower chambers of the legislatures in Maine and North Carolina and both chambers in New Hampshire, where Republican Kelly Ayotte was reelected. The count could grow as results are tallied in additional states.
The National Council of State Legislatures says it’s likely to end up as the election with the most legislative seats and chambers changing parties since the 2010 election, when Republicans took over governments across the country amid the Great Recession.
Democrats will also hold the governor’s office in at least 28 states. Results are still pending in Alaska and Kansas.

title: First measles death in 30+ years reported in this state
text:
MADISON, Wis. (WBAY/Gray News) — The Wisconsin Department of Health Services reports the death of an infant associated with the ongoing measles outbreak in the southwestern part of the state.
It is the first measles death in the state since 1990, according to a DHS news release.
The coroner listed the immediate cause of death as measles, the release said. To protect the privacy of the family and the child, DHS is not releasing any more information about the case or the young patient.
State health secretary comments
“Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease,” said DHS Secretary Kirsten Johnson. “Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family.”
Statewide case count
As of Nov. 3, DHS has reported 431 measles cases in 13 counties so far in 2026, according to the release. The DHS numbers are from Nov. 3, before five cases were confirmed in Green Lake County. The number reflects the highest number of cases seen in the state in more than 35 years.
Nine people have required hospitalization for severe symptoms across those cases, DHS said.
The release said reported case counts may not reflect the full extent of measles spread. Not everyone who becomes ill seeks medical care or gets tested, which means cases may go unreported.
“A disease that can spread that quickly can go from a small problem to a big problem very quickly, and the best way across the whole world that we’ve been able to stop illness and death from measles is to stop it from spreading in the community completely,” says Dr. Ryan Westergaard, the chief medical officer with the Wisconsin DHS.
The state’s total was 335 on Oct. 27, which means it added nearly 100 patients in about one week. A majority of the cases are from what is being referred to as the “Southwest Wisconsin measles outbreak” in Grant, Lafayette, Iowa, and Vernon counties. DHS said the cases are related to out-of-state travel, but the exact source of those infections is unknown.
All but three of the patients were not vaccinated.
Green Lake County cases
Green Lake County has confirmed at least five measles cases, according to a news release from the Green Lake County Department of Health & Human Services. They are the first cases confirmed in Northeast Wisconsin.
The cases are linked to a laboratory-confirmed case in another county, the release said. The Green Lake County Department of Health & Human Services did not name which county the infection spread from.
Green Lake County is adjacent to Marquette County, which has two confirmed measles cases.
All confirmed and suspected cases identified so far in Green Lake County have been among people who were not vaccinated against measles. Known exposures have been limited to private gatherings, and no public exposure locations have been identified at this time.
The state is now recommending an early dose of the MMR vaccine for infants between 6 and 11 months old who face a higher risk of exposure. The usual first dose is given after a child’s 1st birthday.
“Ordinarily, we don’t begin MMR vaccination until a child’s first birthday. But in an outbreak, when we know that an infant may be exposed to measles, there’s a benefit to providing that protection earlier,” said Dr. Westergaard.
Measles symptoms
Measles is a highly contagious, vaccine-preventable disease that can spread from person to person through the air. The virus can stay in the air for two hours after a sick person coughs or sneezes. It can cause serious health complications, including pneumonia, brain damage and deafness, and can sometimes be deadly.
Symptoms typically appear approximately 10 to 12 days after exposure, but in some cases can range from seven to 21 days. Symptoms include:
- Runny nose
- High fever, which may be greater than 104 degrees
- Tiredness
- Cough
- Red, watery eyes or conjunctivitis (“pink eye”)
- Red rash with raised bumps that starts at the hairline and moves to the arms and legs three to five days after symptoms begin
People who develop symptoms should stay home and not go to work, school or shopping or use public transportation. They should call their doctor’s office or clinic before visiting so staff can take precautions to prevent other patients from being exposed.
Vaccination status
People who are unsure whether they are vaccinated against measles can contact their health provider or check the Wisconsin Immunization Registry at dhfswir.org, according to the Green Lake County release.

title: Yarmouth football downs Spruce Mountain to claim 8-man Large South title
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
YARMOUTH — In his first season with the Yarmouth football team, Stephen Connolly has carried the Clippers to a berth in the 8-man Large School final.
Connolly, a junior, rushed 32 times for 410 yards and six touchdowns to lead the Clippers to a 68-34 win over Spruce Mountain on a rainy Friday night.
“I’ve only been here for one year, but the seniors, this means so much,” said Connolly, who attends North Yarmouth Academy. “From the beginning to now, they’ve talked about how much they’ve come through and how much this means to them. And we’re doing it for them.”
The top-seeded Clippers (10-0) will play for the state champion next Saturday at Edward Little High School against the winner of the North final this Saturday between No. 1 Old Town (8-1) and No. 2 Mount Desert Island (6-3).
Yarmouth won the state title in 2022, then failed to make the playoffs in 2024. Last fall, the Clippers lost in the quarterfinals to Mt. Ararat.
“This was the happiest I think I’ve ever been in my life,” Connolly said. “I love these boys more than anything, as you can tell. This is such a family. We work together every day, we worked for this all year, and it means so much.”
The Clippers shut out the Phoenix, 48-0, in the regular season, when Spruce Mountain was without quarterback Dylan Jewett. He made an impact Friday, throwing a touchdown pass and running for a TD.
Connolly scored his first touchdown, a 14-yard run, on Yarmouth’s opening drive, but Spruce Mountain’s Jace McElhaney returned the kickoff for a touchdown. Jewett’s conversion pass to Isiah Ayer gave the Phoenix an 8-6 lead.
Connolly’s second touchdown, a 58-yard run, put the Clippers back in front. Iggy McGrath found Jack Flanagan for a 31-yard touchdown pass with under a minute to play in the first quarter, making it 22-8.
The teams traded scores in the second quarter, and Yarmouth led 44-28 at the half. Spruce Mountain pulled within 10 on a 4-yard run by Owen Kelvey early in the third quarter, but the Clippers scored the next 24 points.
“Spruce Mountain’s a really good team,” Yarmouth coach Nick Orsi said. “That was an awesome first half. That was a really tight game. But I felt like we were battling everything tonight. So battling the elements, battling a great team, battling referees … but these kids never quit. They don’t quit at all. They’ve got just such fortitude and they just refused to lose.”
Yarmouth’s Reed Chapin intercepted three passes, including two in the second half.
The Clippers will try to cap an undefeated season with the fourth state title in program history.
“We just got to do our thing,” Orsi said. “We just got to continue to get better. I feel like when we’re playing at the top of our game, we’re pretty hard to beat.”

title: Looking into how Jackson was able to unseat Collins in Maine's Senate race
text:
Looking into how Troy Jackson was able to unseat Sen. Susan Collins in Maine's Senate race
U.S. Sen.-elect Troy Jackson (D-Maine) did something that no one has been able to do in more than 30 years: defeat Republican Sen. Susan Collins in a statewide election.
In 1994, Collins won the Republican primary for Maine governor, but she ultimately finished third in the general election behind Democratic former Gov. Joseph E. Brennan and the winner, independent Angus King, who is now in his third term as a U.S. senator.
Collins was first elected to the U.S. Senate in 1996 and was seeking her sixth term, but fell short in her reelection bid and ultimately conceded the race to Jackson. The Associated Press called the race for Jackson shortly after 1 a.m. Wednesday. According to the AP, Jackson had a 6.3-point lead over Collins with 94% of votes counted. The official results from the Maine Secretary of State's Office had not been announced as of Friday afternoon.
Jackson was able to win against Collins, the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, despite the fact that he had just over three months to campaign in the Senate race. The former Maine Senate president initially ran for governor in the 2026 election cycle, but he finished third in the Democratic gubernatorial primary. On July 25, the Maine Democratic Party chose Jackson as the new Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, 17 days after the primary winner, Graham Platner, dropped out of the race following allegations of sexual assault.
The final Pine Tree State Poll released before Election Day showed that 54% of likely voters said they would vote or had already voted for Jackson, but there were still questions as to whether the fifth-generation logger from Allagash would win the race. That's because former Maine House Speaker Sara Gideon, a Democrat, found herself in a similar position leading up to Election Day in the 2020 Senate race, but she ultimately lost to Collins by about 8.5 points. Still, that was Collins' smallest margin of victory since her first Senate run in 1996.
Maine's Total Coverage looked at the AP's 2026 election results and the 2020 election results from the Maine Secretary of State's Office to better understand how Jackson was able to unseat Collins.
When examining the AP's election results map, what stands out is the large margin of victory Jackson had in Portland. He received 31,197 votes (84.4%) in Maine's largest city compared to the 5,738 votes (15.5%) that Collins received. Jackson also picked up 11,077 votes (76.3%) in the neighboring city of South Portland, while Collins received 3,431 (23.6%).
In the 2020 election, Gideon also soundly defeated Collins in Portland and South Portland, but the senator did pick up a higher percentage of votes in both cities than she did this year. Gideon received 28,053 votes (66.7%) in Portland, while Collins received 8,659 votes (20.6%). In South Portland, Gideon picked up 10,001 votes (60.8%) while 4,943 votes (30.0%) were cast for Collins.
The big difference Maine's Total Coverage found between the 2020 election and 2026 election is that Jackson performed much better in the biggest cities in the state's 2nd Congressional District than Gideon did. Maine's 2nd District has a stronger Republican voter base than the 1st District, as President Donald Trump has won the electoral vote in CD2 in each of the past three presidential elections.
According to the AP, Jackson outperformed Collins in the cities of Bangor (58.0% to 41.9%), Lewiston (53.8% to 46.1%), Auburn (52.4% to 47.6%) and Augusta (53.2% to 46.6%). In 2020, Collins defeated Gideon in each of those four cities.

title: Looks Like Maine Is Getting Its First Jimmy John's Restaurant
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
It Looks Like Maine Could Be Getting Its First Jimmy John’s Restaurant
It's pretty exciting when a popular restaurant or business that seems to be everywhere else finally makes its way to Maine.
I remember when news about the first Chick-fil-A coming to Bangor in 2016 was a shocking yet pleasant surprise. The lines on that first day were insanely long, too.
Well, it looks like Bangor could be getting another "first" with what appears to be Maine's first Jimmy John's.
Jimmy John's Job Listings Point to a Bangor, Maine, Location
As of November 6, 2026, there are no Jimmy John's restaurants open in Maine.
Yet, there are some clues out there that point to the very first one in the state coming to Bangor.
On both the job website the official Jimmy John's career web page, there are hiring listings for crew members and shift managers in Bangor.
The Jimmy John's page narrows down the location even further to Bangor Mall Boulevard. Exciting!
A Second Restaurant Is Planned Alongside a New Arby's in Bangor, Maine
Back in March 2026, WABI reported that a brand-new Bangor Arby's would be taking over the location where a previous Arby's once was: 57 Bangor Mall Boulevard.
That original Bangor Arby's closed after 32 years in 2015 when its owner chose to retire, according to the Bangor Daily News. Kind of neat to have a revival of a fast-food spot that used to be there, right?
But apparently that's not the only business expected to move into the building.
WABI also revealed that Arby's would only take up half the space at the Bangor Mall Boulevard spot, "with another unknown business slated to take over the other half."
Could Jimmy John's Be Sharing a Location With Arby's in Bangor, Maine?
It certainly appears that Jimmy John's might just be that mystery business moving into 57 Bangor Mall Boulevard with Arby's.
The dots seem to line up.
Additionally, several people have said on the Bangor subreddit that they've driven by the location recently and have seen an Arby's and Jimmy John's sign on the building.
I've emailed Inspire Brands, which owns both Arby's and Jimmy John's, for confirmation but haven't heard an official word back yet.
READ MORE: 9 New Maine Restaurants That Opened in September 2026 You Can Try
Are you excited for a Jimmy John's to come to Maine? The closest one to the state, or even New Hampshire, is in Massachusetts.
I've never had it but certainly interested to check out the popular chain spot. Guess I'll have to pick between the sandwiches and wraps.
And with Bangor seemingly being the place for new "first" national restaurants in the state, fingers crossed a Sonic is next? Maybe? At the very least, just one somewhere in the state?
Anyway, hopefully we'll get more opening timeline details for 57 Bangor Mall Boulevard soon!

title: Meghan Markle's estranged father arrested in child sexual abuse materials case, AP sources say
text:
The estranged father of Meghan Markle was arrested Friday morning by federal agents in Florida on charges related to child sexual abuse material, two people familiar with the matter told The Associated Press.
Thomas Markle Sr. was arrested outside Tampa, according to the people who were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
His arrest follows reports by The Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, that Meghan’s half brother found a collection of child sexual abuse images while clearing out the home of their father in the Philippines.
Meghan Markle, the wife of Prince Harry, recently said she was “deeply distressed” by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her father’s former home. She also revealed that a letter containing “troubling allegations” about him had been sent to London police in 2018.
“It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated,” Meghan said of the letter. “I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them.”
Meghan, an American citizen who starred in the U.S. television drama “Suits,” married Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018. They have two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet.
Her father, a retired television lighting and photography director, did not attend the wedding, prompting extensive coverage in the British media of Meghan’s estrangement from her father.
Thomas Markle Sr. was living in the Philippines earlier this year when he suffered a stroke and had his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the U.S.
The Sun reported that Thomas Markle Jr. recently found “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sex abuse images in boxes at his father’s former home in Cebu City, in the Philippines, when he was clearing out the property.
Markle Jr. told the newspaper that he reported the images to police in the Philippines and contacted the FBI.
“I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years — but that stops now,” Markle Jr. told The Sun. “I won’t speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him.”

title: The Latest: Trump concedes Iran war impact on elections but insists he’d ‘do it again’
text:
As he takes stock of his Republican Party’s midterm drubbing, President Donald Trump faces the difficult question of what to do about his unpopular 8-month-old war against Iran. For weeks, Trump threatened a post-election full-scale bombardment if Tehran didn’t accept his terms. On Thursday, Trump suggested that the election losses aren’t weighing on his calculations.
A handful of remaining Senate and House races, still to be called by The Associated Press, will determine the strength of Democrats’ majority in Congress. Contests in Alaska and Mississippi have narrow margins with votes still outstanding. As the scale of the Democrats’ nationwide victories comes into focus, dozens of House races have not yet been called.
The jockeying to replace Sen. Marsha Blackburn is intensifying after she won the Tennessee governor’s race, with one Republican congressman publicly expressing interest and speculation swirling around Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. But Hegseth is not currently being considered for the seat, according to a person familiar with the matter who discussed the private conversations on condition of anonymity.
The Latest:
US employers created a surprising 165,000 new jobs last month as unemployment dipped to 4.1%
The hiring was far stronger than the 65,000 new jobs that economists had expected.
Friday’s jobs report comes three days after voters frustrated with Trump’s management of the economy — and especially the high cost of living – handed full control of Congress to the Democrats.
America’s economic output and job market have proven resilient in the face of Trump’s double-digit taxes on imports and the war with Iran, which has driven U.S. gasoline prices above $4 a gallon and pinched family budgets.
The gross domestic product advanced at a sprightly 3.4% annual pace from July through September, lifted by strong consumer spending and booming investment in artificial intelligence.
But wage gains haven’t been keeping up with persistently high inflation.
Federal judge orders 14-day delay on any work beginning on Trump’s monumental arch
The temporary restraining order blocking the Trump administration from breaking ground on a towering memorial arch for two weeks represents a major setback for one of Trump’s most prominent projects in his vision to remake Washington.
U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan’s temporary restraining order followed a series of steps taken earlier Thursday by the government, including the final approval of the arch by the National Capital Planning Commission in an 8-4 vote after a 9½-hour hearing where scores of witnesses opposed the construction.
The administration’s court filings made it clear that it was taking the steps needed to begin construction.
In approving the temporary stop, Chutkan said Virginia and the District of Columbia had shown that the immediacy of the construction would cause real harm to the plaintiffs.
Which Senate, governors races are still uncalled by The Associated Press
Just a handful of races for Senate and governor have not yet been called by The Associated Press as of 4 p.m. Eastern time on Wednesday.
In the House, 59 races where party control of the seat is at stake have yet to be called.
In Mississippi’s Senate race, Democrat Scott Colom has a lead of a few dozen votes over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. Several thousand provisional ballots are expected to be counted in the race and the state has until Nov. 10 to resolve those ballots. Those votes will be decisive. In 2022, the state counted about 5,700 provisional ballots. Mississippi does not have an automatic recount process, but a challenger can seek a court order for one.
The AP has also not called Alaska’s Senate contest between incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola, who has a 626-vote lead over Sullivan with an estimated 74% of votes counted. Under Alaska law, if neither candidate gets more than 50% of the vote, then it goes to ranked-choice tabulation.
Trump defends data centers as ‘GOLD’ as newly elected Democrats target them
Trump is doubling down on his support for data centers and warned Friday that states that deny them will lose out on “the riches they bring!”
Tuesday’s midterm elections brought a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths that underpin the artificial intelligence boom. Skepticism of data centers and their impact on electricity prices and overall affordability bolstered successful Democratic campaigns for governor in states such as Texas and Ohio.
Trump has cast data centers as crucial to winning an AI arms race against China but also for lowering taxes and bringing in jobs to communities that allow them.
“As President, I am 100% in favor of Super Intelligence (SI), and will work with the many States in the U.S. that want to become RICH by having them,” Trump said Friday on Truth Social. “They are GOLD, and only foolish leadership will say “NO” to the riches they bring!”
Global shares skid as AI worries send Wall Street tumbling
Global shares tumbled Friday following a broad selloff on Wall Street of shares related to artificial intelligence as the prospect of more regulation in the wake of the US midterm elections compounds fears about high levels of debt and spending in the sector.
Stock markets around the world have been feeling pressure from continued declines for companies that have benefited from the boom in the artificial-intelligence technology industry. Critics also say AI stock prices shot too high and were in a bubble amid concerns about high levels of borrowing and spending as companies race to build the massive computing capacity needed to train AI applications. What might come next remains uncertain, they say.
The Democrats’ win in the US midterm elections Tuesday also raises the prospect of more regulation, including at the state level, where popular resistance to data center construction remains strong.
Clergy candidates’ ‘love your neighbor’ message powers Democrats’ gains
Clergy members and other Democratic candidates with an unapologetically Christian message to “love your neighbor” helped their party flip control of Congress.
It was a striking midterm victory that demonstrated the strength of the religious left as a counter to the stalwart evangelical support for Trump and his fellow Republicans.
“This attempt to corner the market on Christianity by evangelicals was repudiated,” said Brian Kaylor, a Baptist pastor and editor of a progressive faith and politics site.
Instead, American mainline Protestantism, with its less-strident theology, took the election spotlight.
Seminarian James Talarico in Texas, megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton in Kansas and Iowa ministers Sarah Trone Garriott and Lindsay James flipped key seats in the U.S. Senate and House. They’re part of the mainline Presbyterian, Methodist and Lutheran branches with moderate or progressive beliefs.
Unlike the nationalists wanting America to privilege a particular Christian worldview in public life, the mainline candidates in keeping with their Christian values backed church-state separation and sought common ground across religions, Kaylor said.
As Congress returns to Democrats, Trump’s District of Columbia projects are a likely casualty
In his first public appearance after an election that soundly repudiated his policies, Trump turned to a topic both familiar and, given the context, surprising: not his policies or politics, but his efforts to remake pieces of the city that is the backdrop to his presidency.
Despite Trump’s affinity for project management, though, with Democrats taking control of Congress, the work the administration is doing to change the physical face of the District of Columbia is sure to face far more roadblocks than it did for the first two years of his second term.
The potential collision point between an oppositional oversight from Democrats and the president’s preoccupation with the projects was evident in his last message to the American public before the election — and in his first afterward, too.
Both focused to some degree on his projects. On Monday, it was the reflecting pool in front of the Lincoln Memorial; on Wednesday, it was a tour of the under-construction White House ballroom, where he talked columns and steel beams and Corinthian designs.
Latino voters swung left, lifting Democrats to big wins in Texas and nationwide
Latino voters moved sharply to the left in the midterm elections, propelling Democrats to an improbable electoral sweep in Texas and in battleground House races from coast to coast.
It’s a remarkable pivot for a demographic that had shifted toward Trump just two years ago.
“We showed our power and flexed our muscle during this election,” said Democratic Rep. Gabe Vasquez, who won his battleground district in New Mexico by around 17 percentage points after winning by less than 1 percentage point in 2022.
Democrats capitalized on voters’ angst over rising prices and government corruption, riding a wave of frustration to retake control of the House and the Senate.
Hispanics joined in that decisive repudiation of Trump and his Republican Party. In Texas, every county voted more Democratic than it did two years ago, when Trump beat Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris in the presidential race. But the more heavily Hispanic the county, generally the heavier the shift.
Data centers took a beating. A reckoning may be ahead for tech giants
After a campaign season filled with outrage against data centers, the midterm elections ushered in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.
A tougher regulatory environment for artificial intelligence giants and data center developers is expected to follow, even if Trump stalls any federal crackdown.
Data center regulation itself was not on most midterm ballots, and it wasn’t among the top issues for most voters. But hardline stances against the server warehouses were woven into the platforms of many candidates, including the Democrats who upended longtime Republican control of the governorships in Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Nevada and Iowa, many of which are data center hotspots.
Skepticism of data centers and their impact on electricity prices often blended with the fight for affordability — a key campaign talking point for Democrats.
Hegseth is not under consideration for Tennessee Senate seat, AP source says
The jockeying to replace Sen. Marsha Blackburn is intensifying in Tennessee, just days after she won the race for governor, with one Republican congressman publicly expressing interest and speculation swirling around Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Rep. Tim Burchett, a Tennessee Republican who won reelection Tuesday, told The Associated Press that he wants to be considered for the Senate seat when Blackburn becomes governor in January.
Hegseth has also surfaced as a potential replacement, with his future uncertain after Republicans’ sweeping losses in the midterm elections. But Hegseth is not currently being considered for the seat, according to a person familiar with the matter who discussed the private conversations on condition of anonymity.
The person said Blackburn is focused on her transition to the governorship and dismissed the speculation about appointing Hegseth to the Senate seat as baseless chatter.
Meanwhile, Hegseth released a video on social media on Thursday in which he acknowledged the threat of impeachment and argued that it would be “all about the politics of personal destruction” and that “won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”
Trump is left to weigh his next move in Iran war that contributed to GOP debacle
As he takes stock of his Republican Party’s midterm drubbing, President Donald Trump now faces the difficult question of what to do about his unpopular 8-month-old war against Iran.
For weeks, Trump has threatened to return to a full-scale bombardment of Iran once the U.S. elections were in the rearview mirror if Tehran did not come to a settlement under terms acceptable to him.
In his first comments on Wednesday after Democrats’ resounding election victory — a wave powered in part by the American electorate’s dissatisfaction with the war — Trump largely agreed with Vice President JD Vance, who publicly ruminated on the war being a catastrophe for Republicans.
And in an Oval Office exchange with reporters Thursday, Trump suggested that the election losses aren’t weighing on his calculations.
“If we have to do the rest of the Iran thing, we’re very much locked in,” Trump said.
Now, as Trump ponders his next move, the stakes couldn’t be higher for Iran, the Middle East and the global economy writ large.

title: Richmond Rocks Return with Lady Greyhounds in “Ted Lasso” Fourth Season
text:
The highly beloved “Ted Lasso” television series wrapped up their fourth season this October. The show follows an American football coach moving to London to coach the Richmond Greyhounds, a fictional Premier League soccer club. Many thought the show was done for good at the conclusion of the third season in May of 2023, and with it the so-called “arc” planned by the showrunners. That is, until the announcement of a fourth season in March 2025.
At the end of the third season, Ted Lasso (Jason Sudeikis) resigned from his managerial post at Richmond and returned to Kansas City to be with his son. Though the previous season left Lasso’s ending open ended, in season four, he ultimately decides to return to London and embrace a new chapter as a coach once more.
Over the span of ten episodes, the new season tackles the challenges of women’s soccer, corporate backstabbing and the struggles of an unexpected homecoming. It returns to Lasso’s life three years after the third season, the biggest time jump in the show yet. The season begins in the previously unexplored homeland of Ted Lasso, Kansas City, where he works at a local grocery store, argues with his mother and appears to regret returning home.
Thankfully, the show quickly returns to the familiar surroundings of Richmond, where beloved characters Rebecca Welton (Hannah Waddingham), Keeley Jones (Juno Temple) and Leslie Higgins (Jeremy Swift) have been hard at work establishing a women’s team for Richmond, called the Lady Greyhounds.
The characters making up the new women’s team are a range of talented individuals who bring a spark of joy to the season. Assistant Coach Alice Chilton (Tanya Reynolds) is one of the best additions to the season. Throughout the season, Chilton develops from a standoffish coach to self-confident mentor. The character arc feels natural, highlighting the show’s ability to build a fulfilling character and growth journey throughout a season. This arc is further strengthened by Lasso’s continued progression throughout the four seasons. Lasso’s natural openness helps Chilton become a more reliable coach, and she aids him in understanding how to coach players facing different challenges in their home lives that are carried into their sport. Lasso and Chilton grow as coaches together, showing how emotional learning takes teamwork..
However, the show struggles at times to balance the appearances of established characters with new ones. Welton, in particular, struggles with an emotional journey that does not always make sense to the viewer. Major life decisions are made in a way that seems abrupt for a character that we’ve seen agonize over one choice in prior seasons over multiple episodes. She and Jones both have emotional high points that come about with jarringly little buildup. At the same time, it also would have been nice to have more screen time with the women’s players, whether for more team-bonding moments or exploring backstory, such as how they joined Richmond.
While I worried that the inclusion of a women’s team in this season would see the usual tired tropes play out, such as treating the women’s game as different or lesser than the men’s, and portraying it as a less physical sport, it didn’t. Instead, “Ted Lasso” chose to hire a women’s soccer consultant, Leah Williamson, captain of Arsenal Women. Williamson worked to ensure that the storyline reflected the lived experience of women’s soccer players. And it shows, the show insightfully portrays the realities of an overlooked league. The show raises awareness of common issues and barriers that women face in professional sports, from perpetual underfunding of women’s sports, to an ACL tear suffered by the team’s star striker, which in reality is an experience far more common and devastating in women’s sports than in men’s.
Overall, “Ted Lasso”‘s fourth season struck the quintessential funny but poignant tone that made the show so cherished in the first place. Familiar favorites like Welton, Jones, Higgins, and the all-important Roy Kent provided a comfortable launch point. They were complemented by new additions like Chilton, striker Gemma Jay, and captain Lizzie Davies, who brought interesting backstories and challenged the established characters to grow even more. The show also had an authentic edge, developed by Williamson’s wealth of experience in the sport, which contributed to “Ted Lasso”‘s legacy as mainstream sports entertainment that also advocates for equity, on and off the pitch.
Ultimately, the season succeeds by bridging character development and critiques of challenges faced by women’s sports at a structural level. It also brings back the lighthearted and feel-good humor that we expected. Portraying joyful moments alongside questions of belonging and ability to succeed is not easy, but they manage to balance the two ideas well. The show has once again proved that the heart of Richmond still beats strong, leaving audiences eager to see the Lady Greyhounds continue into a potential fifth season.

title: Storms that caused 1-in-1,000 year flood event in Tennessee and Georgia move up Atlantic coast
text:
A storm system that caused what the National Weather Service calls a catastrophic, 1,000-year flood along the Tennessee-Georgia state line moved up the Eastern Seaboard on Friday, prompting flood advisories in coastal areas from North Carolina to Massachusetts.
In McCaysville, Georgia, and Copperhill, Tennessee, residents and crews spent Friday cleaning up alongside the Toccoa River. Rainfall across the surrounding mountain watershed measured 10.28 inches (26.1 cms) over a six-hour period and 11.19 inches (28.4 cms) over 12 hours into Thursday morning, according to the weather service in Atlanta.
Some instances of extreme weather are referred to as 1,000-year events because they have a 0.1%, or 1 in 1,000, chance of happening in a particular place in any given year. While uncommon, “it’s definitely possible to have multiple 1,000-year events in the same year,” the weather service said.
The Toccoa flows into the Ocoee River, where the Tennessee Valley Authority was managing high water levels at three of its hydroelectric dams. Swift-water teams from both states rescued dozens of people before the flooding receded, leaving downtown streets covered in mud and its water treatment plant out of commission.
At least one death was associated with the flooding. Julie Barrs, 56, died while apparently trying to drive her vehicle through floodwaters in a mountainous area of Murray County, Georgia, Sheriff Jimmy Davenport said Friday.
This was the second disastrous flood in three months for the communities — the weather service categorized the early August flood as a 1-in-500 year event — and McCaysville had reopened its renovated police building just last week. Police Chief Michael Otis Earley said his department “lost virtually everything” from the latest flood and that recovering again “will not be easy.”
Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp declared a state of emergency for four counties to make resources available.
Access to the downtown area Friday was restricted to authorized personnel, business owners and residents, and a curfew remains in effect from dusk to dawn, Earley said in a statement.
“This disaster does not define who we are as a community,” Earley said. “How we come together, how we care for our neighbors, how we lift one another up, and how we move forward will define us. McCaysville may be down right now, but we are not defeated.”
With about 1,000 residents in McCaysville and fewer than 500 in Copperhill, the twin towns have been a quaint destination for scenic railroad rides — the Blue Ridge Railway on the Georgia side and the Copperhill Special in Tennessee. Both trains treat tourists to river and mountain views before stopping so visitors can sample the restaurants and shops.
The Copperhill General Store posted on social media that nearly all its wares are covered in mud.
“Thank you for your patience and understanding as we work through this devastating loss,” the store’s statement said.

title: Sisters give birth to sons 30 minutes apart on the same day
text:
Sisters give birth to sons 30 minutes apart on the same day
Two pregnant sisters in Iowa, whose due dates were two weeks apart, gave birth to their sons on the same day, just 30 minutes apart.
Brandy Meisheid, a Linn County supervisor, was at the hospital for an induction when her sister Allison Sweeney’s water broke.
“When she got to the hospital, we knew that she had an appointment that morning. So we almost thought it was a prank that they were at labor and delivery instead of at her appointment, but it didn’t take long to figure out that they weren’t joking,” Meisheid said.
Meisheid’s son Miles was born at 5:48 p.m., followed by Sweeney’s son Cohen at 6:17 p.m.
“It was really cool to call Mom and tell her. Our cousin twins are about to arrive,” Sweeney said.
This wasn’t the family’s first closely timed arrival this year. The sisters’ two other siblings had their babies in June, just three days apart. All four sisters had been pregnant at the same time.
“Being a family of all daughters, we’ve always dreamed of being pregnant at the same time, and even that itself was a miracle just given where we’re all at in the stages of life,” Meisheid said.
The sisters live near each other and often share the ups and downs of raising young families, including late-night texts that new parents know well.
“We call each other. We text in the middle of the night. Are you up? How’s, you know, what, how’s this going? How’s that going? So I think it’s not just special for our children, but it’s really special for us as parents,” Meisheid said.
Adding to the excitement, the family’s calendar is already packed with birthdays. Meisheid said six of the family’s 18 birthdays fall in October.
“It’s really exciting just to hang out on the weekends and kind of watch them grow and share milestones and things like that,” Sweeney said.

title: President Trump declares Oval Office a national monument
text:
President Trump declares Oval Office a national monument
President Donald Trump has declared the Oval Office a national monument.
The executive order is aimed at preventing future presidents from tearing down or making major changes to the Oval Office and Cabinet Room. This follows Trump's demolition of the East Wing to make room for his new ballroom.
"It's going to be the most beautiful ballroom in the world," Trump said Wednesday, referring to his decision to demolish the East Wing to create space for a new ballroom.
The proclamation does not protect the gold decorations or other additions Trump has made to the Oval Office. Future presidents can still redecorate, replace furniture, and add their own personal touches to the space.
However, the designation is not permanent, as a future president could reverse Trump’s proclamation entirely.

title: This 83-year-old minister gives away hand-painted seashells
text:
DANSVILLE, Mich. (InvestigateTV) - Gil Ames calls his Chevy Equinox a $34,000 canvas. The vehicle is painted all over, including tigers on the side.
Inside his home in rural Ingham County, actual paintings on canvas line the walls. Ames made all the picture frames and did all the paintings himself.
Some of his work mimics the masters, including Blue Boy. Other pieces feature his faith, such as Christ at Gethsemane.
An ordained minister, Reverend Ames has not let anything get in the way of his passion for painting. He volunteered with the Red Cross at 52 national disasters, including ground zero in New York.
He also spent 25 years as a long-haul truck driver. He pivoted to something more portable to paint on during that time.
“So that’s when I started painting eggs,” Ames said.
He paints wooden eggs with intricate scenes. Every single one has an angel in it someplace, he said. He also paints thumbtacks, each with an angel.
Ames keeps his own thumbnail painted with an angel design.
His wife Orma has been by his side for 58 years. She said he does amazing things.
“If it doesn’t move, it gets painted,” Orma Ames said. “He’s a true artist, because an artist gets bored and they have to change and do something different.”
About six months ago, Reverend Ames started painting tiny seashells. He said he is running low on a particular size.
The smaller they are, the more he can fit into his shirt pocket. One pocket is full of seashells, probably 50 or more, he said.
Reverend Ames does not sell his seashells. He gives them away for free.
A stop for lunch at the Big Boy in Mason was a place to shell out some kindness.
“It makes me feel loved,” one woman at the restaurant said.
A waitress called the gesture thoughtful and said it brightens people’s spirits.
Ames said he stopped counting after handing out his first thousand seashells. Laughs, hugs and thank yous are the reward.
“Thank you so much and God bless you,” one woman said.
The 83-year-old said making people happy is the motivation that keeps him painting.
“They’re not perfect, but they’re not bad either,” Ames said. “The price is right.”

title: Obituary: Christine (Card) Patton
text:
TOPSHAM – Christine Card Patton, a lover of history and of beauty, of the sea and shore, of trees, gardens, dogs, and birds, of her family and friends, of holidays and celebrations of any kind, and of giving back to her many communities, caring for all who entered her home or her life — died on Friday, Oct. 23, in Newburyport, Mass., after a long illness. She was 93. It was a radiant autumn morning, of the kind she loved. She will be deeply missed.
Born in Medford, Mass. on Dec. 27, 1932, to Esther Bates (Lacount) Card, a French teacher and later parliamentarian, and Philip Weatherbee Card, a dentist, Christine grew up in Arlington, Mass. She was the salutatorian of the Arlington High School Class of 1950, where she met her future husband, Anthony Seavey Patton “Tony’, who would become a cardiovascular surgeon. She graduated from Wellesley College in 1954, going on to earn a master’s degree in social work from the University of Chicago in 1956. On July 14 of that year, Christine and Tony were married at the College Avenue Church in Somerville. Their union would last for 67 years until his death in 2023.
She was a licensed social worker at Massachusetts General Hospital before she became a mother. During Tony’s medical residencies, she and her family lived in Devonshire, England and Salem, Mass. before moving to Danvers, Mass. There, Christine blossomed into the person so many came to know and love. While raising her three children (along with, over the years, a golden retriever, a bloodhound, two chocolate labrador retrievers, two cats, three bunnies, a half-moon parrot, a goat, and many gerbils and fish), Christine led the causes closest to her heart, especially local history. Her deep appreciation for her town’s pre-Revolutionary War heritage stemmed from her own home, a colonial farmhouse built by the physician Caleb Rea in 1756. For over 50 years, she and Tony lovingly restored the house, filling it with antiques from the period. For more than three decades, she gave thousands of volunteer hours to the Danvers Historical Society, providing support and leadership to many important initiatives, including the restoration of Samuel McIntire’s Derby Summer House on the grounds of the Glen Magna Farms. She also worked for numerous humanitarian causes, including mental health awareness and funding for Native American higher education.
At Salem Hospital, she served in the Auxiliary and on the Board of Trustees. There, she championed investments in a renovated chapel and the hospital chaplaincy program, preserving the human element of healthcare amid an increasing industry focus on technology and efficiency. She also served as president of the North Shore Wellesley Club and as a corporator for Danvers Savings Bank. Adoring the natural world, Christine also created community ritual traditions such as the Winter Solstice celebration at the Unitarian Universalist Church of Danvers, where she was a devoted member since it was dedicated in 1967.
Christine’s ability to preserve and celebrate American history led to a professional career later in her life. In 1984, she became the Director of Marketing and Public Relations for the House of the Seven Gables and Settlement Association, serving there in senior leadership until 1995. The “Chris Patton Garden Fund,” established at her retirement from the Gables, has nurtured many blossoms on its grounds.
In 1984, Chris and Tony’s love of the coast of Maine brought them to Boothbay, where they built a summer home on Barters Island by the Sheepscot River. There, with characteristic energy, Christine dove into environmental conservation as a highly active member of the Board of Trustees of the Boothbay Regional Land Trust. She also worked as a contributing reporter for the Boothbay Register.
Chris and Tony extended their retirement life in 2013 to Topsham, where she was an active fundraiser for the Maine Health MidCoast Hospital, while also vibrantly participating in the social life of the Highland Green residential community. Christine’s energetic public service tells only part of her story. Through her gentle smile and conversational ease, she allowed anyone coming into her world to feel relaxed, at peace, welcomed, and loved. She was strikingly elegant, always “put together” in style, usually wearing her sunglasses on her head, even indoors. Even as the cruelties of her dementia slowly eroded her memory and in the end, even her ability to speak, her warmth, twinkle, and social grace held fast.
At Port Healthcare, where she was skillfully cared for during the last two years of her life, she was known for introducing every visitor to her new friends — even if she had only met them only a few minutes earlier. And of course her visitors would invariably be complimented on their outfits.
Christine is survived by her children and their spouses, in birth order, Kimberley Patton and Bruce Beck of Newburyport, Mass., Geoffrey Patton and Karen Kent of Ashland, Mass., and Laurie Patton and Shalom Goldman of Shoreham, Vt. She also leaves her cherished grandchildren and step-grandchildren, Lee Patton and their partner Taylor Epperly, Caitlyn Patton and her wife Cat Kemmett, Christina Calfo and her husband Justin Calfo, Rosemary Beck; Daniel Shai Goldman, his wife Monica, and their three children.
A memorial service to honor her life will be held on Sunday, Dec. 27, at 2:30 p.m., on what would have been her 94th birthday, at the Northshore Unitarian Universalist Church at 323 Locust St., Danvers, Mass.
To share a memory or leave a message of condolence, please visit Christine’s Book of Memories Page at http://www.bibberfuneral.com. Arrangements are in care of Bibber Memorial Chapel, 67 Summer St., Kennebunk, ME 04043.
In lieu of flowers, donations in Christine’s memory may be sent to
The House of the Seven Gables Settlement Assoc. or its Chris Patton Garden Fund (Salem, Mass.),
the Northshore Unitarian Universalist Church (Danvers, Mass.),
the Danvers Historical Society (Danvers, Mass.),
the Boothbay Regional Land Trust (Boothbay),
or Wellesley College (Wellesley, Mass.)

title: Maine private schools file lawsuit against the Maine Department of Education
text:
Maine private schools file lawsuit against the Maine Department of Education
The Maine Association of Independent Schools and several private schools are taking the Maine Department of Education (MDOE) to court over a new rule change regarding state special education regulations.
In a lawsuit filed late last month, plaintiffs asked the court to invalidate the rule change and for the MDOE to remove that standard.
Court records identify Foxcroft Academy, Fryeburg Academy, Lincoln Academy, Thornton Academy, Washington Academy and Spurwink Services among the schools suing the education department.
The emergency rule at the center of this argument is an amendment made to the Maine Unified Special Education Regulation. The change leaves private schools serving students as out-of-district educational placements susceptible to litigation, with the new potential to list them as parties in due process hearings regarding student placement.
"This appears to be yet another attempt by the MDOE to shift legal liability of the Department and public school districts onto private schools, without addressing the core issue of student safety in all schools, public and private alike," said Jeff Burroughs, president of the Maine Association of Independent Schools
Tara Walker, who is representing some of the schools suing, says MDOE and were working on an agreement where students would have placements in independent schools and a process if things became unsafe, but says the department’s new emergency rule did not include any mention of that agreement.
"What we are concerned about is that private schools, who do choose to take these placements, have as much of a voice in that process as the public schools would," Walker said.
Per court documents, attorneys representing the schools argue the change will impact the safety of special education students and staff by restricting schools' ability by restricting a private schools' ability to conduct safety assessments and decide whether or not their school should continue educating a student with destructive behaviors. They say this change will force certain private schools to go to litigation every time student behavior problems arise.
"By issuing the emergency rule without notice or comment from the affected schools, the Department of Education put Special Purpose Private Schools like ours in a nearly impossible position," said Martin Puckett, the executive director of Central Aroostook Association. "Schools like ours exist to serve students with disabilities, often those with the highest needs and most difficult behaviors that public schools are not equipped to educate. By requiring SPPSs to initiate litigation when they determine that, even after extensive efforts, they cannot safely serve a student, the Department shifts a huge amount of potential liability onto SPPSs and makes it unsustainable to continue serving the student population most in need of our services."
When the new rule was implemented, documents show MDOE said students face harm if they continue to be removed from their educational placements if their "stay put" rights are ignored.
Maine's Total Coverage reached out to MDOE for comment but did not immediately hear back.

title: Milford father charged in daughter’s death had repeated visits from child protection
text:
A Milford father charged with manslaughter in the death of his 1-year-old daughter had refused several times to use support services offered by the state’s child welfare system, new police records show.
Eleanora Ray McLaughlin was found dead from hypothermia on the morning of Dec. 28, 2025, in an unheated home, wearing only a thin onesie and a blanket.
Her father, Shane McLaughlin, was arrested last week after being indicted by a grand jury on charges of manslaughter and three counts of child endangerment. His bail was set at $250,000, but Superior Court Justice Bruce Mallonee said on Wednesday that he was planning to lower that amount and allow McLaughlin, 37, to have contact with his other two children, who have been living with their maternal grandmother since Eleanora’s death.
A state prosecutor had originally asked that McLaughlin not have contact with the kids. Police have alleged that he failed multiple times to recognize he was placing them at risk and seek help, despite repeated involvement with child protective services.
The defense argued that McLaughlin had applied and was still waiting for heating assistance when Eleanora died. Police say it was roughly 18 degrees in the home that morning.
Maine State Police Detective Jennifer Fiske wrote in a probable cause affidavit supporting McLaughlin’s arrest that his mother lived roughly a mile away and had heat at the time.
The affidavit mentions four times dating to 2018 when caseworkers from the Maine Department of Health and Human Services investigated the McLaughlin family. One investigation was closed six days before Eleanora’s death.
Caseworkers had been concerned about the children’s growth, Fiske said, and that McLaughlin repeatedly declined offers for support services.
“Shane McLaughlin told me that he hated asking people for help because when you ask someone for help, they want help in return or they run their mouth,” she wrote. “Shane McLaughlin negligently put his pride ahead of the safety of his children.”
CASE HISTORY
The McLaughlin family’s case history, as described in Fiske’s report, started in 2018 when DHHS was investigating the mother of McLaughlin’s three children. Fiske said that case resulted in the mother involuntarily losing parental rights of another child with a different father.
A second case was opened in April 2023 over the family’s living conditions, Fiske wrote. It was closed with no findings.
DHHS opened a third case in July 2025, Fiske said, about a month after the mother left the family to live in another state. The detective said McLaughlin’s former boss had accused him of drinking and driving, which McLaughlin denied.
That case was closed after a caseworker couldn’t substantiate the allegations, with the expectation that McLaughlin would “follow through with supports and services for his children.”
DHHS opened a fourth case that November after a pediatrician reported concerns that McLaughlin wasn’t following through on recommendations from medical providers that he engage in services to improve the children’s growth and development.
Assistant Attorney General Jennifer Ackerman said during the hearing Wednesday that the history of DHHS involvement was reason for concern. The last time the department visited McLaughlin’s home was during an announced visit on Nov. 14, Fiske said. A caseworker noted that the home was “cluttered” but found no safety hazards.
That case was closed on Dec. 22, less than a week before Eleanora’s death.
“I think that speaks more to DHHS than Mr. McLaughlin,” Ackerman said.
Both 2025 cases were open for roughly 45 days, which DHHS says is the maximum amount of time for the agency to investigate.
After Eleanora was found dead on Dec. 28, police said the home was dirty and cluttered with “items piled upon items” that Fiske said would be hazardous for young children who were learning to crawl, walk and play. There was no running water or heat.
McLaughlin told police he had been relying on a space heater in the bedroom to warm himself and the children while they slept, and that he believed it had stopped working overnight.
James Howaniec, one of two attorneys representing McLaughlin, said Eleanora’s death was a tragic accident, not a crime. McLaughlin had applied on Dec. 18 for heating assistance from a Penobscot County nonprofit and was still waiting on it when the girl died, according to court records. Her death was ruled an accident by the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner.
“He’s a single parent living in abject poverty, supporting himself and his children on DoorDash proceeds, and he’s never been in trouble in his life,” Howaniec said.
Fiske’s affidavit doesn’t address whether caseworkers offered to connect McLaughlin with heating help during the Nov. 14 visit.
A different caseworker told Fiske that McLaughlin told them in July that his home didn’t have heat or water. The caseworker who conducted the November visit told Fiske that he hadn’t checked on the water situation, according to the affidavit.
Bobbi Johnson, director of the state’s Office of Child and Family Services, said on Thursday she could not comment specifically on McLaughlin’s case, citing confidentiality laws.
Generally speaking though, Johnson said that caseworkers are trained to recognize when unmet needs are so severe that a child might need to be moved elsewhere, either through a court petition or the parents making their own arrangements. An unmet need may constitute as neglect, Johnson said, depending on a parent’s willingness or ability to provide.
A state law enacted last year clarifies that DHHS cannot consider poverty a form of abuse or neglect. Johnson said caseworkers have been trained to connect families with services when parents might be struggling to provide food, clothing or utilities to the children. They might take a family to a food bank, or connect them with financial resources to get heat or electricity.
REUNIFICATION EFFORTS
The state’s case was at odds with a caseworker’s testimony on Wednesday about McLaughlin’s progress this year in working with DHHS to reunify with his children.
Caseworker Kirstin Batchelder said that McLaughlin has attended every required meeting and that he has been involved in setting up recommended child development programs for his autistic son. He has never tested positive for substances and has been in therapy, Batchelder said. He has had regular, unsupervised visits with the children since late May.
“All the things that we’ve asked him to do per the jeopardy order, he’s continued to do,” Batchelder said.
Howaniec said that McLaughlin’s engagement with DHHS is “evidence of his commitment to his children.”
McLaughlin’s case is one of several prosecutions in Maine stemming from child deaths in homes where there has been prior involvement by child protective services. In every death, lawmakers have routinely called for reform and pressed DHHS for information about these cases. Sen. Jeff Timberlake, R-Turner, announced earlier this year that he was looking into Eleanora’s death.
Some of those same tensions emerged during the bail hearing, when a prosecutor pressed Batchelder on how earlier caseworkers had handled the investigation that was closed days before Eleanora’s death, and whether the criminal charges of child endangerment would give DHHS pause when it comes to allowing McLaughlin unsupervised visits with his other children.
Johnson said law enforcement agencies and DHHS have different legal obligations, and that state law requires her caseworkers to work with parents on reunification, unless a judge issues a “cease reunification” order.
“(Police and prosecutors are) investigating whether or not a crime occurred, and the next step that will happen if it’s found that there was one,” she said. “And our responsibility is to determine the safety of children, and whether abuse or neglect occurred, and then provide rehabilitation and reunification support to address those issues.”

title: Dolly Parton manager moves to withdraw complaint against the country music legend's nephew
text:
Dolly Parton's manager moves to drop complaint accusing late singer's nephew of threatening estate
Dolly Parton’s longtime manager moved Thursday to drop a complaint that accused the late singer’s nephew of threatening her estate and its employees.
She’s Alive, the entity founded to manage and protect Parton’s estate, had secured a temporary restraining order against Bryan Seaver and his security company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services, in September.
A hearing, pushed several times over the course of a month, was slated for Tuesday.
A very brief filing in a Tennessee court Thursday gives no reason why the complaint is being withdrawn.
It says only that a proposed order was being drafted for the judge’s approval to dismiss the case without prejudice, meaning it can be refiled again. A court filing from a day earlier said the two sides had reached an agreement, but that also gave no details.
The Associated Press sent emails seeking comment from lawyers for She’s Alive, Seaver and his company.

title: Ask 8 Investigates: Why wasn’t an AMBER Alert issued for a missing teenager from Turner?
text:
Ask 8 Investigates: Why wasn’t an AMBER Alert issued for a missing teenager from Turner?
A teenager from Turner went missing, prompting a viewer to ask why an AMBER Alert wasn’t issued
Ask 8 Investigates: Why wasn’t an AMBER Alert issued for a missing teenager from Turner?
A teenager from Turner went missing, prompting a viewer to ask why an AMBER Alert wasn’t issued
A teenager from Turner went missing, prompting a viewer to ask why an AMBER Alert wasn’t issued.
In order for police to issue an AMBER Alert, three criteria must be met.
The child must be 17 or younger. Police must have reason to believe the child is in imminent danger of serious harm or death, and police must have information the public could use to help find the child.
The system is intended for abductions, not child custody disputes or cases in which a child ran away or is generally missing. If police believe a child is with a parent who does not have custody, that alone is not enough to activate an alert under state guidelines. Police must also believe the parent is likely to hurt the child.
When a missing child meets the criteria, local police contact Maine State Police, which can activate an alert through the statewide emergency alert system.
