title: Yes, Americans embrace diversity
text:
A few of the firsts associated with the 2026 election have caught my attention.
For the first time, Georgia will have a Black governor, a descendant of slaves. For the first time, America is likely to have a Black Speaker of the House. For the first time, there will be a Muslim in the United States Senate. This list could be extended.
It seems that, at least when confronted with individuals rather than categories, Americans have embraced the value of diversity. Although the badly misunderstood concept of “DEI” has become a political dog whistle, voters seem to realize that diversity makes us smarter and stronger.
Indeed, the diversity of our people has been, since our founding, one of the elements that made America great in the first place. It is nice to see that reaffirmed in these elections.
Kevin Smith, M.L.S., J.D.
North Yarmouth

title: 🧀 HAPPY NATIONAL NACHO DAY, MAINE! Food Network Says These Are the Best Nachos in the State!
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Food Network Names These the Best Nachos in Maine
It's National Nacho Day, which gives us the perfect excuse to celebrate one of America's favorite appetizers. And if you're looking for some nacho inspiration here in Maine, Food Network has a pretty delicious recommendation!
Food Network is a popular American cable channel that focuses on food, cooking, and lifestyle programming. Launched in 1993, it has become a leading destination for food enthusiasts.
Food television has become a massive part of pop culture, with shows covering everything from cooking competitions and restaurant adventures to food-and-travel destinations and reality TV. Shows like Chopped, Beat Bobby Flay, Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives, and Man v. Food have become iconic over the years, propelling everyday dishes and local restaurants into must-try destinations.
So when Food Network named Luchador Tacos' nachos the best in Maine, it makes you more than eager to give them a try, especially on National Nacho Day!
Chef-owner Katherine Mitchell, a Mexican American who grew up in East Los Angeles, started Luchador in 2017 as a tiny roadside food stand in South Paris. She was looking for the LA-style tacos she grew up with and couldn't find them in Maine, so she decided to make them herself. That little trailer eventually grew into full-fledged restaurants around the 207.
Read More: What's Next For Brewer, Maine's Former Ruby Tuesday Building?
Luchador has grown to four locations across Maine:
South Paris — 243 Main St.
Windham — 781 Roosevelt Trail
Auburn — 945 Center St.
Old Orchard Beach — 1 E. Grand Ave.
The menu is tight, focused, and delicious: tacos, burritos, quesadillas, bowls, fries, nachos, and more, all built around grilled steak, chicken, and pork, along with homemade red and green salsas. There are vegan and gluten-free options, too.
But the nachos are the real star of the show here. Loaded with crispy tortilla chips, black beans, melted cheese, roasted poblano-corn crema, your choice of asada, birria, pastor, or calabacitas, plus cilantro, onions, and guacamole, with salsa on the side.
The poblano-corn crema is what really sets them apart and makes folks like Food Network stand up and take notice! It's creamy, smoky, and a little sweet, which is a nice switch-up from the usual sour cream and cheese routine.
These are hearty, loaded-up taco-shop nachos, exactly the kind of dish that feels worthy of a Food Network shoutout. And what better day to give them a try than National Nacho Day?

title: Bedbugs discovery closes Medomak Middle School for days
text:
WALDOBORO, Maine (WABI) - Medomak Middle School in Waldoboro is moving to remote learning for several days after multiple bedbugs were discovered at the school.
In the letter, RSU 40 Superintendent Daniel Welch said that the decision was made “out of an abundance of caution,” and announced that the school would be arranging professional treatment to target the bugs.
Officials said there is currently no indication of an infestation.
Superintendent Welch announced that students will be learning remotely through next Tuesday.
The bedbug treatment is scheduled for next week in accordance with state regulations that mandate five days’ advance notification before treatment can occur.
School officials are asking families to check children’s backpacks, coats and other belongings for signs of bedbugs. Families are also encouraged to inspect bedding, mattress seams and areas where belongings are stored.
The district also said bedbugs are a nuisance but are not known to spread disease.
The school said families should contact the school if they find bedbugs or have questions about the situation.

title: Local baker expanding cookie business to downtown Bangor
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
When Joy Dudley first started her cookie business, she would bring just 20 cookies to the Bangor European Market every Saturday morning to sell at her table.
“I would sell out every weekend,” Dudley said.
The business grew, and now, five years later, she’s opening a second brick-and-mortar storefront, this time in downtown Bangor. It’s one of several local businesses set to open their doors downtown in the winter months.
Baked By Joy, which has a takeout-only store in Hampden, plans to open its Bangor location at 25 Hammond St., where Bangor Sandwich Company sat before moving to the larger space next door earlier this year.
The opening means that Dudley can move her baking operations out of her basement in Hermon and into the Bangor store as she grows her staff and the wholesale side of her business. Local grocers like Danforth’s and Tiller and Rye carry her baked goods, and she’s looking to expand the wholesale side of her business too.
In Bangor, she can add more to her menu and offer seating for customers to hang out with their treats — a space that customers have been asking for since the Hampden store opened in March, Dudley said.
“Bangor is a hub for everybody,” she said. The store’s central location downtown will make it easy for people to stop by, and she thinks the Filipino-inspired flavors on her menu will add something unique to the Queen City. Some of her offerings might be foods her customers can try for the first time.
That menu includes cookies, pan de sal (a type of Filipino bread roll), cakes, matcha, ice cream, boba made with real fruit like strawberry, mango and ube, and lattes and pourover coffee supplied through a partnership with the Deer Isle-based 44 North Coffee.
Dudley plans to start moving into the new store this month with the goal of opening before Christmas, or sometime in January if not then. She’ll do some updates and painting to the store but doesn’t have any major renovations planned. She hasn’t determined what the store’s hours will be yet, but she’s hoping to stay open a bit later to give customers a cafe option in the early evening, a rarity in Bangor.
Two other area residents are planning to open downtown businesses in November and December as well: Burgers & Bad Decisions and the Fireheart Tavern, both on Main Street.
Dudley also wants to host events in the store every month, especially focused around kids and families, like baking classes or the princess day she hosted last winter, when she was using space within the Not So Empty Nest gift shop. About 200 kids showed up, Dudley said.
“It’s kind of hard if you don’t have your own space to do that,” she said. “We’re excited to be in Bangor.”

title: ‘It’s Over’: Adam Driver Says He’s Done With Star Wars
text:
‘It’s Over’: Adam Driver Says He’s Done With Star Wars
Don’t expect to see Kylo Ren back in Star Wars any time soon.
Promoting his new movie Paper Tiger on The Rich Eisen Show, Adam Driver was asked whether there’s a chance he could make a return to the Star Wars franchise. The question is not outrageous, despite how Kylo Ren’s story arc concluded in 2019’s Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker. A few months ago, word leaked into the press that Driver himself had collaborated with filmmaker Steven Soderbergh on a pitch for a Rise of Skywalker prequel they would have called The Hunt for Ben Solo.
Disney ultimately turned down their proposal, a decision that Soderbergh himself publicly called “insane.” But clearly Driver did have interest in a Star Wars return at some point.
Not anymore. Driver told Eisen flat out “no more Star Wars.”
“We tried to do one more,” he added. “But [Disney] were like, ‘No, he’s dead.’”
READ MORE: Every Star Wars Movie, Ranked From Worst to Best
Driver appeared in all three of Disney’s big-screen Star Wars sequels, starting with 2015’s The Force Awakens. Since 2019 and the release of The Rise of Skywalker, just one Star Wars movie has made it to theaters: This summer’s The Mandalorian and Grogu, based on the hit Disney+ series. In between, many projects — including Driver and Soderbergh’s — were developed or discussed by Lucasfilm or Disney. None made it to the finish line.
The franchise’s upcoming big-screen slate does include one confirmed title: Star Wars: Starfighter from director Shawn Levy and star Ryan Gosling. That opens in theaters next May.
After that? Who knows. Driver’s Star Wars co-star Daisy Ridley was supposed to get her own The Rise of Skywalker sequel, directed by Sharmeen Obaid-Chinoy. But that film remains mired in a development Sarlacc Pit. Recently, there were reports that Spider-Man director Jon Watts was working on a new Skywalker saga movie, but there’s been no update on that in a while either.

title: Recalled playsets sold on Amazon and Walmart pose a risk of injury or death, commission says
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(CNN) - Playsets sold on Amazon and Walmart have been recalled because a child’s head or neck could get trapped, posing a risk of serious injury or death.
Arlopu is recalling about 10,000 of its slide playsets.
The Consumer Product Safety Commission said the playsets have openings that a child’s torso can fit through but a child’s head cannot. It said that poses the risk of injury or death due to potential neck entrapment.
Regulators said one of the models also features basketball nets that can detach and pose dangers.
The recalled playsets have model numbers KTCS17 and LY31. They’re for indoor or outdoor use and come in tan, red, blue, yellow, gray and green.
The CPSC said Amazon and Walmart sold the playsets online from April 2023 through August 2026.
Arlopu said it received one report of a child getting trapped in the playset, resulting in abrasions to the child’s neck.
Customers are advised to stop using the playsets and keep them away from their children. They can contact Arlopu for a free repair kit that includes redesigned panels, basketball hoops and installation instructions.

title: Death row inmate asks for a stay of execution until after holidays
text:
COLUMBIA, S.C. (WHNS/Gray News) - A South Carolina death row inmate is petitioning to have his execution pushed back to after the holidays.
Steven Bixby was convicted in 2007 of killing State Constable Donnie Ouzts and Sergeant Danny Wilson of the Abbeville County Sheriff’s Office during a standoff in 2003.
Bixby and his parents were part of a land dispute with the state, which planned to take 20 feet of land from their property to widen a highway.
The dispute escalated into a standoff.
In a petition submitted to the South Carolina Supreme Court, Bixby is asking that the clerk of court not issue a notice of execution until after the winter holidays.
The petition cites a previous stay of execution granted to a death row inmate in 2024, whose execution date would have fallen near Thanksgiving and Christmas.
The South Carolina Supreme Court has not yet made a ruling on the petition.

title: Two strokes haven’t stopped him: Meet the Michigan man greeting his town for 10 years
text:
EATON RAPIDS, Mich. (Aging Untold) — For 10 years, George Doxtader has made a difference in his community by spreading joy with a thumbs-up.
The 78-year-old sits on a bench at the corner of State and Main streets in Eaton Rapids and lifts his thumb to greet passersby.
“He gets up very early, he’s out here a lot of times at 4 a.m.,” his friend, Kurt Norgaard, said. “And you’ll see a lot of waving and beeping, just how it is.”
Community notices when he’s absent
Doxtader is not there every day. He takes breaks for church and other activities.
Norgaard said if Doxtader is missing for any stretch of time, the community takes notice.
“Oh yeah, it comes up in the community. ‘Hey what happened to George? Where’s George at?’” Norgaard said.
Pastor Jenny Rouble of First Congregational Church said Doxtader is not only a member of her congregation but also a friend and a blessing to the community.
“It just makes them happy to see his smiling face and his thumbs-up,” Rouble said.
Drivers honk their horns and call out greetings as they pass.
“I guess you can tell by when the people go by, they’re honking their horns. They know his name,” Rouble said.
Overcoming challenges with positivity
What many might not know is that Doxtader suffered two major strokes 35 years ago.
He has paralysis on the right side of his body and sometimes he has trouble speaking.
“Slow and gradually,” Doxtader said when describing his speech.
Despite his challenges, he smiles and offers a friendly gesture to everyone who passes by.
When he is not greeting passersby, Doxtader passes the time crocheting blankets and pictures, all with his left hand.
He never misses a chance to share his positive perspective on life.
“Yes,” Doxtader said when asked about spreading inspiration.
“Yes, that’s the goal, right? Yeah, that’s the goal is the inspiration in a complicated world,” Rouble added.

title: Friday’s high school football: Windham knocks out Portland in Class A North
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
Jordan Pastore rushed for three touchdowns, quarterback Patrick Davenport gained more than 100 yards on the ground, and third-seeded Windham advanced to the Class A North championship game by upsetting second-seeded Portland, 21-14, in a semifinal Friday night at Fitzpatrick Stadium.
Portland’s offense didn’t get untracked until the second half, after Windham (7-3) built a 21-0 lead. The three-time defending regional champions were frequently hurt by penalties, including two that negated touchdown runs on one drive in the third quarter.
Pastore opened the scoring with a 4-yard run in the second quarter. He added a 2-yard TD run later in the second and a 1-yard run in the third.
David Gomes gave the Bulldogs (7-3) some life with a 15-yard touchdown run later in the third, but Portland’s next drive was hindered by more penalties and eventually ended with a Windham interception.
After Gomes cut the margin to 21-14 when he scored on a 9-yard run with 2:02 remaining, Windham recovered the onside kick. Davenport picked up a first down with a long run on third-and-13, and the Eagles were able to run out the clock.
Windham will play for the regional title next week against top-seeded Oxford Hills.
THORNTON ACADEMY 42, SOUTH PORTLAND 0: Brennan Tabor ran for three touchdowns in the first half, and the top-seeded Trojans (10-0) cruised to a Class A South semifinal win over the Red Riots (4-6) in Saco.
Thornton, the defending Class A champ and the No. 1 team in the Varsity Maine poll, will host Bonny Eagle in the regional final.
Thornton took a 7-0 lead just over a minute into the game. Brody Hadiaris recovered a South Portland fumble on the opening kickoff, and Tabor scored on a 3-yard run. Tabor added a 13-yard touchdown run before the end of the first and a 9-yard run in the second.
Logan LeBlanc took a short pass from Noah Fullerton for a 72-yard touchdown and Josiah Blain returned an interception 50 yards for a touchdown in the third quarter for the Trojans.
GREELY 34, OCEANSIDE 8: The second-seeded Rangers (9-1) took the lead by scoring on back-to-back plays in the second quarter and pulled away in the second half against the seventh-seeded Mariners (5-5) in a Class C quarterfinal in Cumberland.
Greely, the reigning state champion, trailed 8-7 before a 1-yard run by Noah Allen in the second quarter. Oceanside then fumbled the kickoff, and Ethan Kittredge returned it 10 yards for a touchdown that made it 20-8.
Luke Piper added two touchdown passes in the second half — 24 yards to Mitchell Dionne and 14 yards to Kittredge.
The Rangers will be at home next week against No. 3 seed Hermon.
Greely’s Barron Silver opened the scoring with a 33-yard run in the first quarter. Oceanside answered with a 4-yard touchdown run by quarterback Braeden Toothaker, who also ran for the conversion.
FOXCROFT ACADEMY 22, WELLS 8: Preston Hutchinson rushed for two touchdowns in the second half, lifting the fourth-seeded Ponies (8-2) past the fifth-seeded Warriors (6-4) in a Class C quarterfinal in Foxcroft.
After stopping a Wells drive deep in Foxcroft territory in the third quarter, the Ponies drove down the field and took a 16-8 lead on an 8-yard run by Hutchinson, who also rushed for the conversion.
Hutchinson added a 30-yard run in the fourth.
Quarterback Evan Seavey scored on a 1-yard run in the first quarter for Foxcroft, which advances to play No. 1 seed Leavitt in the semifinals.
Wells tied the game in the second quarter on a 37-yard pass from Noah McDonough to Liam Perkins, followed by Quinn Finemore’s conversion rush.
FREEPORT 48, DIRIGO 12: Andrew Thomas ran for three scores and threw for another as the top-seeded Falcons (7-2) earned a Class D South semifinal victory over the fifth-seeded Cougars (3-7) in Freeport.
Thomas had touchdown runs of 3, 51 and 85 yards. His TD pass was a 63-yarder to Sam Willard. Willard scored Freeport’s first touchdown on a 14-yard run in the first quarter. Landon Clark (43 yards) and Colby Chipman (22) also ran for scores for the Falcons.
Hudson Lufkin scored both of Dirigo’s touchdowns — a 1-yard run in the first quarter and a 2-yard run in the second.
Freeport will face No. 2 Winthrop/Monmouth/Hall-Dale in the regional final next week.

title: Rain Moves In This Afternoon & Evening, Wet & Cooler Weekend Ahead
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Our Friday will feature mostly cloudy skies on average with the best chance for some sunshine being over northern locales. Low pressure riding northward along a stalled out cold front will bring increasing rain chances to areas closer to... and along... the coast this afternoon and evening. Areas north of Bangor are expected to stay dry through much of the day. High temperatures will top off in the 60s to near 70°. Rain will spread further inland tonight as low pressure continues to ride northward along the front. It looks like the rain will be confined to areas along and to the south and east of I-95 with the heaviest rain falling near the coastline. Winds will become northeast tonight and increase with gusts to around 20-25 MPH possible. This will usher cooler air into the region tonight with lows dropping to the 40s.
Upper-level energy coming out of the Great Lakes Region tonight will cause a new area of low pressure to develop just south of New England late tonight/early Saturday morning. This new low is forecast to slowly move northward through the Gulf of Maine from Saturday afternoon through Sunday morning then slide to our east Sunday afternoon. This will keep us under the clouds and bring us more widespread periods of rain throughout the day Saturday... Saturday night and into Sunday morning. As the low pushes to our east Sunday... rain will taper off from west to east by late morning into the afternoon. Temperatures on Saturday will be much cooler than today with highs in the mid-40s across the north... upper 40s to low 50s elsewhere. Sunday’s highs will be a bit cooler with temperatures in the 40s... possibly a few upper 30s across the north and west. Rainfall totals from this afternoon through Sunday evening will range from .5″ to 1″ across the north and 1″-2″ from the Capital Region through Bangor and Interior Downeast south to the coast. There could be some higher amounts closer to the immediate coast up to 2.5″-3″.

title: 4 things Maine homeowners should know about installing a standby generator
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
In Maine, preparing for winter is a seasonal ritual. Homeowners clean their gutters, service their heating systems and stock up on supplies before the snow begins to fall.
But there’s another important item to consider adding to the checklist: backup power.
Snow, ice and high winds can bring down trees and power lines, leaving homes without electricity for hours or even days. For households that rely on electricity for heating, water, cooking and food storage, an extended outage can quickly become more than an inconvenience.
A permanently installed standby generator sits outside the home and is connected to its electrical system through an automatic transfer switch. It typically operates on propane or natural gas, powering designated household circuits when utility service fails. For homeowners considering the investment, Robert Cyr, founder and president of DIRFY Generators, offers four things to know.
1. Start with your wish list and your need list
Not every home requires the same amount of backup power. Before selecting a generator, consider which appliances and systems are most important during an outage.
“We tailor each installation to the customer’s goals, and work to fit their budget,” Cyr said.
For some households, the priorities are refrigeration, lighting and internet access. Others depend on electrically powered heating systems, well pumps, sump pumps or septic pumps.
DIRFY has heard from homeowners whose basements flooded when sump pumps stopped working, whose pipes froze without heat or whose refrigerators and freezers spoiled thousands of dollars’ worth of food.
However, homeowners who rarely lose power or experience brief interruptions by living near hospitals or fire and police stations may not need to invest in a standby generator.
2. Bigger homes don’t always need bigger generators
One common misconception is that generator size should correspond to a home’s square footage. In reality, electrical demand is what matters.
“A small house with an electric stove, electric dryer, electric water heater, hot tub, three heat pumps and an electric garage heater could need a much larger generator than a big house with gas appliances,” Cyr explained.
Homeowners can also choose to power only essential circuits rather than the entire house.
“If they just want the basics, we can put in a selected-circuit transfer switch for those specific loads,” Cyr said. “As a result, they can go with a much smaller generator, and it would be much less expensive.”
Depending on the home’s electrical needs, Cyr says that choice could mean the difference between an $8,500 installation and a $17,000 installation.
3. Installation is easier when you plan ahead
The only problem with a seasonal ritual of preparedness is that everyone is planning on the same timeline.
Cyr said his company has the capacity to install 10 generators a week and outside of the busy season, some installations are scheduled within one or two weeks.
“We keep a fairly large amount of inventory, with new inventory coming in regularly, but this time of year, things can change in a matter of a few days,” Cyr said.
DIRFY can coordinate the full installation to startup process, although homeowners may arrange fuel service through their existing provider.
4. Regular maintenance protects your investment
A standby generator operates automatically, but that doesn’t mean it’s maintenance-free.
“Sometimes customers don’t realize that a generator is like a car and needs regular maintenance,” Cyr said. “Cars go by miles; generators go by hours.”
DIRFY has customers whose generators are still operating after 15 to 20 years, thanks in part to proper maintenance.
To help encourage that care, DIRFY offers its own reward program, providing qualifying customers with no labor or travel charges for covered repairs and a 20% discount on parts, without a separate annual program fee. Participation requires specified maintenance.
A standby generator can’t prevent the next major storm, but it can keep essential household systems operating when the power goes out. For Mainers who have experienced flooded basements, spoiled food or days without heat, that reliability can make all the difference.

title: Windham-Raymond school board approves name for new middle school
text:
Windham-Raymond school board approves name for new middle school
School board members voted to name the school Windham Raymond Middle School after rejecting a proposal to honor the late Maine lawmaker Bill Diamond
Windham-Raymond school board approves name for new middle school
School board members voted to name the school Windham Raymond Middle School after rejecting a proposal to honor the late Maine lawmaker Bill Diamond
The Windham-Raymond school board voted Wednesday to name the district's new middle school Windham Raymond Middle School, rejecting a proposal to name it after the late Maine lawmaker Bill Diamond.
The Regional School Unit 14 board voted in favor of Windham Raymond Middle School after a motion to name the building Bill Diamond Middle School failed in a 2-5 vote.
Several community members spoke in support of naming the school after Diamond during the public comment portion of Wednesday's meeting.
During the board discussion, one board member questioned whether the school should be named to honor the legacy of an individual or reflect the communities that helped plan and build it.
"I believe there are many other ways to honor the legacy of Bill Diamond," she said. She suggested several possibilities, including naming a building on the school campus or a community center after Diamond, or establishing a scholarship for graduates in his honor.
Diamond, who died in 2025, served in the Maine Legislature and as Maine's secretary of state. He also worked as a teacher, principal and superintendent for more than 20 years.
During Wednesday's meeting, Diamond's daughter, Karen Diamond, addressed the board about allegations involving the former Elan School, where her father previously worked.
Karen Diamond said her father had no knowledge of abuse at the school during his time there. She also said the family has legal counsel reviewing what she described as false allegations and urged board members to evaluate her father's name based on verified facts.
The decision also drew criticism from Erik's Church, a Windham business, which expressed support for efforts to reverse the outcome in a social media post.
"We will support any initiative to change this outcome," the business wrote.

ICE arrests 23-year-old UC Berkeley student and asylum seeker at San Francisco airport
text:
ICE arrests 23-year-old UC Berkeley student and asylum seeker at San Francisco airport
A UC Berkeley student was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement at San Francisco International Airport Friday while waiting to board a flight to Portland for a vacation with her boyfriend.
Related video above: House passes immigration enforcement bill amid partisan divide in June
Paula Valentina Albornoz Hernandez, 23, is currently being held at ICE’s California City Detention Center, agency records show, while UC Berkeley students and administration mobilize to support her. Attorneys at Centro Legal de la Raza have filed a habeas corpus petition challenging her detention.
The arrest likely represents the first ICE detention of an active UC Berkeley student since the Trump administration began its mass deportation push last year, said both Niko De Bremaeker, a managing attorney at Centro Legal de la Raza, and university spokesperson Aileen Zerrudo.
The business administration student arrived in the U.S. from Colombia in 2022, De Bremaeker said. He said she overstayed her visa and applied for asylum based on experiencing “severe gender-based violence” in her home country, an application that is still pending. She had a valid work permit, De Bremaeker said, and had attended San Jose City College before transferring to Berkeley where she was conducting research on artificial intelligence.
On Friday night, her boyfriend Anthony said, the couple had arrived early at the airport for a weekend getaway that he hoped would help take Albornoz Hernandez’s mind off her heavy course load. They were waiting in the gate area, he said, when an ICE agent in plain clothes approached Albornoz Hernandez and asked her name, saying she looked familiar. Without identifying himself as working for ICE, the agent guessed a couple of different names, Anthony said, to which Albornoz Hernandez said no.
The third time, Anthony said, he guessed right. Once Albornoz Hernandez confirmed her name, ICE agents separated the couple, then told Albornoz Hernandez that her visa was expired and they were going to detain her, Anthony said. (Berkeleyside agreed to identify him by his first name only due to the sensitivity of his girlfriend’s case.)
“It was scary seeing that my partner was getting ripped apart from me and there’s nothing I can do about it,” Anthony said.
Albornoz Hernandez spent most of the weekend at Stockton Detention Center, De Bremaeker said, before being taken to California City, a facility northeast of Los Angeles where earlier this year, a court-ordered investigation found major flaws in the medical care provided to people detained there.
A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security confirmed by email that ICE agents had detained Albornoz Hernandez at SFO.
“She entered the country on September 6, 2022, with legal permission to stay until March 6, 2023. In defiance of our nation’s laws, she did not depart,” wrote the spokesperson, who did not give their name. “She will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.”
The DHS spokesperson denied that ICE agents had failed to identify themselves when approaching Albornoz Hernandez, saying agents “clearly identify themselves as law enforcement in accordance with agency policy.”
Asked why agents had detained someone with a pending asylum application and valid work permit, the spokesperson replied that “work authorization or a pending application does NOT confer legal status in the United States.”
ICE has stepped up arrests at San Francisco International Airport and other airports since the summer, especially targeting people who had overstayed visas in the past. Immigration agents have also held green card holders in a windowless room in the airport for days at a time, a San Francisco Chronicle investigation found.
De Bremaeker said Albornoz Hernandez had no criminal record or previous arrests; a Berkeleyside search of Alameda County and federal court records did not turn up any criminal history.
“This is somebody who was very much known with the government, she had been complying at every step, she was doing everything she was supposed to do and obviously excelling within the community,” De Bremaeker said.
Her arrest “demonstrates the arbitrary nature in which the government is arresting folks and how deeply it cuts into our communities,” he said.
UC Berkeley chancellor asks for student to be allowed to resume studies
In a petition filed in U.S. District Court Monday, attorneys with Centro Legal de la Raza argued that ICE’s arrest of Albornoz Hernandez violated federal law and the U.S. Constitution because officers did not present a warrant and did not interview her to determine whether she was a flight risk before taking her into custody. Berkeleyside has asked DHS for a response to those claims.
The petition asks the court to order Albornoz Hernandez’s release and prevent the government from detaining her again unless it can prove in a court hearing that she poses a flight risk or is a danger to the community.
In a letter of support attached to the petition, UC Berkeley Chancellor Rich Lyons called Albornoz Hernandez “one of our outstanding students.”
“It takes remarkable dedication and perseverance to complete a degree at UC Berkeley,” he wrote. “I am deeply concerned that her current situation will unnecessarily interfere with the opportunity that she has earned, potentially impacting her academic progress.”
“I respectfully request that you make it possible for Paula to resume her studies with us,” he added.
Student was headed to Oregon with her boyfriend for trip hiking in the outdoors
Anthony described his girlfriend as hyper-responsible and studious and said she had long dreamed of attending UC Berkeley. The two met in school, he said: He was working towards his high school diploma and Albornoz Hernandez toward her GED.
“She always talked about Berkeley and how she wanted to get in,” he said. “I just admired how confident she was — she knew what she wanted and was going for it.”
They kept in touch as Albornoz Hernandez went on to San Jose City College, and started dating last summer. After transferring to UC Berkeley, he said, Albornoz Hernandez studied harder as she adapted to a more competitive environment. “She’s always working, day and night,” he said.
Anthony hoped the trip to Portland, which neither of them had visited before, could give her a chance to relax. They both love the outdoors, he said, and looked forward to going hiking, maybe seeing some waterfalls.
He has always been protective of Albornoz Hernandez’s safety, he said, taking time from his own studies and job as a welder to drive her from evening church services in Hayward back to Berkeley, then trekking home to San Jose. Now, he said he is plagued by guilt that the trip he planned unexpectedly led to her arrest, but tries to stay focused on getting her released soon.
Albornoz Hernandez’s friends at UC Berkeley have also helped out, he said, informing professors about her absence so she doesn’t fall too far behind.
“We want her to not miss out on her schooling because this is her dream,” he said.
The Alameda County Immigration Legal Education Partnership is advising anyone with an uncertain immigration status to avoid traveling by plane without consulting an attorney first. They have also urged anyone who is detained or witnesses an ICE arrest to call their hotline.
Albornoz Hernandez is scheduled for a hearing in immigration court on Nov. 17, De Bremaeker said. The immigration case is separate from the federal case challenging her detention.

title: Arizona Democrats gain trifecta to control the state House, Senate and governor’s office for first time in 60 years
text:
PHOENIX (AP) — Democrats in Arizona won control of both legislative chambers and retained the governor’s office, giving the party its first trifecta in the state since 1966 as Democrats made major gains nationwide in this week’s elections and took control of both chambers of Congress.
In her first term, Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs had vetoed more than 540 measures passed by the Republican-led Legislature on policies including taxes, immigration and voting laws. Hobbs has said she’s looking to address water issues and affordability, and take on fraud and abuse in the state’s school voucher program.
The Associated Press called enough legislative races to confirm that both chambers flipped on Friday. The news organization calls races individually and it can take several days after voting, depending on when election officials tally the votes and how close the elections are. There have not been major disputes or disruptions this year.
In Arizona, Republicans have held the House for 60 years and the Senate since the early 1990s.
Overall, Democrats took full control — both statehouse chambers and governors’ offices — in at least six states where they previously shared power with Republicans. Besides Arizona, those wins were in the battleground states of Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Nevada and Wisconsin.
The flips weren’t just in states that are normally competitive. Democrats won control of the Texas House, which Republicans have held since 2003, and elected Gina Hinojosa as the state’s first Democratic governor since George W. Bush ousted Ann Richards in 1994. Republicans held onto the state Senate.
Democrats also flipped the lower chambers of the legislatures in Maine and North Carolina and both chambers in New Hampshire, where Republican Kelly Ayotte was reelected. The count could grow as results are tallied in additional states.
The National Council of State Legislatures says it’s likely to end up as the election with the most legislative seats and chambers changing parties since the 2010 election, when Republicans took over governments across the country amid the Great Recession.
Democrats will also hold the governor’s office in at least 28 states. Results are still pending in Alaska and Kansas.

title: Graphic novel series features Joshua Chamberlain’s Medal of Honor story
text:
ARLINGTON, Virginia (WABI) - A Maine war-hero is having his story told in a national free comic book.
“Medal of Honor: Joshua Chamberlain” is the Association of the United States Army’s latest edition in its graphic novel series.
The novels tell the stories of Army heroes awarded the Medal of Honor throughout history, going with the organizations mission statement.
“It’s a professional and educational organization,” Joseph Craig, book program director of AUSA, said. “The book program works with military publishing to try to, you know, get stories out there that are about the Army or would be of interest to the Army.”
Chamberlain’s edition follows his actions at Little Round Top during the Battle of Gettysburg in the Civil War.
“As we’ve been working on this series, we get suggestions all the time for people that they would like to see covered in the books,” Craig said. “Not surprisingly, Chamberlain has been a very popular figure. A lot of people have been talking about him. He’s used in Army training manuals as examples of great leadership. We want to do a Civil War story, he was long overdue.”
The book was written and illustrated by artists who have worked on mainstream comics such as DC and Marvel.
Craig said the graphic novels hope to share American heroes with younger generations.
“We want to make sure that the younger generation understands about the history of the Army, what it does, its role in keeping America safe,” Craig said. “And these stories have done a great job in doing that. But, we found that, really, people from all generations have been enjoying these stories.”
Craig said graphic novels normally follow a fictional superhero story, but AUSA’s follow real-life superhero stories.
“You know, superheroes in general have been very popular in today’s culture,” Craig said. “We have our own superheroes that are just everyday American citizens who rise up to, you know, do something extraordinary when duty calls.”
“Medal of Honor: Joshua Chamberlain” is free to read digitally. Other installments from the series are also free to read online. AUSA releases four stories a year in the “Medal of Honor” series.

title: LA’s Higgins Runs Away with Class B State XC Championship
text:
Lincoln Academy senior Karen Higgins won the Class B girls cross country state championship in convincing fashion on Saturday, Oct. 31 at Cony High School in Augusta.
Higgins bolted to the front of the pack after the starting gun and never looked back as she led from start to finish, completing the course in 18:58.41.
According to Lincoln Academy head coach Garrett Martin, Higgins is the second girl in Lincoln Academy history to win an individual state title in cross country. Higgins’ victory helped boost the Eagles to an eighth place finish at the state meet with a score of 184.
“We finished eighth in the team standings, and while it wasn’t our best day collectively, there’s a lot to feel good about,” said Martin. “This was our sixth straight trip to the state meet, which means a lot when you consider the program hadn’t been there since 2003 before this run began. We’ve also climbed in the standings each year, from 11th two years ago to 10th last year and eighth this year.”
Unlike her first three opportunities at the state championship meets, Higgins had very few Class B runners during her senior campaign who could challenge her for the state title.
“We knew coming into the state meet that Karen was the favorite, but seeing her step up and deliver on the biggest stage was pretty special,” said Martin. “Karen is an exceptional talent, and we’ve been lucky to coach her. This was a fitting way to finish her high school state meet career, and we’re excited to see what she can do at the New England Championship in two weeks, where she’ll represent Lincoln as our lone qualifier.”
Higgins said runner-up Emma Graves, of Caribou, was probably her biggest threat heading into the race, but added she was not too worried, as her own PR time was about 40 seconds faster. Graves finished the course in 19:28.70.
“I was unsure of how Emma would race on the Cony course, so that definitely factored into how I approached the race and my position early on,” said Higgins. “My strategy was to take it out a little quick and get through the first 2 miles how I normally do, and to especially focus on pushing after the hill and on the downhills. I think that having Emma a little closer than I thought for the first mile made me take it out a couple seconds faster than what I planned, but that was not too big of an issue.”
Higgins has been one of the top cross country runners in Maine since she emerged onto the scene as a freshman at Boothbay Region High School. She placed 19th in Class C as a Boothbay freshman in 2023, runner-up as a sophomore in Class C in 2024, and second in Class B last year as a junior in her first season since transferring to Lincoln Academy.
“It felt amazing to win, especially after so many second-place finishes throughout my career,” said Higgins. “I definitely had a taste of what it felt like to win states from last year’s outdoor season, but I’ve always wanted the cross country state title, and it definitely felt great to achieve that. I would not have been able to do it without the unwavering support of my family, friends, teammates, and amazing coaches and all the friends that I have met through the running community.”
Higgins is known for her work effort and strong commitment to the sport.
“She’s put in an incredible amount of work over the past four years, both physically and in how she approaches the mental side of training and racing,” said Martin.
In her preparation for this year’s cross country season, Higgins focused on consistency in her strength training, workouts, and mileage she built up over the summer.
“I also tried to not get super anxious about races and just remember to have fun, which I think helped a lot and was a change in my mentality from years prior,” Higgins said.
Although the cross country season has concluded, Higgins is already looking forward to competing for Lincoln Academy in the upcoming indoor and outdoor track and field seasons. Further down the road, Higgins is gearing up to join the University of New Hampshire cross country and track and field teams for the 2027-28 season, after announcing her commitment to join the prestigious NCAA Division I program in October.
“I’m really excited to continue my career in college at the (NCAA) Division 1 level,” said Higgins. “I think that it will be a little bit of a shock competing with so many elite athletes, but I’m looking forward to having that level of competition in all of the races. I’m very excited to join the UNH team and compete for Coach Duffy. I really like her coaching strategies and the way that she works with the athletes.”
Despite seeing Higgins run for the last time in Maine in an Eagles cross country uniform, the future is bright for the Lady Eagles team. The senior captain was the only upper classman on the roster for the girls state championship race.
“Four of our seven runners are ninth graders, and some of them had never run competitively before this fall,” said Martin. “They deserve a lot of credit for how hard they’ve worked and how much they’ve grown, both as athletes and as a team. With only one senior graduating, this group has gained valuable experience at this level, and we have a real opportunity to take another step forward next fall.”
Lincoln Academy results
Also scoring points for the Lady Eagles in the state championship meet were Higgins’ younger sister, freshman Jillian Higgins (48th, 22:47.46), sophomore Annabel Garvan-Soto (52nd, 23:03.91), and freshmen August Miller (62nd, 24:00.38) and Daisy Rhodes (67th, 24:11.01).
Also competing for Lincoln Academy were freshman Seneca Angell (81st, 25:26.38), and sophomore Hadley Spekke (83rd, 25:46.44).
“We had some encouraging individual performances,” said Martin. “Daisy (Rhodes) had a breakout race cutting nearly two minutes off her time from two weeks earlier on the same course, and she was our only runner to set a personal best on a hilly, demanding course. Hadley (Spekke) and Annabel (Garvan-Soto) also improved on their times from two weeks ago, by 24 and 21 seconds respectively.”
Following Karen Higgins and Graves, Kulani Granholm, of Mount Desert Island, was third (19:33.46), Freeport’s Ella Oshetski was fourth (19:46.15), and Lily Walsh, of Cape Elizabeth, was fifth (19:52.96).
Freeport won the team Class B girls championship with 67 points. MDI was second (81), Yarmouth placed third (87), Cape Elizabeth was fourth (109), Caribou was fifth (135), Presque Isle took sixth with 144, York placed seventh (162), and Lincoln Academy came in eighth place with a score of 184. John Bapst (9th, 193) and Greely (10th, 221) placed below the Eagles.
Lincoln Academy junior Holden Nehrboss placed 30th in the boys Class B championship race, completing the course in 18:24.86.
The Lincoln boys team failed to qualify at the regional championship race leading up to states, and Nehrboss was the only athlete on the boys team to qualify for the championship race as an individual.
“Holden (Nehrboss) ran his most aggressive race of the season and earned All-State honors by finishing 30th, 27 seconds faster than he ran on the same course two weeks ago,” said Martin. “What stood out was his willingness to attack the downhills. He made up ground there and worked his way back into contention late in the race. It was a great example of racing with confidence and taking chances when it matters most.”
Caribou sophomore Pierce Gorneault won the Class B boys race with a time of 16:26.85, followed by four Yarmouth runners: runner-up Jackie Chalmers (16:36.41), Bowen Mitchell (16:47.22), Eli Chalmers (16:53.70), and Jesse Canfield (17:04.20).
With four runners placing in the top five, Yarmouth ran away from the competition to win the state championship with a low score of 27 points. Freeport was a distant second with 92, Caribou placed third (121), Cape Elizabeth was right behind them in fourth (122), and York rounded out the top five with 130 points.
Medomak Valley results
Medomak Valley senior Colby Daigle raced to a coveted top 10 finish in the Class B state championship race, placing 10th with a time of 17:36.16. Daigle improved upon his 12th place result in the 2025 Class B championship (17:54.24), which was held on the same course.
Daigle’s top 10 finish was the best Panther result in a boys state championship race since his brother Connor won the Class B meet in 2021 with a time of 16:35.75.
“Colby worked hard over the summer building up mileage, which is a must if a high school runner wants to improve,” head coach George Gould said. “I’ve been fortunate to have coached many excellent student athletes and I can safely say that Colby is exceptional. He is a hard worker, “the” leader by example who’s always giving advice and encouragement to his teammates.”
Daigle led the Panthers to an 11th place finish with 255 points. Also scoring points for the Medomak boys were junior Grady Emerson (49th, 19:07.04), freshman Gardner Gillespie (72nd, 20:08.19), junior Tanner Kopishke (81st, 20:51.63), and freshman Max Cordero (88th, 21:35.46). Freshman Rowan Lage also competed in the race, placing 98th (24:54.66).
Elizabeth Robbins was the only Medomak athlete to compete in the girls Class B championship race. Robbins, a junior, placed 46th with a time of 22:43.94.

title: Row house fire in Brooklyn kills 6 people and injures 9
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A fire barreled through a multifamily row house in New York early Thursday, killing six people and injuring nine others, including some firefighters and police officers, the city’s fire department said.
More than 200 first responders descended on the two-story building in Brooklyn’s Sunset Park neighborhood, where Kevin Woods, the department’s chief of fire operations, said they were met with “fire on every floor.”
The severely charred wooden home had “fire blowing out every window, meeting us at the front door,” he said at a news conference. Fire marshals were still investigating what caused the blaze.
Firefighters rescued four people, using a rear entrance in the two-unit home to reach people trapped behind window bars, Woods said. A staircase partially collapsed inside the home, he added.
First responders brought the fire under control in about three hours, and eight people who were displaced were taken to hotels. Woods said the fire spread to one adjacent row house, but damage could be seen on buildings to both its left and right.
Row houses share common walls and exteriors and are usually built in blocks. Fire officials said the Sunset Park home was one in a block of 25 wood-frame homes.
“This was a devastating fire,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at the news conference. “It will take a long time for this neighborhood to mourn the neighbors they lost this morning and to recover from this immense grief.”
The nine injured people were expected to survive, including three firefighters and two police officers who had minor injuries. No names have been released.
The home was built in 1915, according to property records.
City records show that the building was sold by a family a few years ago to a company called One Golden Sunshine Corp. Complaints filed with the city’s building department in 2025 said that the home’s basement level was illegally being converted into an apartment and that construction had been going on without a permit for a month.
City inspectors visited several times, including in August, but were unable to gain access.
A lithium-ion battery was found at the scene, but it was unknown whether it was related to the cause of the fire, the department said.
Last week, an e-bike battery fire killed four people in the Bronx. It is among more than 400 fires in the city that have been linked to lithium-ion batteries this year, leading to at least six deaths and more than 70 injuries, according to fire officials.
Fatal home fires are not uncommon, though the death toll in the Brooklyn blaze was unusually high. A townhome fire in Chicago the same day killed four people, including a teenager.
The U.S. Fire Administration says at least 1,555 people have died in home fires this year. Among them were an Amish woman and her six children who were killed in a swift-moving house fire in April in rural Pennsylvania.
Last month, five people, including four children, died in a mobile home fire in Canton, Texas. And in Riverdale, Utah, a man and his four children were killed Oct. 1 in a house fire started by a power strip that overheated, officials said.
——
McCormack reported from Concord, New Hampshire. Associated Press reporters Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut, Yuki Iwamura in New York and Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City contributed.

title: Madi Cyr and Wyatt Daigle Win Week Nine Athlete Honors
text:
Wisdom’s Cyr and Fort Kent’s Daigle Win Fall Week Nine Athlete of the Week Honors
Nine weeks of nominations, voting and outstanding performances across Aroostook County have brought us to the final weekly Athlete of the Week winners of the fall season.
Madi Cyr of Wisdom and Wyatt Daigle of Fort Kent are your Fall Week Nine Athletes of the Week.
Cyr earns the girls honor after finding the net in back-to-back tournament victories for the Pioneers, while Daigle takes the boys award after delivering with Fort Kent's season on the line during a dramatic penalty shootout.
They emerged from an incredibly deep Week Nine ballot featuring 18 athletes from across Aroostook County.
Boys Athlete of the Week: Wyatt Daigle, Fort Kent
When Fort Kent's Class C North semifinal against George Stevens Academy came down to penalty kicks, Daigle stepped into one of the biggest pressure situations of the season.
He converted the deciding penalty kick, sending the Warriors through to the regional championship.
One kick. One enormous postseason moment. And now a Week Nine Athlete of the Week honor.
Congratulations to Wyatt Daigle of Fort Kent, your Fall Week Nine Boys Athlete of the Week.
Girls Athlete of the Week: Madi Cyr, Wisdom
Cyr made her mark during Wisdom's tournament run by finding the net in consecutive playoff victories.
She scored in the Pioneers' 6-1 quarterfinal victory over George Stevens Academy before scoring again in Wisdom's 5-0 semifinal win over previously unbeaten Sumner.
Those back-to-back postseason goals helped the Pioneers advance to the regional championship and ultimately helped Cyr earn the Week Nine girls honor.

Thank You for an Incredible Fall
Week Nine brings the weekly Athlete of the Week voting to a close for the fall, and there is one more thing that deserves recognition: everyone who took part in it.
Thank you to the coaches, athletic directors, parents, teammates, fans and community members who sent in nominations throughout the season.
Thank you for sending statistics, stories and performances that might otherwise have been overlooked.
And thank you to everyone who came back week after week to read about these athletes and cast a vote.
From Week One through Week Nine, Athlete of the Week gave us the opportunity to recognize athletes from schools throughout Aroostook County and celebrate everything from huge scoring performances and championship races to defense, goalkeeping, leadership and sportsmanship.
Congratulations to every athlete who was nominated this fall and to all of our weekly winners.
And one more time, congratulations to Madi Cyr of Wisdom and Wyatt Daigle of Fort Kent, your Fall Week Nine Athletes of the Week.
The weekly voting may be finished, but we aren't done celebrating this fall season yet.

title: Kimmarie Johnson, actress and Miss USA contestant, dies
text:
Kimmarie Johnson, ‘Beverly Hills, 90210’ actress and Miss USA contestant, dies at 50
Actress and model Kimmarie Johnson died Wednesday, TMZ first reported.
Her niece, Rhonda Scott, confirmed Johnson's death. She was 50.
Video above: Remembering those we lost in 2026
Johnson appeared as Judy on "Beverly Hills, 90210" in 1998 and made her film debut in "Let's Talk About Sex" that same year. Her other television credits include "VIP," "Talk of the Town," and "Wanda at Large."
Her breakout movie appearance came in 2000 with a cameo in "Dude, Where's My Car?"
According to People Magazine, Johnson suffered a heart-related medical emergency at her home in Los Angeles, California, on Oct. 27, and was hospitalized at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, where she was diagnosed with a heart aneurysm condition.
She died Nov. 4.
The Pittsburgh native was named Miss Pennsylvania in 1992 and finished sixth in the Miss USA pageant that year before she moved to New York City. Johnson's modeling career included print and runway work in the United States and Europe.
She was also a business owner who created a line of lifestyle and skincare products.

title: The hidden risks of denial in caregiving: When a loved one’s decline is hard to accept
text:
(Aging Untold) — When a loved one starts to need extra support, admitting how much has changed is one of the hardest hurdles families face.
Denial can step in naturally to protect us from overwhelming grief, but avoiding reality for too long can risk caregiver burnout and compromise care.
Recognizing where you and your loved ones stand emotionally is the first step toward navigating the aging journey with clarity and compassion.
The hidden purpose of denial
“I think denial gets a bad rap,” Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “Denial is a really healthy stage of grief. It’s a shock absorber. It allows the body to kind of catch up and process what’s going on. You can’t let this situation take you all over. And I don’t think people realize that you go in and out of it.”
O’Rourke recalled visiting a client whose husband was actively dying. When she arrived, the wife put the conversation on hold.
“She just stopped me and said, ‘You know, we’re having dinner right now, and we’re enjoying each other,’” O’Rourke noted. “I thought, good for you, and I left, and I was so happy for her that she was aware that she was going to keep it away and enjoy him.”
The caregiver blind spot: ‘I’m not a caregiver’
Denial also shows up when family members take on heavy workloads without acknowledging their actual role as a caregiver.
The National Alliance for Caregiving estimates that 63 million Americans, nearly one in four adults, serve as a family caregiver, but Cradduck said that number is likely higher based on her experience with people who don’t recognize themselves as caregivers.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said many people who are cooking the meals, getting the groceries, keeping the house and paying the bills will tell her that they are not a caregiver. They are doing these tasks for someone who is independent and living alone.
“I’m like OK, when do you become the caregiver? Well, when I give them a shower — when I help with the personal care,’” Cradduck said.
“The denying that someone needs help, or saying ‘I’m fine,’ can be detrimental. Not just the caregiver doing it, but the person themselves,” Cradduck said.
Another facet of denial is when the caregiver who is at a breaking point says they are fine, Cradduck said.
Meeting loved ones where they are
Another facet of denial, aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said, is not facing a loved one’s decline.
If you can’t wrap your head around that, you could actually do harm and have a lot of regrets, she said.
Examples she gave include:
“She’s just being stubborn,” Or, “He’s just giving me a hard time.”
“Because you could be in denial about what is really going on,” Ambrose said.
Seeing a loved one decline is a harsh reality, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
“You really have to meet people where they are. But it’s really, really hard because when you start to accept that, you also start to understand that they can actually change and decline very quickly,” Rogers said.
Ambrose emphasized reorienting your daily mindset: “You want to think about: Who does my loved one need me to be right now, in this moment, and serve them best?”
When older parents are the ones in denial and resist assistance, O’Rourke advises patience over confrontation: “Don’t try to push your way through the denial in that moment.”
She recommends asking gentle, open-ended questions such as, “What do you see?” or “Are you having a hard time?”
Preventing caregiver burnout and collision
True support cannot happen without an honest assessment of both your loved one’s decline and your personal limits.
“We have to reach a point of acceptance even in our grief,” Cradduck said. “I can’t meet you where you’re at if I don’t know where that’s at. I have to be honest enough to say, ‘You know what? You are declining. This is too hard.’”
Unacknowledged stress can lead to exhaustion and relationship friction.
“It’s not just denying that the person themselves is declining and you’re losing someone that you love; it’s how hard and how insurmountable being that caregiver is,” Cradduck said. “When you’re not admitting it, you’re not taking care of yourself. We’re seeing that caregiver burnout and we’re seeing those struggles so frequently because it’s so hard and you’re just saying, ‘Oh, I’m good, I don’t need help.’”
O’Rourke said she also sees people collide at different stages of grief — one person is in denial and the other is in anger.
“They can collide if you’re not really aware of where are you in the stages of grief because everybody is grieving, whether it’s the caregiver or the person,” O’Rourke said.
Key Takeaways
- Denial acts as an emotional shock absorber: Denial is often a stage of grief that shields families from acute crisis and creates space to process painful news at a manageable pace.
- Find value in being present in the moment: Compartmentalizing the illness sometimes helps families block out the crisis and just enjoy the moment.
- Focus on today’s needs: Stop living in yesterday’s memories. Focus instead on the needs of the person in front of you today.

title: First measles death in 30+ years reported in this state
text:
MADISON, Wis. (WBAY/Gray News) — The Wisconsin Department of Health Services reports the death of an infant associated with the ongoing measles outbreak in the southwestern part of the state.
It is the first measles death in the state since 1990, according to a DHS news release.
The coroner listed the immediate cause of death as measles, the release said. To protect the privacy of the family and the child, DHS is not releasing any more information about the case or the young patient.
State health secretary comments
“Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease,” said DHS Secretary Kirsten Johnson. “Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family.”
Statewide case count
As of Nov. 3, DHS has reported 431 measles cases in 13 counties so far in 2026, according to the release. The DHS numbers are from Nov. 3, before five cases were confirmed in Green Lake County. The number reflects the highest number of cases seen in the state in more than 35 years.
Nine people have required hospitalization for severe symptoms across those cases, DHS said.
The release said reported case counts may not reflect the full extent of measles spread. Not everyone who becomes ill seeks medical care or gets tested, which means cases may go unreported.
“A disease that can spread that quickly can go from a small problem to a big problem very quickly, and the best way across the whole world that we’ve been able to stop illness and death from measles is to stop it from spreading in the community completely,” says Dr. Ryan Westergaard, the chief medical officer with the Wisconsin DHS.
The state’s total was 335 on Oct. 27, which means it added nearly 100 patients in about one week. A majority of the cases are from what is being referred to as the “Southwest Wisconsin measles outbreak” in Grant, Lafayette, Iowa, and Vernon counties. DHS said the cases are related to out-of-state travel, but the exact source of those infections is unknown.
All but three of the patients were not vaccinated.
Green Lake County cases
Green Lake County has confirmed at least five measles cases, according to a news release from the Green Lake County Department of Health & Human Services. They are the first cases confirmed in Northeast Wisconsin.
The cases are linked to a laboratory-confirmed case in another county, the release said. The Green Lake County Department of Health & Human Services did not name which county the infection spread from.
Green Lake County is adjacent to Marquette County, which has two confirmed measles cases.
All confirmed and suspected cases identified so far in Green Lake County have been among people who were not vaccinated against measles. Known exposures have been limited to private gatherings, and no public exposure locations have been identified at this time.
The state is now recommending an early dose of the MMR vaccine for infants between 6 and 11 months old who face a higher risk of exposure. The usual first dose is given after a child’s 1st birthday.
“Ordinarily, we don’t begin MMR vaccination until a child’s first birthday. But in an outbreak, when we know that an infant may be exposed to measles, there’s a benefit to providing that protection earlier,” said Dr. Westergaard.
Measles symptoms
Measles is a highly contagious, vaccine-preventable disease that can spread from person to person through the air. The virus can stay in the air for two hours after a sick person coughs or sneezes. It can cause serious health complications, including pneumonia, brain damage and deafness, and can sometimes be deadly.
Symptoms typically appear approximately 10 to 12 days after exposure, but in some cases can range from seven to 21 days. Symptoms include:
- Runny nose
- High fever, which may be greater than 104 degrees
- Tiredness
- Cough
- Red, watery eyes or conjunctivitis (“pink eye”)
- Red rash with raised bumps that starts at the hairline and moves to the arms and legs three to five days after symptoms begin
People who develop symptoms should stay home and not go to work, school or shopping or use public transportation. They should call their doctor’s office or clinic before visiting so staff can take precautions to prevent other patients from being exposed.
Vaccination status
People who are unsure whether they are vaccinated against measles can contact their health provider or check the Wisconsin Immunization Registry at dhfswir.org, according to the Green Lake County release.

title: Maine sets midterm turnout record as more than 730,000 voters cast ballots
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Maine voters set a new turnout record for a midterm election this year, Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said Friday.
More than 730,000 Mainers voted in Tuesday’s election, Bellows said. That compares with 680,909 in 2022, when Maine had the nation’s highest voter turnout percentage for the election cycle.
Election officials are certifying the results from Tuesday’s election.
National comparison still to come
Bellows said Maine won’t know whether it ranked first in the country this year until after states report their results to the federal government in January. She said those reports come out later in the winter.
“What we do know is that more voters turned out to vote than ever before in a midterm election,” Bellows said. “We didn’t quite reach the threshold of the presidential in 2024, but it was pretty incredible.”
More than 842,000 Mainers voted in the 2024 presidential election, Bellows said.

title: Hallowell police chief says he can’t recommend Quarry Tap Room liquor license renewal
text:
HALLOWELL, Maine (WABI) - Hallowell Police Chief Zachary Kindelan said he cannot, in good faith, recommend the renewal of the Quarry Tap Room’s liquor license ahead of a public hearing.
Chief cites concerns about operations
Kindelan said he does not want to see the Quarry Tap Room close, but he has concerns about the bar continuing to operate the way it has been.
Kindelan says since becoming chief last summer, Hallowell Police have responded to 15 incidents at the Tap Room. Eleven of those incidents ended in an arrest or summons.
Kindelan said some of the arrests were for OUIs.
Meeting at business draws no response from leadership
Kindelan said he has spoken with some of the staff and was told things would improve. He said he has not seen any improvements.
He adds this week that he, Code Enforcement, the Fire Chief, and Liquor Enforcement scheduled a meeting at the business to discuss concerns and a way forward. The Tap Room’s leadership did not show up, he said.
The Quarry Taproom’s Response
Friday, The Quarry Taproom put out a statement, saying, “Yesterday, The Quarry Taprooms ownership was made aware that Hallowell Police Chief Kindelan had written a letter to the Hallowell City Council recommending that the Council not renew The Quarry Taprooms liquor license. In the letter, Chief Kindelan mentioned that an email was sent about a visit, but no one responded or was present at the time when he arrived for a walk through. However, today The Quarry Taproom ownership responded via email to the Chief, had a productive phone call with him and is meeting with him for a walkthrough on Monday prior to the public hearing. There are a number of other allegations, statements and arguments in the letter that The Quarry Taproom ownership, employees and loyal patrons will address directly at the public hearing on Monday evening. The Quarry Taproom is committed to providing a fun, comfortable and safe environment for its many return customers, and looks forward to welcoming new customers in the future.”
Public hearing set for Monday
The public hearing for the Quarry Tap Room’s liquor license renewal is scheduled for Monday night.

title: Some patients are choosing self-pay alternatives to medical insurance
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
GREENVILLE, S.C. (Aging Untold) —Some patients are choosing to pay cash for medical procedures rather than file insurance claims, saying it can be significantly cheaper for certain services like MRI scans.
Greta Fuller faced this decision when her 10-year-old son needed an MRI for severe abdominal pain in fall 2024.
His doctor was having difficulty getting insurance approval for the scan so she took her son to Imago in Greenville, which doesn’t accept insurance.
“I was able to get Seth in that day,” Fuller said.
Patients pay about $500 out of pocket for an MRI scan.
“That was amazing because we had talked with friends who’ve spent $2,000 after insurance,” Fuller said.
Growing trend of cash-pay medical facilities
Palmetto Proactive Imaging Center in Spartanburg is another self-pay location.
DJ Horton took his son, Grey, there for a knee MRI after the boy experienced pain from sports activities.
Because they have a membership with Palmetto Proactive Primary Care, they received a discounted rate of about $350 to $400 per knee.
Nonmember MRI costs at Palmetto Proactive are usually $500 to $600.
Hospital pricing comparison
Hospital systems in the area charge about $2,000 for a leg MRI when patients pay cash, often offering discounts when insurance isn’t used. However, using insurance can cost more — around $3,500 for an MRI if the patient hasn’t met their deductible.
Both parents said their children received needed treatment after the MRIs and are healthy again.
“We thought this was a much better economical decision, but it’s also been way more than that,” Horton said.
“We were just really thankful to be able to get that done quickly, affordable, have some information, some thoughts on how to move forward,” Fuller said.
Direct primary care model
Dr. Chris McCarthy from Palmetto Proactive compared it to a subscription service.
He said patients can often schedule same-day appointments and get more time with their doctor.
According to the American Academy of Family Physicians, monthly membership fees range from $50 to $100.

title: Incumbent sheriff ousted in very close Oxford County race
text:
Incumbent Republican sheriff ousted in very close Oxford County race
Democrat Timothy Holland has ousted incumbent Republican Sheriff Christopher Wainwright in a very close race for Oxford County Sheriff.
The unofficial vote total reported by municipalities to the Maine Secretary of State's Office shows Holland with 10,108 votes (34.9%), Wainwright with 10,040 votes (34.7%) and independent candidate Justin Brown with 8,797 votes (30%).
Holland says the Secretary of State's office called him on Thursday to tell him he had won the race.
In a statement on Friday morning, Holland said, "I do not take the responsibility you have entrusted to me lightly. I am truly humbled by the opportunity to serve as your next Sheriff. This election was about more than choosing a person for a position. It was about the future of public safety, the strength of our communities, and the importance of having a Sheriff's Office that remains connected, accountable, and committed to the people it serves."
Holland said he will be working with Wainwright and the current administrative team over the coming weeks as they transition to a new sheriff and administration.
"Our priority is the safety and well-being of the people of Oxford County. As promised during my campaign, we will take the time to understand what is working, identify opportunities for improvement, and build on the foundation already in place. Continuity of operations, support for our employees, responsible leadership, and uninterrupted public safety services will remain at the forefront of our efforts."
Wainwright's reaction
Wainwright shared a statement on Friday morning thanking those who supported him and saying he has been grateful for the opportunity to serve as sheriff.
"When I first started at the Oxford County Sheriff's Office more than 35 years ago, Tim Holland was my first supervisor. We have worked together for more than three decades, and I have a great deal of respect for him," Wainwright said in his statement.
"Throughout this campaign, we kept our focus on the merits of the office and what matters most: serving the citizens of Oxford County. Tim and I had a lengthy conversation this morning about the future of the agency. We agree that the Sheriff's Office is in a great place, and we are committed to ensuring a smooth transition. I congratulate Tim on his election and wish him the very best.
"Over the past eight years, we have worked hard to increase our presence throughout the county, strengthen our operations, expand support for those struggling with substance use disorder, and manage our resources responsibly.
"I am proud of what we have accomplished, but I am especially proud of the men and women who make up this agency. Their dedication to this work and to the people of Oxford County is what makes this office strong. It has meant a great deal to me to work alongside them."

title: This 83-year-old minister gives away hand-painted seashells
text:
DANSVILLE, Mich. (InvestigateTV) - Gil Ames calls his Chevy Equinox a $34,000 canvas. The vehicle is painted all over, including tigers on the side.
Inside his home in rural Ingham County, actual paintings on canvas line the walls. Ames made all the picture frames and did all the paintings himself.
Some of his work mimics the masters, including Blue Boy. Other pieces feature his faith, such as Christ at Gethsemane.
An ordained minister, Reverend Ames has not let anything get in the way of his passion for painting. He volunteered with the Red Cross at 52 national disasters, including ground zero in New York.
He also spent 25 years as a long-haul truck driver. He pivoted to something more portable to paint on during that time.
“So that’s when I started painting eggs,” Ames said.
He paints wooden eggs with intricate scenes. Every single one has an angel in it someplace, he said. He also paints thumbtacks, each with an angel.
Ames keeps his own thumbnail painted with an angel design.
His wife Orma has been by his side for 58 years. She said he does amazing things.
“If it doesn’t move, it gets painted,” Orma Ames said. “He’s a true artist, because an artist gets bored and they have to change and do something different.”
About six months ago, Reverend Ames started painting tiny seashells. He said he is running low on a particular size.
The smaller they are, the more he can fit into his shirt pocket. One pocket is full of seashells, probably 50 or more, he said.
Reverend Ames does not sell his seashells. He gives them away for free.
A stop for lunch at the Big Boy in Mason was a place to shell out some kindness.
“It makes me feel loved,” one woman at the restaurant said.
A waitress called the gesture thoughtful and said it brightens people’s spirits.
Ames said he stopped counting after handing out his first thousand seashells. Laughs, hugs and thank yous are the reward.
“Thank you so much and God bless you,” one woman said.
The 83-year-old said making people happy is the motivation that keeps him painting.
“They’re not perfect, but they’re not bad either,” Ames said. “The price is right.”
