title: 2 Justice Department officials resign in wake of the midterm elections
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The top federal prosecutor in Miami who had been tasked with overseeing an investigation into foes of President Donald Trump has resigned, joining other high-profile Justice Department officials departing in the wake of the midterm elections, officials said Friday.
Jason Reding Quiñones’ resignation follows frustrations among Washington officials with his management of the office assigned to lead the so-called “grand conspiracy” investigation, according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel issues.
The Justice Department’s top national security official, John Eisenberg, also resigned on Friday, Attorney General Todd Blanche said. On Thursday, Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who led a radical overhaul of the department’s Civil Rights Division, also announced her departure.
Quiñones was confirmed by the Senate last year as U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, where the Justice Department had centered its meandering probe into whether former law enforcement and intelligence officials conspired against the Republican president.
His departure comes as the investigation has shown signs of faltering amid a spate of staff turnovers and delays. Investigators in recent weeks have put off scheduled grand jury testimony of several witnesses, according to multiple people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation.
Blanche said in a social media post that the department is grateful for Quiñones’ “leadership in combating violent crime, drug trafficking, sex trafficking, and transnational crime, including the indictment of Raúl Castro.”
Castro, the former Cuban president, was indicted by Quiñones’ office in May on charges related to the 1996 downing of civilian planes flown by Miami-based exiles.
Quiñones said Friday that he is leaving with “immense pride in what we accomplished together and profound gratitude for the opportunity to serve our great Nation.”
“I am grateful to President Trump for his trust and to the extraordinary men and women of the great Southern District of Florida for their dedication, friendship, and unwavering commitment to justice and the rule of law,” Quiñones wrote in a social media post.
The “grand conspiracy” investigation has proceeded in fits and starts for over a year with repeated setbacks and departures. Last April, a lead national security prosecutor in the investigation of former CIA Director John Brennan was replaced on the team after raising questions about the strength of the case.
Shortly afterward, Joseph diGenova, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, took over the probe. DiGenova resigned from the Justice Department in September without bringing any criminal charges.
Eisenberg was sworn in as assistant attorney general in charge of the department’s National Security Division in June 2025 and oversaw cases involving espionage, terrorism, export control violations, cyber crimes and other matters.
Among the division’s most high-profile cases under his watch was the prosecution of former national security adviser John Bolton, who pleaded guilty this year to allegations of mishandling classified information and is awaiting sentencing.
“He has served with distinction, strengthening our nation’s ability to address threats, both foreign and domestic,” Blanche said in a statement.

title: How BofA teamed with Farnsworth to give old paintings new life
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Farnsworth Art Museum in Rockland recently announced that Bank of America was gifting the institution four murals painted by renowned artist N.C. Wyeth in the early 1920s. BofA acquired the paintings when it acquired the Boston bank that commissioned them.
How the paintings ended up at the Farnsworth is a story that involves BofA’s wider efforts to place much of its vast art holdings, along with a bit of ingenuity by curators to transport the massive paintings and prepare gallery space for an exhibition in 2028.
‘Deep connection to Maine’
Christopher J. Brownawell, executive director of the Farnsworth, said the gift was at least two years in the making. Bank of America has been in the process of gifting some of its art holdings.
In a conversation with Mainebiz, Brownawell and Farnsworth chief curator Jaime DeSimone said the bank approached the Rockland museum about the gift.
“The murals have a deep connection to Maine through N.C. Wyeth and the Wyeth family’s legacy, so in many ways, this feels like these paintings are coming home to Maine. The Farnsworth is nationally recognized for preserving and interpreting the family’s work and is in a great position to care for the murals and share them with visitors,” Brian King, president of Bank of America Maine, told Mainebiz in an email.
The N.C. Wyeth murals, painted in 1923-24 at the artist’s Chadds Ford, Pa., studio, depict scenes of maritime trade and commerce and have been in storage in Delaware since the 1970s.
Brownawell talked about the “grand scale” of the paintings, and he’s not kidding. The paintings are more than 14 feet high and a dozen feet wide.
“They’re massive when fully stretched and framed,” he said.
The Farnsworth was initially challenged by the sheer size of the paintings, not only how to transport them but also where to hang them once they were ready to be exhibited at the Rockland museum.
With the first painting to be moved, each mural would have to be laid diagonally in a truck. Only one per truck could be moved that way.
“Each one [would have] needed its own 18-wheeler,” Brownawell said.
DeSimone consulted with a third-party conservator team, Kristin deGhetaldi and Brian Baade, who had worked with Jamie Wyeth last year to transfer a separate N.C. Wyeth mural.
DeSimone traveled to Delaware to see the murals in storage.
“It was like you were in a doctor’s waiting room, waiting. When we went into the viewing room, it was incredible,” DeSimone recalled. “The color in the murals and the scale [were] unbelievable.”
Best of all, the works were in good shape.
After some study, the consensus was the canvases could be safely taken off their “stretchers,” or the wooden framework, and rolled up for shipping. Such a procedure could risk damaging the paintings, but Brownawell was assured it was possible. And that’s how the paintings were shipped to Rockland.
“That’s when we got excited about the potential,” Brownawell said.
“The size of the murals made moving them a significant undertaking,” King added. “Bank of America hired a professional conservator to carefully remove each painting from the large panels on which they were mounted. From there, the murals were carefully rolled, boxed and transported by truck to ensure they could make the journey safely.”
Bank of America covered the cost of the conservation and transfer, King said, so there was no expense to the Farnsworth.
What’s next
In coming months — and leading up to when the murals will be put on display in 2028, conservators will take a closer look at the paintings. They’ll also spend time going through N.C. Wyeth’s studies for the paintings as well as letters and other documents — to tell more of the backstory of how the murals came together.
There’s also an archive of photographs that Margaret Bourke-White shot of the murals in the 1920s in their original Boston bank setting.
“There’s such depth to the story,” Brownawell said.
To prepare the murals to be displayed at the Farnsworth’s Wyeth Center, Brownawell said the scale of the paintings requires the museum to shore up the walls to ensure they can support the weight.
The murals will go on view in a special exhibition at the Farnsworth’s Wyeth Center in June 2028.

title: Cornell faculty vote ‘no confidence’ in university’s leadership over handling of sexual assault allegations
text:
(AP) - Cornell University’s Faculty Senate approved a resolution Friday declaring “no confidence” in the school’s top leaders, a symbolic gesture reflecting deep discontent on campus in the wake of a former student’s lawsuit saying she was gang raped at a fraternity party in 2024.
The resolution passed 75-50, with five faculty senators abstaining and five others not voting, according to an email sent to members of the Faculty Senate on Friday afternoon.
The vote followed weeks of debate among professors over whether Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff and other administrators handled the woman’s allegations properly and whether they’ve done enough to curtail sexual misconduct at the prestigious university.
While the faculty body has no power over the university’s top leaders, backers of the resolution had said they hoped it would pressure Cornell’s trustees to urgently address what they viewed as longstanding institutional failures.
Voting took place electronically over more than a week, with the results released Friday.
The Cornell community has been in a state of distress and dismay since mid-September, when a former student filed a lawsuit against the university and seven former members of the Chi Phi fraternity, saying she was given ketamine and raped at a fraternity house in October 2024.
All of those men have denied her allegations, saying either the sex was consensual or they weren’t involved. The local district attorney initially decided the woman had consented to the encounter, and that no crime had been committed, but the investigation has since been reopened and handed to New York’s attorney general.
Cornell disciplined several of the accused students following a months-long Title IX investigation. Two were expelled, two received suspensions and probation, and two were required to write “reflection” papers and complete bystander training. A seventh man had already graduated and was barred from campus, according to records obtained by The New York Times.
Kotlikoff also convened a task force to study the problem of sexual misconduct on campus, which released certain recommendations.
Some faculty members have been furious with Kotlikoff for not acting more forcefully to strengthen the school’s disciplinary process, push for criminal investigations and change campus party culture.
Paul Ortiz, a labor history professor who co-sponsored the no-confidence resolution, said last week that hundreds of students, staff, alumni and faculty approached the resolution’s sponsors to emphasize that “the Jane Doe case is but a tip of the iceberg” and that “a veritable fortress of silence has been breached” around sexual violence since the resolution’s introduction.
Speaking to Faculty Senate members on the first day that they debated the no-confidence resolution, Kotlikoff pledged to make the university a leader in addressing the problem of sexual assault, and he asked that he be given the time to make more changes.
Kotlikoff defended his leadership, arguing that replacing him would do little to solve complex problems and could damage Cornell’s reputation. He acknowledged he had not read the campus police report, explaining that university policy barred top administrators from interfering in criminal investigations. He also rejected suggestions that he had been indifferent to the woman’s case, though he acknowledged not having known until recently that she left Cornell.
Kotlikoff said the university needed to determine whether fraternities could operate safely and left open the possibility of sweeping restrictions on Greek life. He urged faculty to give him time to make changes, arguing that decisions should be based on research and evidence rather than emotion.
Some professors also urged patience and said faculty should wait until the release of an independent investigation by former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates, whom the university hired to examine both how Cornell responded to the woman’s initial rape report in 2024 and its overall procedures for handling similar reports from other students.
The no-confidence resolution did not call for Kotlikoff’s resignation.

title: Holocaust survivor dies almost a year after being shot in Australia Hanukkah massacre
text:
90-year-old Holocaust survivor dies almost a year after being shot in the Australia Hanukkah massacre
A 90-year-old Holocaust survivor has died almost a year after she was wounded during the massacre of 15 people at a Sydney Hanukkah celebration, officials said Friday.
Video above: Albanese sets out hate speech reforms in wake of Bondi Beach shooting
Romanian-born Eva Geller died Thursday night in a Sydney hospital, Executive Council of Australian Jewry director Evan Zlatkis said.
She was one of around 40 people wounded when two gunmen allegedly inspired by the Islamic State group opened fire on a crowd at Bondi Beach on Dec. 14. Fifteen victims aged 10 to 87 died. One of the gunmen, Sajid Akram, was shot dead by police at the scene.
Rabbi says victim was 'strong and pretty healthy' before she was shot
Rabbi Aron Moss said Geller had been “strong and pretty healthy right up until the Bondi attack where she was shot.”
She had been admitted to the hospital several times in recent weeks due to surgery complications, Moss said.
“She’s a proud mother, grandmother and great grandmother. A beautiful, positive person who even in these difficult months maintained her positivity,” Moss said on the family’s behalf.
“She was told after being shot that she will never walk again by the doctors. But through sheer determination, she got back up and she did walk again,” Moss added.
She walked with a cane following the leg wound, he said.
The surviving alleged gunman, Naveed Akram, the 25-year-old son of the dead gunman, has been charged with 15 counts of murder, 43 of attempted murder and one of committing a terrorist act. He has yet to enter a plea.
It was not yet clear whether Geller’s death would change the charges Akram faces.
Police said in a statement they were awaiting advice from a state coroner, who would investigate the circumstances of her death.
Akram is scheduled to appear in court next on Feb. 24, when prosecutors expect to finalize what charges will go to the New South Wales state Supreme Court for trial.
State government leader says death is ‘heartbreaking’
State Premier Chris Minns offered his condolences to Geller’s family.
“After everything Geller endured, the news of her death is heartbreaking,” Minns said in a statement.
“Almost a year on, we are still living with the pain and aftershock of that evil act. We will never forget Eva or any victim whose life was changed forever,” Minns added.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the devastation of the Bondi attack continued to cause pain for families.
“Eva should have been able to celebrate Chanukah (Hanukkah) in peace and safety and instead, her life was changed forever by an act of terror and antisemitism,” Albanese said in a statement, using a different spelling of Hanukkah.

title: Airport officials discover 3,000 tarantulas smuggled inside dirty socks
text:
Airport officials discover 3,000 tarantulas smuggled inside dirty socks
More than 3,000 tarantulas were discovered stuffed inside dirty socks that were packed in the luggage of travelers as they prepared to board a flight.
Peruvian authorities say the spiders were hidden in labeled stockings inside three suitcases belonging to two German citizens and a Polish citizen on a flight from Lima’s Jorge Chávez International to Germany.
Related video above | Red-eyed, three lipped sea spider species discovered
Officials with the Peruvian National Forest and Wildlife Service, known as SERFOR, said the haul included eggs, young spiders and adults, with some species not yet described by science.
The tarantulas came from several regions of Peru, including Junín, Loreto, Cajamarca, Cusco and La Libertad.
Police arrested the three travelers at the airport as they were checking in, and they face criminal charges related to environmental crimes.
They also will face administrative proceedings, officials with SERFOR said.
One of the detainees is reportedly a well-known tarantula researcher, according to scientific publications cited by the agency.
Authorities suspect the spiders were meant for collectors, research or the pet trade. After they are identified and evaluated, the tarantulas will be transferred to an authorized breeding center.

title: UMaine scientist helps identify one of the oldest Martian meteorites on Earth
text:
ORONO — University of Maine professor Alicia Cruz-Uribe and her colleagues were analyzing a box of rock samples from Mars when they made an unexpected discovery. They would confirm that one sample came from one of the oldest Martian meteorites ever found on Earth.
While examining samples to determine their age, the group selected one from Teghaza 001, an ancient Martian meteorite found by Sahrawi prospectors in the Sahara Desert in 2022. Until recently, little was known about the age and origins of the meteorite.
Most Martian meteorites found on Earth are no more than about 2 billion years old. But in a lab at the California Institute of Technology in summer 2025, Cruz-Uribe and her colleagues measured isotopes showing that Teghaza 001 is 4.1 billion years old.
Only two other known Martian meteorites are older than 4 billion years: Allan Hills 84001 and NWA 7034, also known as Black Beauty.
“I think we actually jumped up and down; full on dance party in the lab,” Cruz-Uribe, Edward Sturgis Grew Professor of Petrology and Mineralogy, said.
In a new study published in Science, Cruz-Uribe and her colleagues confirmed not only Teghaza 001’s age but also that it dates back to the formation of Mars’ crust and mantle — offering a rare window into the planet’s geologic history.
“When you add a third sample, and its geochemistry is really unique compared to the other samples that we have, it lets us see a different part of Mars’s ancient history in terms of what the mantle looked like and what the different mantle sources were on Mars,” Cruz-Uribe said.
A new method for dating rocks
The study is part of a multiyear research project on the formation of Mars’ crust by Cruz-Uribe and colleagues from Caltech, UCLA and the University of New Mexico. It involved a new method Cruz-Uribe developed for dating rock samples.
The technique involves firing a laser beam one-sixth the width of a human hair to drill holes into a sample. It uses helium gas to carry material removed by the laser through a tube and into a mass spectrometer — a machine that allows elements to be separated by mass. Chemical reactions inside the instrument separate the elements so researchers can measure the sample’s composition.
Similar dating methods have been used by other scientists to identify isotopes of uranium and lead, but Cruz-Uribe’s method is unique because it looks for rubidium and strontium. By looking for different elements, scientists can date minerals other than those containing uranium and lead, she said. That was crucial for dating feldspar minerals in Teghaza 001.
At Caltech, Cruz-Uribe and her colleagues discovered that the rubidium-strontium age of Teghaza 001 was the same as the uranium-lead age for zircons from the meteorite.
“When we can’t date a rock by one method, maybe the rubidium-strontium can fill in the gaps,” Cruz-Uribe said. “The other thing that is unique about this method is that it was created specifically for the mass spectrometer at Caltech in the lab of my colleague François Tissot, which is capable of high precision analyses of the isotopes of rubidium and strontium.”
Rubidium-strontium has been one of the most popular geochronologic systems used by scientists for the last six decades, but traditional methods involved weeks, if not months, of chemistry and analysis that would destroy samples. By using laser ablation coupled to mass spectrometers, scientists can save time and preserve their samples, Cruz-Uribe said.
“Instead of taking your bulk sample and dissolving it and separating out rubidium and strontium, this allows you to put your sample into the laser chamber, pick your spot, drill a hole with the laser, and then do the separation chemistry inside of the mass spectrometer,” she said. “A single laser spot typically takes less than one minute.”
The samples used in the study are held at the Institute of Meteoritics at the University of New Mexico and total 22 grams of Teghaza 001. The meteorite’s primary mass, weighing 442 grams, is held by the Maine Mineral & Gem Museum in Bethel.
“We really appreciate having this type of resource in the state of Maine, and we appreciate their generosity in sharing samples with researchers when they need them,” Cruz-Uribe said. “The Maine Mineral and Gem Museum has recently loaned us an additional piece of Teghaza 001 so that we can continue work on this sample both at Caltech and also at UMaine.”
Cruz-Uribe has analyzed this additional sample of Teghaza 001 in UMaine’s MicroAnalytical Geochemistry and Isotope Characterization Laboratory, or MAGIC Lab.
UMaine students applying the research
In addition to studying Martian meteorites, Cruz-Uribe and her students are using her new method to date rocks in Maine, particularly western Maine, to learn more about the state’s geological history and composition.
“Most of the rocks in Maine were studied back in the ‘50s and ‘60s, and a lot of the fundamental work on a large portion of the state was done before the development of any of the modern geochronology tools that we have now,” Cruz-Uribe said, “so we are able to add a huge amount of information to better understand the tectonic history of Maine.”
UMaine students have also helped prepare the meteorite samples Cruz-Uribe and her colleagues have studied in their multiyear project.
“They contribute to this science in real and fundamental ways, and they deserve credit for that,” she said. “We are excited to embody UMaine’s mission as a learner-centered R1 institution by giving students access to cutting-edge geochemistry and geochronology experiences during their undergraduate and graduate educations.”

title: An illegally killed bull moose became an unusual classroom lesson for Maine students
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
East Grand High School students in Danforth got a hands-on lesson in processing wild game Wednesday, learning how to butcher, package and preserve meat from a bull moose.
The Maine Warden Service recovered the moose last week after it was illegally shot in northern Maine during Maine’s antlerless-only moose hunt, which ran Oct. 26-31. Warden Tyler Leach quartered the animal and packed it out of the woods before delivering it to Hatch’s Meat Cutting in Merrill for cold storage.
Rex Crocker, a Danforth resident who previously worked as a professional meat cutter and held several roles at East Grand School over the years, helped students break down the animal. He brought his own cutting tools and shared his experience with the class.
Becky Cropley, an educational technician at the school, demonstrated how to can moose meat, a preservation method that allows it to be stored without refrigeration. Students also learned how to vacuum-seal meat for storage.
The school had not held the activity in several years because it depends on an illegally killed moose being recovered and made available for educational use.
The lesson was part of East Grand’s outdoor education program, which is in its 30th year. The high school elective is open to students in grades nine through 12 and meets every other school day from 8 to 9:30 a.m. Students learn outdoor skills including map and compass navigation, fire building, canoeing and riflery, as well as teamwork and leadership.
This year’s class has 12 students and is taught by Maine guides Dave Conley and Tammi Matula. Matula also teaches physical education and health at the school.
“The students were pretty excited to be involved with the whole process,” Conley said. Each student took home about 25 pounds of meat.

title: These Maine towns still count ballots by hand
text:
MAINE (The Maine Monitor) - Shortly after the polls closed on election night, the town clerk of Cranberry Isles, Ben Sumner, and two volunteers, Barbara Meyers and Beverly Sanborn, began counting the island’s ballots by hand.
With a view of Acadia National Park, Great Cranberry is the largest of five islands that make up the town of Cranberry Isles, which has a population of about 160. On Nov. 3, there were 48 ballots to count — the old-fashioned way, with no electronic tabulators in sight.
Cranberry Isles is one of 88 towns in Maine that still counts its ballots by hand. That is down from 161 towns, or about a third of the state’s voting jurisdictions, that did so in 2024, according to data from Verified Voting, a nonpartisan organization that researches the use of technology in elections. Those towns were quite small — with an average of 248 registered voters — making up 4 percent of the total voters in the state.
This election cycle, 73 of them decided to join the majority of Maine’s municipalities and switch to hand-fed optical scanners, which scan hand-marked paper ballots and tabulate the votes, storing the data on a memory stick.
These scanners are manufactured by a company called Election Systems and Software, which Maine has contracted with since 2012, and provided by the state at no cost to municipalities. Studies have shown these machines are more accurate and more efficient than hand counting, which can be prone to human error.
“More towns opted into tabulators because counting by hand is incredibly time consuming and more subject to human error,” Jana Spaulding, the deputy secretary of state for communications, told The Maine Monitor this week. “Time and time again, towns that make the switch express relief at how easy the tabulators make it to count the votes quickly.”
But it is up to towns whether they want these machines, and, on Great Cranberry, hand counting is still the method of choice.
As a fire crackled in the community center’s brick fireplace, the mantle covered in gourds and dried flowers, another year-round resident, Helen Bertles, dropped by with a homemade cake.
“Sugar, sugar, sugar. Gotta keep moving!” Bertles said before taking a seat to watch.
The clerk began the process by voiding all the town’s unused ballots. They were marked with red X’s and stored to be transported in the town offices on Islesford, a neighboring island and separate voting precinct in the Cranberry Isles.
“On Wednesday morning,” Sumner said, “I combine both precincts and report the results. If a race has to be determined by ranked choice, I’ll take the ballots off to Mount Desert on Thursday so the state police can pick them up and take them to Augusta.”
Next, the election workers opened the absentee ballots and deposited them into the town’s wooden ballot box — which is believed to be at least 100 years old — where they joined the ballots that were cast throughout Election Day.
The box was unlocked, and the group retrieved and organized the ballots. Then it was time to count.
The counting process requires one reader, who examines each ballot and announces the votes, and two counters, who keep a tally as the votes are read aloud. Sanborn, the reader this year, announced each vote, calling out, “senator, Collins,” or “governor, Pingree” as she went. The two counters, Sumner and Meyers, independently tallied the votes. Each time a candidate passed a multiple of five, they said “five” aloud in unison.
At one point, Sanborn encountered a ballot where the voter had marked Collins as their first choice, second choice and third choice, and had done the same for Jackson. Sumner reviewed the guidelines for processing such a ballot and determined it had to be counted as a blank.
As they reached the last ballot, Sanborn laughed.
“You’re going to love this, Ben. You’re a write-in,” Sanborn said.
(The vote would not count, as only votes for declared write-ins are valid.)
After all the ballots were counted, Sumner and Meyers compared their counts to verify that they matched. Then they moved on to counting the referendum votes in the same fashion.
Once those were tallied, cross checked and validated, the ballots were sealed in a lockbox with a tamper-proof lock.
Even with just 48 votes, the counting, sorting, certifying and securing of the ballots stretched to 10 p.m., concluding a 12-hour shift and another typical, if old-fashioned, election for the voters of Great Cranberry Island.

title: Two murders linked to serial killer, police say
text:
PITTSBURGH, Pa. (KDKA) - After nearly five decades, Pennsylvania State Police said they have identified the man responsible for the murders of two young women.
Investigators said DNA evidence has linked two cold cases in the Pittsburgh area.
Susan Rush, 21, disappeared in 1976 on her way to a Thanksgiving Eve dinner. She was later found dead in the trunk of her car.
Brenda Ritter, 18, disappeared in 1977 after leaving her boyfriend’s house. Her body was found on a hillside in South Strabane.
Police said both women had been sexually assaulted and strangled.
“The testing identified the same offender murdered both Susan Rush and Brenda Ritter. This testing confirmed there was a serial killer in Washington County during this time frame,” said Pennsylvania State Police Cpl. James Petrosky.
Investigators have now identified James Richard Clark Sr. as the killer.
Clark died of natural causes in 2023.
State police said Clark had never previously been a suspect in either case.

title: 'An insult to his culture': Italian chef reportedly fired after refusing to put pineapple on pizza
text:
'An insult to his culture': Italian chef reportedly fired after refusing to put pineapple on pizza
Friendships have ended over the age-old discussion: Does pineapple belong on pizza? And now, one Italian chef is alleging he lost his job for emphatically saying "no."
Related video above: New York may ban flour used in thousands of pizzerias and bagel shops
According to a complaint filed on Nov. 3 with Australia's Fair Work Commission, Italian Chef Davide Tamburella was allegedly fired from the La Costa restaurant in Queensland, Australia, on May 20, two weeks after being disciplined by his boss "to address performance concerns."
One of those concerns: refusing to put pineapple on pizza because it was "an insult to his culture."
Putting pineapple on pizza has become increasingly popular in recent years. In a 2017 poll published by pizza delivery app Slice, 46% of the 34,000 people polled said pineapple belongs on pizza — a narrow margin compared to other prompts in the poll, including Chicago-style vs. New York-style and whether anchovies are an acceptable topping.
Pineapple is fairly popular in Queensland, so much so that a large statue of the fruit recently reopened in Sunshine Plantation — a pineapple farm — after being abandoned in 2010. The "Big Pineapple" hosted more than a million visitors per year in the 1970s and '80s, making it Australia's No. 1 tourist attraction.
For Tamburella's boss, Elliot Ingram, the chef's refusal was particularly costly.
"We had a large function come in, and they were spending in excess of $15,000, and the guy paying for the whole thing says: 'Look, I need to get some ham and pineapple pizza,'" Ingram said.
Tamburella acknowledged that this was the third time he had refused this direction, instead requesting Ingram "check how important it is for Italians not to put pineapple on a pizza."
"Do I go and buy a ham and pineapple pizza? It's probably not my absolute favorite," Ingram said. "But I'm not going to turn my nose up at it, that's for sure. And, look, we have had ham and pineapple pizza on the kids' menu previously."
La Costa described itself as an elegant slice of Italy serving "classic Italian dishes." The restaurant closed in July after its lease expired, with Ingram attributing the closure to high operating costs.
According to The Guardian, Tamburella was more than three years into an 186 visa process — an employer-sponsored pathway to permanent residency. Ingram said he waited as long as he legally could to notify authorities that he was no longer hiring Tamburella in the hope that the Italian's visa application would be approved before the restaurateur was legally obliged to withdraw his sponsorship. It did not, meaning he would have to start the process again.
Tamburella is now employed at another Italian restaurant that does not feature pineapple anywhere on its menu.

title: As Americans get older, the need for ‘aging-ready’ homes grows
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ROANOKE, Va. (InvestigateTV) - America’s population is aging and a recent study found there may not be enough senior-friendly homes to meet demand. In 2019, one in six Americans were 65 or older and by 2060 it will be one in four.
A 2019 U.S. Census data analysis found that “the stock of aging-ready homes across the nation may be inadequate for the growing number of older households.”
The Census categorized “aging-ready homes” as dwellings with a bedroom and full bathroom on the first floor and a step-free entryway.
Experts say multi-generational housing is in demand, but inventory is low.
Heather Simon has spent the last 35 years helping thousands of families find homes as a mortgage lender.
She said she’s seen a lot of trends over the years.
However, in the last six to seven years, she’s seen a change in what her clients need in a home.
“Couples that have maybe lived in their house for 30-plus years, and their house no longer is conducive for them to be able to live in it, like multiple levels. It seems to be a problem,” Simon said.
She said many clients who are living in a home with 4,000 to 5,000 square feet of space find themselves needing one level, smaller homes with aging-in-place features, like a master suite on the first floor, wider hallways, fewer stairs and zero-step showers.
Inventory on those types of homes is low.
“Here in Virginia, there does seem to be a lack of one stories, one level, that would be the right size for a couple that’s downsizing,” she explains.
“But all over the country, we’re having problems with moving our parents into the right place that’s going to fit their health needs, their lifestyle,” Simon said.
Beth Powell agrees. She owns Home with Heart and helps clients downsize their homes. She said there’s inventory out there, but not that helps the aging population.
“Some folks will say, well, a patio home is the answer. A patio home is not the answer because, one, they’re not accessible. Two, they’re very expensive. And if somebody has lived in their home and they’ve paid their home off, why should they go into debt at the end of their life for an enormous amount of money?” Powell said.
Both agree experts need to help the aging population do a cost analysis of the pros and cons of their options: retrofitting an existing home, purchasing a new home, or building a home.
But that takes time and planning.
“If you have a couple that have lived in their house for 30, 40, 50 years and they’ve lived in this 5,000 square foot house and now they have to downsize to a 2,000 square foot house. That’s a huge transition. And it’s a very emotional transition and it is also something that takes months of planning,” Simon said.
Powell and Simon both agree finding that right place for loved ones starts with a conversation before a worst case scenario happens.
Experts say too often that worst-case scenario is after a fall or a crisis hits, and the homeowner is forced to make a choice, a choice they say that is both more expensive and more limited in options.
Both agree the best advice is to work with a team that can spend the time to find the right fit for everyone.
Until the inventory for this population increases, retrofitting an existing home to accommodate multiple generations will likely continue to be a growing trend.

title: UMaine asks faculty to retire to address budget shortfall
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This story appears as part of a collaboration to strengthen investigative journalism in Maine between the BDN and The Maine Monitor. Read more about the partnership.
The University of Maine asked 158 faculty members at its campus in Orono and regional campus in Machias this week if they would consider retiring voluntarily in a move to address a steep budget shortfall.
The university told eligible faculty Wednesday that they could receive a one-time payment equivalent to their base salary if they voluntarily retire by next September. Faculty members are eligible if they are at least 55 years old and have 10 years of full-time experience at the school. They have until Jan. 2 to decide whether they want to accept the offer.
Maine’s flagship public university is grappling with a $19 million shortfall projected for the 2028 budget year, which starts in July. University officials said in September that they would need to lay off faculty and staff to address the gap.
So far, officials have said that UMaine will shave $10 million from the university’s academic expenses, which make up about half of the entire budget. In October, officials then announced that UMaine could save an additional $6 million through potential cuts in other units on campus, such as the president’s cabinet, and through new sources of revenue.
The retirement incentive comes after unions and other groups gathered in late October to condemn the cuts and call for administrators to seek alternative measures to solve the budget gap rather than laying off faculty and staff.
At the gathering, union leaders and students also called for the state to increase its appropriation to the university. State Sen. Mike Tipping, D-Orono, who was recently reelected to his seat, also made an appearance and said that public higher education has been underfunded for decades.
University of Maine System spokesperson Samantha Warren said that the system, which oversees the state’s public universities, committed up to $6 million in one-time payout costs to schools, including the UMaine retirement incentive and a separate retirement incentive program that is underway at the University of Maine at Farmington.
Warren said that faculty union members at UMaine and its satellite campus had voted to move this incentive forward, and that officials at UMaine will work with units across the university to find other revenue streams and permanently reduce expenses. Federal labor laws limit the university from speaking further about the retirement initiative, Warren said.
The Maine Monitor was unable to reach two union representatives by press time Thursday.

title: Rockland man arrested following Damariscotta hit-and-run that seriously injured bicyclist
text:
Damariscotta, Maine (WMTW) - A Maine man faces multiple charges in connection with a hit-and-run crash in Damariscotta that left a bicyclist seriously injured.
John Barczak, 67, of Rockland, was arrested and charged with elevated aggravated assault, leaving the scene of an accident involving serious bodily injury and reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon.
The crash happened at about 5:25 a.m. Wednesday at the intersection of Biscay Road and Main Street.
Damariscotta Police Chief Erik Josephson said a 65-year-old woman who was riding a bicycle sustained serious injuries in the crash. The woman was transported by ambulance to Miles Memorial Hospital, but she was later transferred to Maine Medical Center in Portland due to the severity of her injuries.
Josephson said the vehicle involved in the crash had left the scene before first responders arrived.
After examining physical evidence, surveillance footage and vehicle-related information, Damariscotta Police Officer William Smith identified the suspect vehicle, a red Toyota Tacoma pickup truck, which was later found at a local business.
Josephson said that Smith identified Barczak as the driver of the truck through further investigation.
Barczak was interviewed as part of the investigation, and at about 4 p.m. Wednesday, he was taken into custody without incident and brought to the Two Bridges Regional Jail in Wiscasset.
Josephson said the investigation remains active and ongoing. The police chief also acknowledged the assistance the Damariscotta Police Department received from the Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office, Lincoln County District Attorney’s Office, Damariscotta Fire Department and Central Lincoln County Ambulance.

title: ‘An imminent expression of brotherhood’: An inside look at the Morehouse College Glee Club
text:
(Aging Untold) — For more than a century, the Morehouse College Glee Club has uplifted audiences.
They’ve performed at presidential inaugurations, Super Bowls and the Atlanta Olympics. But behind every performance is a deeper mission - their voices rise not just in song, but in leadership.
“At Morehouse College, Glee Club is an immediate expression of brotherhood, a united force of dedication and commitment, and an unselfish labor of love,” said Desmond Thompson, a proud member of the 38-member group.
The Glee Club performed at New Olivet Worship Center in Cordova by invitation from alumnus Pastor Kenneth Whalum Jr. Whalum says when he saw the Morehouse Glee Club perform in Memphis as a young boy, he knew he’d become a Morehouse man.
“There’s something about Black men singing in harmony. It strikes the ear,” Whalum said. “And the comportment of those men in the Glee club. They put in hours and hours and hours of work so that the harmony can be crystal clear and the message of the music can get across.”
That Morehouse message is one of service and leadership, producing men of distinction for nearly 158 years.
“Well, Morehouse traditionally makes men who have a sense of civic responsibility and believe that we are responsible for lifting the entire community,” Whalum explained.
Dr. David Morrow is the current director of the Morehouse Glee Club.
“For sure it is an arm of the college that shows the college off in such a way that we can use it for recruiting and advertising for the school,” he said.
But Morrow emphasizes it’s even more than that. “It’s more of a remembering that you are a part of a community, that you are more than just yourself. You are more than just a member of the Glee club. You are more than just the Blaze, and you are more than just a tie. You are family. You are part of something great.”

title: Houston mayor signs order to limit cooperation with ICE, says 'elections matter'

Houston mayor signs order to limit cooperation with ICE, says 'elections matter'
The mayor of Houston on Friday said the city would limit cooperation with federal immigration authorities, heralding “a new model” of immigration enforcement after Democrats won power in Texas for the first time in decades.
Mayor John Whitmire said the city would go after immigrants “that pose a danger, not those that are going about their family business, work and education.”

A traffic incident "will not even ... you write a citation or you warn them and they go about their way. No contact with (U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement) over nonviolent, non-jailable offenses. It reduces the fear and anxiety.”
Details of the change were to be spelled out in an executive order but the move by the nation’s fourth-largest city is one of the first steps to curb ICE’s powers since Tuesday’s election.
The Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in Houston has sparked protests after an ICE officer fatally shot a Mexican homebuilder this summer and another struck a man with a car.
A grand jury last week indicted ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Prosecutors say Morales intentionally rammed his car into Miguel Parra Hernandez, whose leg was broken. title: Teen accused of killing Maine paddleboarder to be tried as an adult
text:
A Frankfort teenager accused of killing a Maine woman will be tried as an adult.
Deven Young, 19, is charged with murder in the death of 48-year-old Sunshine Stewart. She was found dead in July 2025 near a campground in Union, where she had been paddleboarding. Young was 17 at the time of her death and was originally charged as a juvenile.
During court proceedings Friday, Young agreed to waive his right to a bind-over hearing, where a judge would have heard arguments about the prosecutors’ request to charge him as an adult. Because of scheduling conflicts, that bind-over hearing wasn’t expected to happen until early 2027.
He was taken to Knox County Jail, where he will remain in custody without bail, prosecutors said. Jail staff said Young will likely be transferred to Two Bridges Regional Jail in Wiscasset.
District Court Judge Eric Walker ordered that Young’s case may proceed to adult court, which carries harsher punishment for murder convictions. Walker previously found that Young is competent to stand trial and said Friday that Young is able to make his own decisions, including the decision to be tried as an adult.
Following Friday’s order, Young remained in the courtroom for a second hearing in adult court, during which he agreed to reconvene for a status conference in January.
His case will be presented to a grand jury for potential indictment, said Superior Court Justice Sean Ociepka.
Young’s attorney, Jeremy Pratt, declined to comment about the hearings.
Public records from the Waldo County Sheriff’s Office, unrelated to the murder charge, show that Young had a history of violent behavior and was working with a caseworker. They also showed he had spent three years waiting for behavioral health services from the state.

title: Unannounced armed troops have no place in Portland
text:
William Middleton, a retired librarian, is a resident of Great Diamond Island.
When I arrived at the Casco Bay Lines Ferry terminal on Oct. 27, there were seven uniformed personnel — black shirts, black bulletproof vests, khaki trousers — in the building. They were wearing sidearms, and their vests were marked with “Maine Civil Support.”
I’d never heard of Maine Civil Support. From the way they were dressed, I thought they might be ICE agents. They weren’t.
Maine Civil Support is a unit of the Maine National Guard, specifically the 11th Civil Support Team based in Waterville.
Maine Civil Support works with local, state and federal first responders during natural and man-made disasters. They’re the good guys. The ferry building, a strategic transportation hub vulnerable to both weather and mischief, is exactly the kind of place Maine Civil Support should know well.
The seven troops, however, weren’t exploring the terminal or talking to staff. They were just standing there, as if their simple presence — the presence of armed, uniformed personnel —somehow provided safety.
It didn’t. The presence of armed, uniformed personnel made people feel less safe.
A car alarm provides an analogy. When we’re walking in town, or worse, when we’re asleep, and we hear a car alarm, we don’t think: Oh good, an attempt to steal a car has been stopped; I live in a safe place. Rather we think: I live in a place where auto theft is so common that the prudent car owner purchases an alarm. That is: I live in an unsafe place.
The purpose of a car alarm is safety, but hearing it doesn’t make us feel safe.
The purpose of Maine Civil Support is also safety, but similarly, seeing it doesn’t make us feel safe.
The first job of any government — federal, state, municipal — is to ensure the safety of the people. It’s hard. It’s hard because people don’t just want to be safe, they want to feel safe. Safety is both perceived and real, and the two don’t always align. In fact, some of the things that make us safe — a car alarm, Maine Civil Support — make us feel unsafe.
Nevertheless, government has to address both the perception and the reality.
To keep us safe, the government has been granted a monopoly on violence. In constitutional democracies such as ours, that monopoly is granted by the consent of the governed. By us.
In the hour that I watched Maine Civil Support, they didn’t do anything. They just stood there. Their uniforms, their bulletproof vests, their sidearms, were doing all the work. The work that gear was doing was reminding everyone in the building that the state has a monopoly on violence.
When citizens grant their government a monopoly on violence, they do so with solemnity. It is the single most serious thing a citizen does. So when the government flaunts that monopoly, treats it lightly, as a performance, a flex, citizens can doubt the wisdom of their grant.
Maine Civil Support didn’t need any of their kit. They could have done everything they did unarmed, in civilian clothes. The quality of their training would not have been diminished.
More importantly, had they worn civilian clothes, the perception of safety by the citizens of Portland would not have been lost.
If Maine Civil Support ever has to be deployed for a real event requiring their full battle rattle, the unit should include a public communications element — signage, leaflets, a spokesperson —explaining to civilians who they are and what they’re doing. Not as a courtesy, but as an acknowledgement of the solemnity of that grant from the citizens they serve.
In this instance, Maine Civil Support wasn’t protecting citizens from a real threat. In this instance, in our difficult present moment, Maine Civil Support weren’t stopping the terror; they were the terror.
I refuse to normalize the presence of armed soldiers in my town.

title: These mall walkers are bringing a ’90s vibe back in Oregon
text:
PORTLAND, Ore. (Aging Untold) — In the 1980s and 1990s, the mall was a place to gather beyond shopping, and one Oregon woman is bringing vibes from that era back to the Lloyd Center mall in Oregon.
Krista Catwood started the Food Court 5000 walking group. Participants wearing spandex, windbreakers, sneakers and scrunchies gather every Sunday morning for three and a half miles of power walking.
“We’ve become sort of B-celebrities of the mall,” Catwood said. “I think most people that come here kind of know who we are.”
How the group started
Catwood started the group while searching for a fun way to move. She knew it had to be silly, social and shared with others.
“I knew when I had this idea that it was a good one,” Catwood said. “I had no idea how many people would be interested.”
Members describe what keeps them coming back
The idea drew people in, and the energy, kindness and inclusion keep bringing them back.
“I’m having the time of my life, and I’ll be 81 in two months,” Leslie Kelinson, one of the walkers, said. “I get so much from those two hours, you have no idea.”
She said the meetups are “fun” and “healthy” and “inspiring.”

title: Production of Tesla’s Cybertruck will wind down. Here’s why
text:
(AP) - Production of Tesla’s Cybertruck, a stainless-steel electric vehicle with a polarizing allure for potential buyers, will wind down next year.
In a post on social media, CEO Elon Musk said, “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”
The Texas facility is the only location where the Cybertruck is produced.
Teslas, and the Cybertruck in particular because of its unorthodox profile, became a political touchstone as Musk allied himself with President Donald Trump and some right-leaning causes amid a widening political divide in the U.S. and Europe.
European sales of Tesla vehicles tumbled 49% in the first two months of 2025 even as overall sales of EVs grew. Musk’s endorsement of Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany party in national elections drew broad condemnation.
The vehicle was also plagued by quality-control issues, with a handful of recalls within months of its debut.
Despite enormous anticipation, the Cybertruck never caught on with most buyers, and sales declined almost from the moment it hit the market.
While Tesla does not break out sales of its vehicles by model, Kelley Blue Book estimated that Cybertruck sales declined 48% from 2024 to 2025. From January through September of this year, sales were down 28%, according to Kelley Blue Book.

title: 🧀 HAPPY NATIONAL NACHO DAY, MAINE! Food Network Says These Are the Best Nachos in the State!

Food Network Names These the Best Nachos in Maine
It's National Nacho Day, which gives us the perfect excuse to celebrate one of America's favorite appetizers. And if you're looking for some nacho inspiration here in Maine, Food Network has a pretty delicious recommendation!
Food Network is a popular American cable channel that focuses on food, cooking, and lifestyle programming. Launched in 1993, it has become a leading destination for food enthusiasts.
Food television has become a massive part of pop culture, with shows covering everything from cooking competitions and restaurant adventures to food-and-travel destinations and reality TV. Shows like Chopped, Beat Bobby Flay, Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives, and Man v. Food have become iconic over the years, propelling everyday dishes and local restaurants into must-try destinations.
So when Food Network named Luchador Tacos' nachos the best in Maine, it makes you more than eager to give them a try, especially on National Nacho Day!
Chef-owner Katherine Mitchell, a Mexican American who grew up in East Los Angeles, started Luchador in 2017 as a tiny roadside food stand in South Paris. She was looking for the LA-style tacos she grew up with and couldn't find them in Maine, so she decided to make them herself. That little trailer eventually grew into full-fledged restaurants around the 207.

Luchador has grown to four locations across Maine:

Auburn — 945 Center St.
Old Orchard Beach — 1 E. Grand Ave.
The menu is tight, focused, and delicious: tacos, burritos, quesadillas, bowls, fries, nachos, and more, all built around grilled steak, chicken, and pork, along with homemade red and green salsas. There are vegan and gluten-free options, too.
But the nachos are the real star of the show here. Loaded with crispy tortilla chips, black beans, melted cheese, roasted poblano-corn crema, your choice of asada, birria, pastor, or calabacitas, plus cilantro, onions, and guacamole, with salsa on the side.
The poblano-corn crema is what really sets them apart and makes folks like Food Network stand up and take notice! It's creamy, smoky, and a little sweet, which is a nice switch-up from the usual sour cream and cheese routine.
These are hearty, loaded-up taco-shop nachos, exactly the kind of dish that feels worthy of a Food Network shoutout. And what better day to give them a try than National Nacho Day?

title: School janitor accused of trading vapes for nude photos from girls
text:
KINGMAN, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — A school janitor in northwestern Arizona is accused of giving vape pens and alcohol to girls in exchange for naked photos of them.
The Mohave County Sheriff’s Office said Thursday that Pierce Anthony Eller, 41, is facing more than a dozen charges.
Investigators said Eller works as a janitor at a Kingman-area school through a private contractor, and the vape-for-explicit-photos trades started in February with an underage family friend.
The sheriff’s office said there have been 10 trades between Eller and the victim.
Detectives said the victim then told her friends about the deal, and the friends reached out to Eller on social media.
The sheriff’s office said Eller gave three additional girls, ages 14 to 16, vapes and alcohol in exchange for nude photos of them.
Deputies said Eller admitted to the allegations Wednesday and that they found more evidence on his phone.
He was arrested and booked into jail on 10 counts of sexual exploitation of a minor, four counts of luring a minor and four counts of commercial exploitation of a minor.
While processing digital evidence, investigators said they found that the photos were being shared with a teacher, identified as 57-year-old Ronald Wayne Bowman. Bowman taught for the Kingman Unified School District for 24 years, officials said.
Bowman was detained and allegedly admitted to being involved. He was arrested and faces nine charges of sexual exploitation of a minor.
Deputies said none of the victims were students at the school where Eller worked.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER:Weekend Rain Still Expected, But Will Northern Maine See Much Drought Relief?
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Friday. We’ve made it to the end of another work week, and after enjoying several days of above average temperatures, some changes are on the way heading into the upcoming weekend. Temperatures are expected to fall back closer to average overnight tonight, with much cooler readings expected Saturday and Sunday. We’ve also been keeping a close eye on an approaching area of low pressure expected to bring rainfall to the region this weekend. While I still expect periods of rain across Aroostook County, the latest forecast guidance has shifted the greatest rainfall totals further south and east. Unfortunately, this could mean less drought relief for northern Maine than we were originally hoping for.
Temperatures will continue to cool off overnight tonight as colder air begins working its way into the region. Most locations across Aroostook County should have no problem falling back into the lower to mid 30s by tomorrow morning, with some of our northern and western towns potentially falling closer to the freezing mark. Caribou and Presque Isle are both expected to see temperatures around 36 degrees, while Houlton looks to fall to around 37 degrees. Cloudy skies are expected to remain in place overnight, with some rain showers possible, especially across central and southern portions of the region. I also wouldn’t rule out seeing a few snowflakes mixing in with the rain across northern locations as temperatures continue to cool off.
The upcoming weekend is looking considerably cooler than the weather we’ve enjoyed over the past several days. Saturday is expected to feature mostly cloudy skies, with temperatures struggling to climb out of the lower to mid 40s across much of Aroostook County. While rain remains in the forecast, I think there’s a decent chance that portions of northern and western Aroostook County end up seeing less precipitation than originally anticipated. The best opportunity for steadier rainfall Saturday looks to be across central and southern portions of the region, with a few periods of rain or snow also possible further north. Sunday looks to feature more of the same, with plenty of cloud coverage and additional opportunities for rainfall. Temperatures aren’t expected to warm up much either, with highs generally remaining in the lower to mid 40s. As colder air continues working its way into the region, some snow could mix in with the rain across northern and western locations, although I don’t expect much in the way of snow accumulation. A few lingering showers will also be possible Monday before we begin seeing some improvements in the forecast.
The latest rainfall potential map from the Weather Prediction Center does a nice job illustrating the changes we’ve been seeing in the forecast over the past 24 hours. You’ll notice that the greatest rainfall totals are now expected to remain further south and east, with northern and western portions of Aroostook County seeing considerably less precipitation. This is a fairly significant shift from what we were looking at earlier this week. While I don’t expect northern Maine to completely miss out on rainfall this weekend, I think the chances of receiving substantial rainfall have decreased considerably. The exact track of this developing low pressure system will ultimately determine where the heaviest rain falls, but forecast models have become more consistent in favoring a track that keeps the greatest rainfall totals south and east of Aroostook County.
We have managed to pick up some much needed rainfall across the region over the past week. Fort Kent leads the way among the locations shown on our rainfall report graphic, having picked up 1.19 inches of rain. Caribou has received 0.93 inches, with Allagash and Saint Agatha both reporting 0.92 inches. Presque Isle has also managed to pick up 0.78 inches of rainfall.
These are certainly welcome numbers considering just how dry things have been across northern Maine over the past several months. Unfortunately, the rainfall we’ve received so far isn’t going to be enough to make up for the substantial precipitation deficit we’ve accumulated.
The latest update to the U.S. Drought Monitor really illustrates just how serious our drought situation has become across Aroostook County. Last week’s update showed roughly 85 percent of the county experiencing severe drought conditions, with the remaining 15 percent in moderate drought.
Unfortunately, things have taken another turn for the worse with this week’s update. Extreme drought conditions have now expanded into portions of northern and western Aroostook County, covering just over 19 percent of the county. Severe drought conditions are still being experienced across another 80 percent, leaving less than one percent of Aroostook County in the moderate drought category.
It’s important to point out that the latest Drought Monitor update doesn’t necessarily reflect all of the rainfall we’ve received over the past several days. However, I think it does a good job illustrating just how much catching up we still have to do before we can begin talking about any substantial improvement to our drought conditions. While the rainfall we’ve received this week is a step in the right direction, we’re going to need additional periods of widespread, soaking rainfall to make a meaningful dent in our precipitation deficit.
Looking ahead to the start of the new work week, temperatures are expected to remain much closer to average for this time of year. Monday’s highs should generally reach the lower to mid 40s across northern Aroostook County, with some upper 40 degree readings possible further south. Caribou is expected to reach around 43 degrees, while Presque Isle looks to top out near 46 degrees and Houlton around 48 degrees.
I wouldn’t rule out a few lingering showers Monday, especially during the morning hours, before we begin seeing some improvement in the forecast. Temperatures through the middle of next week look to remain fairly seasonable, with highs generally staying in the 40s.
For more details on the changes to our weekend rainfall forecast, along with what we can expect heading into the new work week, make sure to check out my First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great weekend!

title: Every deer camp has a story about the buck that got away. This was ours.
text:
This story was originally published in November 2025.
It was a cold and crisp November morning, late in the firearms season, when I mounted my stand. The ladder steps were frosted over and the metal slick as I ascended the fifteen feet to my perch. A hard frost had come in overnight, and as I looked up through the tree canopy, the stars were afire against the black backdrop of sky.
The wind was nonexistent and the woods around me eerily quiet, dawn still a half hour away. It was a perfect morning for deer hunting — and not just any deer, but the buck I’d been after for several seasons.
I had logged countless hours scouting the ridge he called home, and the pile of dead trail camera batteries proved just how uncanny he was at slipping past me every step of the way. This year, however, I finally caught him on camera. He was everything I had hoped for and more. My anticipation climbed as the sun twinkled over the ridge and I prepared to start a rattling sequence.
I heard him coming from 200 yards away, snapping branches and breaking through icy puddles below my spot on the hill. My heart was pumping hard — it felt as though it was lodged in my throat. The big buck stepped over the edge of a drop-off, just 75 yards in front of me, into a thick concentration of bramble and deadfall.
All I could see was his head, neck and a short section of his back. I eased my rifle up and put the crosshairs on the neck and waited. He appeared to be looking for the young bucks he heard fighting. Not seeing them, he hung up and wouldn’t come any closer.
It was decision time — risk the heavy cover fouling the shot or hope for another opportunity.
Would I ever get another chance? Would I ever see him in daylight again? A million thoughts raced through my mind in the blink of an eye.
I fired — and missed. The buck turned slowly and made his way back down the ridge before I could cycle the bolt for a follow-up.
Two days later, my hunting partner Harley was feeling under the weather and stayed in camp. His stand was roughly 600 yards north of mine. I hunted my stand until around 10, then got down and still hunted around the bottom of the ridge and back up to Harley’s stand, planning to spend the afternoon there.
I pulled the trail camera card on my way through, figuring I’d check it back at camp that evening. Sure enough, that buck walked right by Harley’s stand at 10 a.m. — striking a pose for the camera. To this day, I’m convinced he was taunting us.
This was the day that buck earned the nickname “Sneaky Pete”.
Over the next two seasons, I kept adjusting my setup, trying to zero in on the best possible ambush spot. No matter what I did, Sneaky Pete was always one step ahead. I’d hear him slip past me before first light one day, then move to the opposite side of the trail the next — only for him to switch sides again that evening.
That buck found a way every day to thread the needle between multiple stands and blinds — both mine and Harley’s. We could hear him, but he was like a ghost.
We told the story of Sneaky Pete at every deer camp at Tucker Ridge, and I challenged my clients to match wits with him. Many hunters tried, but all failed.
Sneaky Pete would skirt past, grunt at a hunter and be gone like the wind. One client, after not seeing a buck for three days, decided to bring his shotgun that morning and take advantage of the abundance of partridge in the area. It was a huge mistake. When he reached the overgrown apple orchard he had been flushing grouse from every morning on his way to the deer stand, who do you think was standing there 50 yards away? Sneaky Pete — high, wide and handsome, and hanging out with a few does.
After three seasons, the legend of Sneaky Pete was firmly cemented in deer hunting lore at Tucker Ridge. Even though I haven’t seen him on camera the past two years, we still talk about him to this day.
Based on his size and age, I am sure he is gone now, and that saddens me. Not because I didn’t capitalize on the one and only opportunity any hunter ever had at taking him, but because I know I’ll never have the chance to dance with him again.

title: Rockland man arrested following Damariscotta hit-and-run that seriously injured bicyclist
text:
Damariscotta, Maine (WMTW) - A Maine man faces multiple charges in connection with a hit-and-run crash in Damariscotta that left a bicyclist seriously injured.
John Barczak, 67, of Rockland, was arrested and charged with elevated aggravated assault, leaving the scene of an accident involving serious bodily injury and reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon.
The crash happened at about 5:25 a.m. Wednesday at the intersection of Biscay Road and Main Street.
Damariscotta Police Chief Erik Josephson said a 65-year-old woman who was riding a bicycle sustained serious injuries in the crash. The woman was transported by ambulance to Miles Memorial Hospital, but she was later transferred to Maine Medical Center in Portland due to the severity of her injuries.
Josephson said the vehicle involved in the crash had left the scene before first responders arrived.
After examining physical evidence, surveillance footage and vehicle-related information, Damariscotta Police Officer William Smith identified the suspect vehicle, a red Toyota Tacoma pickup truck, which was later found at a local business.
Josephson said that Smith identified Barczak as the driver of the truck through further investigation.
Barczak was interviewed as part of the investigation, and at about 4 p.m. Wednesday, he was taken into custody without incident and brought to the Two Bridges Regional Jail in Wiscasset.
Josephson said the investigation remains active and ongoing. The police chief also acknowledged the assistance the Damariscotta Police Department received from the Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office, Lincoln County District Attorney’s Office, Damariscotta Fire Department and Central Lincoln County Ambulance.

title: Dad of 20-year-old co-pilot in Florida Learjet crash says her final radio calls showed 'she's tough'
text:
The father of the 20-year-old co-pilot who died along with eight others when their Learjet crashed in Florida said Friday he has listened to his daughter’s heartbreaking final radio transmissions “many times” since the crash.
Allan Filgueiras, himself a pilot, was searching for answers as to why the plane plunged from the sky on Sunday — but what he found was immense pride in how his daughter, Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, handled the crisis.
“I did listen to that many times trying to find a clue. In my head. How’d that happen? And wow, she’s tough,” Allan Filgueiras said at a news conference Friday, frequently holding back tears.
In her final conversation with air traffic control, she can be heard calmly reporting ice buildup on the plane as the Learjet flew into a thunderstorm and turbulence tossed it up and down by 700 feet (200 meters). The situation quickly escalated as the aircraft fell at breathtaking speed. “Declare an emergency 722-Bravo-Delta. We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute!” she said.
Her father and aviation safety experts have been impressed that Filgueiras continued to call out updates on what was happening even as she realized the plane’s fate was sealed.
“For the family — it’s like having the heart torn from my chest,” her father said in Spanish. “I have to find a way to go on living.”
The family wants to push back against online criticism over whether she had enough experience to be in the cockpit of a Learjet. She had more than 1,300 hours of experience and completed extensive training to earn her commercial pilot’s license.
So her father held Friday’s news conference, which his lawyer said was designed to “preserve not just her memory, but her reputation.”
“She was at the top of her class in everything that she did, and she was perfectly qualified to be the co-pilot on this flight, despite her tender years,” attorney Stuart Grossman said, noting there were no immediate plans to file a lawsuit over the crash.
It’s far too early in the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigation to know what caused the crash. As it fell, the Learjet accelerated beyond its design limits and pieces of the plane’s tail were found miles away from the crash site.
Retired airline pilot John Cox, who is now the CEO of Safety Operating Systems, said he started out flying professionally at age 19, meaning he was in the same situation as Filgueiras when he started his career. He said she was doing quite well to earn the co-pilot’s seat she had.
“To be in the right seat of a Lear 60, she had to impress somebody, because that’s a good ride. I mean, that’s great. I know she loved it,” Cox said.
Her father believes she held up in the midst of a crisis better than most.
“She showed me what it is to be a hero because once you see that coming, a lot of the big boys — military or whatever — they can’t handle. And she was the one over there to the last minute fighting,” Allan Filgueiras said.
The victims included technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson; his wife, Helen Sharp; and their two young children, relatives said. The family’s nanny, Ana María Ramírez Cetina, was also killed. The plane’s captain, who was at the controls as the plane fell, was 55-year-old Jeff Gregory.

title: Help Feed Our Neighbors During the 10th Annual High Five Turkey Drive
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
10 Years of Giving: High Five Turkey Drive Returns to Aroostook County November 12 and 13
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine — For the past decade, Aroostook County residents have shown what can happen when a community comes together to help its neighbors. This November, that tradition continues as the 10th Annual High Five Turkey Drive returns for two days of giving ahead of Thanksgiving.
Townsquare Media, alongside the Aroostook County Action Program (ACAP) and United Way of Aroostook, is inviting residents and local businesses to help make the holiday season a little brighter for families throughout the County.
The mission is simple: collect donations that help local food pantries provide Thanksgiving meals to families who need a little extra support.
Two Days, Two Locations, One Great Cause
This year's High Five Turkey Drive will make stops in Presque Isle and Houlton, giving communities two opportunities to take part.
Thursday, November 12
- Star City IGA, Presque Isle
- 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Friday, November 13
- County Tractor, 708 North Street, Houlton
- 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Whether you're stopping by on your lunch break, heading out to do some shopping, or making a special trip to donate, every contribution helps support the effort.
A Little Help Can Make a Big Difference
Thanksgiving is a time for family, friends, and gathering around the table. But for some households, putting together a holiday meal can be difficult, especially with the everyday expenses that families already face.
That's where the High Five Turkey Drive comes in.
Community members are encouraged to contribute cash donations, grocery store gift cards, turkeys, or other food donations to support local families through area food pantries.
One of the most important parts of this annual tradition is its local impact. Contributions help support the communities right here in Aroostook County, allowing local organizations to assist families during the Thanksgiving season.
You don't need to make a large donation to make a difference. When individuals, families, and businesses all pitch in, those contributions add up.
Ten Years of Neighbors Helping Neighbors
Reaching a 10-year milestone is something worth celebrating, but the real success of the High Five Turkey Drive has always been the people behind it.
From the local businesses that open their doors to the volunteers who lend a hand, and the countless residents who make donations year after year, this event is a reminder of the generosity found throughout Aroostook County.
For ten years, that generosity has helped make Thanksgiving a little easier for families across the region.
And with another holiday season approaching, there's an opportunity to keep that tradition going.
Join Us November 12 and 13
Mark your calendars, spread the word, and consider making a donation during this year's High Five Turkey Drive.
Stop by Star City IGA in Presque Isle on Thursday, November 12, or County Tractor in Houlton on Friday, November 13.
Follow along with 101.9 The Rock, Q96.1, and Big Country 96.9 for coverage of this year's effort.
After ten years, the message remains the same: when Aroostook County comes together, we can make a meaningful difference for our neighbors.
The 10th Annual High Five Turkey Drive is proudly supported by Aroostook County Action Program (ACAP) and United Way of Aroostook, working alongside Townsquare Media to support local food pantries and families this Thanksgiving.

title: Man gets stolen car back, then faces $2,398 fine and other expenses
text:
BALTIMORE, Md. (WJZ) — A Mount Vernon man says his car was stolen in October and returned with damage. He also says he is dealing with fines and tickets that came in while the car was missing. Trace Thompson wants police to do more to track down stolen vehicles.
Car reported missing Oct. 17
Thompson said he was trying to go to work around 6 a.m. on Oct. 17 when he realized his car had been stolen from his Mount Vernon neighborhood.
“I was in a bit of panic. I was trying to get to work at the time. It was about 6 in the morning,” Thompson said.
He called 311 for help. Thompson said the operator told him his car may have been moved for the marathon. He then asked for police to come out. When officers arrived two days later, they determined the car was stolen.
Car found at Wawa in Lansdowne
Baltimore police said the car was tracked on license plate reader cameras in the city. Thompson said he worked with the car manufacturer to track the location to a motel.
Baltimore County police found the car in the middle of the night last Friday at a Wawa in Lansdowne.
“I was actually able to pass my location information to the police department, and two days later, at three o’clock in the morning, I received a call that my car had been found next to a Wawa,” Thompson said.
Police arrested the driver, identified as Bobby Hamlett. He is charged with unlawful taking of a vehicle. Charging documents say Hamlett claimed he knew Thompson and was borrowing the car.
“I don’t think I would ever let somebody borrow my car and take it to a highway motel,” Thompson said.
Damage, tolls and insurance fine
Thompson said he is now dealing with the damage left behind. He described how the car was entered.
“The individual actually, through the left side port window, was able to pop the rubber out and then pried out the window from there,” Thompson said.
Thompson said he received tickets in the mail for unpaid tolls incurred while the car was stolen. He also received a fine from the MVA for lapsed insurance.
“So I got two within an hour of each other between Baltimore Tunnel South and Fort McHenry. I received a fine for $2,398 in the mail for insurance,” Thompson said.
The MVA said the vehicle being reported as stolen triggered the fine notice to be mailed. The agency said it is reaching out to Thompson, who said he had insurance the entire time. Thompson said he is not sure if more tickets are coming.
Thompson said the inside of the car was also damaged.
“In the back there were trash bags full of stuff,” Thompson said.
He said the bags contained trash, drugs and bodily fluids.
“I think the car was more of a crime scene than a vehicle recovery,” Thompson said.
Thompson asks city for action
Thompson is asking the city to do more to protect neighbors from crimes like this.
“If stuff like this keeps happening to your young professionals, we’re going to leave,” Thompson said.
Thompson said he now parks his car in a garage nearly a mile away.
Hamlett is due back in court in December.
