title: ALS is on the rise, tracking cases could tell us why
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, has no cure, and the number of cases is projected to rise. The number of people in the U.S. with the disease is not known because doctors are not required to report cases to their health departments. A growing number of states are making reporting mandatory.
ALS is also known as Lou Gehrig’s disease. It affects the nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord. It is considered a rare disease, and experts say there is no explanation for why the numbers are rising.
Living with ALS
In two years, ALS has taken Jennifer Robb’s ability to walk and to eat most solid food. It is now taking her ability to talk.
Using the text-to-speech tool, Jennifer told us it’s a “constant challenge” where “every day gets harder with loss of function.”
Her hands are her main source of communication, but Jennifer admitted they are getting weaker.
ALS destroys the nerve cells that control voluntary muscle movement. As motor neuron cells die, people lose the ability to walk, talk, swallow and breathe. There is no cure, and the disease is fatal.
Jennifer’s husband, Eric Robb, quit his job as a teacher to become her full-time caregiver. He said the disease is progressing quickly.
“Every month it seems like we have to change up our routine, we have to do things differently,” Eric said. Bedtime for the couple took about 30 minutes when Jennifer was first diagnosed. It now takes two hours to get her to bed and two hours to get her up.
“The disease doesn’t get better. It only gets worse, and that’s what’s tough about it. It’s painful to see somebody go through that because you know that she’s never going to get any of that back,” Eric said.
Research and treatment
Researchers across the country are working to change the course of the disease.
“We hope to put ourselves out of business. We don’t want to be doing this,” said Dr. Stephen Goutman, associate professor of neurology at the University of Michigan and director of its ALS clinic.
Goutman said he has seen people living with ALS for 14 years and has cared for more than a thousand people with the disease. He said the clinic follows close to 300 people at any given time.
Goutman and Ben Murdock, an associate professor of neurology, of the University of Michigan Medical School have spent more than a decade researching the disease. Their work includes constant tests of patients’ blood. The average life expectancy after diagnosis is three years.
“These people are really scared, they’re really terrified by what’s going to happen to them, and it’s really heartbreaking, and so it’s incredibly important to, you know, give people hope or some options,” Murdock said.
Murdock said only a handful of treatments exist for ALS. He said there hasn’t been much meaningful discovery in treatment since the drug Riluzole came on the market more than 30 years ago.
“That’s still the gold standard. It provides an extra, I want to say, two or three months of life,” Murdock said.
Murdock said he would like to see a treatment that provides at least six months to a year, but ultimately the end goal is a cure.
But a cure is much more complicated to find than a treatment, in part because no one knows why people get ALS, how to stop it or what causes it. Among experts, there are suspicions that pollutants in the environment play a role.
“Individuals exposed to metals seem to have this higher risk of ALS, and we don’t entirely know why that is, but it’s giving us something to dig into,” Goutman said.
Researchers said they could better study that if they knew where ALS patients were located.
State reporting requirements
ALS is not a mandated reportable disease. Most illnesses that must be reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention are contagious. Only a few non-communicable diseases, such as cancer, are on the list.
A growing number of states have chosen to require reporting themselves. According to the ALS Association, they are Massachusetts, Vermont, Maine, California, Louisiana, New York, New Jersey and, as of 2025, Michigan.
More than a year after Michigan implemented its rule, the state had not collected a single case.
“We’re waiting on guidance from the health department,” Goutman said.
The Michigan health department declined interview requests. It said that once a pilot collection system is tested at the University of Michigan and is working properly, it will start collecting data statewide.
Goutman and Murdock advocated for the tracking. Murdock said the information will be helpful for studies of environmental exposure.
“Now we can kind of figure out where people have been living, where they come from, and hopefully we can start putting some of those puzzle pieces together,” Murdock said.
Cases are expected to rise nationwide. The projected number of cases in 2022 was nearly 33,000. The projected number for 2026 is 35,000.
Murdock said ALS is the most common rare disease. When asked if it is becoming more common, he said, “Yes, the rates have been going up.”
“The number of people that I care for in the 14 years that I’ve been here has almost doubled, and so there has to be a reason why,” Goutman said.
The rate of ALS is about 1 in every 100,000 people. Jennifer is the third person from her home county in Missouri to get ALS. The county has fewer than 40,000 people.
Missouri health leaders would not know that because it is not among the states tracking the disease.
“I think it needs to be mandated,” Eric Robb said. “People need to be aware of it. And the more they’re aware of it, the more funding there will be, the more help there will be for people with ALS.”
Jennifer told us she thinks the disease is being ignored. When asked if more people with ALS would be seen and the disease would be harder to ignore if reporting were mandated, she said yes.
She advocates for mandated reporting with ALS groups. She said she does not know how much time she has left.
“You have to have hope,” Jennifer said.
National registry and funding
A national ALS registry exists with the CDC. It relies on people self-reporting their disease. The CDC acknowledges it is missing cases because reporting is not mandatory. The CDC also says that even if reporting is mandated, it will rarely capture 100% of cases.
Advocates say more funding could help bring an end to ALS. In early 2026, Congress approved the highest level of funding ever for ALS, $315 million.
Funding for other diseases is in the billions: $8.1 billion for cancer, $3.9 billion for Alzheimer’s disease and $3.3 billion for HIV/AIDS.
The ALS Association says more funding will lead to more answers about ALS and hopefully lead to a cure.

title: Bonny Eagle football heads to A South final with win over Massabesic
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
STANDISH — Standing on the muddy sideline while the night’s steady rain continued to fall, Bonny Eagle football coach Kevin Cooper figured it was time for some high praise.
“We have a lot of good players in Maine,” he said. “I find it hard to believe anyone’s playing better than Lucas Klehn.”
It’s hard to doubt that assertion after Friday night. Klehn ran for 230 yards, threw a touchdown pass and sealed the game with an interception as second-seeded Bonny Eagle took down third-seeded Massabesic, 35-20, in a wet Class A South semifinal.
“If anybody watched this game tonight, they saw what kind of player he is on both sides of the ball,” Cooper said. “He’s a fantastic player. He’s really doing it all for us.”
Klehn wasn’t the only Bonny Eagle player to step up, as a defense that had trouble containing Massabesic’s rushing attack in the first half stood firm in the second. But the senior quarterback took over the game, showing the speed to run around defenders as well as the strength to run through them.
“It feels great. I really needed it, honestly,” said Klehn, who also was 5 of 7 passing for 92 yards. “The last two games, I feel like I haven’t played my best. I really needed to get back on track, and I think I did that today.”
Bonny Eagle (9-1) will play top-ranked Thornton Academy in the regional final. Massabesic, playing its first Class A playoff game since 2009, finishes 6-4.
“Taking the job over last March, I knew it was going to be quite a rebuild. We’ve bridged the gap in a lot of ways,” said first-year Massabesic coach Cory Woodsome. “It’s a true testament to these kids, and their willingness to buy in to the expectations and standards we put forth to them.”
SECOND-HALF SURGE
After ending the first half with a 14-13 lead, the Scots (9-1) picked up steam in the second half. Klehn had runs of 15, 19 and 20 yards — slipping two tackles on the latter run — before barging in from a yard out to make it 22-13 with 4:15 left in the third.
After Massabesic answered with a touchdown on a 1-yard run by Alex Harriman (32 carries, 114 yards), Klehn struck again, faking the handoff to Ben Noe before keeping it himself and racing 54 yards for a touchdown that made it 29-20.
“Every time I get the ball, I (think), ‘Don’t go down on first contact.’ That’s my main goal,” said Klehn, who ran for 143 yards after halftime. “Make somebody miss, because my guys are blocking their heart out for me. I can’t just get tackled by one guy.”
A 4-yard run by Ben Noe (seven carries, 41 yards) made it 35-20 with 6:17 left, and Klehn had an interception on Massabesic’s next drive to seal it.
MAKING ADJUSTMENTS
Bonny Eagle’s offense had success early. On the second drive of the game, Klehn faked the handoff to Noe and hit a wide-open Wes Pinkham, who turned in the slippery conditions and ran 59 yards for a 6-0 lead with 3:47 left in the first quarter.
“First thing I’m thinking is, ‘Don’t slip,'” said Pinkham, who had three catches for 78 yards. “I saw some blocks in front of me and open space. I was just praying no one could catch me.”
The Scots’ defense scuffled early, as Massabesic’s double-wing offense churned up yardage. With 2:10 left in the second quarter, Harriman scored on a 2-yard run to put the Mustangs up 7-6.
A 1-yard touchdown by Klehn, set up by his 61-yard run, put Bonny Eagle back up 14-7 with 45 seconds left in the half, but Massabesic cashed in on a trick play when halfback Dustin Maley took a toss and then hit a wide-open Nate Gray for a 63-yard touchdown with 29 seconds left.
After a halftime film review, however, the Scots stiffened with stops on three of the next four Mustangs drives, including a turnover on downs when Noe, Drew Gervais and Ben Havu teamed to stop Harriman on fourth-and-2 with 11:06 left.
“We completely locked in in the second half. We were able to stop what was killing us,” Pinkham said. “(We started) just playing our gaps, adjusting to their fronts and some of their unbalanced sets.”

title: Trump makes the Oval Office a national monument
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Thursday signed a proclamation that he says will preserve the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as a national monument, his first official action after his party was swept aside in midterm elections on Tuesday.
But the action does not prevent future presidents from restyling the iconic office that Trump has filled to the brim with gold flourishes, nor does it prevent a successor from rolling back the proclamation itself. Trump himself has reversed national monument designations made by his predecessors.
Trump, however, described the Oval Office order in expansive terms. “It will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape,” Trump said. “We like the Oval Office, and it’s a symbol, like the White House itself.”
It was the third day this week that the president, a real estate mogul, delivered remarks fixated on his pet projects in Washington. On Wednesday, a day after Republicans suffered defeats in key races across the country, Trump gathered reporters to sign the final beam being raised during construction of his opulent ballroom project. On Monday, he went to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to talk about his renovation of the landmark.
The proclamation, released after Trump’s remarks, says that nothing in it will “restrict the President’s authority to redecorate the monument, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument’s historic structure or architectural character.”
It orders the Interior secretary to manage the Oval Office and requires “documentation, review, and consideration of alternatives before any action that would substantially alter or demolish the monument.” Trump separately said any major changes would need review from Congress, though such a requirement is not in the document’s text.
“If they want to say, ‘Let’s not have oval anymore, let’s make it square,’ what happens is they have to go back to Congress and hopefully the Congress, the people in Congress, will be smart enough not to let that happen,” said Trump — who notably demolished the East Wing of the White House to make room for his ballroom.
A red baseball cap with “VETO” on the front was sitting on the Resolute Desk as Trump signed the document, a not-so-subtle nod to the shifting of powers in Congress.
His effort to preserve changes at the White House comes as Democrats gear up for new scrutiny of Trump. Connecticut Sen. Richard Blumenthal, the top Democrat on the Homeland Security Committee’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, sent a flurry of letters Thursday to known donors to Trump’s ballroom, demanding that they provide information or face “alternative measures to obtain compliance.”
Since returning to the White House, Trump has overseen numerous design changes to various rooms, including the Oval Office, where he has filled the wall space with portraits, a copy of the Declaration of Independence and numerous golden accents.
As he talked about his interior decorating decisions, Trump highlighted new chandeliers that he says were installed in the Cabinet Room to address “very bad lighting.” His other additions to the Oval Office include numerous gold wall appliqués and gold-framed portraits.
Trump did not elaborate on precisely what he was hoping to prevent but suggested that the Oval Office might face some threat in the future. Trump himself has faced several lawsuits alleging that his Washington beautification projects were done without the necessary approval.
“If anybody ever decides to come and start knocking down walls, you call me wherever I may be,” Trump said, “and I’ll come back here and I’ll make sure it never happens.”

title: ‘ER’ and ‘The Pitt’ are similar enough for lawsuit to move forward, appeals court finds
text:
‘ER’ and ‘The Pitt’ are similar enough for lawsuit to move forward, appeals court finds
A California appeals court has found that “ER” and “The Pitt” have enough similarity that a lawsuit brought by the widow and estate of “ER” creator Michael Crichton alleging “The Pitt” is an unauthorized reboot can move forward.
A three-judge panel from California’s 2nd District Court of Appeal ruled unanimously on Wednesday that the trial court judge was correct to reject a motion to throw out the case from “The Pitt” production company Warner Bros. Television, which also produced “ER.”
But the judges dismissed Noah Wyle — the star of both shows and a producer on “The Pitt” — as a defendant along with two other producers who worked on both series.
The lawsuit is a clash between the makers of multiple Emmy-winning TV series that were each among the most important and acclaimed shows of their eras.
Crichton, the author of “Jurassic Park” and many other novels that became hit movies and TV shows, wrote the pilot script for “ER,” the NBC show about a Chicago emergency room that redefined the medical drama genre and drew tens of millions of weekly viewers in its run from 1994 to 2009.
The lawsuit brought by Sherri Crichton was filed two years ago, before a single episode of “The Pitt” had aired. The HBO Max series that shows a real-time day in the life of a Pittsburgh emergency department has since become perhaps the most lauded series in television, winning two Emmys for best drama for its first two seasons and two best actor Emmys for Wyle.
Along with more technical legal issues, the judges had to decide whether the shows had at least the minimal similarity that would give the lawsuit enough merit to move forward. Their decision applies only to this early legal challenge and they did not rule on whether the plaintiffs had proved the “The Pitt” is derivative of “ER.”
The court agreed with the plaintiff that “both shows provide commentaries on the healthcare system; they focus specifically on the emergency room and the difficult conditions under which the medical staff operates. Both shows take place, with little exception, in the emergency room, as opposed to other medical shows which track patients as they move out of the emergency room, or indeed never enter it.”
The opinion also said that both feature “very fast pacing, and reactions to multiple overlapping crises. The fast-paced dialogue is (to a layperson) frequently incomprehensible shorthand and jargon, lending an air of immediacy and accuracy.”
Warner Bros. Television said in a statement that “WBTV continues to maintain that ‘The Pitt’ is an entirely original series and that the claims against it are without merit. Nothing in the Court of Appeal’s decision establishes otherwise, and WBTV looks forward to defending its position as the case proceeds.”
The defendants argued in legal filings that the shows have “generic similarities” that would exist in “any dramatic story” that features “overworked doctors and staff.”
The panel also unanimously dismissed as defendants Wyle, John Wells, who created “The Pitt” and worked on “ER,” and R. Scott Gemmill, a “Pitt” executive producer who also worked on both shows. The judges found there was no evidence the three men knew the provisions of the Crichton contract that the lawsuit alleges they interfered with.
Sherri Crichton's lawsuit alleges “The Pitt” is a rebranded version of an unauthorized “ER” reboot that she had rejected.
Her husband had secured a coveted “frozen rights” provision in his contract for the series, prohibiting Warner Bros. from proceeding with any sequels, remakes, spinoffs or other productions derived from “ER” without Crichton’s consent, or his estate’s consent after his death from cancer in 2008.
After the production company could not reach an agreement with Sherri Crichton over a proposed “ER” reboot, the TV studio proceeded to develop and produce a series based on the same premise without permission, the lawsuit alleges.

title: InvestigateTV+: Measles outbreaks in the U.S.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Once declared eliminated in the U.S., measles is making a comeback as cases reach a decades-high peak. InvestigateTV+ digs into the highly contagious disease’s return and how one state is fighting its worst outbreak in years.
Plus, Black women who integrated industries during the Civil Rights era reunite at the adult education center that changed their lives.
Then, we visit a tasting room opened by a volunteer firefighter to honor first responders and celebrate the brotherhood of the fire service.
Measles outbreaks in the U.S.
Measles is one of the most contagious diseases on Earth and can cause serious health complications, including death.
Measles is most often associated with a rash and fever, according to the CDC. Health experts warn it can cause severe complications, particularly in babies and young children.
When more than 95% of a community is vaccinated, most people are protected through what’s known as herd immunity.
This school helped break barriers
Just over 60 years ago, the country took a step toward making good on a promise that all Americans are created equal. The passage of the Civil Rights Act in 1964 desegregated schools, workplaces, and public spaces all while creating protections against discrimination.
A year after the signing of the landmark legislation, an adult education center in New Orleans opened its doors to young Black women. Those women would use the skills they learned to integrate major corporate offices across the South.
The need for housing
America’s population is aging and a recent study found there may not be enough senior-friendly homes to meet demand. In 2019, one in six Americans were 65 or older and by 2060 it will be one in four.
A 2019 U.S. Census data analysis found that “the stock of aging-ready homes across the nation may be inadequate for the growing number of older households.”
An old fire station distillery
A Wisconsin family runs a distillery in an old fire station along Highway 96 in Dale, with a business designed to support the fire departments that keep them safe.

title: 4 Cornell lawsuit defendants join effort to oust Letitia James from criminal investigation
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Four men named in a former Cornell University student’s lawsuit are joining a co-defendant’s effort to block New York’s attorney general from leading a reopened criminal investigation into the woman’s gang rape allegations, according to court filings on Thursday.
The co-defendant’s lawyers said the men agreed to be added to a court petition that seeks Attorney General Letitia James’ removal from the case because of social media posts she made prior to her involvement in which she condemned the alleged assault and expressed support for the accuser.
The development comes a day after James appointed Jacqueline Kelly, a former federal prosecutor who oversaw sex crimes cases against music mogul Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs, as outside counsel for the investigation. She and a team of lawyers and investigators will be responsible for evidence gathering, witness interviews and other investigative steps. They will report to James.
A judge heard arguments last week on one of the accused men’s request to remove James but said he wouldn’t rule without knowing if the six other lawsuit defendants backed the effort. He gave the man’s lawyers until Thursday to try to get them to join.
Lawyers for one of the four men agreeing to join had separately filed court papers seeking to have James removed. Two other men named as defendants in the lawsuit didn’t have lawyers who could speak for them and did not provide a response, court filings said.
James’ office declined to comment.
A former Cornell student identified in court papers as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit in September alleging that several men raped her at a fraternity party in 2024. The woman said some of the men pressured her into using ketamine and marijuana and that she drank alcohol that left her too intoxicated to consent. Not all of the men named were accused of rape.
James, a Democrat, posted about the case on X and Facebook on Sept. 28, linking to a news article about the lawsuit. “I’m holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you’re not alone. We stand with you.”
On Oct. 1, Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed James as special prosecutor overseeing the criminal investigation, saying that she had lost faith in the local district attorney, who declined to bring charges in 2024 but had said he would restart the investigation following the former student’s lawsuit.
James initially declined to comment about her social media posts but addressed them at an Oct. 8 debate, saying: “Those comments demonstrate empathy, and what we need now more than ever in our body politic is more empathy.”
In court, the state’s lawyers argued that Hochul has wide latitude to appoint special prosecutors and said she picked James because of her track record handling sensitive cases in the national spotlight.
In a statement on Wednesday, James said she is confident that Kelly “will lead a fair and comprehensive investigation.”
Andrew Miltenberg, a lawyer for the man spearheading the removal effort, said in a court filing that Kelly’s appointment “changes the face of the investigation” but ”does not establish any change in ultimate authority.”

title: Upstream pig poop stymies Maine town’s desire to reopen polluted clam flat
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Soft-shell clams face steep challenges along the coast of Maine, where harvests have fallen by 75% since the mid-1970s amid warming waters and the arrival of invasive green crabs that eat their young.
On the shores of Herrick Bay in the Hancock County town of Brooklin, once its most productive flat, testing suggests harvesters face an additional issue: pig feces washing down into a bay from Selectman David Reiley’s small farm upstream, where remediation efforts have apparently stalled for more than a year.
“This has been ongoing for a long time,” said David Tarr, chair of the town’s shellfish committee.
Only three commercial harvesters now work in Brooklin, which has also seen its soft-shell clam numbers dramatically decline in past decades. Often, state closures due to bacterial pollution result from sources like wildlife waste or faulty septic systems that are harder to control, according to Tarr.
But in this case, residents believe the shores could be at least seasonally opened if the pig waste can be contained, an unusual example of a Maine town that could reclaim some of its shellfish production. Even though few harvesters remain, residents also say they want the water clean for its own sake.
The Maine Department of Marine Resources closes harvesting areas when high levels of fecal bacteria make shellfish unsafe to eat.
In April, it added 26 acres at the head of the bay to a list of areas where harvesting is restricted, meaning no one can dig there without a special permit.
That’s a step further than the conditional, generally weather-based closures that clamming areas are commonly subject to, and a step below a “prohibited” designation.
The department didn’t grant an interview request, but said no source of the pollution has been identified in Herrick Bay. It will continue routine monitoring while residents work to figure out the source and whether it can be remediated, a spokesperson said.
Reiley’s farm is so far upstream that it previously seemed an unlikely culprit, but advances in technology recently identified that feces in the water comes from swine, according to Tarr.
“We feel like we’ve pinpointed [it],” he said. “We feel like we know where it is.”
Reiley had a $12,000 grant from the Natural Resources Conservation Service to help address the problem and planned to move his 30 pigs elsewhere on the property, he told the Rising Tide online news site last fall. Reiley has said there are only 10 pigs there now, Tarr said Thursday.
Much of that money was used for remediation analysis, which said the animals should be moved to a different part of the farm and their pens should be paved with concrete to streamline manure cleanup, according to the Rising Tide.
Reiley did not return a request for comment Thursday.
Tarr, who is 60, remembers when there were clams on all the area’s shores up to Surry, and recalled going out to dig them as an 8-year-old to buy school clothes and earn pocket money. Many of those areas are now at least seasonally closed due to pollution, and numbers are falling.
“It’s not that it’s being dug up,” Tarr said. “It’s just that [the clams] are not there.”
Only two Brooklin residents now clam commercially, both of them part-time, and one nonresident who digs clams full time.
There were up to 14 when Tarr was harvesting commercially himself about a decade and a half ago, he said, and decades before that there were up to 40 or 50. Another 69 people had recreational clamming licenses in 2025, according to the town’s committee reports.
Brooklin’s average landings between 2021 were on the lower end of Hancock County towns, according to state data, though others reported no landings at all.
Clamming wasn’t hugely lucrative for the town before, Tarr said, but about $400,000 worth of clams once came from the flat.
It’s still possible for larger “depuration” operations to take clams from some flats that have been closed, which they do in Brooklin. Those businesses keep clams in clean water until the contaminants cycle out and they’re safe to eat.
The town gets 50 cents per bushel from those operations, according to Tarr. One bushel can be worth $75 to $300 depending on the time of year.
“There’s been a lot of money that came out of there that didn’t go to the town,” Tarr said.
He’d prefer those dollars to stay local, and noted that managing the fishery takes time and money.
Water samples are still failing tests, according to Tarr. The town did some testing of its own by boat, rather than from samples collected from shore, which he said makes them slightly more representative and did lead to the outer area of the bay being reopened. It seems the pig waste only washes out to the bay during heavy rainfall events, rather than in a consistent stream, he said.
Tarr is disappointed it’s taken so long to address and doesn’t want to put a farm out of business, but thinks the problem is fixable.
He believes it’s a matter of money and not knowing what to do, rather than a lack of desire to fix things. Until that happens, however, the town’s avenues are limited.
Tarr sees the larger decline of clam populations as a long-term change due to complex factors.
“I always figured that I could support my family off of what comes off the clam flats in town if I needed to,” he said. But now, he’s not sure, with prices down and numbers declining.
Invasive green crabs that eat larval soft-shell clams broadly get the blame, though Tarr said that when it comes to the complex ocean, it’s also hard to point immediately to a single cause of changes.
While clamming may not be as much of a way of life as it used to be there, residents are still worried about water quality aside from commercial impacts.
“People want the water clean,” Tarr said. “Whether or not they’re going to eat the shellfish out of Herrick’s Bay, they want the water clean.”

title: Jay Rockefeller, former West Virginia governor and US senator, dies at 89
text:
Jay Rockefeller, former West Virginia governor and US senator, dies at 89
Jay Rockefeller, the last member of his family’s political dynasty — and the only Democrat — who served as West Virginia’s governor and later a longtime U.S. senator, has died. He was 89.
Video above: Remembering those we've lost in 2026
Rockefeller died Thursday night at his home in Washington, said Mary Stewart, vice president for external affairs at WETA, the public broadcasting station where Rockefeller’s wife, Sharon, serves as president and CEO.
Rockefeller came from one of the nation’s richest families to spend a half century in public service in one of the poorest states. He arrived in 1964 as a worker in an anti-poverty program, was elected governor a dozen years later and served two terms, then spent 30 years as a U.S. senator.
“I could not imagine a more rewarding career,” Rockefeller said upon his retirement in 2015.
He was born John D. Rockefeller IV in New York City. His great-grandfather, Standard Oil Co. founder John Rockefeller, died a month before Rockefeller’s birth. His father, John D. Rockefeller III, was a well-known philanthropist. Uncles Winthrop (Arkansas) and Nelson (New York) were Republican governors. Another uncle, David Rockefeller, ran Chase Manhattan Bank.
Jay Rockefeller went in a different direction.
A few years out of college at age 27, Rockefeller moved to the West Virginia mining community of Emmons to participate in the Volunteers in Service to America program, a time that Rockefeller said proved transformative.
“It explains every policy I pursued and every vote I have cast. It was where my beliefs were bolted down, and where my passions met my principles,” he said in an emotional farewell speech from the Senate floor on Dec. 4, 2014.
While he intended for his stay in the state to be brief, Rockefeller broke from his family’s Republican tradition and was elected to the state House of Delegates as a Democrat in 1966. By combining money with hard work in a traditionally Democratic state, Rockefeller overcame suspicions of political opportunism and rose from state legislator to secretary of state to governor.
A turning point came after Rockefeller’s only political defeat in the 1972 governor’s race to Republican Arch A. Moore Jr., whose daughter, Republican Shelley Moore Capito, was elected in 2014 to Rockefeller’s Senate seat upon his retirement.
After the defeat, Rockefeller remained in West Virginia, a decision he called the most important of his career. He became the first without a theological degree to become president of West Virginia Wesleyan College in 1973. His popularity there — and a change in his stance to embrace strip mining — translated to a landslide win over Republican Cecil Underwood in the 1976 governor’s race.
As governor, Rockefeller emphasized development of the state’s infrastructure, such as roads, sewers and bridges. Those issues, he said, are “not very sexy things, I grant you but very, very necessary in West Virginia.”
After Rockefeller defeated Arch Moore in a rematch in 1980, he won a U.S. Senate seat in 1984 after the retirement of longtime Democrat Jennings Randolph. It came despite a landslide victory that year for Republican President Ronald Reagan.
Rockefeller and his wife, Sharon, daughter of former Republican Sen. Charles Percy of Illinois, fit easily into the capital’s social scene, purchasing a multimillion-dollar estate for their family. Never shy or apologetic about using his inherited $150 million fortune to win his races, he spent millions upon millions from his own pocket. He won by comfortable margins in each of his five terms.
Rockefeller’s vast wealth was always a source of conversation and an undercurrent in his political races. He spent at least $21 million of his own money in his political campaigns, including $9 million to win a close 1984 Senate race against Republican novice and fellow multimillionaire John Raese. In Rockefeller’s 1980 gubernatorial race against Republican Arch Moore Jr., bumper stickers appeared saying: “Make Him Spend It All, Arch.”
The state’s junior senator for 25 years, Rockefeller carved his own path of influence in Sen. Robert C. Byrd’s immense shadow. Byrd died in 2010 as the longest-serving senator in U.S. history, winning an enduring reputation for steering billions of dollars over many decades to boost his impoverished state.
Rockefeller’s influence was less showy. As chairman of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, he championed consumers’ rights, upgrading broadband infrastructure and sponsoring a bill to block companies from tracking online activity of their customers. He authored legislation in 1997 that created the Children’s Health Insurance Program, which assists poor families whose incomes are too high to qualify for Medicaid.
He also was head of committees on Veterans Affairs and Intelligence, frequently sparring with President George W. Bush over foreign policy. Rockefeller said he regretted his 2002 vote to authorize the war against Iraq.
But Rockefeller also differed with the Democratic administration of President Barack Obama over mining-related regulations. With his state the nation’s second-biggest coal producer, Rockefeller was among several West Virginia officials who opposed the Obama-era Environmental Protection Agency’s oversight of the mountaintop removal method of surface mining.
College studies in Tokyo laid the groundwork for Rockefeller’s efforts to bring business from Japan to West Virginia. He had known Toyota’s founding family since the 1960s and was instrumental in helping the Japanese automaker pick a Buffalo, West Virginia, cornfield for an engine parts plant in 1996. The $2 billion plant now employs about 2,200 workers.

title: Soaking rain along the Maine coast Friday night
text:
Showery through midday Sunday
Much-needed rain continues in Maine with scattered showers Saturday, Saturday night, and Sunday morning.
Showery through midday Sunday
Much-needed rain continues in Maine with scattered showers Saturday, Saturday night, and Sunday morning.
Intermittent showers continue on Saturday, with the steadiest rain falling on the Midcoast and Downeast Maine, where an additional 1 to 3 inches is possible. Elsewhere, an additional 0.25 to 0.5 inches is possible by midday Sunday.
Some patchy fog is also possible Saturday, and temperatures fall gradually during the afternoon. Northerly winds around 10 mph could gust up to 25 mph.
Overnight, showery weather continues, and the higher summits will likely see a changeover to wet snow late night. Elsewhere, spotty showers continue Sunday morning.
Scattered showers wind down by midday Sunday and will likely end by mid-afternoon. Temperatures will top out in the 40s and low 50s, normal for early November. Clouds break up late in the afternoon, with gradual clearing expected Sunday evening.
On Monday, a few hit-or-miss showers are possible in the afternoon and evening, with highs in the 40s to mid-50s. Next week is generally cool and cloudy, with a cold snap likely by the end of the week.
Maine's Total Weather is watching a potential storm that could arrive next Friday or Saturday (November 13/14). With cold air in place, snow is a possibility, along with rain and gusty winds. If the storm trends farther south, Maine would miss out on the precipitation and get more cold air flowing in.

title: Midwife convicted of practicing medicine without license after near-fatal home birth
text:
ATLANTA (WANF/Gray News) - A woman in Georgia was convicted of practicing medicine without a license after a near-fatal home birth in 2022, according to authorities.
Cynthia “Cindy” Rene Morrow, 64, was found guilty of all nine counts she faced Wednesday, according to the Blue Ridge Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, which covers Cherokee County.’
During labor and following the 2022 birth at a Woodstock home, Morrow performed multiple medical procedures she wasn’t licensed to perform, including administering an injection of Pitocin – a drug used to help induce labor – and intravenous fluids, inserting a catheter and performing a manual uterine procedure, prosecutors said.
The mother experienced significant blood loss after giving birth. Despite her worsening condition, Morrow did not tell the woman’s family she was experiencing a medical emergency, and requested a non-emergency medical transport when she eventually called 911, the DA’s office said.
By the time Morrow called 911, the victim was vomiting, had lost consciousness and was experiencing hypovolemic shock.
Cherokee County Fire & Emergency Services stabilized the woman and took her to the hospital for emergency treatment of a severe postpartum hemorrhage.
Medical records show the woman’s blood pressure dropped to 63/55, her heartrate reached 139 beats per minute and she lost approximately 50 percent of her blood, prosecutors said.
Doctors administered medication to control bleeding, provided multiple blood transfusions and performed emergency surgery.
Medical experts who testified at the trial said that they would have taken the woman to a hospital at least five hours earlier, based on her condition.
The jury also heard testimony from two other former clients and their family members. They described similar experiences with Morrow’s midwifery practice in separate incidents that happened outside of Cherokee County.
One of those women nearly died during childbirth, while the other lost her baby. The DA’s office said their testimony gave the jury additional evidence to consider regarding Morrow’s practices and conduct.
Prosecutors also introduced more than 100 exhibits, including the Cherokee County 911 call, the victim’s medical records, client logs Morrow maintained for her business, Birth Servant Midwifery, LLC, along with cellphone records and records showing Morrow was not licensed as a physician, nurse, or certified nurse midwife.
Photographs taken during the execution of the search warrant at the Woodstock home showed expired, dangerous drugs – the Pitocin – and needles, sutures, intravenous supplies and other medical equipment.
Seven of the charges Morrow was convicted of stemmed from the 2022 Woodstock home birth:
- One count of practicing medicine without a license
- One count of practicing nursing without a license
- Two counts of unlawful practice of midwifery
- Two counts of reckless conduct
- One count of possession of a dangerous drug (Pitocin)
Morrow was also found guilty of the “lesser-included offense of criminal attempt (for possession of expired Pitocin that was recovered during a 2024 search warrant of her home)” and unlawful practice of midwifery, involving a second victim in Cherokee County.
Sentencing is set for Nov. 10.

title: Jay Rockefeller, former West Virginia governor and US senator who was part of a dynasty, dies at 89
text:
CHARLESTON, W.Va. (AP) — Jay Rockefeller, the last member of his family’s political dynasty — and the only Democrat — who served as West Virginia’s governor and later a longtime U.S. senator, has died. He was 89.
Rockefeller died Thursday night at his home in Washington, said Mary Stewart, vice president for external affairs at WETA, the public broadcasting station where Rockefeller’s wife, Sharon, serves as president and CEO.
Rockefeller came from one of the nation’s richest families to spend a half century in public service in one of the poorest states. He arrived in 1964 as a worker in an anti-poverty program, was elected governor a dozen years later and served two terms, then spent 30 years as a U.S. senator.
“I could not imagine a more rewarding career,” Rockefeller said upon his retirement in 2015.
He was born John D. Rockefeller IV in New York City. His great-grandfather, Standard Oil Co. founder John Rockefeller, died a month before Rockefeller’s birth. His father, John D. Rockefeller III, was a well-known philanthropist. Uncles Winthrop (Arkansas) and Nelson (New York) were Republican governors. Another uncle, David Rockefeller, ran Chase Manhattan Bank.
A detour from his family’s path
Jay Rockefeller went in a different direction.
A few years out of college at age 27, Rockefeller moved to the West Virginia mining community of Emmons to participate in the Volunteers in Service to America program, a time that Rockefeller said proved transformative.
“It explains every policy I pursued and every vote I have cast. It was where my beliefs were bolted down, and where my passions met my principles,” he said in an emotional farewell speech from the Senate floor on Dec. 4, 2014.
While he intended for his stay in the state to be brief, Rockefeller broke from his family’s Republican tradition and was elected to the state House of Delegates as a Democrat in 1966. By combining money with hard work in a traditionally Democratic state, Rockefeller overcame suspicions of political opportunism and rose from state legislator to secretary of state to governor.
A turning point came after Rockefeller’s only political defeat in the 1972 governor’s race to Republican Arch A. Moore Jr., whose daughter, Republican Shelley Moore Capito, was elected in 2014 to Rockefeller’s Senate seat upon his retirement. Capito on Friday called Rockefeller “a true gentleman” who treated her with respect, kindness and encouragement.
“Over the years, we developed a wonderful friendship that transcended politics, and I will always be grateful for that,” she said in a statement.
After the defeat, Rockefeller remained in West Virginia, a decision he called the most important of his career. He became the first without a theological degree to become president of West Virginia Wesleyan College in 1973. His popularity there — and a change in his stance to embrace strip mining — translated to a landslide win over Republican Cecil Underwood in the 1976 governor’s race.
As governor, Rockefeller emphasized development of the state’s infrastructure, such as roads, sewers and bridges. Those issues, he said, are “not very sexy things, I grant you but very, very necessary in West Virginia.”
Current Gov. Patrick Morrissey said Rockefeller helped shape the state and left a lasting mark on the lives of generations of West Virginians.
“From his early work in some of our state’s most disadvantaged communities to his efforts to strengthen healthcare, protect coal miners and their families, and support our veterans, Senator Rockefeller demonstrated a deep commitment to the people of West Virginia,” Morrissey said in a statement.
Onward to Washington
After Rockefeller defeated Arch Moore in a rematch in 1980, he won a U.S. Senate seat in 1984 after the retirement of longtime Democrat Jennings Randolph. It came despite a landslide victory that year for Republican President Ronald Reagan.
Rockefeller and his wife, Sharon, daughter of former Republican Sen. Charles Percy of Illinois, fit easily into the capital’s social scene, purchasing a multimillion-dollar estate for their family. Never shy or apologetic about using his inherited $150 million fortune to win his races, he spent millions upon millions from his own pocket. He won by comfortable margins in each of his five terms.
Rockefeller’s vast wealth was always a source of conversation and an undercurrent in his political races. He spent at least $21 million of his own money in his political campaigns, including $9 million to win a close 1984 Senate race against Republican novice and fellow multimillionaire John Raese. In Rockefeller’s 1980 gubernatorial race against Republican Arch Moore Jr., bumper stickers appeared saying: “Make Him Spend It All, Arch.”
The state’s junior senator for 25 years, Rockefeller carved his own path of influence in Sen. Robert C. Byrd’s immense shadow. Byrd died in 2010 as the longest-serving senator in U.S. history, winning an enduring reputation for steering billions of dollars over many decades to boost his impoverished state.
Rockefeller’s influence was less showy. As chairman of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, he championed consumers’ rights, upgrading broadband infrastructure and sponsoring a bill to block companies from tracking online activity of their customers. He authored legislation in 1997 that created the Children’s Health Insurance Program, which assists poor families whose incomes are too high to qualify for Medicaid.
He also was head of committees on Veterans’ Affairs and Intelligence, frequently sparring with President George W. Bush over foreign policy. Rockefeller said he regretted his 2002 vote to authorize the war against Iraq.
But Rockefeller also differed with the Democratic administration of President Barack Obama over mining-related regulations. With his state the nation’s second-biggest coal producer, Rockefeller was among several West Virginia officials who opposed the Obama-era Environmental Protection Agency’s oversight of the mountaintop removal method of surface mining.
College studies in Tokyo laid the groundwork for Rockefeller’s efforts to bring business from Japan to West Virginia. He had known Toyota’s founding family since the 1960s and was instrumental in helping the Japanese automaker pick a Buffalo, West Virginia, cornfield for an engine parts plant in 1996. The $2 billion plant now employs about 2,200 workers.
___
Associated Press writer Holly Ramer in Concord, New Hampshire, contributed to this report.

title: Former police officer pleads guilty to child porn possession, gets 100 days in jail
text:
GREENVILLE, N.C. (WITN/Gray News) - A former Greenville police officer pleads guilty to child pornography possession
On Wednesday, Dominic Olivares pleaded guilty in court to two counts of third-degree sexual exploitation of a minor.
Six other counts, including first- and second-degree sexual exploitation of a minor, were dismissed as part of a plea agreement.
Olivares received two consecutive suspended sentences of six to 17 months, meaning he’ll avoid prison unless he violates the terms of his eight years of supervised probation.
The judge did order him to serve 100 days in jail under the state’s Misdemeanant Confinement Program, and he will have to register as a sex offender.
Olivares was arrested in September 2025 by the SBI for two counts of first-degree sexual exploitation of a minor, three counts of second-degree sexual exploitation of a minor, and three counts of third-degree sexual exploitation of a minor.
Arrest warrants were issued at the time that Olivares used a 16-year-old girl to create videos with her engaged in sexual activity.
The 30-year-old Olivares was hired as a police officer in Greenville in May 2020.
A spokeswoman says he was fired on Aug. 5, 2021, two months after the SBI was brought in to investigate a complaint the department received about Olivares.

title: These Maine towns still count ballots by hand
text:
This story appears as part of a collaboration to strengthen investigative journalism in Maine between the BDN and The Maine Monitor. Read more about the partnership.
Shortly after the polls closed on election night, the town clerk of Cranberry Isles, Ben Sumner, and two volunteers, Barbara Meyers and Beverly Sanborn, began counting the island’s ballots by hand.
With a view of Acadia National Park, Great Cranberry is the largest of five islands that make up the town of Cranberry Isles, which has a population of about 160. On Wednesday, there were 48 ballots to count — the old-fashioned way, with no electronic tabulators in sight.
Cranberry Isles is one of 88 towns in Maine that still counts its ballots by hand. That is down from 161 towns, or about a third of the state’s voting jurisdictions, that did so in 2024, according to data from Verified Voting, a nonpartisan organization that researches the use of technology in elections. Those towns were quite small — with an average of 248 registered voters — making up 4% of the total voters in the state.
This election cycle, 73 of them decided to join the majority of Maine’s municipalities and switch to hand-fed optical scanners, which scan hand-marked paper ballots and tabulate the votes, storing the data on a memory stick.
These scanners are manufactured by a company called Election Systems and Software, which Maine has contracted with since 2012, and provided by the state at no cost to municipalities. Studies have shown these machines are more accurate and more efficient than hand counting, which can be prone to human error.
“More towns opted into tabulators because counting by hand is incredibly time consuming and more subject to human error,” Jana Spaulding, the deputy secretary of state for communications, told The Maine Monitor this week. “Time and time again, towns that make the switch express relief at how easy the tabulators make it to count the votes quickly.”
But it is up to towns whether they want these machines, and, on Great Cranberry, hand counting is still the method of choice.
As a fire crackled in the community center’s brick fireplace, the mantle covered in gourds and dried flowers, another year-round resident, Helen Bertles, dropped by with a homemade cake.
“Sugar, sugar, sugar. Gotta keep moving!” Bertles said before taking a seat to watch.
The clerk began the process by voiding all the town’s unused ballots. They were marked with red X’s and stored to be transported in the town offices on Islesford, a neighboring island and separate voting precinct in the Cranberry Isles.
“On Wednesday morning,” Sumner said, “I combine both precincts and report the results. If a race has to be determined by ranked choice, I’ll take the ballots off to Mount Desert on Thursday so the state police can pick them up and take them to Augusta.”
Next, the election workers opened the absentee ballots and deposited them into the town’s wooden ballot box — which is believed to be at least 100 years old — where they joined the ballots that were cast throughout Election Day.
The box was unlocked, and the group retrieved and organized the ballots. Then it was time to count.
The counting process requires one reader, who examines each ballot and announces the votes, and two counters, who keep a tally as the votes are read aloud. Sanborn, the reader this year, announced each vote, calling out, “senator, Collins,” or “governor, Pingree” as she went. The two counters, Sumner and Meyers, independently tallied the votes. Each time a candidate passed a multiple of five, they said “five” aloud in unison.
At one point, Sanborn encountered a ballot where the voter had marked Collins as their first choice, second choice and third choice, and had done the same for Jackson. Sumner reviewed the guidelines for processing such a ballot and determined it had to be counted as a blank.
As they reached the last ballot, Sanborn laughed.
“You’re going to love this, Ben. You’re a write-in,” Sanborn said.
(The vote would not count, as only votes for declared write-ins are valid.)
After all the ballots were counted, Sumner and Meyers compared their counts to verify that they matched. Then they moved on to counting the referendum votes in the same fashion.
Once those were tallied, cross checked and validated, the ballots were sealed in a lockbox with a tamper-proof lock.
Even with just 48 votes, the counting, sorting, certifying and securing of the ballots stretched to 10 p.m., concluding a 12-hour shift and another typical, if old-fashioned, election for the voters of Great Cranberry Island.

title: Judge accepts ex-NFL star Antonio Brown's guilty plea to reduced charge, sentences probation
text:
Judge accepts ex-NFL star Antonio Brown's guilty plea to reduced charge, sentences probation
Former NFL star Antonio Brown pleaded guilty Friday to aggravated assault with a firearm in connection with a 2025 shooting outside a celebrity boxing match in Miami.
Judge Marisa Tinkler Mendez sentenced Brown to three years of probation during which time he will have to attend weekly counseling sessions and not possess a firearm, among other conditions.
He would not have any criminal conviction under the plea and could seek an early termination of probation at about the halfway mark of the sentence so long as all terms are met.
The plea to the reduced charge, which Brown entered in state court in Miami, allows the All-Pro wide receiver to avoid prison time.
Brown had initially been charged with attempted murder after police say he grabbed a handgun from a security staffer at the event and fired two shots at a man he had been in a fistfight with earlier.
Brown maintained he was defending himself from an attack as others were trying to steal jewelry from him.
Florida’s Stand Your Ground law allows people who believe they face death or serious injury to use deadly force to defend themselves without a duty to retreat.
The 38-year-old faced up to 30 years in prison if convicted of the original attempted murder charge.
Brown spent 12 years in the NFL, most of it with the Pittsburgh Steelers. He won a Super Bowl with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in 2021 under quarterback Tom Brady.
The following season, though, Brown effectively ended his career when he inexplicably took off his jersey, shoulder pads and gloves and ran off the field during a game. The Buccaneers released him after the incident.
Brown has dealt with other legal problems in recent years.
He previously was accused of battery on a moving truck driver, faced several domestic violence charges, failure to pay child support and other incidents.
Brown was extradited in November 2025 from Dubai, where he has business interests, after an arrest warrant on the attempted murder charge was issued in June of the same year.

title: Teen accused of killing paddleboarder in Union will be tried as adult
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine (WABI) - The teen accused killing a paddleboarder in Union last summer will be tried as an adult.
A status hearing was held Friday at Knox County Superior Court in the case of Deven Young.
Young is accused of killing paddleboarder Sunshine ‘Sunny’ Stewart, 48, in Union in July 2025. Her body was found in Crawford Pond a day after she went missing. Police say Stewart died from strangulation and blunt force trauma.
Young, now 19, of Frankfort, was 17 at the time police say he killed Stewart.
The decision comes as Young’s attorneys agreed to waive a bindover hearing following months of delays.
At a bindover hearing, both sides make arguments regarding a suspect’s mental status, and a judge decides if they should be tried in a juvenile or adult court.
It was previously ruled that Young is competent to stand trial.
Young has been held in Long Creek Youth Development Center since his arrest. He will now be held without bail at Knox County Jail.
His next court appearance is scheduled for January.

title: ‘An imminent expression of brotherhood’: An inside look at the Morehouse College Glee Club
text:
(Aging Untold) — For more than a century, the Morehouse College Glee Club has uplifted audiences.
They’ve performed at presidential inaugurations, Super Bowls and the Atlanta Olympics. But behind every performance is a deeper mission - their voices rise not just in song, but in leadership.
“At Morehouse College, Glee Club is an immediate expression of brotherhood, a united force of dedication and commitment, and an unselfish labor of love,” said Desmond Thompson, a proud member of the 38-member group.
The Glee Club performed at New Olivet Worship Center in Cordova by invitation from alumnus Pastor Kenneth Whalum Jr. Whalum says when he saw the Morehouse Glee Club perform in Memphis as a young boy, he knew he’d become a Morehouse man.
“There’s something about Black men singing in harmony. It strikes the ear,” Whalum said. “And the comportment of those men in the Glee club. They put in hours and hours and hours of work so that the harmony can be crystal clear and the message of the music can get across.”
That Morehouse message is one of service and leadership, producing men of distinction for nearly 158 years.
“Well, Morehouse traditionally makes men who have a sense of civic responsibility and believe that we are responsible for lifting the entire community,” Whalum explained.
Dr. David Morrow is the current director of the Morehouse Glee Club.
“For sure it is an arm of the college that shows the college off in such a way that we can use it for recruiting and advertising for the school,” he said.
But Morrow emphasizes it’s even more than that. “It’s more of a remembering that you are a part of a community, that you are more than just yourself. You are more than just a member of the Glee club. You are more than just the Blaze, and you are more than just a tie. You are family. You are part of something great.”

title: Letter: New library rules haven’t been justified
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
What is the problem that the state library system is trying to solve with new rules?
Skills and best practices: Are the small libraries mistreating materials borrowed by inter-library loan? Are they abusing the state system? Are mistakes being made in use of the state system that means that it takes time and resources from the state system to square these away? Can problems be demonstrated? Is there evidence? If those are the problems, could training, perhaps county based, conducted using the help and resources of larger libraries help?
Cost control: Is the state trying to reduce the number of libraries in the system to control costs of keeping the inter-library loan system running, specifically the cost of moving books about the state? If so, state that honestly and then work towards a system of reducing costs by things like consolidation. For example, could a request for inter-library loan come from a small library, with the item being delivered to a larger library near the small one.
Be honest about the problem. There could and should be solutions that would preserve the access that many Mainers rely on.
Ben Fuller
Cushing

title: Anderson Noyes’ return gives Cony football a playmaker
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
AUGUSTA — Anderson Noyes sat in the emergency room in August with his father, wondering if his senior season of football at Cony was over. He hoped the injury to his right leg was a high ankle sprain, but if he was being honest with himself, he knew it was much worse, and that was scary.
“I love this game, and it was tough to see it potentially go down the drain,” Noyes said Friday night, walking off Fuller Field in a driving rain storm.
It turned out that Noyes’ right leg was broken in three places. The good news was that it was displaced, and surgery wasn’t needed to set the breaks. Now he’s healed, and he’s ready to be the difference maker for the Rams as they try to reach the Class B state championship game for the second season in a row.
The Class B North semifinal on Friday, a 47-0 win over Skowhegan, was his third game back, and it was his best effort yet.
Noyes accounted for 202 yards in the first half — 131 rushing, 71 receiving — and scored Cony’s first five touchdowns.
Danny Noyes has seen a lot of football. As a player at Colby College in the early 2000s, he was one of the best wide receivers in the New England Small College Athletic Conference. He’s seen players come back from all sorts of injuries.
Noyes has never seen what his son is doing.
“I broke my leg senior year of high school. It was late in the season and I couldn’t come back,” Danny Noyes said. “That he can come back with his teammates and make a run …”
Noyes was interrupted by his son making a play, a 22-yard touchdown catch from Drew Lindquist in the first quarter. It was the second of his five touchdowns.
There was no doubt that Noyes was the best player on the field. There is no doubt that his return could be the X factor that pushes Cony back to Fitzpatrick Stadium on the Saturday before Thanksgiving. The Rams were pretty good without their starting running back. With him, a strong offense has the potential to be that much better.
“For him to break his leg in the preseason, it was just devastating. Honestly, I don’t say that often as a coach, but it was,” Cony coach B.L. Lippert said. “Of course, my mind went to obviously out for the year, but they said six to eight weeks until it’s weight bearing. He had a good recovery, and he’s back, and he’s obviously a pretty special player.”
For his part, Noyes only wants to bring one thing to the Rams.
“Energy,” he said. “I’m not going to do it myself. It starts on the line. We’re really tough in the trenches.”
Initially, doctors told Noyes recovery would take eight weeks. Noyes, as he put it, “ate my vitamins and drank my milk,” working to get back. There were weekly X-rays to monitor the healing process. Noyes focused on his limitations, making sure to not push it and cause a setback.
He returned in week seven of the regular season, running for 109 yards and a pair of touchdowns in a win over Brunswick despite admittedly not being in football shape. In the regular-season finale against rival Gardiner, Noyes ran for 131 yards and three touchdowns.
Cony earned a bye for the first round of the playoffs, giving Noyes time to rest and assess his remarkable progress.
“The last two weeks, it’s almost like restocking the shelves,” Danny Noyes said.
Noyes continues to play with a brace on his right ankle. It gives him a little more stability as he runs over and around defenders, and it also gives him peace of mind. Before the game Friday, Danny Noyes asked his son, “Do you want to take the brace off?”
“No,” Anderson replied. “I’m good with this.”
Noyes’ leg is strong again, and with the Rams heading to the regional championship game next week, that makes them that much stronger.
Staff writer Mike Mandell contributed to this report.

title: Police look for mostly non-verbal man who walked away from a Portland retirement community
text:
Police look for largely non-verbal man who walked away from a Portland retirement community
Police in Portland were looking for a man on Friday who they said was missing from the Holiday Woods at Canco retirement community in Portland.
The community is on Canco Road, between Central Maine Power and Washington Avenue.
David Darman is described as 6 feet 1 inch tall, weighing about 200 pounds with gray hair and a gray beard. Police say he often wears a blue baseball hat with an orange logo and sunglasses.
Police say Darman has early-onset dementia, is largely non-verbal, and has wandered away from the community before. Police said on Friday morning they were concerned for his well-being.
Anyone who sees Darman, or knows where he might be, should call the Portland Police Department at 207-874-8575.

title: NBA player Kristaps Porzingis announces he is stepping away to address health concerns
text:
NBA player Kristaps Porzingis says he is stepping away from basketball to address health concerns
Golden State Warriors' Kristaps Porzingis announced Friday that he is stepping away from basketball to address recent health concerns.
Porzingis announced it on social media.
"This season I was really looking forward to running it with this group, but as I ramped up, my body didn't respond the way I anticipated," Porzingis said. "I've made the decision to prioritize my health and step away from the game I love."
In 2025, Porzingis was diagnosed with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, or POTS, a neurological condition that can be triggered by viral infections, including COVID-19.
The 31-year-old forward first noticed that something was wrong the year before during a playoff run with the Boston Celtics. Suddenly, he couldn't run long distances without getting out of breath. Sometimes not even short distances.
“It hit me and it hit me like a truck,” Porzingis told The Athletic at the time. “The breathing wasn’t good. I did everything I could potentially to feel as good as I could, but my engine wasn’t running the way I wanted.”
Porzingis had a brief stint with the Atlanta Hawks last season before being traded to the Golden State Warriors in February 2026. He played 15 games, averaging 16.1 points and 5.3 rebounds. He signed a two-year, $40-million contract in the offseason to return to the Warriors.
However, Porzingis has not appeared in a game yet this season. Last month, he posted a statement on social media addressing rumors about his health.
"Hello people, I'm working with doctors and experts to figure out how to be fully back to good health asap," he wrote. "Honestly, I'm getting better and better. I just have to stay patient, and I believe I'll be feeling great again soon."
He added, "It has definitely been frustrating dealing with some health stuff that you can't exactly pinpoint, on top of injuries throughout my career, so it has added up for sure, but we will get through it."
It's unclear whether Porzingis is officially retiring from the NBA or will be placed on some sort of exempt list.
The New York Knicks drafted Porzingis in 2015. Despite some fan disappointment with selecting the largely unknown Latvian product, Porzingis took the league by storm. He averaged over 14 points and seven rebounds per game in his rookie season, finishing second in Rookie of the Year voting.
In the following years, he took his game to another level; by his third season, he averaged over 20 points per game and was named an All-Star. However, an ACL tear cut his season short and kept him out the next year as well.
After stops in Dallas and Washington, Porzingis joined the Boston Celtics, where he won an NBA championship in 2024.
