Thomas Markle, father of Meghan, arrested on charges related to child sexual abuse materials
The 82-year-old estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was arrested Friday at a senior care facility in Florida on a charge of keeping child sexual abuse material in storage units in California, authorities said.
Thomas Markle Sr. was in a wheelchair wearing handcuffs when he was transported by ambulance with federal agents, according to video posted by The Daily Mail, a British tabloid newspaper.
Markle's arrest followed the seizure of "approximately 78 items, including slides, film negatives, and books” that contained suspected child sexual abuse images in storage in the Los Angeles area, said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli.
Some images appear to depict him with children, according to an FBI affidavit filed in court.
“These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law,” Essayli said.
Phone and email messages seeking comment from his court-appointed attorney were not immediately returned. After his arrest in Polk County, Markle appeared in federal court in Tampa and was released back to a senior care center with the condition that he be electronically monitored.
U.S. Magistrate Judge Lindsay Griffin also ordered a psychiatric exam, saying Markle might be unable to understand the proceedings or properly assist his lawyer.
Court hearings will eventually move to California "but likely won’t happen for several weeks at least,” the U.S. Attorney's Office in Los Angeles said.
Materials found overseas led to U.S. investigation
Markle's arrest followed reports by The Sun, another British tabloid, that Meghan’s half brother found a collection of child sexual abuse images while clearing out their father’s home in the Philippines. That discovery led to information about two U.S. storage units in the Los Angeles area, which Markle has rented since 2008.
Essayli told The Associated Press that there's no evidence of victims in the United States, based on the seized material, but the investigation was ongoing.
Markle was living in the Philippines earlier this year when he suffered a stroke and had his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the U.S.
The Sun reported that Thomas Markle Jr. found “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sex abuse images in boxes at his father’s home in Cebu City. Markle Jr. told The Sun that he reported the images to police in the Philippines and contacted the FBI.
“I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years — but that stops now,” Markle Jr. said. “I won’t speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him.”
Meghan has distanced herself from her father
Meghan, an American citizen who starred in the U.S. television drama “Suits,” married Prince Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018. They have two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet.
She recently said she was “deeply distressed” by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her father’s former home. She also revealed that a letter containing “troubling allegations” about him had been sent to police in London in 2019.
“It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated,” Meghan said of the letter. “I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them.”
There was no immediate comment from Meghan’s representative on Friday, and Buckingham Palace is not expected to say anything about the arrest.
While Harry is the second son of King Charles III, he and Meghan are not working members of the royal family, meaning they don’t carry out public engagements on behalf of the king. They walked away from royal duties when they moved to California in 2020. After they returned to the U.K. in August, Charles issued a statement saying their status had not changed.
Thomas Markle Sr., a retired television lighting and photography director, has never established a relationship with Meghan’s in-laws. He didn’t attend the wedding after a scandal that emerged when he posed for pictures that were staged by a British tabloid newspaper. Their estrangement has continued ever since.

title: Cornell faculty vote ‘no confidence’ in university leadership after alleged fraternity gang rape
text:
Cornell University’s Faculty Senate approved a resolution Friday declaring “no confidence” in the school’s top leaders, a symbolic gesture reflecting deep discontent on campus in the wake of a former student’s lawsuit saying she was gang raped at a fraternity party in 2024.
The resolution passed 75-50, with five faculty senators abstaining and five others not voting, according to an email sent to Faculty Senate members on Friday afternoon.
The vote followed weeks of debate among professors over whether Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff and other administrators handled the woman’s allegations properly and have done enough to curtail sexual misconduct at the prestigious university.
While the faculty body has no power over the university’s top leaders, backers of the resolution had said they hoped it would pressure Cornell’s trustees to address longstanding institutional failures they identified.
Board of Trustees Chair Anne Smalling said in a statement the faculty vote “reflects the deep anger across our campus” and sent a clear signal that what happened to the woman was unacceptable, but added that Kotlikoff and his administration were the right leaders to “thoughtfully and comprehensively” address the issue.
Thomas Giuffra, an attorney for the woman who filed the lawsuit, said in a statement Friday that “we are hopeful that this will be yet another step forward to educate and support the Cornell community by addressing the longstanding scourge of sexual assault on campus.”
Lawsuit sparked outrage on campus
The Cornell community has been distressed since mid-September, when a former student, identified only by the pseudonym Jane Doe in court documents, filed a lawsuit against the university and seven former members of the Chi Phi fraternity, saying she was given ketamine and raped at a fraternity house in October 2024.
All of the men have denied her allegations, saying the sex was consensual or that they weren’t involved. The local district attorney initially decided the woman had consented to the encounter and that no crime had been committed, but the investigation has since been reopened and handed to New York’s attorney general.
Cornell disciplined several of the accused students following a monthslong Title IX investigation. Two were expelled, two received suspensions and probation, and two were required to write “reflection” papers and complete bystander training. A seventh man had already graduated and was barred from campus, according to records obtained by The New York Times.
Kotlikoff also convened a task force to study the problem of sexual misconduct on campus, which released certain recommendations.
Some faculty members have criticized Kotlikoff for not acting more forcefully to strengthen the school’s disciplinary process, push for criminal investigations and change campus party culture.
Paul Ortiz, a labor history professor who co-sponsored the no-confidence resolution, said last week that hundreds of students, staff, alumni and faculty approached the resolution’s sponsors to emphasize that “the Jane Doe case is but a tip of the iceberg” and that “a veritable fortress of silence has been breached” around sexual violence since the resolution’s introduction.
Cornell’s president defended his leadership
Speaking to Faculty Senate members on the first day that they debated the no-confidence resolution, Kotlikoff pledged to make the university a leader in addressing sexual assault and asked for more time to make changes.
Kotlikoff defended his leadership, arguing that replacing him would do little to solve complex problems and could damage Cornell’s reputation. He acknowledged he had not read the campus police report, explaining that university policy barred top administrators from interfering in criminal investigations. He also rejected suggestions he had been indifferent to the woman’s case, though he acknowledged only recently learning she had left Cornell.
Kotlikoff said the university needed to determine whether fraternities could operate safely and left open the possibility of sweeping restrictions on Greek life. He argued that decisions should be based on research and evidence rather than emotion.
Some professors had said faculty should wait to vote until the release of an independent investigation by former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates, whom the university hired to examine both how Cornell responded to the woman’s initial rape report in 2024 and its overall procedures for handling similar reports from other students.
The no-confidence resolution did not call for Kotlikoff’s resignation.

title: John Bapst soccer girls to play in 1st state title game Saturday
text:
When Greg Bennett took over as the John Bapst High School soccer coach three years ago, he installed a possession-based style of play and began building a Class B North contender.
Then he received some good fortune.
Sophomore Naia Studley transferred to John Bapst from Hampden Academy. And the missing piece to the puzzle was in place.
Striker Studley has scored 41 goals and also assisted on six more goals and is part of one of the state’s most prolific and dynamic scoring tandems with junior attacking midfielder Quinn Bennett, the coach’s daughter.
Quinn Bennett has scored 17 goals and dished out 26 assists.
The Crusaders are 16-0-1 and will be playing in their first state championship game at 1:30 p.m. Saturday at Cameron Stadium in Bangor against South champ Cape Elizabeth, 15-1-1.
“Naia truly works hard,” said Greg Bennett. “If you put the ball out there and it’s not directly to her, she will find a way to get her foot on the ball to keep possession going for us. Not many people can do that or are willing to do that because, truly, you have to put your body into certain positions and extend yourself and put yourself out there, and she is willing to do it.”
And the tireless Studley has a gritty side to her. Even though she is only 5-foot-3, she never shies away from contact and wins a lot of balls with her physicality.
Greg Bennett said his daughter has “definitely been a special player for us.”
“She has a great touch and an awareness around her,” the coach said. “She has been amazing.”
Quinn Bennett is instrumental in launching the attack and makes good decisions with the ball. She is also an aggressive, highly-skilled attacker who wins most of the 50-50 balls.
Quinn Bennett and Studley played soccer and basketball together on travel teams and school squads together growing up.
Greg Bennett said the key to his team’s success has been the fact they have “played as a team and trusted one another.”
“We started the program in regards to a possession-based system, and, this year, we’ve introduced getting off more shots and being able to take advantage of the situations we’ve been given,” he said. “If someone is open, we pass the ball. We don’t try to force things.”
Studley is joined up top by junior Ella Williams, who has 14 goals and nine assists. Senior Stella Goetz has come off the bench and produced eight goals.
Senior Rylie Soucy and sophomore Dani Brasslett are the holding midfielders, and the outside midfielders are junior Maggie Robichaud and either senior Carlie Soucy or junior Ella Johnson. The Soucys are twins.
The play of the midfield has been a vital key to their success.
The three starting backs are senior center back Reese Monnier along with junior left back Elza Cahn and junior right back Khloe Grass.
“I love our back three. They don’t get enough recognition,” Greg Bennett said. “I’m very appreciative of all of our backs and how hard they work.”
Sophomore Abby-May Turner, who had been a fullback on the jayvee team last season, has become the starting goalkeeper.
“She has learned a ton since the beginning of the season,” Bennett said. “I am so happy about how much she has (developed) over the years.”
Bapst has allowed only 11 goals while scoring 95. The Crusaders have posted 10 shutouts and held opponents to one goal or less 15 times.
Studley was named the Penobscot Valley Conference Class B Player of the Year and was joined on the All-PVC first team by Bennett, Robichaud and Monnier. Rylie Soucy was a second team selection, and Greg Bennett was the Coach of the Year.
He said he doesn’t know much about Cape Elizabeth, but said the team’s coach, Branden Noltkamper, coached in the Bangor area previously.
“They are obviously a strong team. Branden loves to have a good possession-based team, similar to us. It should be a good game,” Bennett said.
The John Bapst boys will also be seeking a state B title as the Crusaders will face Yarmouth at 11 a.m. Saturday at Cameron Stadium.
The Class A boys state final between Brunswick and Thornton Academy of Saco will kick off at 11 a .m. Saturday from Kennebunk; the C final featuring Fort Kent against Hall-Dale of Farmingdale will be played at 11 a.m. Saturday at Lewiston; the D state game between Monmouth Academy and Madawaska will be played at 11 a.m. Saturday at Messalonskee High in Oakland; and the Eight-Player final will pit Telstar of Bethel against Wisdom of St. Agatha in Presque Isle at 11 a.m. Saturday.
On the girls side, in addition to the John Bapst-Cape Elizabeth B final, Camden Hills of Rockport will face Scarborough at 1:30 p.m. Saturday in Kennebunk in the A title game; Fort Kent and Maranacook of Readfield will play at 1:30 p.m. Saturday in Lewiston for the C crown; the Penobscot Valley girls from Howland will seek a fourth straight state title against Monmouth Academy at Messalonskee beginning at 1:30 p.m. Saturday in the D title game; and the Eight-Player girls final will see Bangor Christian and Wisdom squaring off at 1 p.m. Saturday in Presque Isle.

title: Ken Fredette wins back his old job leading Maine House Republicans
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine — Republicans in the Maine House of Representatives returned former Minority Leader Ken Fredette to his old job Friday, turning to a key figure from the era of former Gov. Paul LePage to rebuild after a Democratic wave.
Fredette, a 62-year-old lawyer from Newport, beat Reps. Rachel Henderson of Rumford and Jack Ducharme of Madison in a closed-door caucus vote. He replaces Rep. Billy Bob Faulkingham, R-Winter Harbor, who won an open Maine Senate seat Tuesday.
The leadership races were the first test of how Republicans will respond to an election that gave Democrats a two-thirds majority in the Senate and a majority of 87 seats in the lower chamber. It gives Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree a firm hold on the State House as she faces down major governing challenges, including a two-year budget gap of more than $1 billion.
Fredette led House Republicans for the last six years of LePage’s tenure. His caucus often withheld the two-thirds majority needed to override the governor’s record-setting number of vetoes. When he filed to return to the Legislature in 2024, he said he did not plan to seek his old leadership post.
But on election night, he pointed toward a different approach than his caucus took in the era of LePage, who is on track to be one of Republicans’ lone bright spots on Tuesday’s election after Democrat Matt Dunlap conceded to him in the 2nd Congressional District. Rep. Alicia Collins, R-Sidney, will be his assistant leader.
“I think the reality is that you have to govern, and I don’t think you can just be the party of no,” Fredette said. “I don’t think being the party of no is going to help us rebuild.”
In the Senate, Minority Leader Trey Stewart, R-Presque Isle, held off a Friday challenge from his own No. 2, Assistant Minority Leader Matt Harrington, R-Sanford. Sen. David Haggan, R-Hampden, beat Faulkingham for the assistant leader post.
Hours before the vote, Harrington’s wife and LePage’s daughter, Republican National Committeewoman Lauren LePage, wrote on X that the party “left incumbents without resources or support” this year. It was an implicit criticism of Stewart, whose caucus spent little to defend Sens. Scott Cyrway of Albion and Bruce Bickford of Auburn, both of whom lost Tuesday.
“The lessons we learned on Tuesday are clear: Republicans have to focus on the issues important to Maine people, listen to what they are telling us, adjust our strategy to make it clear we have a plan to improve their lives and work together to ensure that plan is carried out,” Stewart said in a statement.
Democrats kept Senate President Mattie Daughtry of Brunswick, Majority Leader Teresa Pierce of Falmouth and Assistant Majority Leader Jill Duson of Portland after leadership elections on Friday. Their caucus said it will hold 24 of 35 seats, its first supermajority since 1985.
On Thursday, House Democrats kept Speaker Ryan Fecteau of Biddeford and Majority Leader Matt Moonen of Portland and picked Rep. Ambureen Rana of Bangor as assistant leader.
The picks become official when the Legislature is sworn in on Dec. 2.

title: Obituary: Joseph “Joe” Anthony Rinaldi
text:
BUXTON – Joseph “Joe” Anthony Rinaldi, 97, of Buxton, was born on Sept. 2, 1929, and was reunited with the love of his life, Marjorie Gallagher, on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026. Joe passed away at his home surrounded by his dedicated and loving family. He was a devoted husband, father, son, brother, uncle, Papa, Grampy, veteran and friend whose love, loyalty and commitment for his family defined his life.
Joe was a corporal in the United States Army and served his country during the Korean War. He worked at Coca-Cola for 40 years before retiring in 1991. He was also a volunteer fire fighter for over 30 years and served as the assistant fire chief for 10 years at the (Groveville) Buxton Fire Department.
Joe was not all work, no play! He enjoyed roller skating and candlepin bowling with his wife and was even part of a dance roller skating group. He loved to camp and was lovingly referred to as “Island Joe” by his camping family. His grandson, Steven, was his sidekick at camp and loved his Papa’s famous chicken fish.
In 1951 he met his future wife, Marjorie Gallagher and the two eloped on Christmas Eve in Virginia. They went on to create a large Catholic family with six children. Above all, Joe was a proud and loving father to his children Alphonso (Yvonne), Bridget Nguyen, Anthony (Christine), Joseph, Nancy (Steve) Talbot, and Paulette Rinaldi. He loved his many grandchildren Marguerite, Joey, Jessica, Mikey, Nick, Angie, Maria, MarkVo, Steven, Tasha, Cathy and CJ. He also had many great-grandchildren Keegan, AnthonyN., AnthonyR., Aiden, Oscar, Anna, Grace, Chloe, Charlotte, Katherine, Francis, Lewis, Liz, Josephine, Stanley, Lucille, Parker, Allie, Isabelle, Zayda, Xen, Viela, Tia, Desiree and Kiersten. Joe also leaves behind his younger brother Sammy Rinaldi, many cousins, neighbors, and friends, as well as his best friend JoJo Kitty.
Joe saw the world change in so many ways. Raised in Portland as a first generation American-Italian by his parents Bridget Maronne and Alfonso Rinaldi of Sicily. He and his seven siblings created the lives their parents hoped they would. As a young man, Joe picked potatoes up North in a suit! To the most recent years when he would take selfies and facetime with his family.
Joe’s family was his foundation and he created many treasured memories with them.
He was predeceased by his loving wife Marjorie; and their son, Joseph Rinaldi. May his reunion with them and all his other loved ones who have predeceased him be joyous.
He will be forever deeply missed by many.
Visiting hours will be held from 1 to 4 p.m. on Sunday, Nov. 8 at Jones, Rich & Barnes Funeral Home, 199 Woodford St., Portland. A Mass of Christian Burial will be celebrated at 10 a.m. on Monday, Nov. 9, at St. Peter’s Roman Catholic Church, 72 Federal St., Portland. Burial with Military Honors will follow at Calvary Cemetery in South Portland.
Please visit http://www.jonesrichandbarnes.com to sign Joseph’s online guest book.

title: UMaine men’s hockey frustrated by UMass
text:
Freshman goalie Ethan Eskit made 46 saves as UMass skated to a 2-1 win over UMaine in a Hockey East game Friday night in Orono.
The Minutemen (5-4-1, 2-0 Hockey East) took the lead just 3:09 into the game on a goal by Jack Galanek. Maxim Masse made it 2-0 with a power-play goal in the second period.

title: U.S. adds 165,000 jobs in October as hiring rebounds
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - U.S. job growth accelerated in October, beating economists’ expectations, while the unemployment rate edged lower.
Employers added a seasonally adjusted 165,000 jobs, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday. That was nearly three times the 59,000 economists surveyed by Dow Jones had expected, according to CNBC.
The unemployment rate fell from 4.2% in September to 4.1% in October.
However, the U-6 rate, a broader measure of unemployment that also includes discouraged workers and people working part time for economic reasons, rose from 7.6% to 7.9%.
The report, released three days after the midterm elections, also showed stronger job growth in the months leading up to the vote.
The bureau revised August’s job gains upward by 53,000, from 133,000 to 186,000. It revised September’s gains upward by 31,000, from 29,000 to 60,000.
Together, the revisions show employers added 84,000 more jobs over those two months than previously reported.
Professional and business services led October’s gains with 70,000 jobs, followed by health care with 42,000. Transportation and warehousing added 25,000 jobs, and manufacturing added 19,000.
Average hourly earnings rose 3.1% from a year earlier, more than economists expected but below the latest reported inflation rate.
October’s consumer price report is due Tuesday and will show how those wage gains compare with inflation over the same period.

title: Woman went on a first date and never returned. Now, more of her remains have been found
text:
MILWAUKEE (Gray News) - A jawbone found in Milwaukee has been identified as belonging to a 19-year-old woman who was killed and dismembered after a first date.
Sade Robinson’s mother, Sheena Scarbrough, said at a news conference Thursday that a pedestrian found her daughter’s jaw and teeth on a rock at Warnimont Park in Cudahy.
The Milwaukee County Sheriff’s Office confirmed the discovery and told WISN 12 News that testing matched the jaw to Robinson.
“Our condolences go out to Robinson’s family as they absorb this news and reflect on her memory,” the sheriff’s office said in a statement.
Robinson went on a first date with Maxwell Anderson on April 1, 2024. She was never seen again.
Investigators said Anderson killed Robinson, dismembered her body and scattered her remains around Milwaukee County. They also said he burned her car to conceal evidence.
A jury found Anderson guilty of killing Robinson on June 6, 2025.
He was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of extended supervision.

title: Van Buren outage to affect power, water pressure
text:
VAN BUREN, Maine (WAGM) - Van Buren Water & Light District Manager Bill Schofield is notifying residents of an extended power outage scheduled for Thursday, Nov. 12, beginning at 7 a.m.
Transformer replacement planned
The outage is expected to last approximately 8 to 12 hours as crews work to replace a malfunctioning substation transformer.
Schofield said the transformer has been acting up and needs to be replaced. The work is planned to take place during the scheduled outage.
Water pressure may be reduced
The outage will also affect the district’s water pumps, which means residents may experience reduced water pressure throughout the day. Schofield said water will likely continue to trickle into homes, but at a lower pressure than normal.
Restoration and contact information
Power and water pressure are expected to return automatically once the work is complete.
If electricity or water pressure does not return to normal, residents can contact the Van Buren Water & Light District at 207-868-3321.

title: Jayson Tatum scores 34, Celtics improve to 2-0 in NBA Cup play
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. — Jayson Tatum had 34 points, nine assists and eight rebounds, Derrick White added 18 points and the Boston Celtics demolished the Charlotte Hornets 119-80 on Friday night for their seventh win in eight games.
Boston shot 17 of 31 from 3-point range in the first half to build a 31-point lead and improved to 2-0 in NBA Cup play. The Hornets fell to 0-2.
Naz Reid had 14 points for Charlotte, which has lost six straight since coach Charles Lee benched Reid — the team’s biggest offseason acquisition — in the second half of a game against the Detroit Pistons because he did not meet “team standards.”
This one was over early.
Tatum erupted for 18 points in the first quarter on three 3s and White added 10 as the Celtics bolted to a 40-20 lead. Boston made 9 of 17 3s in the first quarter.
Charlotte couldn’t do anything right.
The Hornets shot 28% from the field in the opening half while turning the ball over eight times.
Tatum remained in the game until the final minute of the third quarter with Boston up 42 as the Celtics padded their point differential numbers for the NBA Cup.
He drew “MVP!” chants from the pro-Celtics crowd after drawing what appeared to be a shooting foul as he swished a 3 from 33 feet. The basket was waived off after officials ruled the foul was on the floor.
The Hornets played without starters Kon Knueppel and Moussa Diabate, and Brandon Miller left the game in the second quarter because of right groin soreness and did not return.
Miller was 3 of 10 from the field with eight points before departing and appeared frustrated at times in the first half as Boston pressured him relentlessly.
Lee did not offer a timetable for Knueppel’s return after last year’s NBA rookie of the year runner-up reinjured his hamstring on Wednesday night at Brooklyn. It was Knueppel’s first game of the season.
Up next
Celtics: At Milwaukee on Sunday night
Hornets: Host Cleveland on Monday night

title: Watch Bangor native hit clutch 3-pointer for Princeton men’s basketball
text:
Bangor native Landon Clark’s clutch 3-pointer lifted Princeton over Hofstra on Thursday night.
The Tigers were down 10 with just over a minute and a half to play in the second half, then battled back to give themselves a shot down the stretch. Dalen Davis found Clark on the left wing for the score, which put them up one, 58-57, with 18.2 seconds to play.
The 3-pointer was Clark’s only basket of the game, but proved to be the most important, as it completed Princeton’s double-digit comeback. The Tigers ended up winning, 60-58, to improve to 2-0 on the season.
Clark, who played for the Maine United AAU basketball team alongside the likes of Ace and Cooper Flagg, tallied six points, six assists and two steals in Princeton’s season-opening win against Carnegie Mellon on Monday. The Tigers next play Sunday at Siena.
Clark, a sophomore, was a basketball, baseball and football standout at Bangor High School before transferring to St. Paul’s School in New Hampshire, where he played hoops for three seasons and was a 1,000-point scorer. Clark is the son of Husson University football coach Nat Clark.

title: Maine drought puts pressure on Kittery water supply
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine drought puts pressure on Kittery water supply
The town manager says the Kittery Water District is reviewing and restricting new water connections as the town balances water availability with future growth
Maine drought puts pressure on Kittery water supply
The town manager says the Kittery Water District is reviewing and restricting new water connections as the town balances water availability with future growth
An ongoing drought is putting significant pressure on Kittery's water supply, prompting the local water district to review and restrict new water connection, according to the town manager.
In a statement Thursday, Town Manager Amie Hendrix said the Kittery Water District's decision reflects its responsibility to maintain reliable service for existing customers.
Hendrix said the town continues to face a need for housing, economic development and infrastructure investment despite challenges with its water supply.
The Water District is conducting long-term planning and investigating additional water sources to better understand future supply options.
Hendrix also emphasized that Kittery has not imposed a town-wide development moratorium.
Town officials say water availability, wastewater capacity and future growth must all be considered as the community plans for its future.

title: UMaine announces retirement incentive for 158 faculty amid budget shortfall
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The University of Maine announced a voluntary Special Retirement Incentive (SRI) on Thursday, Nov. 5, for 158 eligible faculty members as part of ongoing efforts to address a projected $19 million budget deficit for fiscal year 2028. Faculty who choose to participate will receive a one-time payment equal to 100% of their annual base salary upon retirement on Sept. 1, 2027. A University of Maine System (UMS) official and the UMaine Faculty Senate president provided statements to the Maine Campus about the retirement incentive.
The announcement came in a letter to university employees signed by UMaine President Joan Ferrini-Mundy, Executive Vice President for Academic Affairs and Provost Gabriel Paquette and Vice President for Human Resources Nicole Lawrence.
According to the letter, faculty members at UMaine and its regional campus in Machias are eligible if “they are at least 55 years old and have at least 10 years of full-time equivalent service” as of Nov. 1, 2026. Faculty who are participating in a Partial Phased Retirement Plan will receive a prorated payment. The letter does not specify whether the university plans to replace retiring faculty members or leave their positions vacant.
UMS committed up to $6 million in one-time funding to support the incentive, with a portion of that funding also available for a SRI program at UMaine Farmington.
This new incentive was approved by the Associated Faculties of the University of Maine (AFUM), which is a union representing faculty members. According to the letter, represented and nonrepresented faculty members were notified of their eligibility earlier this week.
In a Nov. 6 written statement to the Maine Campus, UMS Chief External and Governmental Affairs Officer Samantha Warren confirmed that eligible faculty have until Jan. 2, 2027, to decide whether to participate. Warren stated that the number of faculty who accept the incentive, along with “resulting budgetary impacts for FY28 and future years” will remain unknown until after the deadline.
Warren added that “student affordability and State appropriations that have not kept pace with rising operating costs,” has resulted in “financial and enrollment pressures across Maine’s public universities.” She wrote that these pressures, attributed in part to “changes in federal funding and policy” is not a challenge unique to UMaine — citing similar budget deficit issues at schools like the University of Minnesota and the University of Oregon.
Participation in the SRI program is voluntary. The UMaine President’s Office stated this is “a deeply personal decision” for the 158 contacted individuals and that “no faculty member will be treated differently because of the choice they make.”
The move follows months of concerns over potential faculty and staff reductions at UMaine. On Sept. 17, the UMaine President’s Office announced plans to address the projected $19 million budget gap through measures that could include faculty retrenchments and staff layoffs. That initial proposal called for $10 million in reductions to Academic Affairs expenses, including the elimination of vacant positions and potential cuts to academic programs.
UMaine United, a coalition of university unions and organizations, responded by holding an emergency town hall on Oct. 26 to oppose the proposed cuts. Faculty, staff, students and state lawmakers spoke about the potential effects on academic programs and student services.
At the meeting, UMaine Faculty Senate President Brian McGill criticized the administration’s lack of shared governance in addressing the budget deficit.
“How’d we get here, where are we going, what are the consequences of these cuts and what’s the impact gonna be?” asked McGill. “We’re taxpayers and this is a public institution and every single taxpayer has the right to know this information.”
In a Nov. 6 written statement to the Maine Campus, McGill said he does not expect many eligible faculty members to accept the retirement incentive, citing the lack of continued health insurance coverage.
”I do not anticipate a high acceptance rate. There is no bridge for health insurance — so you basically have to be 65 and qualify for Medicare or be married to somebody who gets insurance,” wrote McGill.
Democratic state Rep. Amy Roeder, who represents House District 23 and is an adjunct theater professor at UMaine, raised the question of the budget deficit’s impact on students at the Oct. 26 emergency town hall.
“I have a question about these proposed cuts. What exactly are students supposed to get less of? Less feedback on their work, less help finding the courses they need to graduate, longer waits for counseling, fewer people answering their financial aid questions?” said Roeder.
According to the UMaine President’s Office letter, university officials will work with academic and administrative leaders to “plan for continuity in teaching, research, student support, university operations and service to the state.”
UMaine’s fiscal year 2028 budget proposal is due to the University of Maine System in late January 2027. According to Warren, the UMS Board of Trustees will review the proposal and provide “multiple opportunities for public input before a final vote in May.”
Additional budget updates will be provided as more information becomes available. Budget materials, previous presentations and a form for submitting suggestions are available on the UMaine president’s website.
This story is developing and updates will be provided as they become available. Email news@mainecampus.com with any relevant information.

title: Husson University offers free tuition to five Aroostook County students
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Husson University is offering free tuition to five qualified high school students from Aroostook County through a new scholarship.

title: Judge accepts ex-NFL star Antonio Brown's guilty plea to reduced charge, sentences probation
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Former NFL star Antonio Brown pleaded guilty Friday to aggravated assault with a firearm in connection with a 2025 shooting outside a celebrity boxing match in Miami.
Judge Marisa Tinkler Mendez sentenced Brown to three years of probation during which time he will have to attend weekly counseling sessions and not possess a firearm, among other conditions.
He would not have any criminal conviction under the plea and could seek an early termination of probation at about the halfway mark of the sentence so long as all terms are met.
The plea to the reduced charge, which Brown entered in state court in Miami, allows the All-Pro wide receiver to avoid prison time.
Brown had initially been charged with attempted murder after police say he grabbed a handgun from a security staffer at the event and fired two shots at a man he had been in a fistfight with earlier.

title: 21-unit condo complex approved in Gorham
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Gorham officials approved a 21-unit condominium development this week at 157 South St. near the town’s center.
The townhouse-style development, called Southridge Condominium Association, will replace an abandoned home on the 4.3-acre property. It will consist of five structures and 29 parking spaces that will be concentrated close to the front of the parcel, with the back area remaining wooded. The two-story condos will be 1,020 square feet and have two bedrooms.
Developer Anthony Fernandez, a Gorham resident, said the goal of the subdivision is to provide more affordable housing. The units will be priced between $370,000 and $430,000, and the complex will cost over $7 million to construct.
Fernandez said he is unsure when construction will start due to the town’s post-approval process and the winter approaching. He has built a few houses and rents some properties in Gorham, and has helped work on small subdivisions in Old Orchard Beach and Saco.
The condos will have dark siding, white covered porches out front and decks in the back, according to Fernandez.
“I drive by it every day, so I want it to look decent and (be) something I can be proud of,” Fernandez said.
Fernandez said he will add a small trail loop in the woods on the property and a lawn with a picnic table and park benches.
Some neighbors wrote to the Gorham Planning Board expressing concerns about a townhouse-style complex disrupting the character of a neighborhood of primarily single-family homes.
“We respectfully ask the developer to reconsider this approach and provide more substantial and inviting porches, along with a more interesting and visually pleasing façade, that will help the development better blend into the existing neighborhood,” wrote Nathan Frazee and Alison Frazee, who live nearby.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: One More Warm Day Friday Before Rain and Colder Temperatures Return This Weekend
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Thursday. We’ve enjoyed another unusually warm day across the region today, with temperatures climbing well above average for this time of year. Despite plenty of cloud coverage, southerly winds have continued to introduce warmer air into the region, keeping temperatures in the 60s for many locations. We’re looking at one more day of above average temperatures tomorrow before some noticeable changes arrive heading into the upcoming weekend. Another area of low pressure is expected to bring widespread rainfall to the region Saturday and Sunday, along with much cooler temperatures. While this isn’t necessarily the best news for anyone with outdoor plans this weekend, the additional rainfall could provide some much needed relief from our ongoing drought conditions.
Temperatures overnight tonight aren’t expected to cool off very much, with the warmer air mass we’ve been enjoying remaining in place for another night. Most locations across Aroostook County should have no problem staying in the upper 40s to lower 50s, which is considerably warmer than our average low temperatures for early November. Caribou, Presque Isle and Houlton are all expected to see temperatures hovering around 53 degrees overnight tonight. For comparison, the average low temperature in Caribou for this time of year is only around 30 degrees. We’ll also be watching for some lingering shower activity across the region this evening, although I expect most of this activity to taper off as we work our way through the overnight hours. Mostly cloudy skies will remain in place, with some patchy fog also possible heading into tomorrow morning. Winds will remain relatively light, generally coming from a southwesterly direction.
Friday looks to feature another round of unusually warm temperatures across the region. We’re still looking at plenty of cloud coverage throughout the day tomorrow, but some breaks of sunshine will be possible during the morning and early afternoon hours. High temperatures for most locations should have no problem reaching the lower to mid 60s, with Caribou and Presque Isle expected to reach around 64 degrees, while Houlton could climb to 66 degrees. To put those readings into perspective, the average high temperature in Caribou for November 6th is only around 44 degrees. That means we’re looking at another day with temperatures running nearly 20 degrees above average. I think we’ll have a decent opportunity to get outside and enjoy the warmer weather tomorrow before things take a turn for the worse this weekend. While I can’t completely rule out an isolated shower, I’m expecting most locations to remain dry during the daytime hours Friday.
Unfortunately, the warmer temperatures aren’t expected to stick around much longer. A developing area of low pressure will begin approaching the region Friday night, bringing a return to more unsettled weather. As this system approaches, winds will begin shifting to a more northerly direction, allowing cooler air to work its way back into Aroostook County. Rain chances are expected to increase Friday night, especially across central and southern portions of the region, before spreading northward throughout the day Saturday. I expect Saturday to be a rather gloomy day across the region, with plenty of cloud coverage and periods of rain. Temperatures will also be noticeably cooler, with highs struggling to climb out of the lower to mid 40s for many locations.
The latest rainfall potential map from the Weather Prediction Center does a nice job illustrating where the greatest rainfall totals are expected over the next week. You’ll notice that the higher totals are generally favored across central and southern portions of the region, while northern and western Aroostook County are expected to receive somewhat less rainfall. Given the ongoing drought conditions across much of northern Maine, any additional rainfall is certainly welcome news. We’ve already managed to pick up some beneficial rainfall earlier this week, and another round of widespread rain this weekend could help us continue making some progress. Unfortunately, I don’t think this will be enough to completely eliminate our precipitation deficit, but it’s certainly a step in the right direction.
For more details on tomorrow’s unusually warm temperatures and what to expect from our next round of widespread rainfall this weekend, make sure to check out my First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening!

title: Scientists discovered an unknown baby right whale off Canada. They say it's a cause for joy
text:
PORTLAND, Maine (AP) — It would seem difficult to miss a 15,000-pound (6,804-kilogram) baby, but for months scientists who study rare whales did just that, and now they couldn’t be happier.
Researchers in Canada captured images of an unidentified baby North Atlantic right whale, one of the rarest sea mammals in the world, off Anticosti Island in Quebec in September. Scientists with the New England Aquarium in Boston said this week that after analyzing photos and data about right whales, they have determined it was a calf likely born months ago that went unseen during winter surveys for the giant animals.
The discovery puts the number of baby right whales discovered from the most recent birthing season at 24, the most productive year for the whales since 2009 and the fourth-highest count on record, the aquarium said. The whales number only about 380 in the world, and their population has fallen since 2010.
The whale was seen with its mother, a 38-year-old whale known to researchers as Silt, scientists said. Right whales give birth off the southeastern U.S. in winter before venturing north to New England and Canada to feed.
The whales are extensively cataloged with photography by researchers because they are so rare. It’s also rare for the researchers who study the whales to miss a baby, but the discovery was a welcome surprise, said Amy Warren, a scientist at the New England Aquarium’s Anderson Cabot Center.
“Silt was briefly seen in the southeastern U.S. calving grounds in February 2026, so it’s possible she had the calf there but snuck away before they were documented together. This is an exciting discovery for us so late in the year,” Warren said.
Baby right whale births are closely tracked by scientists because the tiny population needs successful calving years to remain viable. There are only about 70 reproductive-age females left in the population, and scientists have said the whales have reached 20 calves in a season only a few times since 2010.
That was when their numbers started falling, as they lost about 25% between 2010 and 2020. The whales are vulnerable to collisions with large ships and entanglement in commercial fishing gear, and the warming of the ocean has heightened those threats because they have strayed from protected areas, scientists have said. They also suffered a disastrous year in 2018 when no babies were born.
Recent years have been slightly more encouraging, as the whales have gained back some of their population since 2020. But conservationists have decried recent moves by the U.S. government to delay new protections for the whales for a decade in favor of commercial fishing interests.
The baby whale sighted off Quebec was spotted by researchers with Mingan Island Cetacean Study, a nonprofit research organization in the province’s coastal Côte-Nord region. The whale wasn’t seen by researchers despite boat-based and aerial surveys along the U.S. East Coast all spring and summer, the New England Aquarium said.
Scientists are celebrating the animal’s addition to a successful breeding season for the rare whales, said Richard Sears, founder and director of Mingan Island Cetacean Study.
“It just goes to show you how big the ocean is, and how those animals can get lost out there,” he said.

title: Farmers' Almanac Predicts Thanksgiving Weather For Maine
text:
Believe it or not, Thanksgiving is right around the corner. Thanksgiving remains one of the busiest travel holidays during the year meaning the weather forecast is ultra important.
While local weather professionals in Maine will wait much closer to the actual holiday to make their predictions, the Farmers' Almanac never hesitates to make their Thanksgiving weather outlook available early.
And for 2026, the Farmers' Almanac prediction brings good news.
Farmers' Almanac Predicts Good Weather Over Thanksgiving Weekend For Maine
Typically, Thanksgiving weekend forecasts are not sunshine and rainbows. But the Farmers' Almanac weather prediction for Thanksgiving this year really is sunshine.
The Farmers' Almanac predicts that weather from Maine through New York will be fair. The temperatures could be cool but those that travel both short and long distances should not expect much, if any, precipitation.
The only exception will be places in higher elevation, where snow flurries are part of the Thanksgiving forecast from the Farmers' Almanac.
Farmers' Almanac Has Already Predicted a 'Tricky' Winter For Maine
The Farmers' Almanac 2026-2027 winter forecast is rather bleak for the entire country. The effects of El Nino will be felt from coast to coast.
Throughout New England, the Farmers' Almanac calls for lots of precipitation. In Maine, inland areas and the mountains should see regular snowstorms which will be great for skiers.
It's the coast that is in for a 'tricky' winter. The Farmers' Almanac predicts that the heavy dose of storms from El Nino will bring mixed precipitation to Maine's coast. That will come in form of sleet and the dreaded freezing rain.
The Farmers' Almanac also predicts more dramatic cold snaps for Maine than the state has seen in recent years. Those cold snaps typically produce single-digit or below-zero temperatures.

title: Online magazine Salon, an early staple of internet discourse, announces it will shut down
text:
Online magazine Salon, an early staple of internet discourse, announces it will shut down
Salon, one of the early internet's most influential websites that featured sharp voices and political and cultural journalism with a liberal sensibility, announced Thursday it would shut down after 31 years of publication. "It has been an extraordinary privilege," the outlet said in a farewell note.
The announcement, seen as a surprise, cited the fact that "the business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years." It did not immediately indicate what would become of its employees, though some reported they had lost their jobs. A spokesperson for the outlet said 19 full-time employees had been affected, as well as a handful of private contractors.
"Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own," the unsigned farewell note said. "Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives."
It began shortly after the internet went big
Salon began its life in the mid-1990s, barely three years after the internet itself went mainstream and a time when the "World Wide Web" was still written out in that fashion. It launched a decade before the newspaper and print magazine markets imploded — and a decade, too, before the rise of social media fragmented the journalism world.
As its name suggested, Salon was initially styled as an online magazine and meeting place, a site where more provocative opinions and stories that might not be at home in daily newspapers or even then-dominant newsweeklies like Time or Newsweek could surface and generate discussion. It quickly became a place where writers wanted their work to appear.
"The timing was right — readers were tired of bland, market-tested media products, and the internet allowed us to launch something original, something with a strong voice," founder David Talbot said on the outlet's five-year anniversary in 2000.
It drew a cadre of high-profile writers and people who would become famous, including Jake Tapper and Glenn Greenwald. Two of its editors-in-chief, Talbot and Joan Walsh, went on to become prominent progressive political voices as well.
As the internet grew, so did Salon's competition. Slate emerged the following year, and soon after, online magazines became the order of the day. Eventually, older print publications like The Atlantic began putting more content online and the marketplace of online ideas grew. Salon used Princess Diana's death in 1997 to go beyond its culture-and-criticism roots and wade into breaking-news coverage.
Salon'sarchives will remain online for now
Salon told The Associated Press that it had no immediate plans to take down its online archives, which include three decades of stories from across the world and across topics and genres.
In its statement, Salon also made a point of thanking its readers.
"You came to Salon for the journalism, the dialogue, the essays, the criticism, the unexpected discoveries and the sense that there was a place on the internet where ideas mattered," it said. "You read, shared, challenged, subscribed, wrote to us and kept coming back. Your engagement made Salon a publication and a community, and it gave our work meaning. We are so grateful for the time you spent with us."
—
Noveck reported from New York.

title: New limits on federal student loans are steering many borrowers toward private lenders
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — New limits on federal student loans filled Chloe Frabotta with anxiety as she began studying in New York City to become a physician assistant.
The changes that took effect this fall include caps on loans for particular programs as well as limits on the amount parents can borrow to pay for their children’s schooling. Up until weeks before Frabotta, 25, started her program, it was up in the air whether it would count as a “professional” program with higher loan limits.
Amid the uncertainty, she borrowed around $6,000 in federal loans for her first trimester, taking out private loans for the rest with her mother as a cosigner.
“At least in my circles a lot of people were like, ’I guess that’s what I’m going to have to do, and I’m going to try to make it work,’” Frabotta said.
Students have been turning to private lenders to make up the difference between the cost of their educational programs and the amount they can borrow from the federal government, which offers more flexible repayment terms, the possibility of forgiveness after 10 years in public service, and — for many — lower interest rates.
It’s showing up in banks’ bottom lines. Private lender SoFi reported in late October that student loan originations hit $2.9 billion in the third quarter, nearly doubling from a year earlier. Days earlier, Sallie Mae, which controls more than half of the private student loan market, said graduate loans were up 119% year-over-year.
Trump’s ‘Big Beautiful Bill’ put new caps on student loans
President Donald Trump’s “Big Beautiful Bill” slashed the amount new graduate students can borrow. Programs designated as professional degrees face federal student loan caps of $200,000, while other graduate programs are capped at $100,000. Previously, graduate students had been able to take out federal loans up to the full cost of their degree.
For new borrowers, the changes include an overall lifetime borrowing cap of $257,500 and limits to the amount parents can borrow to pay for their children’s schooling.
When all the changes are fully phased in, more than half a million borrowers are going to need to borrow an extra $20,000 a year from somewhere other than the federal loan program, estimated Jordan Matsudaira, the director of the Postsecondary Education & Economics Research Center at American University. The hardest-hit students are in expensive programs like medicine, law and dentistry and states with a high cost of living, an analysis by the center found.
The Trump administration has argued the new limits will curb “excessive borrowing” and force schools to evaluate their costs, describing uncapped access to federal student loans as a driver of the soaring cost of college. Since the loan caps took effect, at least 40 schools have cut the cost of at least some of their programs, according to the conservative American Enterprise Institute.
But critics say most colleges cannot afford to lower tuition and have raised concerns that the changes will add new hurdles for students from poor families in particular.
Colleges are stepping in to help
At South Carolina Student Loan, graduate student borrowing increased 400% this year as it rolled out more options to help students. Some schools, like the law school at the University of Kansas, got into the lending game, too. So far, it has approved eight loans, with more in process.
Steven Freedman, associate dean of admissions at the University of Kansas School of Law, said the loans are important to help provide access to all students.
“Now, frankly, private banks get to choose who goes to law school,” he said.
At Lewis & Clark College, a private liberal arts school in Portland, Oregon, the student aid office has been seeing more private student loans. Its graduate school of education and counseling also began offering a new scholarship this fall for students in financial need because of the loan caps.
Anastacia Dillon, associate vice president for financial aid, described the changes as “really disruptive.”
At the University of Mount Saint Vincent in the Bronx, more first-year students are relying on private loans, even as the school boosted aid to students in financial need.
The private loan market boomed in the 1990s and early 2000s during an era of loan limits. After Graduate PLUS, a federal program, extended how much students could borrow up to the full cost of attendance, private lending began to collapse. But critics argue that Graduate PLUS ushered in new problems, contributing to high default rates because students were borrowing more than they could repay.
Some groups predicted the new loan caps could lead to large numbers of borrowers being denied loans from traditional lenders. But students on the whole appear to be finding ways to finance their education, even if they are turning more to private lenders, said Marc Schoonover, general manager of the lender ELFI.
“What we’re hearing and seeing now is that the number of students who truly can’t find an option is a lot smaller than many initially feared,” Schoonover said during a media call organized by the National Council of Higher Education Resources.
Students struggle to understand changes
A legal fight over which graduate programs would be deemed professional — and therefore eligible for larger loans — extended until just days before the new rule was set to take effect. Ultimately, students pursuing graduate degrees in nursing, physical therapy and several other fields were deemed eligible to take out higher federal student loan amounts — at least for now — after a federal judge blocked part of a Trump administration rule that held them to lower limits.
But that slowed software updates needed to process loans, said Kristina Ortiz Donohue, vice president for strategic enrollment and retention at the University of Mount Saint Vincent.
The last-minute changes also caused schools to delay delivering financial aid packages, Jon Witter, the CEO of Sallie Mae, said on an earnings call with investors. He said the peak lending season extended into October as a result.
Dr. Robert Harrington, dean of Weill Cornell Medicine and provost for medical affairs of Cornell University, said the school received dozens of calls from confused students and their families.
Frabotta’s physician assistant program was ultimately deemed professional and eligible for up to $50,000 annually in federal loans. But she decided to borrow just a fraction of that from the federal loan program, fearful of other changes that might be in store.
Before returning to school, she earned a bachelor’s degree from Boston College and worked as a medical assistant in a dermatology practice.
“This is what I want to do, so if this is the means of how I get there, then if I have to sacrifice at some point,” she said.
Madison Jessen, another first-year Weill Cornell Medicine physician assistant student, said the uncertainty around loan caps prompted her to use most of her savings to pay for her first semester out of pocket. Jessen said she has several younger friends who had planned to go to PA school but pivoted when the loan caps took effect.
That’s Harrington’s biggest fear.
“What we don’t want to see,” said Harrington, himself a first-generation college graduate, “is our programs just becoming the purview of people whose family can afford to pay that bill.”

title: Sheriff’s Determine Cause of Littleton Rollover
text:
AROOSTOOK COUNTY, Maine (WAGM) - An update on Tuesday’s rollover crash in Littleton that injured a Monticello man.
The Aroostook County Sheriff’s Office says it has determined the likely cause of the rollover crash on Route 1 in Littleton. The crash occurred at 5:53 p.m. Tuesday. Officials say the driver, a 65-year-old Monticello man, likely suffered a medical event and lost control of his vehicle causing it to go off the roadway and roll over. Officials say he wasn’t wearing a seat belt, but the air bags did deploy. He was taken to Houlton Regional Hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. The vehicle was towed from the scene, and one lane was partially blocked during the response. The first rollover crash that occurred on Tuesday is still under investigation.

title: Medomak Middle School Closes For Bedbug Treatment, Classes Move Remote
text:
Maine Middle School Closes To Address Bedbug Issue
Several bedbugs were found in a school Waldoboro this week, prompting school officials to close the school down to have the school professionally treated.
What's the issue?
According to the RSU 40 website, classes at the Medomak Middle School, which shares it's campus with the Medomak Valley High School on Manktown Road, were cancelled for part of this week after the insects were found.
Read More: What Led To Bangor Mall's Sudden Condemnation
School officials say there is no indication of an infestation, as of yet, on the campus, which serves over 350 middle school students from area towns of Friendship, Waldoboro, Union, Washington and Warren. But administrators are proactively addressing the situation before it can spread into something bigger that affects not only the school, but students and staff.
"We are following established protocols to minimize any potential spread and are monitoring the situation closely. Out of an abundance of caution, we have also made the decision to arrange for a comprehensive professional treatment of the entire school."
"Although there is no evidence of a larger problem, we feel this proactive approach is the best way to provide peace of mind to our students, staff and families."
How will this impact students and teachers?
Classes were canceled entirely on Thursday. Families were informed that students would take part in remote learning Friday, and continue remote learning Monday and Tuesday of next week. Schools were already scheduled to be closed for Wednesday November 11th in observance of Veterans Day.
The notice went on to recommend that all families and staff members check their own home and belongings for signs of bedbugs.
What should families be looking for at home?
The U.S. Department of Environmental Protection (aka the EPA) says finding bedbugs early can help you prevent an infestation that could get costly to clear out later. Here are some of the things they suggest you look for:
The first thing they say to check the actual bodies of people living in your home for bedbug bites.
"Bed bug bites can look like bites from other insects (such as mosquitoes or chiggers), rashes (such as eczema or fungal infections), or even hives. Some people do not react to bed bug bites at all."
The second thing you should check is your bedding and furniture.
Read More: Bangor School Buses Canceled As Flu Hits Drivers
"A more accurate way to identify a possible infestation is to look for physical signs of bed bugs. When cleaning, changing bedding, or staying away from home, look for:
Rusty or reddish stains on bed sheets or mattresses caused by bed bugs being crushed, dark spots (about this size: •), which are bed bug excrement and may bleed on the fabric like a marker would, eggs and eggshells, which are tiny (about 1mm) and pale yellow skins that nymphs shed as they grow larger, and live bed bugs."
If you find signs of bedbugs, the school asks that you reach out them and let them know, and then contact professionals immediately to begin treatment.
Here's a good video that explains how and what to look for when it comes to bedbugs.
The Centers for Disease Control says that while they are certainly not fun to deal with, as they can interrupt your sleep (they feed on your blood at night. I know, not pleasant to even think about!) the silver lining is bedbugs are not known to carry or spread disease. So I guess that's a plus? While some folks aren't bothered by their bites, others can have allergic reactions to them, so checking often for bedbugs or signs of bedbugs is advised.

title: Man convicted of 2004 killing is put to death in Florida’s 19th execution this year
text:
(AP) - Florida carried out a record-tying 19th execution of the year in an unusual instance of three states administering the death penalty on the same day.
Jesse Guardado was pronounced dead at 6:13 p.m. following a three-drug injection at a state prison in Starke. He had pleaded guilty to fatally stabbing 75-year-old Jackie Malone inside her Walton County home in 2004 before stealing her jewelry box, $80 and other valuables to buy drugs. The woman had helped him get a job and housing.
Hours earlier, Indiana executed a man for killing two children in a house fire in 2010, and in Alabama, a man was scheduled to die by injection later Thursday evening for his conviction in a fatal home robbery.
The executions were taking place the same day California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced he will commute all 548 death sentences in his state, saying that he believes “state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values.”
The announcement was a sharp contrast to Florida, where outgoing Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors. His state has carried out more than half of the 34 executions so far this year in the U.S., where capital punishment has come under renewed scrutiny following Tennessee’s failed execution of Christa Pike in September.
It is the second time since August that three states had organized executions on a single day, although it remains unusual. Prior to this year, the last time it happened was 2010.
Florida inmate apologized before receiving lethal injection
Guardado, 64, was already strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm when the curtain to the Florida death chamber went up promptly at 6:00 p.m. Asked if he had any last statement, he replied, “I would like to once again apologize for the pain and suffering I’ve caused to the victim’s family and my own family as well.”
The drugs began flowing immediately after that. About a minute later, Guardado began breathing heavily, followed by some sputtering and twitching for another minute. As the twitching subsided, the execution team warden shook Guardado and shouted his name, but got no response. A medic checked for a pulse soon after and pronounced Guardado dead.
A federal appeals court said in 2024 that Guardado received a “full and fair” hearing during the death penalty phase of his case. The U.S. Supreme Court denied his last appeal without comment earlier Thursday.
DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said he wants to bring justice to victims’ families who have often waited decades for death sentences to be carried out. He signed the death warrants that led to a state record of 19 executions in 2025. The state will set a new record if two more executions are carried out as planned later this year.
The victim’s son, Patrick Malone, spoke briefly to media witnesses after the execution. Instead of discussing his mother or her murder, he questioned those who oppose the death penalty.
“Do such people ever think about what happened to the victim or consider the unending aftermath the victim’s family endures and relives every time that terrible event comes up?” Malone said.
Alabama man drew the death penalty for a double killing
In neighboring Alabama, Michael Taylor, 54, was set to receive a lethal injection later Thursday. The state changed the execution method after a judge declared a nitrogen gas method unconstitutional.
Taylor’s attorneys objected to the last-minute switch to lethal injection since he selected nitrogen gas as his method years ago, but a judge ruled against Taylor.
In 1991, Taylor, then 19, fatally beat two people, ages 83 and 79, with a metal bar during a robbery in their Gadsden, Alabama, home. Police arrested him with the victims’ Cadillac an hour away in Birmingham.
Death penalty opponents had urged Republican Gov. Kay Ivey to reduce Taylor’s sentence to life in prison, noting his age and immaturity at the time. She declined.
Lawyers had asked for a life sentence for Indiana man
In Indiana, Jeffrey Weisheit, 50, was pronounced dead at 12:45 a.m. at the state prison in Michigan City, said Noelle Russell, spokesperson at the Department of Correction. He had no final words.
Weisheit had publicly acknowledged killing his girlfriend’s two children in a house fire in the Evansville area in 2010 but had hoped Gov. Mike Braun would grant clemency and change his sentence to life in prison. Braun declined.
Lawyers failed to persuade Braun, a Republican, to allow Weisheit to undergo brain scans in an effort to reinforce their argument that he has a history of head injuries and mental health problems that should prevent execution.
Weisheit’s last objection centered on the state’s planned use of lethal drugs purchased from a pharmacy that is facing a disciplinary hearing next week at the Indiana Pharmacy Board. The Indiana Supreme Court declined to intervene Wednesday night, though two of the five justices wanted a 10-day stay for more information about the drugs’ expiration and storage.
The execution provided “long-awaited justice for Alyssa Lynch and her brother Caleb, two innocent children whose lives were stolen in an act of unspeakable cruelty,” Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita said.
Americans have long been uneasy over the death penalty
Americans have long been divided over the death penalty, with nearly half of states banning capital punishment outright and just a handful of others carrying out most of the nation’s executions each year.
____
This story has been updated to correct that Christa Pike’s failed execution was in September, not October.
____

title: 52% of Americans think inflation will ruin the holidays, survey finds
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — More than half of Americans, about 52%, think inflation is going to ruin their holiday season, according to a WalletHub survey.
John Kiernan, managing editor at WalletHub, described the finding this way.
“We found that more than half, around 52% of Americans think inflation is going to ruin Christmas or whatever holiday you celebrate,” Kiernan said.
The survey also found 79% of respondents have a holiday budget that is the same size as last year or smaller. One in four say they are still paying off debt from last holiday season.
That is one reason getting an early start on holiday shopping may be appealing. Kiernan said 41% of people usually start shopping in October or earlier, and that it is not too late for those who have not started.
“So, we found that 41% of people said they usually start shopping for the holidays in October or earlier. If you haven’t started shopping by now, that’s fine. There’s still plenty of opportunities to save money. And that’s the main thing that people are trying to do when they start shopping earlier versus the last minute. More than two in three people believe early holiday shopping saves them money overall,” Kiernan said.
Most people surveyed say they have a holiday budget. Kiernan said it is important to plan ahead, take time looking for deals and stick to what you can afford.
WalletHub’s survey also found 56% of people do not trust AI to help them with their holiday shopping.

title: Buckets, chickens and worms: Schools reduce cafeteria food waste through compost, shared tables
text:
LAWRENCEVILLE, Ga. (AP) — At Lovin Elementary School in Lawrenceville, Georgia, students play with their food. Sort of.
Some walk around the cafeteria with buckets collecting leftover lunch scraps. These apple cores, banana peels and grape stems ultimately head to Lovin’s outdoor compost bin. Others put unopened milk in a shared refrigerator for students to grab as a snack or take home. Uneaten salad scraps are dumped into the school’s chicken coop.
Lovin Elementary, 40 miles (64 kilometers) east of Atlanta, is one example of the many U.S. schools composting, using share tables and tailoring food choices to cut how much cafeteria food ends up in the trash.
“Now there’s not a lot going to the landfill, and there’s not just scraps everywhere,” said student Aissatou Brown. “And it feels like we’re saving the planet.”
Public schools serve more than 30 million lunches each day, according to federal figures. The vast majority come from the Agriculture Department’s National School Lunch Program. But experts say tons of cafeteria food is wasted each year, costing the schools and contributing to methane in landfills. Recovery, recycling and composting have cut waste, despite challenges.
Sometimes the solutions are as simple as picking better chicken nuggets, or using clear trash bags to make the waste more visible, said Carmen Byker Shanks, director of scientific strategy at the Center for Nutrition and Health Impact.
“The reason why food waste might be happening in one school is probably different than other schools,” she said.
“When everybody’s at the table and the students are coming up with solutions, and the nutrition staff are responding to them, and the teachers are helping facilitate the conversations, I think those interventions have been pretty successful,” she added. “When we reduce food waste by helping kids eat more of their meal, we’re essentially supporting learning.”
Putting solutions into place
Lovin, which serves around 900 students, conducted its first food audit in 2018 after receiving funding through the World Wildlife Fund’s Food Waste Warriors program. Students who sorted cafeteria waste found 589 pounds (267.2 kilograms) of discarded food, including 74 pounds (33.6 kilograms) of fruit and vegetable waste and 120 pounds (54.4 kilograms) of recoverable items during one two-hour lunch period, said Gerin Hennebaul, who leads agriculture and science initiatives at Lovin.
In response, students brainstormed announcements and posters to reduce waste. Lovin introduced the designated table and refrigerator for sharing unopened cafeteria items. Food waste dropped by nearly one third in its next food audit months later.
In fall 2021, Lovin received a grant for on-site composting. Now, students collect and weigh their scraps, and Lovin’s master gardener takes them to the bin outdoors.
Volume grew as composting was expanded to each grade level, so Lovin built vermicomposting bins — using worms — and began sharing its waste with a local nonprofit, Creative Enterprises, for use in its garden.
Shared items that are unclaimed at the end of the week now stock Lovin’s food pantry for community members in need. Now, it’s not unusual for Lovin to compost around 100 pounds (45.4 kilograms) of produce waste in a week, and students often collect around 100 share table items each lunch.
“Our cafeteria, it’s just really turned into another classroom and … they don’t realize they’re even learning, but they’re learning every day,” Hennebaul said. “Hearing the kids come in and say, ‘we’re composting at our house now,’ or ‘we built a chicken coop at our home,’ or ‘hey, my family brought in XYZ for the food pantry today’ … that’s been the biggest thing, and we want to see this happen in other schools all over.”
Starting education before food even hits the plate, and other initiatives
Many schools in Baltimore City Public Schools, a district serving more than 76,000 students, have share tables, and some have composting.
Its biggest initiative is a 33-acre (13.4-hectare) learning farm that encourages students to be less wasteful by teaching them about what resources go into making food.
“It’s not really fair to expect students to be curious or excited about fruits and veggies in their cafeteria or healthy options in the cafeteria in general, if they’ve never really had a hands-on experience to interact with fruits and vegetables, harvesting, planting, tasting them right out of the ground,” said Anne Rosenthal, a farm-to-school specialist for the district.
She said many students are familiar with environmental justice issues and pollution, so reducing waste hits close to home.
“We see this as a really important step in empowering students to be part of the solution, and we’ve seen them pick it up really, really quickly in the cafeterias,” she said.
The district is also a participant in the Food Waste Warriors program, which is one of the larger independent resources helping schools fight food waste. The World Wildlife Fund program has worked with more than 1,000 schools, and it says that some have cut waste by as much as 70%.
In 2019, WWF analyzed the food waste of 46 schools in eight states, and used the data to estimate that schools nationwide could be wasting about 530,000 tons (480,807.5 metric tons) of food per year, costing them $1.7 billion, though it acknowledged it was extrapolating from a small sample of schools.
School districts are limited in what they can implement
The Agriculture Department also provides resources for schools to reduce waste, and many of the approaches overlap with those used by the schools in Baltimore and Lawrenceville. Its website includes guides for conducting food waste audits, creating share tables and giving students greater choice. Other tips include scheduling recess before lunch and extending lunchtime.
A spokesperson for the department said in an email that it also recommends schools reassess how they buy and prepare food to reduce waste.
School budgets can be a barrier to implementing new strategies, with administrators already facing tough choices on teacher salaries and classroom materials. Composting, especially when required under some state laws, might also necessitate extra staff.
Districts are also bound by federal requirements for well-balanced meals and food safety rules. Experts say those rules are important but can lessen flexibility in trying new approaches.
“There’s a ton of constraints and a ton of reasons why this doesn’t get a lot of attention,” said Pete Pearson, a World Wildlife Fund vice president. He said the current cafeteria setup doesn’t always prevent kids from throwing edible food away — even as millions of children are food insecure across the nation.
Bringing students into the process is a key part of the solution, Pearson said.
“The more that we involve the students in this whole journey, the more it’s just going to really light up.”
