title: 1 officer killed, 3 wounded in a shooting on a transit bus
text:
LAKEWOOD, Colo. (AP) — A suburban Denver officer was killed and three others were wounded during a firefight on a transit bus that ended with police fatally shooting the gunman, law enforcement authorities said Friday. A bystander also was injured.
The Lakewood officers had responded to a call Thursday evening about a suspicious person attempting to get on a public bus, police spokesperson John Romero said during a news conference. The person may have been involved in a hit-and-run earlier that day, he said.
The man began shooting when officers boarded the Regional Transportation District bus and they fired back, killing the man, authorities said in an update on social media.
The three surviving officers were in stable condition at local hospitals, police said. The bystander’s condition wasn’t known, and it wasn’t clear how they were injured. The names of those involved have not been released.
“Words cannot express the profound sorrow our department and community feel tonight over the loss of our fallen hero, who made the ultimate sacrifice in service to Lakewood,” the police department posted on social media. “Our hearts are heavy, and we stand shoulder-to-shoulder with their loved ones, lifting them up in unwavering support, love, and prayer during this unimaginable time.”
Police said they planned to give another update on Friday.
The shootout happened at a busy intersection about 5 miles (8 kilometers) west of downtown Denver.
A witness, Teddy O’Brien, told NBC affiliate KUSA-TV that he and several other drivers were stopped next to the bus at a red light when the shooting happened. He said several police cruisers surrounded the bus before officers rushed to it with guns and flashlights drawn.
“They hopped on and then shots instantly started ringing from there,” he said. “I instantly just saw shots firing and I ducked down, because you know I’m freaking out at that point.”
O’Brien said he saw only one or two people on the bus besides the driver. He said he heard about 30 or 40 gunshots and saw smoke and flashes of light coming from both the front and back of the bus.
At a hospital after the shooting, dozens of area police officers gathered outside and a bagpiper played “Amazing Grace” in tribute to the officer who was killed. A long procession of police vehicles then left the hospital.
Condolences to the officers and their families poured in on social media.
Gov. Jared Polis and others said they were heartbroken.
“Law enforcement put their lives on the line for our safety everyday,” Polis said in a statement. “Thank you to law enforcement who run into danger to keep us safe and to protect our communities.”
Denver Mayor Mike Johnston said police from his city were assisting Lakewood officials.
The Regional Transportation District said it is deeply concerned by the shooting and is fully cooperating with police as they conduct their investigation.
Colorado State Patrol said in a statement that their hearts are broken over the death of the officer.
“To the three additional Lakewood Agents who were injured in tonight’s shooting, we are sending our deepest prayers, strength and best wishes for a full recovery,” the statement said.

title: 4 Cornell lawsuit defendants join effort to oust Letitia James from investigation
text:
4 Cornell lawsuit defendants join effort to oust Letitia James from criminal investigation
Four men named in a former Cornell University student’s lawsuit are joining an effort to block New York’s attorney general from leading a reopened criminal investigation into the woman’s gang rape allegations, according to court filings on Thursday.
The men agreed to be added to a co-defendant’s court petition seeking Attorney General Letitia James' removal from the case because of social media posts she made prior to her involvement in which she condemned the alleged assault and expressed support for the accuser.
The development comes a day after James appointed Jacqueline Kelly, a former federal prosecutor who oversaw a sex crimes case against music mogul Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs, as outside counsel for the investigation. She and a team of lawyers and investigators will be responsible for evidence gathering, witness interviews and other investigative steps. They will report to James.
A judge heard arguments last week on one accused man’s request to remove James but said he wouldn't rule without knowing if the six other lawsuit defendants backed the effort. He gave the man’s lawyers until Thursday to try to get them to join.
Four agreed to join, including one whose lawyers had previously filed court papers seeking to have James removed. The two others didn't have lawyers and did not respond, court filings said.
James' office declined to comment.
A former Cornell student identified in court papers as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit in September alleging that several men raped her at a fraternity party in 2024. The woman said some of the men pressured her into using ketamine and marijuana and that she drank alcohol that left her too intoxicated to consent. Not all of the men named were accused of rape.
James, a Democrat, posted about the case on X and Facebook on Sept. 28, linking to a news article about the lawsuit. “I’m holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you’re not alone. We stand with you.”
On Oct. 1, Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed James as special prosecutor overseeing the criminal investigation, saying that she had lost faith in the local district attorney, who declined to bring charges in 2024 but had said he would restart the investigation following the former student’s lawsuit.
James initially declined to comment about her social media posts but addressed them at an Oct. 8 debate, saying: “Those comments demonstrate empathy, and what we need now more than ever in our body politic is more empathy."
In court, the state’s lawyers argued that Hochul has wide latitude to appoint special prosecutors and said she picked James because of her track record handling sensitive cases in the national spotlight.
In a statement on Wednesday, James said she is confident that Kelly “will lead a fair and comprehensive investigation.”
Andrew Miltenberg, a lawyer for the man spearheading the removal effort, said in a court filing that Kelly's appointment “changes the face of the investigation" but "does not establish any change in ultimate authority.”

title: Voters in 8 Maine towns approved measures capping or freezing mobile home lot rents
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Voters in eight Maine towns approved measures on Election Day that will cap or freeze lot rent increases for mobile home park residents.
Most residents own their mobile homes but not the land underneath them. And as more out-of-state corporations have purchased Maine mobile home parks recently, many residents are facing drastic rent increases.
Voters approved rent stabilization measures in Augusta, Eliot, Farmington, Jay, Oakland, Standish and Wells. Wiscasset residents also approved a six-month moratorium on lot rent increases.
Lynzy Kosmes lives in Blueberry Ridge Mobile Home Park in Wells and said she paid $325 a month five years ago. Her lot rent has since nearly doubled after a New-York based company, Philips International, purchased the park.
And Kosmes said that’s too much for many of her older neighbors on fixed incomes.
“My neighbor next door has Parkinson’s. She lives off $1,200 a month. We’re now at $625, which means half of her income goes to lot rent,” Kosmes said. “It’s really coming down to, at this point, can I heat my house? Can I buy groceries? Can I afford my medication?”
In Oakland, Rhonda West said she now pays $600 a month to rent the land beneath her home at Breens Mobile Home Park. She said monthly lot rents have increased by more than $200 since another out-of-state company purchased the park a few years ago.
It wasn’t hard to convince Oakland residents to support a measure that would provide residents with some relief, West said.
“They’re like, wait a minute, you’re paying what? And you own your home? I said yes, I own my home. I’m paying this much for a lot,” she said.
A total of 16 towns in Maine have passed mobile home rent stabilization measures in response to an influx of corporate buyers that are raising rents in some parks.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: NFL Week 9 schedule, predictions and more
text:
NFL Week 9 schedule, predictions and more
NFL Week 9 schedule, predictions and more
The halfway point of the NFL season is here. See who is gaining momentum for a second-half push and who should be ready to rebuild for 2027.
Video above: Can Patriots build on win against Dolphins?
As it currently stands in the AFC, the Bills, Jaguars, Broncos, Bengals, Chiefs, Steelers and Patriots would be in the playoffs. In the NFC, the 49ers, Bears, Giants, Buccaneers, Vikings, Lions and Seahawks would be in the playoffs.
However, no team is officially mathematically eliminated (not even the 0-7 Los Angeles Chargers).
There are 151 games left on the regular-season schedule, along with 13 playoff games. The marquee matchup of the week comes on Monday night, but before that, everything is fairly evenly matched.
Here's a look at what's ahead this week, as Matthew Peaslee of the Hearst National Team continues his predictions. Peaslee went 11-3 in his Week 8 predictions and sits at 74-46-1 on the year.
All game times are in Eastern Standard Time.
Thursday, Nov. 5
Jacksonville Jaguars (5-2) vs. Baltimore Ravens (4-4), 8:15 p.m.
The injuries continue to pile up for the Ravens. With Lamar Jackson out, Baltimore traded for quarterback Jacoby Brissett. Derrick Henry is still the centerpiece of the offense, but he can only do so much. Quarterback Trevor Lawrence leads the Jacksonville offense. In seven starts, he has completed 65.7% of his passes for 1,690 yards and 17 touchdowns. Jaguars running back Bhaysul Tuten scored a pair of rushing and receiving touchdowns, running for a career-high 104 yards on 16 carries. The Jacksonville defense forced three turnovers in a dominant win last week and should do the same on the road.
Prediction: Jaguars 28, Ravens 3
Sunday, Nov. 8
Cincinnati Bengals (5-2) vs. Atlanta Falcons (3-5), 1 p.m.
The Bengals are riding a three-game winning streak into Spain. The Falcons have been up and down this year, but are still within earshot of the AFC South lead. Both offenses have been inconsistent this season, but the Bengals are more talented from top to bottom. Joe Burrow remains the leader Cincinnati needs him to be, and that intangible sets the Bengals apart from the Falcons. His 2,115 passing yards rank him No. 4 in the NFL right now.
Prediction: Bengals 28, Falcons 21
Denver Broncos (6-2) vs. Carolina Panthers (3-4), 1 p.m.
The Broncos' dramatic win against the Chiefs last week proved that they're the real deal. Some may say that this is a trap game as they travel across the country, but the Denver defense should smother the Panthers. Alex Singleton's 101 tackles lead the league and the unit ranks fifth in the NFL with 23 sacks. This should be a low-scoring game.
Prediction: Broncos 17, Panthers 10
Dallas Cowboys (3-5) vs. Indianapolis Colts (2-6), 1 p.m.
Battered and bruised, these teams need something to bounce their way. The Cowboys blew a two-touchdown lead against the Cardinals last week, and the Colts are among the lowest-scoring offenses in the league. Dak Prescott is better than he's shown so far and should bounce back in this game. He completed 19 of 29 passes for 195 yards and a touchdown and added a five-yard rushing score, but Dallas managed only 261 total yards. Daniel Jones isn't the answer for the Indianapolis offense, but the Colts have no other suitable options.
Prediction: Cowboys 28, Colts 7
New York Jets (2-6) vs. Kansas City Chiefs (5-2), 1 p.m.
The Chiefs are 3-0 at home and need a dominant win at Arrowhead Stadium after losing their past two road games. Patrick Mahomes completed 30 of 41 passes for 321 yards, three touchdowns, including a 73-yard touchdown to Emmett Johnson. The Kansas City defense let the team down in last week's loss at Denver. The Jets also let one slip away against the Raiders but don't have the ability to bounce back like the Chiefs do this week.
Prediction: Chiefs 37, Jets 14
Detroit Lions (5-2) vs. Miami Dolphins (1-6), 1 p.m.
The Lions handed the Vikings their first loss of the season last week. This week, they can take their foot off the gas in Miami. Detroit leads the league with 395 yards per game behind Jahmyr Gibbs and Jared Goff. For as good as the offense has been, the Detroit defense has been a disappointment. But so has the Dolphins defense, as they both rank at the bottom of the NFL. The Lions defense has been battling injuries, however, and will still be shorthanded in this game.
Prediction: Jaguars 38, Colts 0
Cleveland Browns (5-3) vs. New Orleans Saints (2-5), 1 p.m.
The Browns had an opportunity to show they're for real against the archrival Steelers last week, but they blew it. Another letdown could be waiting for them this week. Deshaun Watson is likely out this week, and the offense must regroup. The Saints offense has found a solid playmaker in wide receiver Chris Olave, who is No. 5 in the NFL with 636 receiving yards. Tyler Shough is also emerging as a formidable quarterback.
Prediction: Saints 24, Browns 16
New York Giants (4-2-1) vs. Philadelphia Eagles (2-6), 1 p.m.
The Eagles are almost two years removed from a Super Bowl win, but it sure seems like it was even further off than that. The struggles have been real, and so have the calls for a change in the coaching staff. Philadelphia can get back on track with a solid win this week. It's been hard to overcome all their injuries, but after three games, Tanner McKee may have finally settled in at quarterback. Another fill-in quarterback, J.J. McCarthy, has filled in wonderfully for New York. McKee could have his opportunity to get those same accolades this week.
Prediction: Eagles 17, Giants 13
Los Angeles Rams (4-4) vs. Washington Commanders (2-4-1), 1 p.m.
This may not be the best year to brag about a win against the Eagles, but the Commanders were dominant in a primetime victory last week. If that momentum can be sustained this week, a win against the Rams would be even more impressive. But that's not likely to happen. Los Angeles should be able to get above .500 with another big game from quarterback Matthew Stafford, who has thrown for 2,146 yards this season. The Rams are fourth in the league with 384.4 yards of total offense per game. The Commanders have a strong defense and should expect another big game from quarterback Jayden Daniels, who hasn't shown many signs of slowing down. The Rams should be able to pull out a close one.
Prediction: Rams 34, Commanders 30
Houston Texans (2-5) vs. Los Angeles Chargers (0-7), 4:05 p.m.
The last team to start a season 0-8 was the 2020 New York Jets. Six years later, the Chargers are set for that same fate. Houston's pass rush remains one of the NFL's most dangerous units, led by Will Anderson Jr., who has recorded 7.5 sacks through seven games. Justin Herbert is coming off his best game of the season last week against the Rams, as he completed 75 percent of his passes for 257 yards, but he did not throw a touchdown pass and had two interceptions. The Texans' defense should make things even harder for him to get over the hump.
Prediction: Texans 22, Chargers 14
Las Vegas Raiders (4-4) vs. San Francisco 49ers (6-1), 4:25 p.m.
Kirk Cousins has been the heart and soul of the Raiders, who have already surpassed their win total from a year ago. However, Brock Purdy of the 49ers is playing at the highest level of his five-year career. For as good as Purdy has been, the San Francisco defense has been the backbone of their success, with the defense allowing just 19.9 points per game. The Raiders defense hasn't kept up with its offense, allowing 28.8 points per game.
Prediction: 49ers 38, Raiders 32
Green Bay Packers (5-3) vs. New England Patriots (5-3), 4:25 p.m.
Jordan Love vs. Drake Maye presents one of the best quarterback matchups of the season. Love has been showcasing his arm in Green Bay's recent wins as he now leads the league with 2,246 passing yards. With a 5-3 record, it's also hard to believe the Packers are last in the NFC North — it's just such a competitive division. The Patriots' 5-3 record puts them in second in the AFC East, way ahead of the Jets and Dolphins and slightly behind the Bills. The Packers' defense gives them a slight edge.
Prediction: Packers 30, Patriots 17
Arizona Cardinals (3-5) vs. Seattle Seahawks (4-4), 4:25 p.m.
The Seahawks are heavy favorites at home. Seattle's defense is led by Ernest Jones, who is third in the NFL with 81 tackles, as the unit is first, allowing just 250 yards per game. But it's the Seahawks' offense that has been so consistent, with Jaxon Smith-Njigba's 985 receiving yards.
Prediction: Seahawks 38, Cardinals 24
Tampa Bay Buccaneers (3-5) vs. Chicago Bears (6-2), 8:20 p.m.
The Bears have been playing confidently and should have enough moxie to come out with a win in front of a raucous night crowd. Chicago is third in the league in total offense with 387 yards per game and should run all over the struggling Tampa Bay defense.
Prediction: Bears 27, Buccaneers 17
Monday, Nov. 9
Buffalo Bills (6-1) vs. Minnesota Vikings (6-1), 8:15 p.m.
The Vikings' defense should lead them to victory in a marquee matchup. While the Bills do have the second-best offense in the league, Minnesota has the second-best defense. And though the Bills enter on a three-game winning streak and the Vikings have stumbled a bit in the weeks following their bye, the home crowd should lift Minnesota to the best record in the NFL.
Prediction: Vikings 27, Bills 17

title: Police rule Aroostook pedestrian death accidental
text:
Glare from the setting sun caused an Oct. 3 crash that left a Presque Isle pedestrian dead, a city official said Friday.
Shelby Sanborn, 68, was walking west on the Ginn Road at about 6:18 p.m. when a westbound 2015 GMC Sierra pickup, driven by 18-year-old Silas Baser, hit him from behind, city spokesperson Kim Smith said in a release.
The Presque Isle Police Department ruled the crash accidental because Baser had been blinded by the setting sun.
Investigators simulated the scenario under matching light conditions, which revealed that someone in Sanborn’s position on the road, wearing a reflective vest, couldn’t be seen by a driver until they were about 100 feet away, Smith said.
Police determined Baser was neither impaired nor speeding. There also were no adverse weather, traffic or road conditions.
Baser had been on a hands-free phone call, which had ended before the crash, Smith said.
Maine State Police approved the Presque Isle police crash reconstruction, she said.
No charges will be filed.
Police urged drivers to slow down when the sun is low and for pedestrians to walk facing oncoming traffic and wear bright or reflective clothing.

title: Houston mayor signs order to limit cooperation with ICE, says 'elections matter' after Democrats win
text:
HOUSTON (AP) — The mayor of Houston on Friday said the city would limit cooperation with federal immigration authorities, heralding “a new model” of immigration enforcement after Democrats won power in Texas for the first time in decades.
Mayor John Whitmire said the city would go after immigrants “that pose a danger, not those that are going about their family business, work and education.”
A traffic incident “will not even … you write a citation or you warn them and they go about their way. No contact with (U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement) over nonviolent, non-jailable offenses. It reduces the fear and anxiety.”
The move by the nation’s fourth-largest city is one of the first steps to curb ICE’s powers since Tuesday’s election.
Under the mayor’s new directive, Houston police should contact ICE only if the person it stops is arrested on a charge that is subject to jailing or if ICE issues an administrative warrant, which is an order signed by a senior ICE official indicating that the person is wanted by immigration officials.
“The fact that a person is, or is suspected to be, subject to immigration enforcement shall not, by itself, be a basis to contact ICE, to prolong any detention, or to take any person into or hold any person in custody,” the two-page order states.
The Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in Houston has sparked protests after an ICE officer fatally shot a Mexican homebuilder this summer and another struck a man with a car.
Spokespersons for ICE did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment on the mayor’s announcement.
A grand jury last week indicted ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Prosecutors say Morales intentionally rammed his car into Miguel Parra Hernandez, whose leg was broken. ICE has asserted that Parra Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle, an account that prosecutors say is contradicted by video.
Despite a one-time $75 billion infusion from Congress, ICE remains heavily dependent on local police to find people subject to deportation and turn them over. It has done so partly by signing about 2,600 agreements — many in Texas — to deputize local police and other state and local agencies to enforce immigration laws. Texas has been a primary target for ICE arrests.
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott has closely aligned the state with the Trump administration to collaborate on enforcing federal immigration laws. He lost his bid for a fourth term to Democrat Gina Hinojosa.
FIEL, an immigrant rights group in Houston that has been working with the family of Parra Hernandez, planned to hold a press conference Friday afternoon in light of the announcement.
“Today Houston won. The City of Houston city council had already decided this months ago,” said Cesar Espinosa, executive director of FIEL Houston, adding that it was time to follow through.
—-
Wilder reported from Austin, Texas; Spagat reported from San Diego.

title: Owner charged after several horses die in flood; refused to let neighbors help move animals to higher ground, sheriff says
text:
CAMP VERDE, AZ (AZFamily/Gray News) — An arrest has been made following an investigation involving several horses that died during recent flooding in Arizona.
The Camp Verde Marshal’s Office said on Thursday that the suspect, whose name has not been released, is facing animal cruelty charges.
On Sunday, first responders were called to a property following reports that several horses were trapped in rising floodwaters. Investigators said emergency personnel and neighbors offered to help move the horses to higher ground, but the owner refused to release them from their enclosures.
The marshal’s office said the owner received repeated warnings about worsening weather but didn’t move the horses before floodwaters overtook them.
Crews spent the following days searching for the horses. While four horses were rescued, three were found dead. Four other horses are missing and presumed dead.
Investigators collected evidence, spoke with witnesses and emergency responders and reviewed veterinary evaluations before arresting the horses’ owner.
“The Camp Verde Marshal’s Office recognizes and appreciates the extraordinary efforts of Copper Canyon Fire and Medical Authority, Emergency Equine Evacuation, veterinary professionals, neighboring residents, and volunteers who worked tirelessly under extremely dangerous conditions to save these animals,” the agency posted on Facebook. “Animal welfare is a responsibility that should never be taken lightly. Animals depend on their owners for appropriate care, protection and safety, particularly during emergencies and natural disasters.”
More than 100 homes were damaged, a dozen of which are a total loss, after severe flooding in Camp Verde.

title: Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms adds Tyler Perry to transition team
text:
Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms adds Tyler Perry to transition team
Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms won her election Tuesday, defeating Republican Rick Jackson. She will become the first Black woman to serve as governor in U.S. history.
On Friday, she announced her first steps to prepare for office, which include establishing a transition team. One of the most prominent names on that team will be actor and producer Tyler Perry.
Bottoms introduced Perry as "an entertainment mogul who is also a huge philanthropic part of our Georgia community and owns Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta."
Perry, born in Louisiana, has lived in Atlanta for most of the past 35 years. He founded Tyler Perry Studios in 2006 and opened the first location in 2008. The production moved to a much larger location in 2019, where he has shot many of his projects since. "House of Payne," the long-running TV show that he created, is also set in Atlanta.
In recent years, Perry has faced allegations of sexual misconduct. In June 2025, Derek Dixon, an actor in a couple of Perry's productions, filed a lawsuit accusing Perry of committing acts of sexual assault and sexual battery against him since 2021.
Dixon requested $260 million in damages.
In December 2025, another actor who appeared in a Perry-led movie, Mario Rodriguez, filed a $77 million sexual battery lawsuit in California state court against both Perry and Lionsgate. However, text messages were later released that seemed to discredit some of Rodriguez's claims against Perry.
Other notable names on Bottoms' transition team include Arthur Blank, co-founder of Home Depot and owner of the Atlanta Falcons, and Roz Brewer, the former CEO of Sam's Club and COO of Starbucks.
Before winning the gubernatorial election, Bottoms served as mayor of Atlanta and as an advisor in the Biden administration.

title: Inside Alcor’s bid to pause death and the questions still unanswered
text:
SCOTTSDALE, AZ (InvestigateTV) — People frozen for years then thawed out and awake in a different time. It’s a common scene in popular science fiction movies.
But this isn’t the script of a blockbuster, a nonprofit in Arizona is attempting to make it a reality. Since the 1970s, Alcor has specialized in cryonics, defined as the practice of preserving life by pausing the dying process using subfreezing temperatures.
Alcor is betting on future science to do what today’s cannot.
In an unassuming building tucked inside an industrial section of Scottsdale, a small team at the Alcor Life Extension Foundation is working on something that can sound like science fiction: preserving people, and even pets, at ultra-low temperatures with the hope that future medicine may one day be able to repair and revive them.
For Alcor member and author Rick Lemler, the idea isn’t about certainty. It’s about possibility.
“It’s something I choose to believe,” Lemler said. “It’s something I believe in and am willing to gamble.”
Lemler said his fascination with sci-fi goes back to childhood, and now, he’s taken steps to make what once felt like a fantasy part of his real-life plan. He has signed up to be cryopreserved after legal death, joining hundreds of Alcor members whose bodies or heads are stored in large vacuum-insulated containers called dewars.
“Here I am almost becoming a real-life character of my own books,” Lemler said. “So that’s kind of cool.”
The concept has long drawn skepticism—and controversy—because of the central question: Are they trying to bring people back to life?
Alcor CEO James Arrowood said that framing misses the point.
“I think the question really is, how does this make any sense,” Arrowood said. “Are we trying to bring people back from the dead? That’s actually a crude understanding of what this is.”
Alcor’s goal is to preserve cells and tissue as intact as possible through a process called vitrification, using chemicals and controlled cooling to prevent the ice crystals that typically form during freezing and can destroy cellular structures. Arrowood said one of the key solutions used, called M22, helps prevent ice from forming inside the tissue.
“In simplest terms, this is sort of a biological antifreeze,” he said. “Just like you put in your car engine, so it doesn’t crack—there’s literally ice outside of this. There is no ice inside of it.”
If vitrification can reliably preserve healthy cells without damage, Arrowood said it could have implications beyond cryonics, particularly in organ donation and transplantation, where time and tissue degradation are constant obstacles.
Rapid response after death
When an Alcor member dies, Arrowood said a specialized response team moves quickly. The team, often referred to as the “DART” team and made up of medically trained personnel, including former military members, begins cooling the body and preparing it for vitrification as soon as legally possible.
From there, Alcor’s internal medical staff continues a process that can take about a week, including replacing blood with preservation solutions and gradually lowering the temperature so the patient can be stored in liquid nitrogen.
Members can choose whole-body preservation or “neuro” preservation, which stores only the head, based on the belief that the structures associated with memory and identity are housed in the brain.
Once preparation is complete, patients are placed inside a dewar, a large container designed to hold liquid nitrogen at roughly -320 degrees Fahrenheit.
A wall of faces and unanswered questions
Inside Alcor, photos of members line the walls.
Arrowood said that when Lemler’s time comes, his picture will be added, alongside people from around the world, including one of Alcor’s youngest members: a 2-year-old girl from Thailand who died from brain cancer.
The organization’s history includes high-profile disputes that still circulate online, including legal battles and calls for greater regulation decades ago. Arrowood acknowledges the past but said much of what people cite is old.
“Many of these things are 30 to 40 years old,” he said. “That’s not uncommon anytime you’re in the technology space.”
He said that in more recent years, the conflicts that arise are often tied to logistics and finances—particularly life insurance policies used to fund preservation.
Not everyone believes cryonics can deliver what many consumers imagine.
Dr. Arthur Caplan, a bioethicist with NYU Grossman School of Medicine, called the idea of freezing a body, or a head, with the expectation of revival far-fetched.
“If you’re selling something and saying, ‘I can freeze your body. Someday doctors of the future will wake it up,’ or ‘I can freeze your head and someday doctors of the future will wake it up and stick it on another body or a robot’—what I say is preposterous,” Caplan said.
Caplan points to several barriers he believes science has not solved. The freezing process itself, achieving the correct chemical balance for preservation, and then, especially in neuro preservation, figuring out how a brain could function if it were ever removed from storage and placed elsewhere.
“If you were going to sort of take your brain and put it on another body,” Caplan said, “you are going to get signals coming in from the nerves of that body. That the old brain isn’t going to know how to process.”
Still, Caplan said one related goal could become realistic: using advanced preservation to improve organ banking and medical repair.
“Could we get someday to the point where we could freeze a kidney, freeze some cells that could be used to repair the heart? Yes,” he said. “I think that is possible.”
Arrowood is blunt about the uncertainty.
“I am the president and I am telling you that I don’t know if this will ever work,” he said. “And it may not work for me at all. In fact, I am perfectly OK with that.”
He compared the gamble to early medical breakthroughs with steps that initially seemed impossible but paved the way for modern medicine.
“The first heart transplant patient knew he would die a week or two later,” Arrowood said. “He did it because 30 years forward, his grandchildren—if they needed a heart—could get one and would live a full life.”
For Lemler, the choice is deeply personal, but rooted in the same idea, that the alternative is final.
Asked whether he fears it may never work, Lemler said he thinks of it differently.
“Concerned,” he said. “I know there is a good chance that it might not. But I don’t feel like I’m losing anything in the bargain here.”
What it costs
Cryonics isn’t cheap. Whole-body preservation typically costs about $220,000, while neuro preservation generally ranges from $80,000 to $90,000.
For those who sign up, it’s an investment in a future that may never arrive but one they hope science can someday reach.

title: Longtime Presque Isle grocery store to reopen next week as Hannaford
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Hannaford Supermarkets will unveil its newest store in Presque Isle two weeks before Thanksgiving.
The Scarborough-based grocery chain will reopen the former Graves’ Shop ‘n Save on Friday, Nov. 13.
It will be Hannaford’s 69th Maine location and will kick off a new chapter for a longstanding neighborhood grocery store.
Graves Shop ‘n Save has been part of everyday life in Aroostook County for generations, first opening in Mars Hill by the Graves family in 1935. The independent grocer has been in Presque Isle since 1959 and in its current location at 797 Main St. since 1970.
Many people in the community worked their first jobs at the store and others built careers there, the Graves family said in a recent message to the community.
The family sold the store to Brandon Hopkins in December 2021, but remained involved.
“We know that change can bring emotion, questions and uncertainty, especially with a business that has been part of the community for so long,” the family said. “But we want this message to be a positive one.”
Hannaford plans to build on the family’s legacy, Hannaford spokesman Zach Blanchard said Thursday.
“Customers will continue to see many familiar faces and products, including our selection of high-quality Hannaford brand items,” Blanchard said. “We’re proud to begin this next chapter and deepen our connection with the Presque Isle community.”
Following the acquisition of Graves Shop ‘n Save earlier this year, the New England supermarket giant has been planning upgrades throughout the 35,000-square-foot store, officials said.
To prepare for the Nov. 13 grand opening, the Presque Isle store will temporarily close at 2 p.m. on Monday, Nov. 9, and reopen under the Hannaford banner at 7 a.m. Friday, Nov. 13.
The Presque Isle Pharmacy, an independently operated pharmacy inside the store, will continue to operate during the closure, according to officials. Customers can directly access the pharmacy or opt for curbside pickup, Blanchard said.
A full-service Hannaford pharmacy will open in December. Any active prescriptions will automatically transfer to Hannaford.
“This pharmacy has proudly served the Presque Isle community for years,” Wendy Boynton, director of pharmacy operations at Hannaford, said. “We know how important it is for our customers to feel welcome and supported when it comes to their health. As we look ahead to this next chapter, we’re committed to continuing to serve the community with care.”
Blanchard expects the store to employ approximately 80 Hannaford staff, including many of the same people who have worked there for years. They will also be hiring for some positions, he said.
“This store has earned the trust of generations of customers and we’re honored to carry that legacy forward,” Todd Bullen, Hannaford vice president of retail operations, said in a previous interview. “Our focus is on preserving what customers value most while continuing to deliver fresh, quality products, dependable value and exceptional service in a welcoming environment.”
The Presque Isle store raises Hannaford’s number of locations to 189 in New England and New York. The company has expanded its reach in northern Maine in recent years, acquiring Paradis Shop ‘n Save stores in Fort Kent and Madawaska in 2024. Hannaford also runs supermarkets in Caribou and Houlton.
Before buying the Presque Isle site, Hannaford acquired four other Graves’ stores — Camden, Dover-Foxcroft, Hampden, and Bar Harbor — in 2005, according to previous news accounts.
With the new store opening two weeks before Thanksgiving, staff are working hard to help customers stay within their budgets, Blanchard said.
In addition to store coupons and weekly flyer sales, shoppers registered for the My Hannaford Rewards program earn 2% rewards on private brand items that are redeemed at the register quarterly.
“Shoppers can look to our weekly flyer for the latest savings,” he said. “We [also offer] our Thanksgiving Meal for 8 under $40.”
Graves had a similar Loyalty Rewards program that must be redeemed by Nov. 8.
The Presque Isle Hannaford will be open Monday through Saturday from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. and Sunday from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. For more information about the Presque Isle Hannaford, visit Hannaford.com.

title: How Medicare for All would work in practice
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WMTW) - Senator-elect Troy Jackson said establishing Medicare for All is one of his top goals in Congress, but how would such a program work, and how much support would it have in Congress?
Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced a Medicare for All bill in 2025 that could serve as a framework. If enacted, it would create a single-payer healthcare system in which the government pays for covered care for U.S. residents of all ages.
People would be automatically enrolled at birth or when they establish U.S. residency. Coverage would include primary and preventive care, emergency services, mental health treatment, vision, dental and prescription drugs.
The bill would eliminate copays and coinsurance for covered services, though people above a certain income threshold could pay up to $200 a year for prescription drugs.
Private insurance would still exist, but insurers could only sell coverage for services not included in the national health insurance program.
“We’re going to get more spending, more inefficiency and lower quality care, rather than what Medicare for All advocates are promising,” said Michael Cannon, a health policy expert at the Cato Institute.
Some policy experts like Cannon argue Medicare for All is not the right path to universal coverage, saying private options create competition that pushes providers to offer higher-quality care.
“It would leave us with less freedom, less control over our health care,” Cannon said. “It would enrich inefficient healthcare providers. It would reduce the quality of care.”
An analysis by the Congressional Budget Office also outlined potential concerns about single-payer systems, though it noted that such a system would reduce the number of people who are uninsured and could encourage people to seek more frequent preventative care since they wouldn’t have gaps in coverage.
Including Sanders, the bill had 19 cosponsors, and 18 are expected to return to Washington, D.C., next year.
They would be joined by at least four incoming senators who have expressed support for Medicare for All, including Jackson. Supporters would need to recruit dozens of other lawmakers in both chambers to pass the proposal.

title: 52% of Americans think inflation will ruin the holidays, survey finds
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — More than half of Americans, about 52%, think inflation is going to ruin their holiday season, according to a WalletHub survey.
John Kiernan, managing editor at WalletHub, described the finding this way.
“We found that more than half, around 52% of Americans think inflation is going to ruin Christmas or whatever holiday you celebrate,” Kiernan said.
The survey also found 79% of respondents have a holiday budget that is the same size as last year or smaller. One in four say they are still paying off debt from last holiday season.
That is one reason getting an early start on holiday shopping may be appealing. Kiernan said 41% of people usually start shopping in October or earlier, and that it is not too late for those who have not started.
“So, we found that 41% of people said they usually start shopping for the holidays in October or earlier. If you haven’t started shopping by now, that’s fine. There’s still plenty of opportunities to save money. And that’s the main thing that people are trying to do when they start shopping earlier versus the last minute. More than two in three people believe early holiday shopping saves them money overall,” Kiernan said.
Most people surveyed say they have a holiday budget. Kiernan said it is important to plan ahead, take time looking for deals and stick to what you can afford.
WalletHub’s survey also found 56% of people do not trust AI to help them with their holiday shopping.

title: Maine Credit Unions celebrate Kind Day through community service and giving
text:
WESTBROOK – Maine credit unions put their People Helping People philosophy into action this October, participating in the state’s second annual Credit Union Kind Day through acts of kindness, volunteerism and charitable giving.
Observed on or around Oct. 12, Credit Union Kind Day brought credit union employees together to support local nonprofits, recognize community heroes and brighten the lives of their neighbors. From food donations and care packages to volunteer projects and unexpected gestures of generosity, credit unions found meaningful ways to give back.
Among this year’s activities:
Cumberland County Federal Credit Union packed 550 pounds of food for Freeport Community Services and made additional donations to local hunger relief efforts.
Dirigo Federal Credit Union joined the Maine Credit Union League and Synergent to volunteer at Good Shepherd Food Bank, sorting and packing 3,020 pounds of food, equivalent to approximately 2,013 meals.
Franklin-Somerset Federal Credit Union surprised 100 members with $25 grocery gift cards, while Sabattus Regional Credit Union covered purchases at local coffee shops and delivered meals to first responders.
KV Federal Credit Union assembled 100 “Bags of Hope” for individuals experiencing homelessness, while PeoplesChoice Credit Union and Community Credit Union prepared activity and care kits for patients and families at MaineHealth Barbara Bush Children’s Hospital.
OTIS Federal Credit Union employees volunteered to clean historic gravestones at Jay Hill Cemetery, while Midcoast Federal Credit Union recognized local first responders with meals and messages of appreciation.
Additional efforts included charitable donations from Casco Federal Credit Union to nonprofits including Make-A-Wish Maine and the Maine Cancer Foundation, and a collection drive organized by Acadia Federal Credit Union to support survivors of domestic violence.
“CU Kind Day is a wonderful reflection of what makes credit unions so special,” Elise M. Baldacci, president of the Maine Credit Union League, said. “Every day, our credit unions demonstrate their commitment to the communities they serve. This initiative gave us an additional opportunity to celebrate that generosity and show how even small acts of kindness can make a meaningful difference.”
Originally established in Minnesota in 2018, Credit Union Kind Day has grown into a nationwide celebration of the credit union movement’s commitment to service and community.
The Maine Credit Union League is a nonprofit, professional trade association that exists to serve Maine’s credit unions. Founded in 1938, the League’s mission is to help credit unions succeed and improve the financial lives of their members. As the trade association for Maine’s credit unions, the League provides advocacy, education and other resources designed to assist credit unions in meeting the needs of their membership. For more information, visit www.mainecul.org.

title: Police seek aid in locating missing Portland man
text:
The Portland Police Department is seeking the public’s aid in locating a missing Portland man.
David Darman went missing from Holiday Woods at Canco, a Portland retirement community, the department said in a social media post Friday.
Police described Darman as being 6 feet, 1 inch tall, about 200 pounds, and having gray hair and a gray beard. He often wears a blue baseball hat with an orange logo and sunglasses.
“David has early onset dementia, is largely nonverbal, and has wandered away from the community in the past,” the department said in its post.
Those with information about his whereabouts are requested to contact the Portland Police Department at 207-874-8575.

title: Two murders linked to serial killer, police say
text:
PITTSBURGH, Pa. (KDKA) - After nearly five decades, Pennsylvania State Police said they have identified the man responsible for the murders of two young women.
Investigators said DNA evidence has linked two cold cases in the Pittsburgh area.
Susan Rush, 21, disappeared in 1976 on her way to a Thanksgiving Eve dinner. She was later found dead in the trunk of her car.
Brenda Ritter, 18, disappeared in 1977 after leaving her boyfriend’s house. Her body was found on a hillside in South Strabane.
Police said both women had been sexually assaulted and strangled.
“The testing identified the same offender murdered both Susan Rush and Brenda Ritter. This testing confirmed there was a serial killer in Washington County during this time frame,” said Pennsylvania State Police Cpl. James Petrosky.
Investigators have now identified James Richard Clark Sr. as the killer.
Clark died of natural causes in 2023.
State police said Clark had never previously been a suspect in either case.

title: How measles outbreaks are impacting people across the U.S.
text:
(InvestigateTV) — The CDC reported 4,852 measles cases in the U.S. between Jan. 1 and Oct. 30, 2026, the most the country has seen since an outbreak that stretched from 1989 to 1991. According to the CDC, cases are at a 35-year high.
Measles is one of the most contagious diseases on Earth and can cause serious health complications, including death.
Measles is most often associated with a rash and fever, according to the CDC. Health experts warn it can cause severe complications, particularly in babies and young children.
One out of every 1,000 cases will develop encephalitis, which often results in permanent brain damage, the CDC said.
Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine offer the strongest protection against measles, according to the CDC.
When more than 95% of a community is vaccinated, most people are protected through what’s known as herd immunity.
Families describe complications
Christine Castle said her sister Fonda is a ball of energy and often smiles and giggles. Fonda is 66 years old. Her room is filled with baby dolls and cartoons.
“She has a lot of love to give,” Castle said. “She basically just didn’t develop past a five or six year old.”
Castle said their mother was seven months pregnant with Fonda when she contracted rubella, a virus different from measles that causes similar symptoms. According to the CDC, a rubella infection during pregnancy can lead to serious illness and developmental delays for babies after birth.
“She can’t read or write. She can kind of memorize colors,” Castle said.
Fonda was born during the U.S. rubella epidemic. According to the National Foundation for Infectious Diseases, between 1965 and 1966, more than 11,000 pregnant women lost their babies and 20,000 were born with congenital rubella syndrome, including Fonda.
“They can basically look at the timeframe when my sister’s brain stopped developing,” Castle said.
Another family carries the effects of measles. Emmi Herman said her sister Marcie was a pianist.
“She was a wonderful piano player. My parents bought her a piano, which went wherever she went,” Herman said.
Herman said that in 1960, Marcie became ill with measles at age 9 and developed encephalitis. The CDC estimates this happens to 1 in every 1,000 children who contract measles.
“She had to learn to walk again; she had to learn to feed herself,” Herman said.
Herman said Marcie faced mental health challenges until her death in 2020 from COVID-19.
“You don’t know about the hardships and the heartaches and the way measles in particular can break up a family and really change the trajectory of that person’s life and also shape the future of the siblings’ and the parents’ lives,” Herman said.
Marcie contracted measles three years before a vaccine became available to the public, according to the World Health Organization. Herman was 6 years old at the time of Marcie’s diagnosis.
South Carolina outbreak timeline
Dr. George Haddad Jr. and Dr. Jennifer Grier are professors at the University of South Carolina School of Medicine – Greenville. They studied medicine in the 1990s and early 2000s, when national measles cases were at their lowest in years.
“I never saw it in training, and I never saw it in practice... until now,” Haddad said.
“I didn’t really think about measles too much other than it’s sort of a disease you see in the textbooks,” Grier said.
According to the S.C. Department of Public Health:
- South Carolina’s first measles case was reported July 9, 2025.
- By Oct. 1, state health officials confirmed five new infections were related, meeting the criteria for an outbreak, defined as three or more linked cases.
- New cases peaked by mid-January 2026, and hundreds of people were in quarantine or isolation.
- State health officials declared the outbreak over April 26, 2026.
A total of 997 people contracted measles during the outbreak.
“Many of them, the majority being children, especially some young children who were sick,” said Dr. Brannon Traxler, the department’s chief medical officer, who oversaw the state’s effort to fight measles.
Traxler said 15 of the 21 hospitalizations were children.
“As a parent myself I can imagine the anguish of the family, of the parents,” Traxler said.
No one died during the outbreak, which Traxler said came to an end largely due to an aggressive vaccination campaign.
“Everything from, you know, making new connections with faith-based, you know, entities, and non-profits,” Traxler said.
Partnerships produced mobile vaccine units, including one at Mount Moriah Baptist Church in Spartanburg. Spartanburg saw a 94% year-over-year increase in MMR vaccinations.
Of the 997 cases in the outbreak, more than 93% (932) were unvaccinated.
Daughter’s reaction to the vaccine
For some South Carolinians, vaccine hesitation is rooted in personal experience.
“She was a completely healthy toddler,” Deidre Downs said of her daughter, Shaylee.
Downs said that a few weeks after Shaylee received the MMR vaccine in 2024, she developed immune thrombocytopenia purpura, also known as ITP. According to Johns Hopkins, ITP is a disorder that affects the ability to form blood clots.
“And within a 24-hour period, they went from small bruises to her whole body covered in bruises,” Downs said.
According to the CDC, ITP can happen after a natural measles infection and after the MMR vaccine. The agency says it occurs in 1 in every 40,000 vaccinated children.
“It doesn’t feel like a rare occurrence when it happens to your child,” Downs said.
Downs said Shaylee is now symptom-free. According to Johns Hopkins, ITP typically doesn’t return. Downs said that after her daughter’s reaction, she will never be too sure of the odds.
“As a whole when this hot topic comes up, I would just like there to be more understanding and compassion,” Downs said.
Castle said she wonders about her sister’s life had the MMR vaccine been available when their mother was infected.
“We don’t know who is going to be affected and who is not, but we definitely would not want a five-year-old for the rest of your life, it is very difficult,” Castle said.
Castle, Herman and Downs each shared a different experience. All three have one message for parents with questions about measles or the vaccine: speak with a trusted doctor.
“If that could save one life, it’s a legacy that, you know, many people can’t claim,” Herman said.

title: Man arrested with guns near White House reported voices telling him to kill President Trump
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray News) - A man was arrested Thursday evening after he reportedly told law enforcement the voices in his head told him to kill President Donald Trump.
The Department of Homeland Security said Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos, who was in the country illegally from Venezuela, was spotted “acting suspicious” while in his car, parked near the White House.
Officials said the car was reported stolen and Chrinos admitted to having weapons.
Law enforcement reported finding three guns and dozens of rounds of ammunition.
Chrinos was then arrested and charged with:
- Carrying a rifle outside of a home or business
- Unlawful transportation of a firearm (three counts)
- Unregistered firearms (three counts)
- Unregistered ammunition (three counts)
- Possession of certain dangerous weapons
- Carrying a pistol without a license
- Unauthorized use of a motor vehicle
- Theft
- Receiving stolen property
“This incident reflects the heightened threat environment in which we operate, as well as the continued number of armed individuals who are drawn to the White House complex,” U.S. Secret Service Director Sean Curran said in an issued statement. “While our personnel are trained to respond to situations like this and we remain confident in our tactics, we are alarmed by the increase in threat cases that continue to arise.”
Chrinos entered the country illegally in 2024 and was arrested by the United States Border Patrol before being released.
Following his arrest in Washington, he was placed under an immigration detainer with the U.S. Marshals Service.

title: Supporters of naming Windham-Raymond middle school after late senator vow to press on
text:
Supporters of the effort to name a new middle school serving Windham and Raymond after late Sen. Bill Diamond vowed to press on after the Regional School Unit 14 school board rejected the proposal at its Nov. 4 meeting.
Diamond, who died last year at 80, served in Maine government for nearly half a century. First elected as a Democrat to the Maine House of Representatives in 1976, he was elected in 1982 to the first of 10 nonconsecutive terms in the state Senate, representing a district encompassing Windham, Raymond, Standish and Casco, among other towns. From 1989-97, he served as Maine’s secretary of state under Govs. John McKernan and Angus King.
In addition to his public service, Diamond was, in his later years, devoted to the cause of preventing child abuse. He was the founder of Walk a Mile in Their Shoes, a nonprofit dedicated to advocating for the welfare of Maine’s children, as well as the co-founder of Windham Neighbors Helping Neighbors nonprofit to provide emergency assistance for Windham residents in need of heating fuel. Diamond was also a lifelong educator, serving as principal of Jordan Small Middle School and superintendent of Raymond public schools.
A majority of residents at the meeting spoke in favor of naming the school after Diamond.
Cumberland County Sherriff Kevin Joyce, although not a resident of Windham, spoke about his strong personal connection with Diamond, a former teacher of his who provided guidance well into adulthood. Joyce called Diamond a “pillar of the community,” and said there was no other person who met the criteria.
Char Jewell, chair of the Raymond Select Board, said that a lot of parents in her town are upset about the closure of Jordan Small Middle School, as well as the longer school bus rides they have to face. Jewell supported naming the new middle school after Diamond, and argued that the idea of naming the new school Windham Raymond Middle School would create a sense of division between the two towns.
Opposition to naming the school after Diamond primarily stemmed from resistance to naming an educational institution after a person.
Resident Debbe Kelley cited the example of the multiple institutions named for former Sen. George Mitchell, and the decisions to remove his name following the revelation of his ties to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein. Board member Grace Leavitt agreed, saying that naming institutions after people has lost support, but she hoped the town will find another way to honor Diamond’s legacy.
There were also concerns related to Diamond’s employment at the Élan School, where Diamond served as superintendent and director of government relations.
Karyn Diamond, Bill Diamond’s daughter, said at the school board meeting that the family recognized the severity of the abuse at the school, but said her father’s affiliation with the school was limited to serving as a government liaison, and he had no knowledge of what occurred there.
Ultimately, the board rejected a motion to name the school after Diamond, and approved a motion naming the school Windham Raymond Middle School.
Following the meeting, John Cressey, leader of the effort to name the school after Diamond, vowed to press on, pledging to set up a petition to rename the school, and urging supporters of the renaming effort from both Windham and Raymond to do a “show of unity” at the next school board meeting.

title: Ellsworth council candidate requests recount after losing by 7 votes
text:
An Ellsworth City Council candidate has requested a recount after losing Tuesday’s election by just seven votes.
Tiffany Dilda Gaspar, a business owner and outspoken critic of council spending who spearheaded the springtime recall petition of five sitting councilors, has requested a formal recount of Tuesday’s election.
It marks the second year in a row that Ellsworth will perform a recount of the City Council race. Last year, the city’s recount confirmed the initial results: area businessman and conservative activist John Linnehan — who was elected to the city’s school board this year after decades of failed runs for state and local public offices— lost by just two votes.
Gaspar received 1,801 votes, seven votes short of Robert Grant Sr., who was elected to his first term on the council. Former Councilor Casey Hanson was elected with 1,903 votes, and incumbent Councilor Nancy Smith came in fourth place, falling short in her reelection bid with 1,704 votes.
The city announced the recount Thursday evening but had not yet confirmed when the process, which will be conducted in council chambers and open to the public, would take place. Last year’s recall was held roughly 10 days after the election.
Hanson and Grant will not be sworn into their roles until after the recount takes place. In the interim, the current city councilors will retain their positions, the city said.
The city said it would foot the bill for the recount because the race is so close. The city expects the recount to cost roughly $10,000, the same as last year.
Gaspar and Grant were the two fiscally conservative candidates on this year’s ballot. Both promised to reduce council spending while prioritizing the city’s infrastructure needs.
Gaspar led the recent recall petition to oust five councilors, including Smith, who voted to censure fellow Councilor Steve O’Halloran after a city investigation alleged he had harassed city staff.
Grant did not sign the petition, he previously said.
Gaspar and her followers have said the petition resulted in the council’s frivolous spending habits, including the roughly $14,000 spent on a rebranding package of the city logo.

title: Mother and daughter killed by grizzly bear while hiking in Canada
text:
(AP) - Selah Reed’s family first knew something was wrong when the 20-year-old missed a routine Saturday night call with her sister.
When no one had heard from Reed or her mother, Jenny Balcarras, by the next morning, they asked the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to check on their home in Bella Coola on British Columbia’s central coast. Balcarras’ car was gone and the doors were locked. They found the car at a trailhead up the road, but Balcarras and Reed were nowhere to be found.
Family members across Canada and the U.S. started mobilizing. Jenny Balcarras’ brother, Matt, headed north from Vancouver Island, and his brother left from Calgary. They met and drove through the night but got a call late Monday that their sister had been killed, likely by a grizzly.
When they arrived at the trailhead Tuesday morning, ready to join the search for Reed, her remains had also been found. The search was now a tragic recovery effort.
The killings of Jenny Balcarras, 48, and her daughter happened only 3 to 4 kilometers (1.8 to 2.4 miles) from where a grizzly attacked a group of schoolchildren and teachers last year as they walked on a trail. Eleven were injured, two of them critically, in the Nov. 20, 2025, attack.
Jeff Tyre, an inspector with the Conservation Officer Service, said that aggressive bear was never captured, but officials were able to collect its DNA. Officials have set new traps in the hopes of catching the bear involved in last weekend’s attack and to learn whether it was the same bear from a year ago. They also are not sure whether more than one bear was involved.
Terry Webber, chief administrative officer for the Nuxalk Nation, said the killings were triggering for the families who were traumatized by last year’s attack.
“Our community is still healing,” he said, adding that they’ve imposed a curfew and are providing mental health services for the community. “Our priority is to ensure they’re safe and ensure our community is supported.”
Bear attack complicated the search
The delay in finding the remains of the two women was complicated by difficult terrain, even though it was close to the trailhead, and the grizzly bear’s behavior.
Searchers found Jenny Balcarras first, then her daughter. The search was helped by more resources and a cadaver dog, Matt Balcarras said.
Searchers found his niece’s remains in a bear cache — a place where bears stash food, sometimes by digging a small hole and covering it with branches and vegetation to keep other animals and birds away.
“Even though it was within 100 or so meters (330 feet), locating remains in a cache is difficult,” he said.
By the time officials located his niece, she could only be identified by her clothing, he said. His sister was in a similar condition, but they knew who she was thanks to several tiny tattoos, he said.
“There’s no obvious body to identify,” he said. “The coroner’s investigation will include DNA and dental work. But there is no doubt that the remains that were found are theirs.”
Balcarras was comfortable in challenging environments
Grizzly bears are common in the area surrounding the Bella Coola community, officials said. Conservation officials maintain a hotline where people can report problem bears, but no calls had been received recently, Tyre said during a media briefing.
Balcarras, an art therapist, had moved to Bella Coola during the summer. She had previously lived in Alaska, where her children were born, and was “the central organizing person in our family,” Matt Balcarras said.
“In classic, strong single-mother style, she scraped together a career and a life for herself and her kids,” Balcarras said. She was small in stature but strong in character and physical abilities, he said.
She was comfortable living among the wildlife, he said.
“She lived in the Bush when her kids were babies,” he said. “She and my niece were not naive or foolish or uninformed. They’ve lived in these areas and have been around animals of countless types for years and years and decades.”

title: Inside Alcor’s bid to pause death and the questions still unanswered
text:
SCOTTSDALE, AZ (InvestigateTV) — People frozen for years then thawed out and awake in a different time. It’s a common scene in popular science fiction movies.
But this isn’t the script of a blockbuster, a nonprofit in Arizona is attempting to make it a reality. Since the 1970s, Alcor has specialized in cryonics, defined as the practice of preserving life by pausing the dying process using subfreezing temperatures.
Alcor is betting on future science to do what today’s cannot.
In an unassuming building tucked inside an industrial section of Scottsdale, a small team at the Alcor Life Extension Foundation is working on something that can sound like science fiction: preserving people, and even pets, at ultra-low temperatures with the hope that future medicine may one day be able to repair and revive them.
For Alcor member and author Rick Lemler, the idea isn’t about certainty. It’s about possibility.
“It’s something I choose to believe,” Lemler said. “It’s something I believe in and am willing to gamble.”
Lemler said his fascination with sci-fi goes back to childhood, and now, he’s taken steps to make what once felt like a fantasy part of his real-life plan. He has signed up to be cryopreserved after legal death, joining hundreds of Alcor members whose bodies or heads are stored in large vacuum-insulated containers called dewars.
“Here I am almost becoming a real-life character of my own books,” Lemler said. “So that’s kind of cool.”
The concept has long drawn skepticism—and controversy—because of the central question: Are they trying to bring people back to life?
Alcor CEO James Arrowood said that framing misses the point.
“I think the question really is, how does this make any sense,” Arrowood said. “Are we trying to bring people back from the dead? That’s actually a crude understanding of what this is.”
Alcor’s goal is to preserve cells and tissue as intact as possible through a process called vitrification, using chemicals and controlled cooling to prevent the ice crystals that typically form during freezing and can destroy cellular structures. Arrowood said one of the key solutions used, called M22, helps prevent ice from forming inside the tissue.
“In simplest terms, this is sort of a biological antifreeze,” he said. “Just like you put in your car engine, so it doesn’t crack—there’s literally ice outside of this. There is no ice inside of it.”
If vitrification can reliably preserve healthy cells without damage, Arrowood said it could have implications beyond cryonics, particularly in organ donation and transplantation, where time and tissue degradation are constant obstacles.
Rapid response after death
When an Alcor member dies, Arrowood said a specialized response team moves quickly. The team, often referred to as the “DART” team and made up of medically trained personnel, including former military members, begins cooling the body and preparing it for vitrification as soon as legally possible.
From there, Alcor’s internal medical staff continues a process that can take about a week, including replacing blood with preservation solutions and gradually lowering the temperature so the patient can be stored in liquid nitrogen.
Members can choose whole-body preservation or “neuro” preservation, which stores only the head, based on the belief that the structures associated with memory and identity are housed in the brain.
Once preparation is complete, patients are placed inside a dewar, a large container designed to hold liquid nitrogen at roughly -320 degrees Fahrenheit.
A wall of faces and unanswered questions
Inside Alcor, photos of members line the walls.
Arrowood said that when Lemler’s time comes, his picture will be added, alongside people from around the world, including one of Alcor’s youngest members: a 2-year-old girl from Thailand who died from brain cancer.
The organization’s history includes high-profile disputes that still circulate online, including legal battles and calls for greater regulation decades ago. Arrowood acknowledges the past but said much of what people cite is old.
“Many of these things are 30 to 40 years old,” he said. “That’s not uncommon anytime you’re in the technology space.”
He said that in more recent years, the conflicts that arise are often tied to logistics and finances—particularly life insurance policies used to fund preservation.
Not everyone believes cryonics can deliver what many consumers imagine.
Dr. Arthur Caplan, a bioethicist with NYU Grossman School of Medicine, called the idea of freezing a body, or a head, with the expectation of revival far-fetched.
“If you’re selling something and saying, ‘I can freeze your body. Someday doctors of the future will wake it up,’ or ‘I can freeze your head and someday doctors of the future will wake it up and stick it on another body or a robot’—what I say is preposterous,” Caplan said.
Caplan points to several barriers he believes science has not solved. The freezing process itself, achieving the correct chemical balance for preservation, and then, especially in neuro preservation, figuring out how a brain could function if it were ever removed from storage and placed elsewhere.
“If you were going to sort of take your brain and put it on another body,” Caplan said, “you are going to get signals coming in from the nerves of that body. That the old brain isn’t going to know how to process.”
Still, Caplan said one related goal could become realistic: using advanced preservation to improve organ banking and medical repair.
“Could we get someday to the point where we could freeze a kidney, freeze some cells that could be used to repair the heart? Yes,” he said. “I think that is possible.”
Arrowood is blunt about the uncertainty.
“I am the president and I am telling you that I don’t know if this will ever work,” he said. “And it may not work for me at all. In fact, I am perfectly OK with that.”
He compared the gamble to early medical breakthroughs with steps that initially seemed impossible but paved the way for modern medicine.
“The first heart transplant patient knew he would die a week or two later,” Arrowood said. “He did it because 30 years forward, his grandchildren—if they needed a heart—could get one and would live a full life.”
For Lemler, the choice is deeply personal, but rooted in the same idea, that the alternative is final.
Asked whether he fears it may never work, Lemler said he thinks of it differently.
“Concerned,” he said. “I know there is a good chance that it might not. But I don’t feel like I’m losing anything in the bargain here.”
What it costs
Cryonics isn’t cheap. Whole-body preservation typically costs about $220,000, while neuro preservation generally ranges from $80,000 to $90,000.
For those who sign up, it’s an investment in a future that may never arrive but one they hope science can someday reach.
