title: Philadelphia foster mother charged with murder in death of 10-year-old girl
text:
Philadelphia foster mother charged with murder in death of 10-year-old girl
The foster mother of a 10-year-old girl, whose disappearance sparked a massive search before her body was found across state lines nearly two weeks later, has been charged with murder, Philadelphia officials said Thursday.
Malayshia Alford was last seen alive at her home in West Philadelphia on Oct. 22. Four days later, she was reported missing, triggering an intense search by locals, the police department and the FBI.
On Wednesday, her body was found in the trunk of a car around 20 miles away in New Jersey after a turning point in the case: video surveillance was obtained from the early morning hours of Oct. 26 showing what authorities believed to be her body being moved out of the home in a bag, Philadelphia Assistant District Attorney Ashley Toczylowski said at a news conference Thursday.
The video pointed police to a witness who ultimately led them to Malayshia’s body in Lindenwold, New Jersey, Toczylowski said. Her cause of death is believed to be blunt force trauma and her manner of death was ruled a homicide, officials said.
“We do have an indication that there were instances of abuse happening, and that items were used to carry out that abuse,” Toczylowski said.
Malayshia’s foster mother, 36-year-old Caprice Williams, has been charged with murder, endangering the welfare of a child, criminal use of a communication facility, possession of an instrument of crime, recklessly endangering another person, tampering with evidence and abuse of a corpse, Toczylowski said.
Williams did not have a criminal record, according to Philadelphia District Attorney Lawrence Krasner.
“She deserved safety. She deserved to be loved. She deserved a chance to grow up,” Philadelphia Police Commissioner Kevin J. Bethel said about Malayshia at the news conference.
Philadelphia Mayor Cherelle L. Parker said authorities will continue to investigate the tragedy and seek justice.
“As a mother, this has shaken me to my core,” Parker said in a statement. “I can’t stop thinking about this precious baby and the heartache and turmoil that her immediate village will endure.”
Surveillance video led authorities to her body
Authorities say they believe Malayshia was removed from her home after she was last seen there on Oct. 22. She was then placed in one car and later transferred to another, Toczylowski said.
Police, the FBI and the community scrambled to find the missing girl. Wayne Jacobs, Special Agent in Charge of FBI Philadelphia, said the “around-the-clock effort” included witness interviews and a review of digital evidence.
The surveillance video recovered Wednesday then eventually led to the grim discovery.
“It was that video that then led law enforcement officials to a suspect vehicle, which then led law enforcement officials to find that vehicle and find a person that they wanted to speak to related to that vehicle,” Toczylowski said.
That witness was interviewed by police and the FBI, which “ultimately led law enforcement officials to her body.”
The charges against Williams are a result of the discovery and “what this witness said to law enforcement,” Toczylowski said.
When Malayshia’s body was found around 11 p.m. Wednesday “it was immediately apparent that she had been there for a while,” Toczylowski said.
Krasner said his office will be in touch with the Philadelphia Department of Human Services, the county’s child welfare agency, and they “look forward to speaking to them further about this.”
Malayshia’s family expressed their grief at the news conference, saying they loved her and are going through a “very hard time.” Neighbors and community members placed pink balloons and teddy bears in front of a memorial honoring Malayshia.
“There are few things more heartbreaking than a loss of a child. A young life filled with promise, possibilities in the future that should have been hers to experience,” Jacobs said. “To lose a child under circumstances like these, in a place where she should have been safe, it’s almost impossible to comprehend.”

title: Portland to map out growth, development in new 10-year plan
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Portland city officials are developing a plan to guide growth and development in Maine’s largest city over the next decade.
Portland’s Plan 2040 will shape city policy, investment and development over the next decade, addressing housing, economic growth, climate change, infrastructure and public spaces.
“From the rising cost of housing and the changing needs of our local economy to the impacts of climate change, Portland faces important challenges that will shape our community for years to come,” said Portland Mayor Mark Dion.
“We need to ensure that Portland remains a place where people from all backgrounds can afford to live, where businesses can thrive and where our neighborhoods remain strong and welcoming, he added. “Portland’s Plan 2040 is an opportunity to confront these challenges and work toward a more affordable equitable, and resilient future for our city.”
Dion conveyed that same message in an interview with Mainebiz at City Hall earlier this year.
“I’m about as pro-business a mayor as you’re going to get, because I think that’s the lifeblood that makes everything else work,” he said at the time.
The planning process will include multiple phases focused on community engagement, collaboration among city departments and in-depth analysis of key topics.
Residents, businesses, and community organizations are encouraged to participate in the planning process and help inform the development of the updated plan.
More information
To learn more about the project timeline, upcoming public engagement, and to sign up for email updates, visit the official project website at www.portlandscomprehensiveplan.me.

title: I was inside Susan Collins’ campaign in its final hours. Here’s what I saw.
text:
The Bangor Daily News was the first to report this story. What you’re reading here would likely not be made public without the efforts of professional journalists asking questions, interviewing sources and obtaining documents.
I’ve photographed U.S. Sen. Susan Collins for the Bangor Daily News for the past 30 years, documenting campaigns, public appearances, political events and the many moments that come with life in public office.
But there was one moment I had never been able to capture with Collins, or any other politician: what happens behind closed doors on election night, away from the cameras, crowds and campaign celebrations.
That changed Tuesday, when I was given the opportunity to step behind the scenes with Collins as she and her family watched results pour in for an election that would ultimately end her five-term Senate career.
For a photojournalist, access like this is rare. So much of political life takes place in public, where every appearance is orchestrated. Being invited into a private space offered something different — an opportunity to document the quieter, more personal side of an evening that carries enormous significance for those in the room.
There were two reasons I believed Collins might be the one politician willing to trust me with such access. First, Collins has been among the most engaging public figures I’ve photographed, often mingling with the public and media during her appearances. Second, I had heard rumors that she liked my photography.
With those thoughts in mind, I made my request to her press secretary and chief of staff at her election night watch party.
Not long after, her press secretary waved me over and told me we were going up to the senator’s room.
When I walked into Collins’ hotel suite at the Hilton Garden Inn in Bangor around 10:40 p.m., she greeted me and asked what I would like to see. I told her I simply wanted to capture what politicians do on election night when they’re away from their campaign parties.
She chuckled and replied, “This is it.”
Collins and about 10 family members sat and watched CNN report live election results on a TV that hung on a wall. Every seat in the sitting room was filled and some people spilled over into an adjoining room and were watching another TV while sitting on a bed.
The atmosphere was relaxed and people chatted quietly. Phones were checked often. Beverages, including Polar seltzers, sat on a coffee table with whoopie pies and other baked goods.
After about 15 minutes of observing and photographing Collins and the room, I thanked her and her family for allowing me behind the scenes. Collins came over to say goodbye.
About an hour after I left the room, Collins called her opponent, Democrat Troy Jackson, to concede the race in a result that sent shockwaves through Maine and the nation.
For me, it was more than another assignment. It was the completion of a story I had been trying to tell for three decades — a reminder that sometimes the most meaningful photographs happen when someone is willing to open a door and let you in.

title: Trump announces new Chief of Staff-Stephen Miller
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump announced Friday he’s making a major personnel change - promoting Stephen Miller to White House Chief of Staff.
Trump announced the move Friday in a Truth Social post. Miller’s first day on the job will be Monday. He’s replacing outgoing Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, who will join Trump’s political operation. Wiles was the first female White House Chief of Staff in American history.
Miller, who served in both Trump administrations, has been the Deputy Chief of Staff since Trump began his second term Jan. 20, 2025. He’s been a long-time aide to the president, serving in a variety of roles in both the first and second term. His appointment sends a very strong message to the new 120th Congress, which will be controlled by Democrats. Miller is not the conciliatory type, which means there will be lots of battles between the White House and the new Congress over the next two years.
“President Trump is the most transformative political leader in American History — and he has single-handedly saved America from those who would destroy it. It has been the privilege of my lifetime to have served on his team from Day One, and I am honored beyond words to serve as his White House Chief of Staff.I want to thank the incomparable Susie Wiles for her years of devoted service to the President and the Country, and for her friendship. The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic,” Miller posted on X Friday.
The move comes days after Democrats scored major wins in the midterm elections, which included flipping control of both the House and Senate by wide margins. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) both criticized the move on X.
“Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands. His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today,” Jeffries wrote.
“Donald Trump learned nothing from his historic defeat. Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn’t have made a worse choice. Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way,” Schumer wrote.
As for Susie Wiles, she merely expressed her gratitude for the opportunity to serve, writing, “More than anything, I’m grateful for the extraordinary people I’ve had the privilege of working alongside. While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will.”

title: Maine must not soften the message on Gaza genocide
text:
Laurie Hudson lives in South Paris.
Permit me to have what I’m sure is not the last word on the issue of genocide.
Dr. Peter Stein recently wrote two op-eds which seemed to contradict each other. Stein’s first, “Maine Democrats must now check their egos at the door” (July 24), suggested that we listen to each other.
His second, telling us to stop whining about genocide, seems to be in contradiction on the subject of stifling our egos, despite our strongly held convictions, in order to vote for change (“‘Genocide’ can hurt. I will still vote for Maine Democrats.” Oct. 28).
I believe that the issue of genocide has been the biggest ego-driven element of this past U.S. Senate campaign.
Let me first say that I consider Dr. Stein a friend, in a bizarre world where opposites tend to make strange bedfellows during political campaigns.
I saw him coming out of a fundraiser before a Portland event and saw him again in a Lewiston event (both for Troy Jackson) and we started talking. I suggested a meeting of the minds from the opposite ends of the political spectrum.
Maybe we could find common cause, without abandoning our better judgment, and issue some sort of joint statement that could help Troy on an issue he started to avoid discussing?
We couldn’t be further apart on this issue, I thought, but Stein assured me we saw it similarly. But do we? He seemed to despise Netanyahu. But calling genocide what it is? Genocide? It seems to be a trigger for him.
I’m an anti-war, anti-Zionist former candidate who ran against Susan Collins in 2008. Stein is progressive, but is among Troy’s influencers who wanted him to soften the message on genocide while he was campaigning.
We came to think, after discussions and meeting a few times, and sharing confidences, that there was place for mutual respect and even trust. Ideologically, we remain at a standstill.
Those who try to avoid taking a side simply end up enabling the status quo. That’s all the invitation a bully needs to reassert their lost power, as we will see in Israel. And that’s because you must soundly defeat those who reject the rule of law.
There was a song sung for Troy Jackson at his event in Bath. The songster put Troy’s name into the lyrics of the old labor song “Which Side Are You On?” Choosing sides comes at a cost.
I still believe that the issue of firm opposition to genocide must be unyielding. To stand for humanity, we must oppose Netanyahu as a war criminal, just as we support truth tellers on other hard issues of our day, such as the Epstein victims and Donald Trump’s criminality.
We must keep pressing for candidates to stand up on the hard things that are avoided in campaigns when everybody wants to come together. There are, however, certain things you cannot compromise on.
I’d like to remain friends with Dr. Stein, and will continue to regard him as a kind, generous and humane being. I cannot agree, though, with his idea of softening the message on Gaza and genocide.
Israel’s leadership is inextricably linked to our government and President Trump’s horrific legacy in siding with them and funding their barbaric wars with the support of Sen. Susan Collins and others. If we do not condemn these atrocities, they grow until it becomes an insane mindset that becomes a plague on all mankind, as we have now seen.
How do you reconcile two opposing forces? Let’s hope we can all pick up the pieces, now, and figure it out.

title: Scientists discovered an unknown baby right whale off Canada. They say it’s a cause for joy
text:
PORTLAND, Maine (AP) - It would seem difficult to miss a 15,000-pound (6,804-kilogram) baby, but for months scientists who study rare whales did just that, and now they couldn’t be happier.
Researchers in Canada captured images of an unidentified baby North Atlantic right whale, one of the rarest sea mammals in the world, off Anticosti Island in Quebec in September. Scientists with the New England Aquarium in Boston said this week that after analyzing photos and data about right whales, they have determined it was a calf likely born months ago that went unseen during winter surveys for the giant animals.
The discovery puts the number of baby right whales discovered from the most recent birthing season at 24, the most productive year for the whales since 2009 and the fourth-highest count on record, the aquarium said. The whales number only about 380 in the world, and their population has fallen since 2010.
The whale was seen with its mother, a 38-year-old whale known to researchers as Silt, scientists said. Right whales give birth off the southeastern U.S. in winter before venturing north to New England and Canada to feed.
The whales are extensively cataloged with photography by researchers because they are so rare. It’s also rare for the researchers who study the whales to miss a baby, but the discovery was a welcome surprise, said Amy Warren, a scientist at the New England Aquarium’s Anderson Cabot Center.
“Silt was briefly seen in the southeastern U.S. calving grounds in February 2026, so it’s possible she had the calf there but snuck away before they were documented together. This is an exciting discovery for us so late in the year,” Warren said.
Baby right whale births are closely tracked by scientists because the tiny population needs successful calving years to remain viable. There are only about 70 reproductive-age females left in the population, and scientists have said the whales have reached 20 calves in a season only a few times since 2010.
That was when their numbers started falling, as they lost about 25% between 2010 and 2020. The whales are vulnerable to collisions with large ships and entanglement in commercial fishing gear, and the warming of the ocean has heightened those threats because they have strayed from protected areas, scientists have said. They also suffered a disastrous year in 2018 when no babies were born.
Recent years have been slightly more encouraging, as the whales have gained back some of their population since 2020. But conservationists have decried recent moves by the U.S. government to delay new protections for the whales for a decade in favor of commercial fishing interests.
The baby whale sighted off Quebec was spotted by researchers with Mingan Island Cetacean Study, a nonprofit research organization in the province’s coastal Côte-Nord region. The whale wasn’t seen by researchers despite boat-based and aerial surveys along the U.S. East Coast all spring and summer, the New England Aquarium said.
Scientists are celebrating the animal’s addition to a successful breeding season for the rare whales, said Richard Sears, founder and director of Mingan Island Cetacean Study.
“It just goes to show you how big the ocean is, and how those animals can get lost out there,” he said.

title: Some patients are choosing self-pay alternatives to medical insurance
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
GREENVILLE, S.C. (Aging Untold) —Some patients are choosing to pay cash for medical procedures rather than file insurance claims, saying it can be significantly cheaper for certain services like MRI scans.
Greta Fuller faced this decision when her 10-year-old son needed an MRI for severe abdominal pain in fall 2024.
His doctor was having difficulty getting insurance approval for the scan so she took her son to Imago in Greenville, which doesn’t accept insurance.
“I was able to get Seth in that day,” Fuller said.
Patients pay about $500 out of pocket for an MRI scan.
Growing trend of cash-pay medical facilities
Palmetto Proactive Imaging Center in Spartanburg is another self-pay location.
DJ Horton took his son, Grey, there for a knee MRI after the boy experienced pain from sports activities.
Because they have a membership with Palmetto Proactive Primary Care, they received a discounted rate of about $350 to $400 per knee.
Nonmember MRI costs at Palmetto Proactive are usually $500 to $600.
Hospital pricing comparison
Hospital systems in the area charge about $2,000 for a leg MRI when patients pay cash, often offering discounts when insurance isn’t used. However, using insurance can cost more — around $3,500 for an MRI if the patient hasn’t met their deductible.
Both parents said their children received needed treatment after the MRIs and are healthy again.
“We thought this was a much better economical decision, but it’s also been way more than that,” Horton said.
“We were just really thankful to be able to get that done quickly, affordable, have some information, some thoughts on how to move forward,” Fuller said.
Direct primary care model
Dr. Chris McCarthy from Palmetto Proactive compared it to a subscription service.
He said patients can often schedule same-day appointments and get more time with their doctor.
According to the American Academy of Family Physicians, monthly membership fees range from $50 to $100.

title: Bangor movie theater employee brings characters to life to make moviegoers smile
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - As “The Cat in the Hat” arrives on the big screen, one Bangor movie theater employee knows how much a character can bring to the experience.
Clyde Simmons works at Bangor Mall Cinemas 10, where he dresses up as different characters to bring smiles to moviegoers’ faces. His costumes have included a shark and the Mandalorian.
For Simmons, it’s about giving people a little extra happiness when they come to the movies to take a break from the world.
“You know there’s enough going on in the world as it is and I just like to make a little more happiness in their life,” Simmons said. “You know you come to the movies to forget about things for two hours you know and so I just try to add to that. I want to add to their experience.”
Simmons said the experience means something to him, too.
“It just touches my heart because you know it’s something that I enjoy,” he said.

title: Lewiston immigrant community jubilant after 2026 election
text:
Lewiston’s immigrant community is reflecting over what many are describing as an overwhelmingly successful outing Tuesday despite a fraught early election atmosphere.
“It was a very intentional, authentic, grassroots, door-to-door organizing,” community organizer Safiya Khalid said of getting people to the polls. “The immigrant community really was determined to elect people who were welcoming, who were progressive, who were tolerant and who really supported immigrants.”
Khalid said some 30 volunteers helped with canvassing, rides and other voter outreach. Fellow organizer Ifraax Saciid-Ciise Lugoole said volunteers spent endless hours training interpreters and helping voters overcome other potential barriers to voting, namely transportation to polling stations.
And they said people showed up determined to cast their vote regardless of friction at the polls.
Accusations of both voter harassment and electioneering in the week leading up to the election reached the Secretary of State’s Office and the U.S. Department of Justice.
Complaints included filming and photography by a right-wing media organization of interpreters assisting non-English speakers at the voting booths, possibly meant to intimidate them. And claims were made that interpreters were assisting voters and telling them how they should vote, which is illegal.
As members of the Secretary of State’s Office and Lewiston City Clerk’s Office kept an eye on the polls for harassment and illegalities, the federal government requested City Hall video of early voting action to review claims of electioneering and the DOJ assigned several poll watchers to the city’s four polling stations on Election Day.
The presence of DOJ poll watchers on Tuesday at the polls caused a tense atmosphere early in the day. However, Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, who visited polling places in Lewiston, said election efforts statewide, and in the city, went smoothly.
“The last year was really brutal and harsh for the immigrant community with constant bullying and blame for things out of our control,” Lugoole said, referencing the city’s uptick in youth gun violence.
Lugoole said a handful of bad actors have painted all immigrants as lawless instigators rather than as the peaceful neighbors the vast majority are. She also referenced what she described as ongoing harassment by a right-wing news media outlet over the past 12 months.
“We’ve been used as scapegoats for a long time,” Khalid said. “We’ve been harassed based on our ethnicity and our nationality and where we were born and based on our language.”
As a result, Lugoole said, the immigrant communities have responded.
“They went out in numbers, more than double than last time,” Lugoole said. “They wanted to respond to all of these political attacks. This is how we used our voices. You can try to scare us, but we are strong, we are resilient and we have overcome a lot.”
The city of Lewiston reported that about 60% of all registered voters either cast early ballots or went to the polls — 5% more than in the 2024 general election and 13% more than for the 2022 midterm election.
Khalid said the post-election energy is high, seeing “big wins in Maine and across the country, too.”
“It’s incredible seeing Troy Jackson win as well as Hannah Pingree,” Khalid said. “Most of the (local) candidates that we supported have won their races. We are just overjoyed. …
“Everyone was saying we should do a celebration at Kennedy Park, that we should hold a party just to celebrate all of our efforts, because we’ve all contributed to this big win.”

title: Jay Rockefeller, former West Virginia governor and US senator who was part of a dynasty, dies at 89
text:
CHARLESTON, W.Va. (AP) — Jay Rockefeller, the last member of his family’s political dynasty — and the only Democrat — who served as West Virginia’s governor and later a longtime U.S. senator, has died. He was 89.
Rockefeller died Thursday night at his home in Washington, said Mary Stewart, vice president for external affairs at WETA, the public broadcasting station where Rockefeller’s wife, Sharon, serves as president and CEO.
Rockefeller came from one of the nation’s richest families to spend a half century in public service in one of the poorest states. He arrived in 1964 as a worker in an anti-poverty program, was elected governor a dozen years later and served two terms, then spent 30 years as a U.S. senator.
“I could not imagine a more rewarding career,” Rockefeller said upon his retirement in 2015.
He was born John D. Rockefeller IV in New York City. His great-grandfather, Standard Oil Co. founder John Rockefeller, died a month before Rockefeller’s birth. His father, John D. Rockefeller III, was a well-known philanthropist. Uncles Winthrop (Arkansas) and Nelson (New York) were Republican governors. Another uncle, David Rockefeller, ran Chase Manhattan Bank.
A detour from his family’s path
Jay Rockefeller went in a different direction.
A few years out of college at age 27, Rockefeller moved to the West Virginia mining community of Emmons to participate in the Volunteers in Service to America program, a time that Rockefeller said proved transformative.
“It explains every policy I pursued and every vote I have cast. It was where my beliefs were bolted down, and where my passions met my principles,” he said in an emotional farewell speech from the Senate floor on Dec. 4, 2014.
While he intended for his stay in the state to be brief, Rockefeller broke from his family’s Republican tradition and was elected to the state House of Delegates as a Democrat in 1966. By combining money with hard work in a traditionally Democratic state, Rockefeller overcame suspicions of political opportunism and rose from state legislator to secretary of state to governor.
A turning point came after Rockefeller’s only political defeat in the 1972 governor’s race to Republican Arch A. Moore Jr., whose daughter, Republican Shelley Moore Capito, was elected in 2014 to Rockefeller’s Senate seat upon his retirement. Capito on Friday called Rockefeller “a true gentleman” who treated her with respect, kindness and encouragement.
“Over the years, we developed a wonderful friendship that transcended politics, and I will always be grateful for that,” she said in a statement.
After the defeat, Rockefeller remained in West Virginia, a decision he called the most important of his career. He became the first without a theological degree to become president of West Virginia Wesleyan College in 1973. His popularity there — and a change in his stance to embrace strip mining — translated to a landslide win over Republican Cecil Underwood in the 1976 governor’s race.
As governor, Rockefeller emphasized development of the state’s infrastructure, such as roads, sewers and bridges. Those issues, he said, are “not very sexy things, I grant you but very, very necessary in West Virginia.”
Current Gov. Patrick Morrissey said Rockefeller helped shape the state and left a lasting mark on the lives of generations of West Virginians.
“From his early work in some of our state’s most disadvantaged communities to his efforts to strengthen healthcare, protect coal miners and their families, and support our veterans, Senator Rockefeller demonstrated a deep commitment to the people of West Virginia,” Morrissey said in a statement.
Onward to Washington
After Rockefeller defeated Arch Moore in a rematch in 1980, he won a U.S. Senate seat in 1984 after the retirement of longtime Democrat Jennings Randolph. It came despite a landslide victory that year for Republican President Ronald Reagan.
Rockefeller and his wife, Sharon, daughter of former Republican Sen. Charles Percy of Illinois, fit easily into the capital’s social scene, purchasing a multimillion-dollar estate for their family. Never shy or apologetic about using his inherited $150 million fortune to win his races, he spent millions upon millions from his own pocket. He won by comfortable margins in each of his five terms.
Rockefeller’s vast wealth was always a source of conversation and an undercurrent in his political races. He spent at least $21 million of his own money in his political campaigns, including $9 million to win a close 1984 Senate race against Republican novice and fellow multimillionaire John Raese. In Rockefeller’s 1980 gubernatorial race against Republican Arch Moore Jr., bumper stickers appeared saying: “Make Him Spend It All, Arch.”
The state’s junior senator for 25 years, Rockefeller carved his own path of influence in Sen. Robert C. Byrd’s immense shadow. Byrd died in 2010 as the longest-serving senator in U.S. history, winning an enduring reputation for steering billions of dollars over many decades to boost his impoverished state.
Rockefeller’s influence was less showy. As chairman of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, he championed consumers’ rights, upgrading broadband infrastructure and sponsoring a bill to block companies from tracking online activity of their customers. He authored legislation in 1997 that created the Children’s Health Insurance Program, which assists poor families whose incomes are too high to qualify for Medicaid.
He also was head of committees on Veterans’ Affairs and Intelligence, frequently sparring with President George W. Bush over foreign policy. Rockefeller said he regretted his 2002 vote to authorize the war against Iraq.
But Rockefeller also differed with the Democratic administration of President Barack Obama over mining-related regulations. With his state the nation’s second-biggest coal producer, Rockefeller was among several West Virginia officials who opposed the Obama-era Environmental Protection Agency’s oversight of the mountaintop removal method of surface mining.
College studies in Tokyo laid the groundwork for Rockefeller’s efforts to bring business from Japan to West Virginia. He had known Toyota’s founding family since the 1960s and was instrumental in helping the Japanese automaker pick a Buffalo, West Virginia, cornfield for an engine parts plant in 1996. The $2 billion plant now employs about 2,200 workers.
___ Associated Press writer Holly Ramer in Concord, New Hampshire, contributed to this report.

title: Dementia care educator Teepa Snow explains ‘brain change’ and what it means for caregivers
text:
(Aging Untold) — Dementia can change how families talk, plan and get through a normal day, and many caregivers are working out what to do in real time.
Teepa Snow, a nationally recognized dementia care educator, occupational therapist and founder of Positive Approach to Care, joined Aging Untold to talk about what she has taught families and care teams for decades.
She discussed why she uses the term “brain change,” how she approaches refusals such as taking a shower and why written reminders may not help.
Why Snow says ‘brain change’
Snow said people with dementia lose some abilities but change others, and she uses “brain change” instead of language that focuses on decline.
“Although people are losing some abilities, they’re actually changing others,” Snow said.
For example, some people who never swore may begin to, and people who would never have asked strangers for help may walk up and say they need to get home, Snow said.
“People think all the time of brain failure and brain loss, and I talk about brain change because the reality is neuroplasticity exists whether you have dementia or you don’t,” Snow said. “So let’s use what we have and let’s use what they have.”
What to try when someone refuses a shower
Gerontologist and Aging Untold expert “Sam” Cradduck presented Snow with a challenge families might face – how would she respond if a parent with dementia continually refused to shower, take medication or get dressed?
Snow said she would not try to force a shower.
Instead, Snow said, ask the loved one for help with a smaller task.
She presented this as an example:
“I have no business trying to force you to take a shower. That’s ridiculous. What I would ask you is, you’ve got something like right here,” Snow said, pointing to her cheek. “And I don’t know if it’s from breakfast or what. It’s out here on this outer edge. Let’s go to the bathroom, look in the mirror I’m going to give you a washcloth and see if you can’t get that off.”
Another example she offered was to ask the person to wash their hands before cooking dinner.
Snow said that if a person will not take part in those smaller steps, a shower is unlikely.
“I’ve got to back up a little bit and try to figure out what’s getting in our way of the interaction,” Snow said.
Why sticky notes may not work
Cradduck brought up written reminders, such as sticky notes and reminders labeled “coffee cups” and “plates,” and why they don’t work.
Snow said families may think they can take written information and translate it into an action.
But following a written sequence requires the hippocampus, which she described as the learning and memory center, to access and use what the person just did and what the next step is. And the front of the brain is trying to sequence, she said.
Snow said families should recognize that the person likely needs more support for completing tasks.
The one thing Snow wants families to know
Asked what one message she would give every family affected by dementia, Snow said both the person with dementia and the caregiver are doing the best they can.
“You’re both doing the best you can, and if you want something to change, one of you is going to have to change,” Snow said.
She said the person with dementia is already experiencing brain change, so caregivers will need to build awareness, knowledge and skills they may not have expected to need.
And recognize, Snow said, that not every family member is suited to be the person providing hands-on care.
“You can be great at organizing care because not every family member is built for this,” Snow said. “I mean, it’s hard work.”

title: Man arrested with guns near White House reported voices telling him to kill President Trump
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray News) - A man was arrested Thursday evening after he reportedly told law enforcement the voices in his head told him to kill President Donald Trump.
The Department of Homeland Security said Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos, who was in the country illegally from Venezuela, was spotted “acting suspicious” while in his car, parked near the White House.
Officials said the car was reported stolen and Chrinos admitted to having weapons.
Law enforcement reported finding three guns and dozens of rounds of ammunition.
Chrinos was then arrested and charged with:
- Carrying a rifle outside of a home or business
- Unlawful transportation of a firearm (three counts)
- Unregistered firearms (three counts)
- Unregistered ammunition (three counts)
- Possession of certain dangerous weapons
- Carrying a pistol without a license
- Unauthorized use of a motor vehicle
- Theft
- Receiving stolen property
“This incident reflects the heightened threat environment in which we operate, as well as the continued number of armed individuals who are drawn to the White House complex,” U.S. Secret Service Director Sean Curran said in an issued statement. “While our personnel are trained to respond to situations like this and we remain confident in our tactics, we are alarmed by the increase in threat cases that continue to arise.”
Chrinos entered the country illegally in 2024 and was arrested by the United States Border Patrol before being released.
Following his arrest in Washington, he was placed under an immigration detainer with the U.S. Marshals Service.

title: Aging Untold: What older adults should know about sexual health and protection
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we address sexual health after 60, discussing essential screenings and how older adults can stay protected while dating.
We explore how creative outlets like music, dance and art can support mood, dignity and connection for loved ones living with dementia.
Finally, we celebrate the historic Morehouse College Glee Club and its century-old legacy of brotherhood, leadership and community service.
“Getting older does not make you immune to getting a sexually transmitted disease,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said. “Just because you retired, your sexual health didn’t.”
If you are dating again for the first time in decades, there have been changes in sexual health.
Rogers said appearances do not show whether someone has a sexually transmitted disease, and age does not change the risk.
So older adults have to take precautions to protect themselves against several diseases, and condoms are about more than preventing pregnancy, she said.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said she has seen the impact the arts can have on people with memory impairments.
She saw it with a client when a caregiver took her to art classes and the woman started creating pictures and watercolors.
Music, dance, poetry, storytelling and art can tap into emotion and long-held experiences for someone with dementia. While they do not cure dementia, they can support mood, dignity and connection.
O’Rourke said families can begin by searching for available resources in their own area.
Some patients say they find that paying cash for medical procedures rather than filing insurance claims can be significantly cheaper for certain services.
When Greta Fuller’s 10-year-old son needed an MRI for severe abdominal pain in fall 2024, they went to a provider that doesn’t accept insurance.
Patients pay about $500 out of pocket for an MRI scan.
“That was amazing because we had talked with friends who’ve spent $2,000 after insurance,” Fuller said.
The Morehouse College Glee Club has performed at presidential inaugurations, Super Bowls and the Atlanta Olympics.
Behind every performance is a deeper mission — their voices rise not just in song, but in leadership.

title: Help Feed Our Neighbors During the 10th Annual High Five Turkey Drive
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
10 Years of Giving: High Five Turkey Drive Returns to Aroostook County November 12 and 13
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine — For the past decade, Aroostook County residents have shown what can happen when a community comes together to help its neighbors. This November, that tradition continues as the 10th Annual High Five Turkey Drive returns for two days of giving ahead of Thanksgiving.
Townsquare Media, alongside the Aroostook County Action Program (ACAP) and United Way of Aroostook, is inviting residents and local businesses to help make the holiday season a little brighter for families throughout the County.
The mission is simple: collect donations that help local food pantries provide Thanksgiving meals to families who need a little extra support.
Two Days, Two Locations, One Great Cause
This year's High Five Turkey Drive will make stops in Presque Isle and Houlton, giving communities two opportunities to take part.
Thursday, November 12
- Star City IGA, Presque Isle
- 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Friday, November 13
- County Tractor, 708 North Street, Houlton
- 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Whether you're stopping by on your lunch break, heading out to do some shopping, or making a special trip to donate, every contribution helps support the effort.
A Little Help Can Make a Big Difference
Thanksgiving is a time for family, friends, and gathering around the table. But for some households, putting together a holiday meal can be difficult, especially with the everyday expenses that families already face.
That's where the High Five Turkey Drive comes in.
Community members are encouraged to contribute cash donations, grocery store gift cards, turkeys, or other food donations to support local families through area food pantries.
One of the most important parts of this annual tradition is its local impact. Contributions help support the communities right here in Aroostook County, allowing local organizations to assist families during the Thanksgiving season.
You don't need to make a large donation to make a difference. When individuals, families, and businesses all pitch in, those contributions add up.
Ten Years of Neighbors Helping Neighbors
Reaching a 10-year milestone is something worth celebrating, but the real success of the High Five Turkey Drive has always been the people behind it.
From the local businesses that open their doors to the volunteers who lend a hand, and the countless residents who make donations year after year, this event is a reminder of the generosity found throughout Aroostook County.
For ten years, that generosity has helped make Thanksgiving a little easier for families across the region.
And with another holiday season approaching, there's an opportunity to keep that tradition going.
Join Us November 12 and 13
Mark your calendars, spread the word, and consider making a donation during this year's High Five Turkey Drive.
Stop by Star City IGA in Presque Isle on Thursday, November 12, or County Tractor in Houlton on Friday, November 13.
Follow along with 101.9 The Rock, Q96.1, and Big Country 96.9 for coverage of this year's effort.
After ten years, the message remains the same: when Aroostook County comes together, we can make a meaningful difference for our neighbors.
The 10th Annual High Five Turkey Drive is proudly supported by Aroostook County Action Program (ACAP) and United Way of Aroostook, working alongside Townsquare Media to support local food pantries and families this Thanksgiving.

title: Obituary: Esther Jane Leck
text:
WOOLWICH – A woman possessed of remarkable talents, energy, and faith, Esther Jane Leck, began her journey to Heaven on Oct. 25, 2026, surrounded by her loving family.
Born Esther Jane McCandless on Feb. 16, 1938 in Antigo, Wis., she was a child of the Midwest, but Maine became her true home, first when her husband served as an Air Force physician during the Cold War at Loring Air Force Base in Limestone in the very early 1960s, and again in July 1970, after brief sojourns in Denver, Colo. and Moline, Ill. while her husband finished his medical training and began his pathology practice. She met her husband, Richard C. Leck, in Hyde Park, Chicago, Ill. in 1958 when she was an undergraduate at the University of Chicago and he was a medical student there. They married on Valentine’s Day 1959 and with that wedding date, how could it not have been a love story for the ages?
Devoted to one another for almost 68 years, Esther and Richard, upon their return to Maine in 1970, created a loving home for their five children in an 1820 farmhouse in Woolwich that Esther redesigned and remodeled, largely with her own hands and brain. Teaching herself architectural drawing, historical house design, painting, tiling, wallpapering, and even basic masonry, Esther learned whatever skills were needed to get the house built.
In the early years of her marriage, as a young mother, Esther threw herself into learning all she could about nursing, natural childbirth, and nutrition. At a time when most pediatricians recommended infants start feeding with formula, she joined the nascent La Leche League in Chicago, Ill. Esther took all she learned about breastfeeding from La Leche and natural childbirth from Lamaze courses she took, and became a leader and teacher of both those philosophies and techniques to countless young mothers, fathers, and families who sought her guidance and wisdom about how to safely and successfully birth, nurse, and care for young children. In the early 1970s, shortly after her return to Maine, Esther served as La Leche League’s Regional Leader for the entire Eastern United States.
As her children grew, Esther threw herself into their care, supporting their interests through her countless talents. A truly gifted seamstress and handicrafts expert, Esther sewed and knitted many of her children’s clothes–even woolen coats!–making costumes for their Halloween celebrations and their school plays, and serving as the sewing instructor for her daughters’ 4-H groups. Driven by her own intellectual interests, Esther also became a docent at the Art and Peary-MacMillan Arctic Museums at Bowdoin College, eventually becoming president of the Docent Society. She audited many classes at the college, too, particularly in music, having studied and played classical piano for much of her life.
When her children began to leave home for boarding school and college, Esther’s boundless energy turned towards care for the natural world and others. She became the founder and president of the Bluebird Society of Maine, working tirelessly to bring this beautiful species, whose population was in severe decline, back to health. She sent bluebird house designs, and occasionally bird houses, along with feeding tips and information about habitats and breeding to hundreds of people. Her work was the catalyst for the now healthier population of these beautiful birds we see frequently in Maine today.
A devoted full-time mother for many years, Esther became a realtor after her children were grown, earning the top score on her real estate exam in Washington State (at the age of 54), where she lived for five years during the final years of her husband’s medical career. Her work in real estate became an extension of her integrity and personal philosophy that finding a home or land to create something the client loved was more important than the commission.
Throughout her life, Esther possessed a keen interest in gardening and horticulture. She was a member of the Garden Clubs of both Wiscasset and Bath, and she served as president of both clubs. Her deep, almost encyclopedic knowledge of plants was extraordinary, and she served as the classification chair, identifying and tagging plants, at many plant sales and garden club events. Her own expansive and exquisite gardens, including a sunken one created from the foundation of the original barn on the farm she called home in Woolwich, were a source of inspiration and pride. She was never happier than when she was working in a garden.
Her passion and expertise in gardening became a source of solace for hundreds of others when, after her own battle with breast cancer in 2006, she was the chief architect, driving force, and creator of the Healing Garden at Midcoast Hospital’s Cancer Treatment Center in Bath. Esther knew first-hand that a beautiful, serene, natural space would provide comfort and peace to all people affected by cancer, be they patients or caregivers, and her efforts were recognized when she received the Spirit of Life Award from the Maine Cancer Foundation in 2011.
Esther’s accomplishments were all driven by her remarkable intelligence and curiosity. An autodidact and quiet leader who could teach herself almost anything, she leaves a legacy of accomplishments, love, and beauty to her family, friends, and the Midcoast community.
She is survived by her husband, Richard Leck of Woolwich; along with four children, Kristin Harman of Newcastle (David Harman), Derek Leck of Portland, Elise Smith of Bethesda, Md. (Brooke Smith), and Heather Leck of Nashville, Tenn. and East Boothbay.
Her youngest child, Richard Brandenburg von Hasseln Leck, predeceased her.
She also leaves six grandchildren, Lauren Gallo White of San Francisco, Calif. (Luke White), Max Gallo of Sacramento, Calif. (Lisa Frank), Collin Smith of Boston, Mass., Charlotte Smith of Bethesda, Md., and Gunnar Leck and Tristin Leck of Bedford, N.H.; along with four great-grandchildren, Calvin, Ray, and Enna White, and Leon Frank Gallo.
A celebration of Esther’s life will be held at the First Congregational Church UCC of Wiscasset on March 20, 2027 at 11 a.m.
Arrangements are under the direction and care of the Strong-Hancock Funeral Home, 612 Main St., Damariscotta, ME 04543. Condolences, and messages for her family, may be expressed by visiting: http://www.StrongHancock.com.
In lieu of flowers, donations may be made to the Garden Club of Wiscasset, the Healing Garden at Midcoast Hospital in Brunswick, or the First Congregational Church UCC of Wiscasset.

title: Cooper Flagg records double-double in Mavs’ win
text:
DALLAS — Cooper Flagg scored 21 points and Kyrie Irving added 14 after a sluggish first half for both stars as the Dallas Mavericks beat the Utah Jazz 112-100 in an NBA Cup game Friday night.
P.J. Washington scored 22 of his season-high 26 points in a first half that ended in a 57-all tie, setting the stage for Flagg and Irving to take over after the break.
Flagg, of Newport, scored 17 in the second half, while Irving had all but two of his points after halftime after starting 1 of 11 from the field. While Flagg’s scoring lagged before the break, he had six rebounds and assists in the first half before finishing with 10 and seven, respectively.
Lauri Markkanen scored 24 points and rookie Darryn Peterson had 21 for the Jazz, who lost their seventh straight game to drop to 1-8.
Flagg and Irving scored 21 of the points on a 22-10 run that turned a one-point Dallas deficit into an 81-70 lead late in the third quarter. Flagg had 13 points and Irving eight.
The Mavericks kept the run going after Irving went to the bench.
Morez Johnson Jr. had a one-handed, alley-oop dunk to clinch his first double-double, and the Dallas lead reached 16 before Utah’s Josh Okogie beat the third-quarter buzzer with a 3-pointer. Johnson tied his season best of 13 points and had 17 rebounds.
Washington was 5 of 6 from 3-point range and made all five of his free throws in the first half. His sixth and final 3 helped Dallas maintain a double-digit lead throughout the fourth quarter.
Dallas’ Santi Aldama had eight points and nine rebounds in his first game since Feb. 4 last season with Memphis. The 7-footer was part of a six-team trade in the summer. Aldama had right knee surgery in March.
Up next
Jazz: At Minnesota on Sunday.
Mavericks: Host Brooklyn on Sunday.

title: Maine’s CD2 ranked choice process moves forward after concession; Bellows outlines cost-saving plan
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - The ranked choice voting process in Maine’s 2nd Congressional District will begin Monday in Augusta, even though Democrat Matt Dunlap has conceded the race to Republican Paul LePage.
Election officials since neither candidate has reached a majority of the vote, state law requires that the ranked choice process play out.
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said law enforcement collected ballots and memory sticks from every city and town in the district Thursday and Friday.
Officials will first verify the results. If LePage remains below the 50% plus one threshold, they will run the ranked choice tabulation, Bellows said.
Plan to limit costs
Bellows said since it seems unlikely that the ranked choice tabulation will change the final outcome, her office thought it was wise to reduce costs.
“We are going to be frugal in the ranked choice voting tabulation,” Bellows said. “We are not going to require staff to work overtime or on the weekend to conduct this count. We are going to do it during business hours as part of the certification process. That will keep costs down.”
The process begins at 10 a.m. Monday, is open to the public and will be livestreamed. Bellows said she expects it to take about a week.

title: Federal judge orders 14-day delay on any work beginning on Trump’s monumental arch
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge late Thursday blocked the Trump administration from breaking ground on a towering memorial arch for 14 days.
The temporary restraining order by U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan halting the work represents a major setback for one of President Donald Trump’s most prominent projects in his vision to remake Washington.
The decision followed a series of steps taken earlier Thursday by the government, including the final approval of the arch by the National Capital Planning Commission in an 8-4 vote after a 9 ½ hour hearing where scores of witnesses opposed the construction.
The administration said the work could begin as soon as the approval and the Interior Department issued a final decision authorizing construction and the proper notification was published by the National Park Service.
In approving the temporary stop, Chutkan said Virginia and the District of Columbia had shown that the immediacy of the construction would cause real harm to the plaintiffs.
“The harm is certain,” she wrote. ”Defendants initially notified the court that construction could begin as early as November 5, 2026, if the NCPC approves the project at its meeting that day and the Department of the Interior authorizes construction.” In their filing, Virginia and D.C. warned of traffic pattern distortions as well as concerns about the impact on mutual aid emergency calls if the arch were to proceed.
“Second, the District and Virginia will incur high unrecoverable costs. As soon as construction begins, DDOT will need to expend staff time and operating resources to affirmatively and proactively manage temporary detours, crashes or disabled vehicles,” Chutkan wrote.
The judge ordered the government to provide a status report next Monday to ensure they are complying with the order.
The judge’s decision came just over an hour after the National Capital Planning Commission hearing ended. The vote by the commission broke along federal and local lines. Those in favor worked for the administration or were connected to the president, who was pushing for the immediate construction. Opponents represented the city of Washington.
The remote, call-in hearing — which crashed repeatedly in the first few hours and was accompanied by a nearly universally negative comment section — drew witnesses who gave impassioned comments opposing an arch they said would destroy the solemnity of the nearby Arlington National Cemetery, where hundreds of thousands of fallen service members and military veterans are buried.
The panel’s Trump-appointed chairman launched the meeting with a gushing appraisal of the towering monument and lauded Trump for wanting to build it.
“President Trump understands as president and a superb builder that it’s important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments,” said Mark Paoletta, the commission’s chairman.
As Trump has often remarked, “the great cities around the world have arches: Paris, Rome, London,” said Paoletta, who also serves as general counsel for the White House Office of Management and Budget.
Commissioner Paul Ingrassia, a lawyer for the General Services Administration, said the arch was “not about politics. It’s about remembrance. It’s about celebrating our history. It’s about commemorating veterans. And it’s really something that’s a noble tribute to our nation and something that we can all rally behind.”
But D.C. City Council Chairman Phil Mendelson, who also serves on the planning panel, said the project has not received required approval from Congress, nor has Congress appropriated any money for it. The plan submitted to the commission does not include a reference to military use cited by Trump and other administration officials, Mendelson said.
“We cannot approve final site and building plans until we have the final site and building plans,” he said.
The commission oversees construction on federal land in the city and began reviewing the arch plan in June.
The arch is one of several projects around Washington that the Republican president has undertaken as he alters the capital to his tastes — from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Those projects could soon face intense scrutiny after Democrats gained control of Congress in the midterm elections this week.
Rep. Jared Huffman, a California Democrat who is set to chair the House Natural Resources Committee, called the project ill-advised and illegal.
“This arch would dishonor America,” Huffman told the commission. He called the proposed arch “a tribute to Donald Trump,” not veterans, as Trump administration officials claim. The monument is similar to those built for emperors or kings, Huffman said, adding that Trump was using veterans as a pretext to build a memorial to himself.
Other critics, including the plaintiffs, argue that the Trump administration must seek congressional approval. The administration maintains that Congress cleared the way for a monument at Memorial Circle decades ago.
Several members of the Planning Commission used that logic in approving the project. Paoletta said it was a “national disgrace” that a memorial arch had not been placed there, despite a 1925 law that designated such a memorial, he said.
Chutkan rejected that argument in her ruling: “The sheer improbability that a 100-year-old statute would contain authority, unknown to every previous administration, to erect a 250-foot arch at a principal location in the Nation’s capital indicates how far defen

title: New video shows NTSB investigators recovering Learjet wreckage pieces from Florida crash crater
text:
NTSB finds portion of one engine in Learjet crash site as more suspected debris discovered on roofs of homes and buildings
Go onto the roof where suspected Learjet wreckage landed, damaging a West Palm Beach triplex. Meanwhile, new video shows NTSB investigators recovering pieces of the plane from the crash crater.
NTSB finds portion of one engine in Learjet crash site as more suspected debris discovered on roofs of homes and buildings
Go onto the roof where suspected Learjet wreckage landed, damaging a West Palm Beach triplex. Meanwhile, new video shows NTSB investigators recovering pieces of the plane from the crash crater.
New video shows investigators painstakingly retrieving pieces of a Learjet from the enormous crater left behind when the aircraft crashed onto a roadway in Florida on Sunday, killing all nine people aboard.
NTSB confirmed they found a portion of one engine, and debris has been found away from the impact location and on the roofs of homes and buildings near the crash site.
Sister station WPBF's investigative team went onto the roof of a nearby triplex where a long, twisted piece of metal believed to be from the doomed jet slammed into the shingles. The suspected wreckage left a hole in the roof, and part of a neighbor's kitchen ceiling later collapsed.
The National Transportation Safety Board has not publicly confirmed whether that particular piece came from the Learjet.
Anthony Blackmon, who lives in the triplex, said he witnessed the plane's final moments and heard the deafening explosion.
"It was really, really loud," Blackmon said.
He said he looked outside after hearing a buzzing noise and saw the aircraft plunging toward the ground.
"I just looked out my window because I heard a buzzing sound. I just want to see what's going on. And then that's when I seen the actual plane coming down and fall, and the explosion was huge," Blackmon said.
He described flames shooting an estimated 100 to 150 feet into the air.
"It was pretty crazy. Really shook the whole house. Debris fell everywhere," he said.
The following day, after part of his neighbor's kitchen ceiling collapsed, Blackmon climbed onto the roof to investigate.
There, he discovered a twisted piece of metal with screws, approximately a foot long, that he believes came from the aircraft.
"It was like a metal piece with screws. And it was like, pretty like this length," Blackmon said, gesturing to show its size.
Blackmon said sheriff's deputies subsequently recovered the metal from the roof.
Investigators recover wreckage from massive crater
New video obtained by WPBF shows NTSB investigators working inside the crash crater after water was pumped out, carefully collecting small fragments of the aircraft.
The Learjet was destroyed when it slammed into the roadway Sunday afternoon.
Investigators are examining the recovered wreckage for evidence that could help explain what caused the jet to crash.
The NTSB previously confirmed that significant pieces of the aircraft's left elevator, a control surface on the tail, separated before impact and were recovered as far as 3.8 miles from the crash site.
Investigators have not determined whether those pieces broke away because the aircraft was already out of control or whether their separation contributed to the loss of control.
Neighbors describe widespread damage
Blackmon said the violent crash affected more than just the roadway where the aircraft struck.
"My window was hit by a couple of debris. My neighbors are affected. Everybody's affected in this area," he said.
He described the aftermath as shocking, with residents still trying to process what happened so close to their homes.
"It's a really tragic moment for everybody. May they rest in peace," Blackmon said.
Military Trail remains closed between Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue, with access limited to residents.
If you have found or collected any debris from the Learjet 60 crash, please do not keep it or attempt to move, alter or dispose of it. Even small pieces of the wreckage may contain important evidence that could help investigators determine what happened. We ask that you contact the NTSB at witness@ntsb.gov to arrange its recovery. Please include a photo of the debris, if possible, in your email. Recovering all available wreckage is critical to the investigation and helping to determine the cause of the crash.

title: Penobscot County Jail relocation measure fails by thin margin
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A referendum that would have allowed Penobscot County to search for a site to build a new jail outside Bangor has failed, according to county officials.
Referendum results
Voters across the county’s 63 municipalities voted down the measure with 32,219 yes votes and 32,334 no votes, county officials said. That’s a difference of just 115 votes. Overseas voters widened that gap to 136, bringing the results of the unofficial count to 32,503 no votes and 32,367 yes votes.
Law requires a public vote to build a facility outside the county seat.
County leaders were eyeing a parcel of land in Hampden at the Ammo Industrial Park for a new facility.
“The voters of Penobscot County have spoken, and it is now our responsibility to ensure the results are reviewed and certified in accordance with Maine law,” Penobscot County Commission Chair David Marshall said. “Given the close margin and the unique circumstances surrounding certification of a county referendum question, the Commissioners are committed to a transparent, deliberate, and legally sound process that maintains public confidence in the integrity of the election.”
The commissioners will be briefed on potential next steps. Further announcements are expected once the commissioners consult with legal counsel.
Proponents of the measure cited aging facilities and a lack of room, while detractors advocated for money that would be allocated to building a new jail instead be used for diversion programs.

title: How the BDN tracked down every vote in Penobscot County’s tight jail referendum
text:
More than 65,000 Penobscot County voters weighed in on the jail question. It came down to 60 votes and clerks I talked into driving back to their town offices to read me their results.
Voters narrowly rejected moving the county jail out of Bangor. That sends commissioners back to look for a site after years of planning a new jail in Hampden.
Most people don’t think about how a newspaper gets results on election night. Many news outlets rely on The Associated Press, whose reporters collect results from towns and feed them to newsrooms. At the Bangor Daily News, we chase the results ourselves and call high-profile races with our partners at Decision Desk HQ.
Each town counts its ballots. Local clerks share their results with us however they choose: an email, a PDF, a photo of a handwritten tally sheet or a post on the town’s Facebook page. This is how you generally learn the winners; the state compiles official results later.
The jail question was different. On top of our normal election night work, it took two more days of calling clerks.
Penobscot County has 63 voting units. Bangor, the county seat, cast more than 11,000 votes on the question. Drew Plantation cast 11. In between are dozens of small towns, plantations and townships: Seboeis Plantation cast 20 votes, Webster Plantation 25 and Maxfield 57.
Some don’t even report on their own. Argyle Township’s votes are counted with Old Town’s. Springfield, Kingman Township and Prentiss Township report to the state as one precinct, though each filled out its own return on the jail question.
Those three were the last to report. Springfield’s clerk, Lisa Kettle, also works another full-time job. She told me she drove back to the town office twice, a 20-minute trip each way, to get me the results.
When I reached Maxfield’s part-time clerk, Karen Carson, by phone Thursday, she also had to go back to the town office. She couldn’t go until she got out of her full-time job at 5 p.m.
Getting every result wasn’t the end of it. With a margin this close, every number had to be right.
I went back through my inbox and matched each town’s total against the clerk’s return. That covered 49 towns. For the 13 with no documentation, such as those whose clerks called in their results, I called town offices to confirm their numbers.
With every town double-checked, no led by 39 votes. Military and overseas ballots reported by Secretary of State Shenna Bellows’ office pushed the margin to 60.
Penobscot County officials have their own unofficial results, which differ from ours. They also show the measure failing. County Administrator Blair Tinkham said commissioners are waiting on legal guidance before certifying the vote, and the county has not said whether it will seek a recount.
It’s a reminder that every ballot counts, and that we’ll keep calling until we’ve tracked them all down.

title: Letter: We can’t afford to get AI development wrong
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
After reading Dario Amodei’s recent essay about artificial intelligence, something occurred to me.
The situation we are in is caused by the tech culture we’ve seen develop beginning in the early 2000s, whereby these companies move very fast inside a culture of “make it, break it, fix it, continue.” This method of development gave us the amazing technology we see today — and has made billionaires. The problem was that most of this technology wasn’t inherently dangerous.
The analogy I would pose is nuclear weapons and nuclear energy: Imagine if during its development, we were not aware of how truly dangerous it was and used the same mentality of rapid progress “make it, break it, fix it” or if Boeing had the same approach of building aircraft.
My prayer is that the news of late, and the dire warnings within, will force these tech geniuses to slow down, realize that they are creating something akin to a nuclear bomb and that they can’t screw it up, or its armageddon.
I think this will be humanity’s biggest test since we harnessed the power of the atom.
They all need this Hindu quote posted on the front of their laptops, from the Hindu text, famously quoted by J. Robert Oppenheimer when he witnessed the first atomic bomb explode: “Now I am become death, destroyer of worlds”
Joshua Reynolds
Carrabassett Valley

title: Hearing scheduled in Deven Young murder case as prosecutors seek adult trial
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine (WMTW) - A status hearing is scheduled for Friday at Knox County Superior Court in the case of Deven Young, the man accused of killing paddleboarder Sunshine ‘Sunny’ Stewart in Union in July 2025.
Prosecutors and the defense team are expected to address issues related to a potential bind-over hearing, which would determine whether Young is tried as an adult or a juvenile.
Young, now 19, was 17 when Stewart was killed. He is charged with one count of intentional or knowing or depraved indifference murder in Stewart’s death.
The Maine Attorney General’s Office is seeking to have Young tried as an adult. A judge would make that determination after a bind-over hearing, where the court considers evidence including the seriousness of the alleged offense and evaluations of the defendant.
The specific bind-over issues scheduled for discussion in Rockland Friday have not been made public.
Bind-over hearing could still be months away
At a status conference in September, a judge expressed frustration with the delays in scheduling a bind-over hearing after Young’s defense team said they needed more time to evaluate Young at the Long Creek Youth Development Center in South Portland. The judge originally had wanted to schedule a bind-over hearing in December.
However, the defense said their expert needed about three months to complete a report after meeting with Young, and the Attorney General’s Office would then need time to review it.
The judge then said the process could push the eventual bind-over hearing into 2027. Court officials have indicated that the bind-over hearing itself could take two to three days.
Sunshine Stewart’s death on a pond in Union
Stewart, 48, was found dead by Maine Game Wardens on July 3, 2025, on or near 100-Acre Island in Crawford Pond in Union, one day after she went paddleboarding.
Authorities said a medical examiner determined that Stewart died from strangulation and blunt force trauma.
Young was arrested in connection with the death and remains held at Long Creek Youth Development Center.
A judge ruled in April that Young is competent to proceed with the case, finding that he has a factual and rational understanding of the proceedings and is able to consult with his attorneys.
Much of the evidence in the case remains sealed because the prosecution began while Young was a juvenile.
What happens next
If Young is ultimately bound over to adult court and convicted, he could face a sentence of at least 25 years and up to life in prison.
If the case remains in the juvenile system, Young would remain subject to juvenile penalties and could not be held in a juvenile facility beyond age 21.

title: Two strokes haven’t stopped him: Meet the Michigan man greeting his town for 10 years
text:
EATON RAPIDS, Mich. (Aging Untold) — For 10 years, George Doxtader has made a difference in his community by spreading joy with a thumbs-up.
The 78-year-old sits on a bench at the corner of State and Main streets in Eaton Rapids and lifts his thumb to greet passersby.
“He gets up very early, he’s out here a lot of times at 4 a.m.,” his friend, Kurt Norgaard, said. “And you’ll see a lot of waving and beeping, just how it is.”
Community notices when he’s absent
Doxtader is not there every day. He takes breaks for church and other activities.
Norgaard said if Doxtader is missing for any stretch of time, the community takes notice.
“Oh yeah, it comes up in the community. ‘Hey what happened to George? Where’s George at?’” Norgaard said.
Pastor Jenny Rouble of First Congregational Church said Doxtader is not only a member of her congregation but also a friend and a blessing to the community.
“It just makes them happy to see his smiling face and his thumbs-up,” Rouble said.
Drivers honk their horns and call out greetings as they pass.
“I guess you can tell by when the people go by, they’re honking their horns. They know his name,” Rouble said.
Overcoming challenges with positivity
What many might not know is that Doxtader suffered two major strokes 35 years ago.
He has paralysis on the right side of his body and sometimes he has trouble speaking.
“Slow and gradually,” Doxtader said when describing his speech.
Despite his challenges, he smiles and offers a friendly gesture to everyone who passes by.
When he is not greeting passersby, Doxtader passes the time crocheting blankets and pictures, all with his left hand.
He never misses a chance to share his positive perspective on life.
“Yes,” Doxtader said when asked about spreading inspiration.
“Yes, that’s the goal, right? Yeah, that’s the goal is the inspiration in a complicated world,” Rouble added.
