title: South Portland schools may temporarily ban AI
text:
Some South Portland students may not be able to use generative artificial intelligence for the rest of the school year, both in the classroom and on assignments.
The School Board will vote Monday on whether to institute a moratorium on the use of AI through the 2026-27 school year for students in pre-kindergarten through 8th grade until it can develop an appropriate policy. Other cities, such as New York and Los Angeles, have enacted similar temporary bans.
If the resolution passes, all staff members would be required to receive two hours of AI awareness training and three hours of AI literacy training by the end of the school year, and afterward, teachers would only be able to use tools sanctioned by the school district on school-issued devices. No teacher would be required to use student-facing AI.
The proposal doesn’t include a plan for enforcement, and there is some concern that students could find ways to work around it. But Claire Holman, the board member who brought forth the resolution, said the district needs to start somewhere.
There are currently no official guidelines for AI use in South Portland schools. An AI committee began meeting a few years ago, but it’s been more focused on information sharing than policy creation, according to Holman, a member of the committee.
There is currently no statewide policy or ban on the use of AI in schools. The Maine Department of Education supports “thoughtful, ethical integration of AI in education,” per its website, and it put together a toolkit to help school districts and administrators determine their own policies. The governor’s office launched a 21-person task force on AI, with an education subgroup, that released a report with recommendations last fall.
Other towns and districts, including Yarmouth, Maine School Administrative District 75 (which serves Harpswell, Topsham, Bowdoin and Bowdoinham) and Gorham have embraced conditional use of AI in the classroom with policies and handbooks.
Some community members support AI tools that can tailor lessons to individual learners, and help prepare students for an increasingly tech-driven economy.
But Holman says schools should move cautiously.
“ChatGPT is only a couple of years old,” she said. “So people are trying to figure out what we should do now.”
UNDERSTANDING NEW TECHNOLOGY
School Board member Daniel Feller said he’s been asking questions about AI use in schools, such as which students, if any, should be able to use it, and whether there should be different policies for different grade levels and subjects. He thinks community members, teachers and administrators need to consider these issues as well.
Feller describes himself as a “power user” of AI, using it as a “genius sidekick” to help him with administrative tasks. His background is in biomedical informatics, so he’s been researching and thinking about AI for about a decade.
But he recognizes that he doesn’t use his brain as much as he used to.
“We don’t want to have a wait-and-see approach of seeing what the impact on our kids will be,” he said. “We really want to be confident that we’re doing it in an intentional way with something as powerful as AI.”
Holman’s first proposed moratorium last month would have temporarily banned the use of AI for all grade levels. She said she was worried about the repercussions if young people don’t develop critical thinking skills on their own.
“They don’t learn to struggle and push through when something gets difficult,” Holman said.
Research has shown that students who use AI can answer questions correctly and quickly, but when the technology is taken away, their test scores drop.
The American Federation of Teachers recommends that elementary schoolers not use chatbots, and educators should prioritize hands-on learning.
A CASE FOR AI
The board excluded high schoolers from the moratorium because they heard from some teachers and community members about the positive use of the tools.
A couple of years ago, South Portland started using MagicSchool, per Technology Director Andy Wallace’s guidance, a closed program that doesn’t train itself on user information. The AI tools are focused instead of open-ended, and the teacher can control what the student sees.
Students can use the software to work through math problems, proofread essays and ask questions when they’re stuck.
Different teachers have integrated artificial intelligence into their classrooms to varying degrees, according to Sarah Gay, an English teacher and president of the teacher’s union. She’s used software to simplify texts to a student’s reading level, she said. And she uses it to help translate for families of multilingual learners in a way that is culturally sensitive.
“I do think that there are cases to be made for some of the tools,” she said. “And I think the most commonly used are probably also the most benign, I hope.”
The moratorium would not apply to technology used by students with disabilities and English language learners, and there could be exceptions for approved instruction, like coding and simulations.
Many teachers’ recent professional development has incorporated sessions about AI, Gay said. But teachers need more training about the tools and how to teach students with access to the technology, she said.
“Our collective knowledge of what it can do and should do is virtually non-existent,” she said.

title: Bangor Firefighters Halt Center Street Fire Before It Reaches Nearby Home
text:
Firefighters Keep An Early Morning Fire On Center Street In Bangor From Spreading To Other Buildings; Outbuilding Destroyed
Hard work and a quick response by the Bangor Fire Department kept an early morning fire on Center Street from spreading to other buildings nearby.
Read More: Two Fires Strike Belfast Area Over One October Weekend
Authorities say an explosion and a fire at 382 Center Street was reported just before 2:30 AM Friday morning. Within 5 minute, firefighters from Station 6 and Central Station were on the scene.
When they arrived, they found an outbuilding fully engulfed in flames. Directly next to the fire were two buildings, a home and a garage.
"Crews quickly contained the fire to the building of origin and kept it from spreading to the exposure buildings."
Within 15 minutes of their arrival, firefighters had the blaze under control. We're told that most of the personnel were able to clear the scene by 4 AM.
According to Bangor Fire, no on was injured in the firefighting effort.
"The outbuilding is a total loss. The garage and house sustained minor exterior damage because they were so close to the fire...The explosions are believed to have been caused by items stored in the outbuilding."
Read More: Generator Enclosed In Box Sparked West Bath Halloween Fire
Authorities are still investigating the fire, but don't believe it to be suspicious. The property was insured.
Bangor Fire Officials say that last month alone, they responded to a total of 1,050 incidents.
On October 25th, the Bangor Fire Department transitioned to 24-hour staffing. Within the first week of that changeover, they responded to over 60 incidents.

title: Dementia care educator Teepa Snow explains ‘brain change’ and what it means for caregivers
text:
(Aging Untold) — Dementia can change how families talk, plan and get through a normal day, and many caregivers are working out what to do in real time.
Teepa Snow, a nationally recognized dementia care educator, occupational therapist and founder of Positive Approach to Care, joined Aging Untold to talk about what she has taught families and care teams for decades.
She discussed why she uses the term “brain change,” how she approaches refusals such as taking a shower and why written reminders may not help.
Why Snow says ‘brain change’
Snow said people with dementia lose some abilities but change others, and she uses “brain change” instead of language that focuses on decline.
“Although people are losing some abilities, they’re actually changing others,” Snow said.
For example, some people who never swore may begin to, and people who would never have asked strangers for help may walk up and say they need to get home, Snow said.
“People think all the time of brain failure and brain loss, and I talk about brain change because the reality is neuroplasticity exists whether you have dementia or you don’t,” Snow said. “So let’s use what we have and let’s use what they have.”
What to try when someone refuses a shower
Gerontologist and Aging Untold expert “Sam” Cradduck presented Snow with a challenge families might face – how would she respond if a parent with dementia continually refused to shower, take medication or get dressed?
Snow said she would not try to force a shower.
Instead, Snow said, ask the loved one for help with a smaller task.
She presented this as an example:
“I have no business trying to force you to take a shower. That’s ridiculous. What I would ask you is, you’ve got something like right here,” Snow said, pointing to her cheek. “And I don’t know if it’s from breakfast or what. It’s out here on this outer edge. Let’s go to the bathroom, look in the mirror I’m going to give you a washcloth and see if you can’t get that off.”
Another example she offered was to ask the person to wash their hands before cooking dinner.
Snow said that if a person will not take part in those smaller steps, a shower is unlikely.
“I’ve got to back up a little bit and try to figure out what’s getting in our way of the interaction,” Snow said.
Why sticky notes may not work
Cradduck brought up written reminders, such as sticky notes and reminders labeled “coffee cups” and “plates,” and why they don’t work.
Snow said families may think they can take written information and translate it into an action.
But following a written sequence requires the hippocampus, which she described as the learning and memory center, to access and use what the person just did and what the next step is. And the front of the brain is trying to sequence, she said.
Snow said families should recognize that the person likely needs more support for completing tasks.
The one thing Snow wants families to know
Asked what one message she would give every family affected by dementia, Snow said both the person with dementia and the caregiver are doing the best they can.
“You’re both doing the best you can, and if you want something to change, one of you is going to have to change,” Snow said.
She said the person with dementia is already experiencing brain change, so caregivers will need to build awareness, knowledge and skills they may not have expected to need.
And recognize, Snow said, that not every family member is suited to be the person providing hands-on care.
“You can be great at organizing care because not every family member is built for this,” Snow said. “I mean, it’s hard work.”

title: Trump names Stephen Miller new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles
text:
Trump names Stephen Miller new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles
President Donald Trump announced Friday that he is replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff. Her replacement: Stephen Miller.
Trump announced the shake-up on social media.
"I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday," Trump wrote.
Miller has served as White House deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security advisor since 2025.
Acknowledging Wiles' contributions, Trump added, "Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!"
Wiles also released a social media statement Friday.
"Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First,” Wiles said in a social media post shortly after Trump’s announcement. She added that her commitment to “the President and the mission” will not change.
Wiles, a longtime Trump adviser, was the first woman ever to serve in that post. Her departure comes almost immediately after the GOP's midterm thrashing on Tuesday.
The departure also came months after Wiles indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease, a diagnosis she went public with in March 2026.
Wiles is Trump's longest-serving White House chief of staff, as he cycled through four during his first four-year term.
Miller is one of Trump’s closest and longest-serving advisers, joining his longshot 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. Among his many policy involvements, Miller is most closely aligned with Trump’s immigration approach and rhetoric.
Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: UMass hockey edges UMaine
text:
ORONO, Maine — The University of Maine’s hockey team generated plenty of scoring chances in Friday night’s Hockey East game against UMass.
But freshman goalie Ethan Eskit, who entered the game with the nation’s 16th lowest goals-against average (1.67) and 14th best save percentage (.944), made 46 saves and the Minutemen earned a 2-1 victory at the Alfond Arena.
UMass is now 5-4-1 overall and 2-0 in Hockey East while UMaine fell to 4-5 and 0-3 and has lost three straight.
The teams will play again Saturday at 7.
Albin Boija made 20 stops for UMaine in a solid performance..
Calgary native Eskit was exceptional. He made several stellar saves and did a good job controlling rebounds.
He received a first-period unassisted goal from sophomore center Jack Galanek and a second-period power play goal by Maxim Masse.
UMaine’s Jaden Lipinski pulled UMaine within one when he came out of the penalty box and scored on a breakaway with 3:04 left in regulation off a Thomas Pichette feed. It was his first of the season.
But the Black Bear couldn’t get the equalizer.
Galanek capitalized on a Max Scott turnover to give the Minutemen a 1-0 lead just 3:09 into the game.
Scott lost the puck off his stick and it rolled right onto the stick of Galanek in the low slot.
The wide open Galanek had time to take a stride and he beat UMaine’s Albin Boija with a rising 20-foot wrist over the goalie’s glove.
It was his fourth goal of the season.
The Minutemen carried the play for the first six minutes of the game, holding a 4-2 edge in shots on goal.
But the Black Bears began taking the game over and generated 11 of the next 13 shots on goal to hold a 13-6 advantage after the opening 20 minutes.
But the Black Bears couldn’t put the puck behind Eskit.
Loic Usereau’s screened shot from the right point glanced off Eskit’s mask and, moments later, he made an exceptional left pad save off an Owen Fowler one-timer from the middle of the slot.
He also was able to make a glove save on a power play wrister from the midpoint off Ross Campbell.
The free-wheeling second period featured a combined 30 shots on goal with UMaine producing 17 of them.
Eskit got his stick and blocker on an Alexander Bales wrist shot from the left faceoff dot early in the period and then it was Boija’s turn to come up with some nice saves.
He came up with a good stop off Larry Keenan’s shot from the high slot and Francesco Dell’Elce’s follow-up shot hit the crossbar.
Boija robbed Galanek with a stacked pad save as the UMass center was alone cruising down the left wing and tried to steer the puck past Boija.
Eskit came up with a good right pad save off Fowler, who took a wrister from the right circle off a two-on-one.
UMass went on its first power play with 4:43 left in the middle period and Masse expanded the lead with a blistering one-timer from the left circle off a cross-ice pass from Egor Barabanov.
It was his second goal of the season.
UMaine had a power play in the third period but couldn’t generate any good chances.
UMaine was without point-producing defenseman Lukas Peterson, who is sidelined with an upper body injury.

title: Federal judge tells Trump administration it cannot begin work on Washington arch for 14 days
text:
Federal judge orders 14-day delay on any work beginning on Trump's monumental arch
Federal judge tells Trump administration it cannot begin work on Washington arch for 14 days
Federal judge orders 14-day delay on any work beginning on Trump's monumental arch
Federal judge tells Trump administration it cannot begin work on Washington arch for 14 days
A federal judge late Thursday blocked the Trump administration from breaking ground on a towering memorial arch for 14 days.
The temporary restraining order by U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan halting the work represents a major setback for one of President Donald Trump’s most prominent projects in his vision to remake Washington.
Video above: Trump speaks about White House ballroom project in first public comments since GOP's losses in midterm elections
The decision followed a series of steps taken earlier Thursday by the government, including the final approval of the arch by the National Capital Planning Commission in an 8-4 vote after a nine-hour hearing where dozens of witnesses opposed the construction.
The administration said the work could begin as soon as the approval and the Interior Department issued a final decision authorizing construction and the proper notification was published by the National Park Service.
In issuing the temporary stop, Chutkan said Virginia and the District of Columbia had shown that the immediacy of the construction would cause real harm to the plaintiffs.
“The harm is certain," she wrote. "Defendants initially notified the court that construction could begin as early as November 5, 2026, if the NCPC approves the project at its meeting that day and the Department of the Interior authorizes construction.” In their filing, Virginia and D.C. warned of traffic pattern distortions as well as concerns about the impact on mutual aid emergency calls if the arch were to proceed.
Video below: Trump Triumphal arch revised design approved
“Second, the District and Virginia will incur significant unrecoverable costs. As soon as construction begins, DDOT will need to expend staff time and operating resources to affirmatively and proactively manage temporary detours, crashes or disabled vehicles,” Chutkan wrote.
The judge's decision came just over an hour after the National Capital Planning Commission hearing ended. The final vote by the planning commission came after 9 ½ hours and scores of people opposing it. The vote by the commission broke along federal and local lines. Those in favor work for the administration or are connected to the president, who was pushing for the immediate construction. Opponents represented the city of Washington.
The remote, call-in hearing — which crashed repeatedly in the first few hours and was accompanied by a nearly universally negative comment section — drew witnesses who gave impassioned comments opposing an arch they said will destroy the solemnity of the nearby Arlington National Cemetery, where hundreds of thousands of fallen service members and military veterans are buried.
The panel's Trump-appointed chairman launched the meeting with a gushing appraisal of the towering monument and lauded Trump for wanting to build it.
“President Trump understands as president and a superb builder that it’s important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments,” said Mark Paoletta, the commission's chairman.
As Trump has often remarked, “the great cities around the world have arches: Paris, Rome, London,” said Paoletta, who also serves as general counsel for the White House Office of Management and Budget.
Commissioner Paul Ingrassia, a lawyer for the General Services Administration, said the arch was “not about politics. It’s about remembrance. It’s about celebrating our history. It’s about commemorating veterans. And it’s really something that’s a noble tribute to our nation and something that we can all rally behind.”
But D.C. City Council member Phil Mendelson, who also serves on the planning panel, said the project has not received required approval from Congress, nor has Congress appropriated any money for it. The plan submitted to the commission does not include a reference to military use cited by Trump and other administration officials, Mendelson said.
“We cannot approve final site and building plans until we have the final site and building plans,” he said.
The commission oversees construction on federal land in the city and began reviewing the arch plan in June.
The arch is one of several projects around Washington that the Republican president has undertaken as he alters the capital to his tastes — from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Those projects could soon face intense scrutiny after Democrats gained control of Congress in the midterm elections this week.
Many of the plans are being challenged in the courts, and three lawsuits have been filed opposing the arch.
Rep. Jared Huffman, a California Democrat who is set to chair the House Natural Resources Committee, called the project ill-advised and illegal.
“This arch would dishonor America,” Huffman told the commission. He called the proposed arch “a tribute to Donald Trump,” not veterans as Trump administration officials claim. The monument is similar to those built for emperors or kings, Huffman said, adding that Trump was using veterans as a pretext to build a memorial to himself.
Associated Press videographer Nathan Ellgren contributed to this report

title: Foster mother charged with murder after missing 10-year-old girl found dead
text:
PHILADELPHIA -- Philadelphia officials announced Thursday that the foster mother of a 10-year-old girl who went missing last month has been charged with murder.
Caprice Williams, 36, the foster mother of Malayshia Alford, is charged with murder, abuse of a corpse and several related offenses, authorities said. Authorities said Alford was found dead in New Jersey late Wednesday night.
Search and discovery
Alford was last seen at her Philadelphia home Oct. 22. Her disappearance led to a search by locals, the police department and the FBI.
On Wednesday, law enforcement found surveillance video from the early morning hours of Oct. 26.
“There was video that shows what we believe to be her body being moved out of the home. It was that video that then led law enforcement officials to a suspect vehicle,” said Ashley Toczylowski, assistant district attorney with the Philadelphia District Attorney’s Office.
Investigators found Alford’s body late Wednesday night in the trunk of a car in New Jersey.
“It was immediately apparent that she had been there for a while,” Toczylowski said.
Officials said Alford’s cause of death is believed to be blunt force trauma.
Community reaction
A community in Philadelphia reacted with shock and grief after authorities said Alford was found dead.
Malcolm Jordan, who helped search for Alford, said, “I wanted to cry. I wanted to cry.”
“It’s just so heartbreaking that this is the end result. I just wish it was a different result, man, and uh we just got to do what we can to prevent this stuff from happening,” Jordan said.
A neighbor, who was not named, said, “Everybody failed this baby. Everybody.”
Alford’s uncle, Nafis Horne, spoke Thursday.
“I need everybody held accountable, from the foster parents who were picked to take care of my niece. I want you held accountable,” Horne said.
CNN is working to determine whether Williams has legal representation.
